PIN code of the world (1-1-1-4) — Population in billions: Americas 1, Europe 1, Africa 1, Asia 4. By 2100 → 1-1-4-5. (Ch 5)

Possibilist — Someone who "neither hopes without reason, nor fears without reason," resisting both optimism and pessimism. (Ch 2)

Recovery position — Laying an unconscious person prone so vomit drains; correct for soldiers but wrongly generalized to sleeping babies. (Ch 6)

Risk = danger × exposure — Real risk equals how dangerous a thing is times how exposed you are — not how scared it makes you feel. (Ch 4)

Single perspective instinct — Attraction to one cause/solution that explains everything; blinds you to disconfirming information. Control: get a toolbox, not a hammer. (Ch 8)

Size instinct — Misjudging importance: a lonely number looks big, a visible victim outweighs statistics. Control: get things in proportion. (Ch 5)

Slow change is not no change — 1%/yr doubles in 70 years; small annual changes compound into transformation. (Ch 7)

Statistics as therapy — Plain official data, shown to people with a too-negative worldview, makes them feel better ("a new kind of happy pill"). (Ch 2)

Straight line instinct — Assuming a trend continues straight; most trends don't. Control: remember curves come in different shapes. (Ch 3)

Urgency instinct — A decision feeling "now or never" when it rarely is; drives drastic, untested action. Control: take small steps. (Ch 10)

View from up here — From Level 4, Levels 1–3 all look equally poor — like looking down from a tall building. (Ch 1)

patterns.md

Factfulness — Techniques & Patterns

The ten instinct-control techniques, each with how to apply it. Use these whenever you read news, evaluate a claim, make a forecast, or prioritize resources.

1. Look for the Majority (Gap Instinct)

When to use: A claim splits the world into two opposed groups (rich/poor, us/them, developed/developing), or cites "the gap."

How:

  • Replace the binary with the Four Income Levels.
  • Beware comparisons of averages (check the spreads — they usually overlap).
  • Beware comparisons of extremes (the majority is in the middle).
  • Beware the view from up here (from the top, everything below looks equally small).

Trade-off: Real gaps occasionally exist (apartheid South Africa) — verify before dismissing.

2. Expect Bad News (Negativity Instinct)

When to use: You feel the world is getting worse, or a story implies decline.

How: Separate level (bad) from direction (better). Ask: "If an equally large improvement had happened, would I have heard about it?" Distrust rosy memories of the past.

Trade-off: Don't over-correct into rosy positivity — aim for accuracy, not a feel-good counterweight.

3. Don't Assume Straight Lines (Straight Line Instinct)

When to use: Extrapolating any trend into the future.

How: Ask which of five shapes it is — straight, S-bend, slide, hump, doubling. Get a third data point (1,2,3 is linear; 1,2,4 is doubling). Remember the part of a curve you see on Level 4 may not apply on Levels 1–3.

Trade-off: Some lines really are straight (income↔health) — identify, don't assume.

4. Calculate the Risks (Fear Instinct)

When to use: Fear is driving attention or a decision.

How: Compute Risk = danger × exposure, not the feeling. Distinguish frightening (perceived) from dangerous (real). When afraid, get calm before deciding — make as few decisions as possible until panic subsides.

Trade-off: Fear is useful when aimed at real risks; don't suppress it entirely.

5. Get Things in Proportion (Size Instinct)

When to use: A single number looks impressive, or one victim dominates attention.

How: Compare (vs. last year, vs. a comparable region) and Divide (into a per-person rate). Use the 80/20 rule on lists/budgets — handle the biggest items first.

Trade-off: Numbers, but not only numbers — keep the human reality in view.

6. Question Your Categories (Generalization Instinct)

When to use: A claim treats a group (nation, religion, "Africa") as uniform, or generalizes from one example.

How:

  • Look for differences within groups and similarities across groups.
  • Beware "the majority" (51% or 99%? ask for the number).
  • Beware vivid/exceptional examples; ask for more, or flip the example.
  • Assume you are not "normal" and others are not idiots ("In what way is this smart?").
  • Don't generalize from one group to another (soldiers ≠ babies).

Trade-off: We must categorize to function — aim for better categories (the Four Levels), not none.

7. Remember Slow Change Is Still Change (Destiny Instinct)

When to use: Someone says a culture/country/religion "will never change" or "it's their culture."

How: Track gradual improvements (1%/yr doubles in 70 yrs). Update your knowledge (social facts expire). Talk to Grandpa (compare generations). Collect counterexamples of cultural change.

Trade-off: Slow ≠ instant — change is real but takes decades; stay patient and possibilistic.

8. Get a Toolbox, Not a Hammer (Single Perspective Instinct)

When to use: One idea (free market, equality, one metric, one technology) is offered as the answer to everything.

How: Test your ideas against people who disagree. Respect limited expertise (experts only within their field). Watch hammers and nails (tool overuse). Use numbers but not only numbers. Beware simple solutions — answer is usually "both, case-by-case."

Trade-off: Simple ideas are seductive and time-saving; trade speed for accuracy when it matters.

9. Resist Finding a Scapegoat (Blame Instinct)

When to use: Something went wrong (or right) and you're reaching for a villain (or hero).

How: Look for causes, not villains — understand the interacting system. Look for systems, not heroes — ask whether the good outcome would have happened anyway. Look in the mirror. Credit institutions and technology.

Trade-off: Accountability still matters; the point is to find the system, not to excuse everyone.

10. Take Small Steps (Urgency Instinct)

When to use: A decision feels "now or never," or you're being pushed to act immediately.

How: Take a breath (ask for time and information). Insist on the data (relevant and accurate). Beware fortune-tellers (demand a range of scenarios; round to your disadvantage). Be wary of drastic action (ask the side effects; prefer step-by-step + evaluation).

Trade-off: A few risks are genuinely urgent — the five global risks — but even those need cool heads, not panic.

Meta-pattern: Test for ignorance

When to use: In your own organization, field, or community.

How: Ask "What are the most important facts here, and how many people know them?" Pose a few multiple-choice fact questions humbly. Expect worse-than-random results — and an avalanche of curiosity once revealed.

Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Four Thousand Weeks

Burkeman's judgment distilled into decision rules. The throughline: you can't do everything; choose your neglect consciously and the rest gets better.

The One Rule Behind Everything

When you feel overwhelmed, the answer is never "do more / get more efficient." It's "confront the limit and choose what to drop." Efficiency surfaces more demands; acceptance ends the spiral.

Decision Rules

When you…Don'tDo (because…)
feel "too much to do"try to fit it all inaccept you can't, then pick what to consciously neglect (the to-do list is infinite by design)
clear your inbox / deckscelebrate being "on top of it"expect more to flow in — efficiency speeds the conveyor belt
evaluate a productivity tipask "does it fit more in?"ask "what does it let me neglect?" — that's the only real help
face a tempting opportunityqueue it for "later"run Buffett 25/5: top-5 → yes; bottom-20 → actively avoid (it's a trap, not a backlog)
have a high-value goalwait for spare timepay yourself first — do it today, first; spare time never comes
juggle many projectskeep all irons in the firecap WIP at ~3; finish or drop before adding
want "work-life balance"chase it (nobody achieves it)decide in advance what to fail at; choose deliberate imbalance
get distracted from hard workblame the appnotice you're fleeing the task's discomfort (the intimate interrupter) — stay with it
feel a project is derivativejump to a new directionstay on the bus — routes diverge into originality only past the shared stretch
rush a problem / personforce the pacelet it take its time; tolerate not-knowing (impatience backfires)
feel guilty about leisurejustify rest as recovery for more worktreat rest as an end in itself (atelic) — that's the point of the time
feel insignificant / behinddespairuse cosmic insignificance therapy — lower the bar to human scale; relief, not pressure
crave certainty before actingwait for the guaranteeact wholeheartedly without it — "I don't mind what happens"
have a generous impulsedefer to do it perfectlyact now, imperfectly — the gift you make beats the one you don't

Thresholds & Defaults

  • Lifespan budget: ~4,000 weeks (80 yrs). The number is the reframe, not a countdown to optimize.
  • Closed list cap: ~10 items; add only by completing.
  • WIP limit: ≈3 active projects (≤1 work + ≤1 non-work for big serialized projects).
  • Buffett split: top 5 of 25 ambitions; avoid the other 20.
  • Daily creative stint (radical incrementalism): small and fixed; never more than ~4 hrs; stop on time even with energy left; weekends off.
  • Work boundaries: set start/stop hours in advance; let the container do the deciding.
  • "Do nothing" practice: 5–10 min.

Tells & Smells (you're avoiding finitude when…)

  • You're "keeping your options open" → really avoiding the commitment that would make life meaningful.
  • You feel you must do more than you can → logically impossible; the inner taskmaster is simply wrong.
  • You're busy but nothing important advances → you're using busyness to numb the discomfort of choosing.
  • You live in "when I finally…" → instrumentalizing the present; the future is a place you never arrive.
  • You can't sit still / must act → you'll make bad choices just to feel in control (practice doing nothing).
  • Every cause feels equally urgent → the attention economy talking; consolidate your caring.

Good vs Bad Procrastination

  • Bad: avoiding a project to dodge the fear of doing it imperfectly / facing your limits (the architect who never builds).
  • Good (creative neglect): consciously choosing what to not do so you can finish what matters. Procrastinate on the right things, on purpose.

The Liberating Reframes (use when stuck)

  • "I'll never get on top of everything" → good news: stop berating yourself; start choosing.
  • "Missing out is guaranteed" → that's exactly what makes a choice mean something.
  • "I have far less control than I want" → and confronting that is the most effective time-management move there is.

glossary.md

Glossary — Four Thousand Weeks

Active patience — Patience reframed not as passive resignation but as an "almost muscular state of alert presence." (Ch 11)

Art of creative neglect — The decision discipline of deliberately, calmly choosing what not to do; treating neglect as a skill, not a failure. (Ch 4)

Atelic activity — An activity with no end point or external goal, valuable in itself (a walk, listening to music). Contrast telic. (Ch 9, via Kieran Setiya)

Attention economy — The system in which companies profit by capturing your finite attention, incentivized to show you enraging or distracting material. (Ch 5)

Being-toward-death — Heidegger's idea that authentic living means facing mortality rather than fleeing it; finitude defines human existence. (Ch 3)

Buffett's 25/5 rule — List 25 ambitions, keep the top 5, and actively avoid the other 20 as traps. (Ch 4, Appendix tool 3)

Causal catastrophe — Valuing present activities only for what they cause/lead to, never for themselves — so the present is endlessly sacrificed to a future that never arrives. (Ch 8)

Clock time — Treating time as an abstract, measurable resource separate from life, to be spent efficiently; the modern default. Contrast deep time. (Ch 1)

Closed / open lists — A two-list system: an unbounded "open" list of everything, and a "closed" list capped (~10) you can only add to by completing an item. (Appendix tool 1)

Consolidate your caring — Deliberately narrowing the causes/worries you engage so your finite capacity for care makes a real difference. (Appendix tool 5)

Conveyor belt of time — Edward Hall's image: time as a belt delivering containers (hours/weeks) we must fill; becoming "productive" just speeds the belt up. (Ch 0–1)

Cosmic insignificance therapy — The relief of recognizing your life matters far less on a cosmic scale than your ego demands, freeing you to live a meaningful human-scale life. (Ch 13)

Creative neglect — See art of creative neglect. (Ch 4)

Deep time — The expansive, timeless absorption in reality that comes from forgetting the abstract yardstick of the clock ("living in deep time," Richard Rohr). (Ch 1)

Decide what to fail at — Strategic underachievement: pre-selecting domains where you'll deliberately not seek excellence. (Appendix tool 3)

Done list — A list that starts empty each day and fills with what you accomplished, countering "productivity debt." (Appendix tool 4)

Efficiency trap — The pattern where becoming more efficient surfaces more demands rather than freeing time. (Ch 2)

Eigenzeit — German for "the time inherent to a process itself"; letting things take the time they take. (Ch 1)

Fixed-volume approach — Designing your work around hard, predetermined limits (work hours, list caps) instead of trying to expand capacity. (Appendix tool 1)

FOMO / JOMO — Fear of missing out vs. joy of missing out; since missing out is guaranteed, it's what makes choices meaningful. (Ch 3–4)

Helsinki Bus Station Theory — Arno Minkkinen's parable: early work resembles others' until you "stay on the bus" long enough for your route to diverge into originality. (Ch 11)

Human disease, the — The compulsion to demand certainty and cosmic reassurance about the future. (Ch 14)

Impatience spiral — The self-reinforcing loop where demanding speed erodes our tolerance for slowness, making everything feel more frustrating. (Ch 10)

Instantaneous generosity — Acting on a generous impulse immediately rather than deferring it (the only donation that counts is the one you make). (Appendix tool 9)

Instrumentalizing time — Treating each moment merely as a means to a future end. (Ch 8)

Intimate interrupter, the — The inner source of distraction: we flee toward distraction to escape the discomfort of a finite, difficult task. (Ch 6)

Joyless urgency — Marilynne Robinson's phrase for the modern compulsion to always be getting more done. (Ch 0–1)

Limit-embracing life — Organizing your days knowing you definitely can't do everything, and making hard choices consciously. (Ch 1)

Paradox of limitation — The more you chase total control over time, the worse life gets; the more you confront finitude, the better it gets. (Ch 1, the book's thesis)

Pay yourself first (with time) — Do your most-valued activity today, first, instead of hoping for leftover time. (Ch 4, Appendix tool 1)

Practice doing nothing — Training the capacity to not-act, so you stop making poor choices just to feel like you're acting. (Appendix tool 10)

Radical incrementalism — Robert Boice's finding: sustained creative output comes from short, fixed daily sessions, stopping on time. (Ch 11)

Researcher in relationships — Adopting curiosity (not a desired outcome) toward other people and the future. (Appendix tool 8)

Rocks-in-the-jar lie — Covey's "big rocks first" parable is rigged: reality has more big rocks than any jar can hold. (Ch 4)

Serialize — Work one big project at a time, finishing before starting the next. (Appendix tool 2)

Sisyphus's inbox — The endlessly refilling task list; the work is never done by design. (Ch 2)

Strategic underachievement — See decide what to fail at. (Appendix tool 3)

Task orientation — Pre-clock way of living where rhythms emerge from tasks themselves, not an abstract timeline. (Ch 1)

Telic activity — An activity aimed at a goal/end point, valued for its completion. Contrast atelic. (Ch 9)

Work in progress (WIP) limit — Capping active projects (≈3) so new work waits until a slot frees. (Ch 4, Personal Kanban)

You are time — We don't have time as a possession; our existence is time, so "managing" it as a resource is a category error. (Ch 3)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Four Thousand Weeks

The book's concrete, repeatable practices. Most come from Chapter 4, Chapter 11, and the Appendix. These are practices, not insights — pick one or two and run them this week.

The Two-List System (fixed-volume productivity)

When to use: your to-do list is bottomless and you never feel "on top of it."

How: Keep an open list (everything, however long) and a closed list capped at ~10. You may only move a task from open→closed when you complete one already on the closed list. Optionally add an "on hold" list for items awaiting others.

Trade-offs: forces conscious prioritization and a felt sense of completion; requires accepting the open list will never empty.

Predetermined Time Boundaries

When to use: work expands to fill all available hours.

How: Decide in advance your start and stop times (e.g., start by 8:30, hard stop 5:30). Let the fixed container force wiser choices. (Newport: "you could fill any arbitrary number of hours with what feels to be productive work.")

Trade-offs: the constraint is the whole point; resist the urge to extend "just this once."

Pay Yourself First (with time)

When to use: a high-value pursuit keeps getting deferred to "leftover" time.

How: Do an hour of your most-valued work first, before email/meetings. Block recurring calendar "meetings" with yourself. Claim time; don't try to find it — spare time never arrives.

Trade-offs: something else gets less of you, on purpose.

Limit Work in Progress (WIP ≈ 3)

When to use: you keep starting things and bouncing between them when one gets hard.

How: Cap active projects at ~3. New demands wait in a queue until a slot frees by completion or deliberate abandonment. Name slots as next achievable steps ("draft ch4 outline"), not giants ("write book").

Trade-offs: from Personal Kanban; converts the false comfort of many open projects into real completion.

Buffett's 25/5

When to use: too many moderately attractive options compete for your finite life.

How: List your top 25 ambitions, rank them, circle the top 5. The other 20 are avoid-at-all-costs, not a someday list — they're appealing enough to distract, not important enough to build a life on.

Trade-offs: the hardest "no" is to things you genuinely want.

Serialize

When to use: anxiety tempts you to start everything at once.

How: One big project at a time (at most one work + one non-work). Consciously postpone everything else and tolerate the resulting anxiety. Only truly essential maintenance (bills, school run) is exempt.

Trade-offs: feels worse short-term, finishes more long-term.

Decide in Advance What to Fail At (strategic underachievement)

When to use: "work-life balance" feels impossible because everything demands excellence.

How: Pre-select domains to deliberately neglect (lawn, tidy kitchen) with zero shame. In essential domains, fail cyclically — bare minimum at work for two months while you focus on kids, then switch.

Trade-offs: replaces impossible balance with deliberate, confident imbalance.

Keep a "Done List"

When to use: you can never feel good because work is never finished ("productivity debt").

How: Start each day with an empty list; log what you actually accomplish. In a rut, lower the bar ("made coffee" counts). Leverages the motivating power of "small wins."

Trade-offs: a reframe, not more output — but small wins compound.

Radical Incrementalism (Boice's method)

When to use: long-horizon creative/knowledge work prone to bingeing and burnout.

How: A fixed, modest daily block (Boice's academics: sometimes 10 min, never >4 hrs). Show up every day; stop when the block ends, even mid-flow, to preserve the appetite to return. Take weekends off.

Trade-offs: slower on any single day, far more sustainable over a career; beats all-day binges.

Stay on the Bus (Helsinki Bus Station)

When to use: your work looks derivative and you're tempted to start over in a new direction.

How: Assume you simply haven't ridden far enough; keep committing to your route. Routes diverge into originality only past the shared early stretch of imitation and skill-building.

Trade-offs: requires enduring a long unoriginal phase; restarting resets you to the station.

Consolidate Your Caring

When to use: social media makes you feel you must care about every crisis at once.

How: Pick your battles — devote spare capacity to a couple of causes for a couple of years. Not because others don't matter, but because real impact needs focus.

Trade-offs: deliberately ignoring worthy causes; the attention economy pressures every cause to claim uniqueness.

Make Technology Boring

When to use: focused work keeps losing to one-swipe-away distraction.

How: Remove social apps; set the phone to grayscale (Settings > Accessibility > Color Filters); use single-purpose devices (Kindle). Strip the seductive escape from limitation out of your tools.

Trade-offs: less convenience, more reclaimed attention.

Seek Novelty in the Mundane

When to use: years feel like they're accelerating and collapsing.

How: Don't cram in exotic experiences — pay deeper attention to ordinary life. New route to work, unplanned walks, photography, journaling, "I Spy" with a kid. Novel attention lays down memory.

Trade-offs: subtle; works through presence, not novelty-chasing.

Be a Researcher in Relationships

When to use: you're trying to control how time with others (or the future) unfolds.

How: In a hard or boring moment, switch to curiosity — "who is this person?" Curiosity is satisfied whether they please you or not; a demand for outcomes is frustrated each time. Choose curiosity over worry about the future too.

Trade-offs: relinquishes control of outcomes.

Instantaneous Generosity

When to use: a generous impulse arises (give, praise, check in).

How: Act now, imperfectly. The donation/message you actually send beats the perfect one you never do. We defer not from meanness but from control-seeking.

Trade-offs: none worth mentioning — it also makes you happier immediately.

"Do Nothing" Meditation

When to use: you can't tolerate not-acting, so you make poor choices just to feel active.

How: Set a 5–10 min timer; sit; stop trying to do anything. Each time you notice you're "doing" something (even thinking, or focusing on the breath), stop doing it. Keep stopping until the timer ends.

Trade-offs: rebuilds autonomy from the urge to evade how reality feels right now.

HBR Guide to Persuasive Presentations

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Duarte's Judgment Calls

Thresholds & Defaults

DecisionDuarte's number
Content vs. slot lengthPlan for 60% (40 min of a 60-min slot)
Audience patience ceiling30–40 min before squirming
Executive summary slides~10% of appendix length (50 appendix → 5 summary)
Executive rehearsal frameBuild for 30, rehearse as if cut to 5
Slide comprehension3 seconds (glance test)
Text field costDefault text box ≈ 80 words ≈ 20 sec of lost listening at 250 wpm
Typefaces per deck1, at most 2
Colors per deck3 complementary + 2 neutrals
Quote slide length≤ 30 words, one quote at a time
Cutting an hour to 40 minCut ~1/3 of slides
Slide count, high-energy style~5/min (145 slides in 40 min); moderate = 1–2/min
Remote slide change interval~20 seconds
Interpreter (any type)Prepare half the material for the slot
Interpreter lead timeNotes sent 1 week ahead; hiring up to 1 month ahead
Tech setup minimum30 minutes, walkthrough preferred
Calming breath cycle4 deep hold-and-slow-release breaths (<1 min)

Decision Rules

  • If it's a topic, not a sentence with POV + stakes → you don't have a big idea; don't generate content yet.
  • If an idea doesn't support the big idea → cut it, however interesting. If you don't filter, the audience will — and resent you.
  • If the audience is senior → lead with conclusions and recommendations; a big reveal at the end will be interrupted away.
  • If the content is understandable without a presenter → it's a document. Circulate it; don't project it.
  • If a slide takes more than 3 seconds → it's a document, a build, or two slides.
  • If bullets on a slide don't need to be associated → give each its own slide. Slides are free.
  • *If bullets do feel related* → circle the verbs/nouns, name the relationship, replace with a diagram.
  • If the data has no z-axis → no 3-D. Ever.
  • If one number carries the message → show that number, huge, with no chart.
  • If you're deemphasizing chart context → you must supply it out loud; don't redistribute that slide.
  • If you don't know a Q&A answer → say so and commit to follow up. Never fake it; they see through it.
  • If a question seems trivial → look for the question behind the question before dismissing it.
  • If the room's body language turns → change course mid-talk; enduring it costs more than admitting it.
  • If the backchannel turns hostile → engage and acknowledge; make people feel heard rather than ignoring or defending.
  • If you're tempted to flag your own sound bite for sharing → don't. Overt flagging reduces sharing.
  • If your first visual metaphor arrives instantly → discard it; it's everyone's first idea.
  • If you're running long → drop to the false ending. That's why you planted it.

Choosing the Vehicle

  • Two direct reports, informal → conversation or whiteboard, no deck
  • Venture capitalists, small room → formal stand-up presentation
  • Analysts → a carefully written memo may outperform slides
  • Young professionals / broad reach → video, streamed or posted
  • Decision still open, want input → sketch live; a slick deck signals "final"
  • Commencement, eulogy, wedding toast, layoff announcement → no slides
  • Status update → distribute a document; don't hold a meeting to read it

Analytical vs. Emotional Mix

TopicAudienceLean
Layoffs, launchesAnyEmotional, but never sentimental
Science, engineering, financeSpecialistsAnalytical + at least one human anchor
Cost cuttingManagers who must fire peopleEmotional first, numbers second, or you read as inhumane
Cost cuttingExecutives owning the bottom lineNumbers first — but acknowledge the human cost

Resistance Diagnosis

SignalTypeResponse
Counterarguments, competing data, "have you seen X?"LogicalRead the opposition; build a nuanced POV
Bias, dogma, moral objection, raw nerveEmotionalProceed carefully; explicitly honor the value at risk
"We can't afford / reach / staff that"PracticalName the sacrifice; visibly shoulder part of it

Tells & Smells

  • Deck ends with a "why it matters" slide → self-focused structure; move it to the front.
  • You can describe the talk as a noun phrase → no big idea.
  • Middle of the talk is all one side of the contrast → tension collapsed; add toggles.
  • Ending is a task list → the new bliss is missing.
  • Slide won't fit on a sticky note → concept too complex for one slide.
  • Eye doesn't know where to start on a slide → hierarchy failure, not content failure.
  • Audience leaning back, arms crossed → resistance. Fidgeting, checking e-mail → boredom.
  • No laughs, no nods, no notes across several minutes → you're not connecting; intervene.
  • You can't find the verbal tic → you haven't watched yourself on video yet.
  • Nobody asks a question → they've disengaged, or you never made room; either is a problem.

glossary.md

Glossary

Analytical/emotional balance — the deliberate mix of logical and emotional content, set by topic and audience; no presentation should be devoid of emotion (Ch 3)

Anti-cliché rule — discard the first visual concept you think of, since it occurs to everyone else too (Ch 8)

Appropriate drama — matching a story's emotional scale to the stakes of the room, so you don't read as manipulative (Ch 6)

Audience as hero / presenter as mentor — the stance that the audience is the protagonist and the presenter is the Yoda-like mentor giving a gift, a tool, and a way to get unstuck (Ch 1)

Backchannel — the stream of online chatter before, during, and after a talk (Ch 12)

Backchannel revolt — coordinated online rejection of a speaker's message (Ch 12)

Big Idea — the one key message, stated as a complete sentence containing your point of view and what's at stake (Ch 2)

Build — animating a list so each item appears as you cover it, controlling pacing (Ch 8, Ch 9)

Clean surface — a blank slide with master prompts turned off, used as the starting point for design (Ch 8)

Comfort monitor — the presenter-facing teleprompter screen showing notes the audience never sees (Ch 7, Ch 10)

Common ground tiers — lots / moderate / minimal, describing how much overlap you share with an audience (Ch 1)

Concrete comparison — a simile or metaphor used as a sound-bite device, or a physical analogue used to convey magnitude (Ch 3, Ch 9)

Consecutive interpretation — the interpreter shares the stage and translates after each point (Ch 11)

Controlling idea — screenwriting's term for the big idea (Ch 2)

Convergent thinking — the elimination phase: sorting and filtering generated ideas against the big idea (Ch 3)

Curator of content — the presenter's role once the highest-leverage audience subgroup is chosen (Ch 1)

Divergent thinking — the generation phase, where new options emerge (Ch 2, Ch 3)

Dynamic opposites — canonical contrast pairs (sacrifice/reward, stagnation/growth, budget/quality) used to build tension (Ch 2)

Emotional texture — emotion layered onto an otherwise analytical case, usually via story (Ch 3, Ch 6)

Emotive anecdote — a gripping personal story used as a S.T.A.R. moment (Ch 6)

Executive summary slides — front-loaded summary at roughly 10% of deck length, with the rest as appendix (Ch 1)

False ending / real ending — two rehearsed exit points allowing a graceful early close (Ch 7)

Five arrangement principles — flow, contrast, white space, hierarchy, unity (Ch 9)

Five segmentation lenses — politics, demographics, psychographics, firmographics, ethnographics (Ch 1)

Four calls to action — the audience acts as doers, suppliers, influencers, or innovators (Ch 2)

Glance test — the standard that any slide be comprehensible in three seconds (Ch 8)

Grandmother test — rework language until a non-expert would understand the central terms (Ch 3)

Graphic recorder — a practitioner who visually synthesizes a talk in real time on a large mural (Ch 7)

Inventory of Personal Stories — a catalog of remembered events and the emotions they summon, built from prompts and reused across talks (Ch 6)

Mind mapping — solo associative brainstorming producing a web of concepts and connections (Ch 2)

New bliss — the rewarded state the audience reaches by adopting your idea; the destination of the ending (Ch 4, Ch 5)

Physical cues — involuntary audience body language read as live feedback (Ch 12)

Planted question — a question a facilitator raises because the audience is too intimidated to ask it (Ch 11)

Pre-selling — meeting tough critics in advance so their objections don't surface as roadblocks (Ch 2)

Pressure-testing — handing your big idea to someone else to attack (Ch 2)

Reciprocity — the currency of social media; spreading others' ideas so yours will spread (Ch 12)

Reexperiencing — narrating a story from inside the moment rather than reporting it (Ch 11)

Resistance types — logical, emotional, practical (Ch 2)

Resonance / resonant frequency — the physics metaphor for tapping something already inside the audience so they move on their own (Ch 1)

Rhythmic repetition — a sound-bite device repeating a phrase across sentences or slides (Ch 3)

Simultaneous interpretation — booth-based real-time translation delivered to audience earphones (Ch 11)

Slide cemetery — a holding area at the end of the file for cut slides, available during Q&A (Ch 7)

Slideument — Garr Reynolds' term for a text-dense document masquerading as a slide deck (Ch 7)

Slogan — a concise, memorable statement engineered for pickup (Ch 3)

Sound bite — a crafted, repeatable phrase delivered without fanfare (Ch 3)

S.T.A.R. moment — Something They'll Always Remember: a climactic shocking statistic, evocative visual, memorable dramatization, or emotive anecdote (Ch 6)

Subtext (in Q&A) — the larger issue or unspoken motive behind a surface question (Ch 11)

Toggling — alternating between what is and what could be through the middle of a talk (Ch 4, Ch 5)

Transformation arc — the mapped move from where the audience starts to where you want it to end up (Ch 1)

Verbal tic — a filler word substituting for a pause (Ch 11)

Visual taxonomy — the five diagram relationship types: network, segment, join, flow, stack (Ch 9)

Walk-in / walk-out slide — the slide displayed as people arrive, and the one left up as they leave (Ch 8)

What is / what could be — the juxtaposition of status quo and better way that generates a presentation's conflict (Ch 4, Ch 5)

Whispering interpretation — the interpreter whispers audience comments to the presenter (Ch 11)

White space — open space around elements; raises perceived value and sharpens focus (Ch 9)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques

Audience-as-Hero Reframe

When to use: Any draft that reads as a list of things the audience must do for you.

How: Recast yourself as mentor. Deliver a gift (insight that improves their lives), a magical tool (a skill or mind-set serving their objectives and yours), and a way to get unstuck (a solution to a painful situation). Rewrite the opening so "why this matters to you" precedes the nitty-gritty.

Trade-offs: Takes longer to prepare and cedes the spotlight; in exchange you get willing advocates instead of grudging compliance.

Audience Segmentation and Curation

When to use: Mixed-role rooms; internal decision meetings.

How: Profile along politics, demographics, psychographics, firmographics, ethnographics. Identify who most affects adoption. Write mostly to that subgroup, keeping enough general content to avoid alienating the rest. Prepare responses for known objectors and pre-sell the saboteurs.

Trade-offs: Over-specialize and you lose the room; under-specialize and you move no one.

The Executive Compression

When to use: Senior executives, short slots, decision meetings.

How: Build for the allotted time, then rehearse as if cut to 5 minutes. Lead with findings, conclusions, recommendations, and call to action. Set expectations up front ("5 minutes of summary, then discussion"). Front-load executive summary slides at ~10% of deck length; the rest is appendix you pull from on demand. Rehearse with someone who succeeds at that level.

Trade-offs: You surrender narrative suspense — which executives don't want anyway.

Big Idea Sentence Construction

When to use: Before generating any content.

How: Start from the topic. Add your point of view. Add what's at stake. Result must be one complete sentence with a subject (often "you") and a verb. Use pain words to make the status quo uncomfortable and reward words to lure.

Trade-offs: Committing to a POV invites disagreement — which is the point.

Divergent–Convergent Brainstorm Loop

When to use: Content generation for any substantial talk.

How: Alone (mind map on paper), then group (fast facilitation, one idea per sticky note, no judgment), then alone again to develop latent ideas. Then converge: filter every idea against the big idea and cut mercilessly.

Trade-offs: Slow, and produces material you'll discard — quantity is the mechanism, not waste.

Resistance Triage

When to use: Before finalizing content; again before Q&A prep.

How: Classify likely objections as logical (read the opposing literature), emotional (identify the bias, dogma, or moral code your idea violates and address the value at risk), or practical (name the sacrifice, share the burden visibly). Pre-empt in the talk; pre-sell the loudest critics privately.

Trade-offs: Raising objections yourself risks planting doubt — but it demonstrates an open mind and invites reciprocity.

What Is / What Could Be Toggle (Sparkline)

When to use: As the skeleton of any presentation meant to change belief or behavior.

How: Establish what is until heads nod. Introduce what could be, opening a gap. Toggle repeatedly through the middle, drawing rows from your dynamic-opposite pairs. End in the new bliss. Never announce the transition.

Trade-offs: More work than a linear report; the only structure that reliably moves people.

Three-Level Ending

When to use: The close of any persuasive talk.

How: Describe future rewards at three levels — benefits to them, to their sphere (peers, reports, customers), and to the world. Then, and only then, action items.

Trade-offs: Can read as grandiose if the third level is a stretch; skip it rather than inflate it.

Emotional-Impact Story Template

When to use: Converting a dry supporting point into something that lands.

How: When/who/where → context → conflict → proposed resolution → complication → actual resolution. Place discomfort stories on the what-is side and awe/inspiration stories on the what-could-be side.

Trade-offs: Costs time in a tight slot; buys retention and retelling.

S.T.A.R. Moment Design

When to use: Once per talk, at the climax.

How: Choose one of four — amplified shocking statistic, evocative visual contrast, memorable dramatization (props, live demonstration), or emotive anecdote. Tie it directly to the big idea.

Trade-offs: Two S.T.A.R. moments dilute each other; a S.T.A.R. moment serving showmanship rather than the idea reads as manipulation.

Vehicle Selection Before Software

When to use: Before opening PowerPoint or Keynote.

How: Match medium to how the audience processes information and to the venue: memo, video, whiteboard conversation, props, handouts, demo, or deck. Use low-tech deliberately when you want to signal that thinking is still formative.

Trade-offs: A polished deck signals finality — sometimes desirable (investors), often not (collaborative decisions).

The 60% Time Budget

When to use: Every talk with a defined slot.

How: Plan content for 60% of the slot. Cut deck by a third, moving slides to a slide cemetery. Rehearse with the clock counting up while trimming; switch to counting down once in range, with quarter-mark time stamps. Plant a false ending and a real ending.

Trade-offs: Feels like leaving value on the table; nobody has ever been faulted for ending early.

Glance Test Pass

When to use: On every slide.

How: Can it be understood in three seconds? Start from a clean surface with master prompts off, justify each added element, limit and enlarge text, unify typeface and palette, align and size deliberately.

Trade-offs: Sparse slides carry less standalone information — which is why documents exist.

Sticky-Note Storyboarding

When to use: After the title outline, before building anything.

How: Sketch each idea on a 1.5″ × 2″ note. One idea per slide. Concepts that overflow the note are too complex — eliminate and re-brainstorm.

Trade-offs: Feels like a detour; it saves more time than it costs and surfaces reusable diagram ideas.

Bullets-to-Diagram Conversion

When to use: Any slide with a related bullet list.

How: Circle the verbs or nouns and identify the relationship. Match it to network, segment, join, flow, or stack. Replace the list with a diagram from that category.

Trade-offs: Diagrams take longer to make and can over-formalize a loose grouping.

Data Clarification Pass

When to use: Every data slide.

How: Decide the one thing to be remembered and give it visual emphasis; gray out the rest; mute gridlines, borders, axes, labels. Kill 3-D where there's no z-axis; keep axis proportions honest. Choose the chart for the argument (matrix for relationships, line for trajectory). Consider showing one huge number instead. Explain why and how, not just what. Anchor big magnitudes in concrete comparisons.

Trade-offs: Deemphasized context must be supplied by you, so it doesn't survive redistribution — send a document for that.

Rehearsal Stack

When to use: Every talk that matters.

How: Honest feedback from a skilled presenter on a printed deck; a rehearsed short version; continued slide tweaking as familiarity-building; runs in slide-show mode; and on-camera recording reviewed for presence, gestures, and tics.

Trade-offs: Time-expensive. Memorizing instead is cheaper and worse — it produces stiffness.

Technology Walkthrough Checklist

When to use: 30+ minutes before every in-person talk.

How: Befriend the AV person; test projector, clicker, audio; bring your own backups plus cloud, drive, and paper copies; prerecord demos; click through every slide in-room; verify comfort monitor legibility from the stage; confirm all media files transferred and play; confirm aspect ratio and projection direction, taping the floor; check for remote attendees.

Trade-offs: Pure overhead when nothing breaks; the one time it does, it's the whole talk.

Q&A Control

When to use: Every business presentation — trim content to make room.

How: Decide up front when questions come. Prepare answers to mundane through hostile questions. Answer the subtext, not just the surface. Admit ignorance and commit to follow up. Use a moderator or a one-question-per-person rule; acknowledge hostile questioners while answering to the rest of the room; use a filtering facilitator for charged topics. Close with a summary that recaps the new bliss.

Trade-offs: Taking questions throughout breaks your build; saving them all risks a pile-up.

Remote Presence Manufacturing

When to use: Any webinar, teleconference, or streamed talk.

How: Camera at eye level, stand, eyes on the lens, gestures kept in frame. Break content into small bites and change slides ~every 20 seconds. Build in interactivity and rewards. Vary voices with a co-host. Pause strategically to cut through white noise. Picture (or photograph) real faces. Test slides on the presenting machine — webinar software breaks builds and animations. Suppress personal, environmental, visual, and communal noise. Use a facilitator.

Trade-offs: High preparation cost for an audience whose attention you only partly control.

Backchannel Engagement

When to use: External talks with broad audiences (never confidential or client meetings).

How: Create and display a hashtag; invite use before, during, and after. Assign a quick-witted moderator to tweet key phrases, raise questions, redirect drift, and post slide links. Repeat and validate audience sentiment. Stream the talk. Post photos live. Invite bloggers. Don't flag your own sound bites, and be novel.

Trade-offs: The channel that spreads your idea can also organize against it; participation is the mitigation.

Structured Follow-Up

When to use: Immediately after every talk that asked for something.

How: Handwritten notes; thank-you e-mail recapping big idea, key points, call to action, and new bliss; open-door or lunch accessibility; promised materials sent immediately; one-on-one calls with people carrying the burden; a next-steps working meeting; and further presentations to other groups.

Trade-offs: Sustained effort long after the adrenaline stops — which is exactly why most presenters skip it and lose the adoption.

HBR's 10 Must Reads on Communication

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules

First branch: what kind of communication problem is this?

  • You need one person to say yes → Ch 1 (classify their decision style) + Ch 4 (audit your credibility first)
  • You need many people to change behavior → Ch 2 (six principles) + Ch 7 (springboard story)
  • People are not saying what they think → Ch 5 (spiral of silence) + Ch 3 (linguistic style, not competence)
  • You have to stand up and deliver → Ch 6 (rehearse intent) + Ch 9 (the five messages)
  • The conversation itself is the hard part → Ch 10 (three stressful types)
  • You are selling a creative idea → Ch 8 (pitcher types)

Decision styles: how to argue (Ch 1)

Style% of execsLead withNeverLatency
Follower36%Precedent, proven-elsewhere casesNovelty framed as untestedDays
Charismatic25%The exciting result, then risks you name yourselfOversellingFast, then verifies
Skeptic19%Credibility borrowed from someone they trustContradicting them publiclyDays or on the spot
Thinker11%Methodology and alternatives consideredJumping to conclusionsWeeks–months, 2 meetings
Controller9%Structured linear memos, problem dataRequesting the meeting yourselfMonths; wait for a trigger
  • If you cannot classify them, they are a follower — the other four announce themselves.
  • ~80% of presentations are pitched at skeptics and controllers, who are 28% of executives. Assume your default is wrong.
  • Sequence to a thinker is roughly the reverse of the sequence to a charismatic.

Cialdini: which principle fits (Ch 2)

SituationPrincipleMove
New relationship, no historyLikingSurface a genuine similarity; give real praise
You want future helpReciprocityGive first, visibly and without a ledger
Peers resist a changeSocial proofLet a respected peer speak, not the boss
Behavior must persist unsupervisedConsistencyActive + public + voluntary written commitment
Audience does not know youAuthorityMake real credentials visible before influencing
Information favors acting nowScarcityExclusive and loss-framed, only if true
  • Never on a false premise. Detection kills the offer and reciprocity returns the dishonesty.
  • Combine principles in one interaction; do not deploy them serially.

Conger: order of operations (Ch 4)

  1. Credibility — if absent, stop and buy it. Steps 2–4 are futile without it.
  2. Common ground — if no shared advantage exists, change the position, not the framing.
  3. Vivid evidence — data alone does not move people; supplement with story, metaphor, analogy.
  4. Emotional connection — match their state, not yours. End on hope, not doom.

Four ways not to persuade: hard sell up front; refuse to compromise; rely on argument alone; treat it as an event rather than a process. Enter with concessions already prepared.

Story selection (Ch 7)

GoalDetailToneForm
Spark actionMinimal — secondsPositive + evidencedSpringboard
Communicate who you areRichEitherFull narrative, told in person
Transmit valuesRich, believableEitherOnly works if you live it
Foster collaborationMoving, sharedEitherThen open the floor
Tame the grapevineEnough to expose incongruityHumorOnly if the rumor is false
Share knowledgeDetailed on the fixNegativeProblem/fix, no hero
Lead into the futureVague on specificsPositiveNever predict particulars
  • Goal is action → subtract detail. Goal is trust → add detail.
  • Rumor true or plausible? Do not ridicule — admit, reframe, move on. Denying gives it credibility.

Pitching: is your type working for you? (Ch 8)

  • Categorization happens in under 150 ms; character judgment inside 30 minutes.
  • ~1% of ideas survive the initial pitch; ~25% of pitchers avoid fast elimination.
  • Negative cues outweigh positive ones → eliminate pushover / robot / used-car salesman / charity case before optimizing anything else.
  • Have a track record? Lead with it and skip type-play entirely. Do not fake the artist — genuineness is the credibility.
  • Catcher's rule: if you feel swept away by a positive type match, start testing — showrunners are the favorite and the most dangerous.

Silence: speak or stay quiet? (Ch 5)

Invert the default. Ask "is this one of the rare times to stay quiet?" Stay quiet only if:

  • the issue is forgettable within a week or a month, or
  • the relationship is short-lived and unimportant.

Defer (with a stated time) when emotions are hot or a deadline is imminent — indefinite postponement guarantees the difference returns. Never resolve conflict by dividing the work. Tell: chronic gossip about someone you have never confronted means you are already in a spiral.

Stressful conversations (Ch 10)

TypeGambitOpening line shape
"I have bad news for you"Honor thy partnerAcknowledge your own share, then state the news plainly
"What's going on here?"Disarm by restating intentions"I can see how you took it that way. That wasn't what I meant."
"You are attacking me!"Fight tactics, not peopleName the behavior's effect, not their character
  • The opening determines the conversation. Never ease into bad news with small talk.
  • Clarity is not brutality: content is not brutal, delivery is. Default tone is neutral.
  • If it is not an emergency, split it — raise in meeting one, discuss in meeting two.
  • Improvement is unilateral: prepare against your predictable vulnerability, not their unpredictable behavior.

Leader's defaults (Ch 9)

  • Announce reorgs whole and fast; never preview (HP's preview cost ~a full quarter).
  • Cap each direct report at 3 initiatives per quarter. The enemy is starting the 85th thing.
  • Withhold your own theory in problem-solving meetings — the boss's answer stifles the room.
  • Define winning numerically, not adjectivally.
  • Treat missed results as a diagnostic, never as a blame trigger.

Cross-cutting tells

  • "Poor communication" → assume differing linguistic styles until shown otherwise (Ch 3).
  • Confidence judged from speech is unreliable — public claims diverge from private ones (Ch 3).
  • Rehearsed gestures lagging the words is what audiences read as fake (Ch 6).
  • There is no one best way to communicate — outcome depends on situation, culture, relative rank, and the interaction of two styles.

glossary.md

Glossary

84 Great Things — 7 direct reports x 3 doable initiatives per quarter x 4 quarters; the yearly output cap that keeps a team from over-starting (Ch 9)

Answer man trap — a leader whose identity rests on having the answer, which suppresses everyone else's thinking (Ch 9)

Antistory — the cynical counter-narrative an audience invents when a story sounds implausibly rosy (Ch 7)

Artist — pitcher type who inverts the power differential by commanding the catcher's imagination with thought experiments (Ch 8)

Authority — Cialdini principle: people defer to visible, genuine expertise as a shortcut through complexity (Ch 2)

Buffered feedback — praise-then-criticism ritual; literal listeners hear only the praise (Ch 3)

Buzzwords — style-specific vocabulary that holds a particular decision maker's attention (Ch 1)

Catcher — the executive who judges a pitch; judges the pitcher's creativity, not only the idea (Ch 8)

Charismatic — decision style: exuberant, visual, risk-seeking, short attention span; decides on balanced information (Ch 1)

Clarification technique — grant the other person's perception, own the words/intent mismatch, resume the substance (Ch 10)

Coalition-building — testing a concern with one savvy peer before voicing it upward (Ch 5)

Commitment (active, public, voluntary) — the three-part test a commitment must pass to bind future behavior (Ch 2)

Common ground framing — stating a position in terms of tangible benefit to the audience; if none exists, change the position (Ch 4)

Consistency — Cialdini principle: people align with commitments they have gone on record for (Ch 2)

Controller — decision style: abhors ambiguity, implements only his own ideas, avoids accountability (Ch 1)

Conversational rituals — conventionalized exchanges (ritual apology, ritual opposition, compliment exchange) that break when taken literally (Ch 3)

Creative collaborator — the catcher recast as co-author of the idea, which sharply lowers rejection odds (Ch 8)

Credibility (expertise + relationships) — Conger's two sources; the prerequisite to any persuasion attempt (Ch 4)

Credibility transfer — borrowing trust by having someone the audience already trusts deliver the message (Ch 1, Ch 4)

Danger zone — a conversation or counterpart you already know you handle badly (Ch 10)

Default mode of decision making — the style a person reverts to under complexity and consequence (Ch 1)

Definitional control — claiming a loaded term's meaning before rumor supplies one (Ch 9)

Deviant act — deliberately violating a silencing norm, e.g. asking the hard question nobody asks (Ch 5)

Emotional matchmaking — tuning emotional intensity to the audience's current state, not your own (Ch 4)

Five Messages Leaders Must Manage — hierarchy, financial results, the leader's job, time management, culture (Ch 9)

Follower — decision style: largest group, risk-averse, decides by precedent; wants innovative-yet-proven (Ch 1)

Four Aims / intents — Morgan's rehearsal targets: be open, connect, be passionate, listen (Ch 6)

Four Essential Steps of Persuasion — establish credibility, frame on common ground, reinforce with vivid evidence, connect emotionally (Ch 4)

Grapevine — the informal river of organizational communication; steer it rather than dam it (Ch 7)

Hip-pocket phrases — pre-rehearsed lines you can recall under pressure (Ch 10)

Honor thy partner — opening a bad-news conversation by acknowledging your own share of the problem (Ch 10)

Indirectness — meaning without spelling it out; used by the powerful as softened orders as much as by subordinates (Ch 3)

Knowledge duet — the showrunner's give-and-take of shared references before landing the idea (Ch 8)

Knowledge-sharing narrative — plotless, heroless, negative-toned problem/fix account; the workhorse story (Ch 7)

Liking — Cialdini principle: people comply with those similar to them and who like them (Ch 2)

Linguistic style — a person's characteristic speaking pattern: directness, pacing, pausing, jokes, questions, apologies (Ch 3)

Loss language — framing around what is forfeited by inaction rather than gained by action (Ch 2)

Maximalist account — the fully rendered story; engrossing but action-suppressing (Ch 7)

Mental opt-out — comply while contributing nothing; the terminal state of a silence spiral (Ch 5)

Neophyte — pitcher type who exploits the power differential by asking boldly for help (Ch 8)

Person prototypes — stereotype sets used to categorize a stranger in under a second (Ch 8)

Persuasion as learning and negotiating — an iterative move toward a shared solution, not a one-shot convincing (Ch 4)

Practical intelligence — feel for which ideas will actually work commercially; the showrunner's edge (Ch 8)

Reciprocity — Cialdini principle: people repay in kind; give first what you want to receive (Ch 2)

Red zone — a thwarting tactic paired with your own known vulnerability (Ch 10)

Results as diagnostic — treating a missed number as a root-cause investigation, not a punishment trigger (Ch 9)

Ritual apology — "I'm sorry" as expressed concern rather than admitted fault (Ch 3)

Ritual opposition — testing ideas through verbal combat; over when it's over (Ch 3)

Scarcity — Cialdini principle: people want more of what is less available; exclusive information outperforms common information (Ch 2)

Second conversation — the nonverbal channel, which fires before words and wins whenever the two conflict (Ch 6)

Showrunner — pitcher type who levels the power differential with a knowledge duet; the catcher's favorite and most dangerous type (Ch 8)

Silencing — declining to confront a difference, in yourself or in others (Ch 5)

Skeptic — decision style: combative, suspicious of anything challenging his worldview; decides fast on gut (Ch 1)

Social proof — Cialdini principle: people follow similar others, not distant strangers (Ch 2)

Speed trap — deadline pressure produces silencing, which produces worse decisions and more pressure (Ch 5)

Spiral of silence — silence, resentment, disconnection, self-protection, more fear, more silence (Ch 5)

Splitting the conversation — raising an issue in one meeting and discussing it in a later one (Ch 10)

Springboard story — minimal-detail, true, recent story with one protagonist that makes listeners leap to "why not here?" (Ch 7)

Status/rapport dynamic — every utterance both conveys ideas and negotiates relative position (Ch 3)

Substitute credibility — credibility borrowed from consultants, independent research, pilots, or allies (Ch 4)

Thinker — decision style: cerebral, risk-averse, data-hungry; slowest and toughest to persuade (Ch 1)

Thought experiment — the artist's invitation into an imagined world (Ch 6, Ch 8)

Thwarting tactics — shouting, accusation, distortion, digression, manipulation used to derail a conversation (Ch 10)

Vivid evidence — stories, metaphors, and analogies that make data land emotionally (Ch 4)

patterns.md

Patterns

Concrete techniques from across the ten articles.

Style-Matched Persuasion (Ch 1)

When to use: You have one identifiable chief decision maker and a proposal that has already failed on merit alone.

How: Classify the person (charismatic, thinker, skeptic, follower, controller). Keep the content constant; change sequence, format, pacing, and vocabulary. Charismatic: lead with the exciting result, then undersell by naming each risk yourself. Thinker: lead with methodology and alternatives considered, reserve two meetings. Skeptic: establish credibility before you open your mouth. Follower: show precedent and a proven track record. Controller: send structured linear memos, never request the meeting.

Trade-offs: Misclassification costs you the proposal. If a person resists classification, treat them as a follower.

Credibility Audit (Ch 4)

When to use: Before beginning any persuasion effort, especially with a new audience.

How: Ask two expertise questions (do I have a track record here, does the audience know it) and two relationship questions (do they see me as helpful and trustworthy, will they listen). Validate the answers with a colleague who will be honest. Where either is thin, buy it: hire an outside expert, cite independent research, run a visible pilot, or recruit a trusted sponsor.

Trade-offs: Slow and ego-bruising. Most managers considerably overestimate both scores.

Listening Tour Before Framing (Ch 4)

When to use: You need a position that carries real shared advantage, not a rationalized version of your own.

How: One-on-one conversations with key stakeholders to gather perspective, explicitly not to pitch. Then frame the position in terms of the benefit they named. If no shared advantage exists, change the position.

Trade-offs: Months of calendar time. Frequently reveals that your original proposal was wrong.

Active, Public, Voluntary Commitment (Ch 2)

When to use: You need behavior to persist without supervision.

How: Have the person summarize the agreement in their own words in writing, circulate it, and connect it to a value they already hold. Applied pressure voids the effect.

Trade-offs: Worthless if coerced. Coerced agreement is a burden, not a commitment.

Peer Testimony Over Boss Speech (Ch 2)

When to use: Veterans resist a new initiative and your positional authority is the wrong lever.

How: Find a respected long-tenured colleague who genuinely supports the change and have them raise it at the team meeting.

Trade-offs: You surrender control of the framing.

Structure the Meeting, Not the Person (Ch 3)

When to use: Capable people are consistently silent in mixed or hierarchical groups.

How: Control turn-taking, recognize speakers explicitly, do not reward whoever needs the shortest pause. Track who originated each adopted idea separately from who spoke longest.

Trade-offs: Less spontaneous, slower. But telling individuals to change their style asks them to change who they are.

Ritual Test Before Attribution (Ch 3)

When to use: Someone's behavior seems inexplicable — a fight that evaporates, an apology with no fault attached.

How: Ask "is this literal or is this a form?" and interpret it in the speaker's system before assigning motive.

Trade-offs: Risks over-excusing genuinely bad behavior.

Leader-Goes-First Debrief (Ch 5)

When to use: After a visible failure, to break a spiral of silence.

How: The authority figure names their own specific contribution to the failure before asking anyone else. Then redirect what surfaces from individual blame to systemic cause.

Trade-offs: Requires real vulnerability from the person with power; hollow versions backfire badly.

Rehearse Intent, Never Gestures (Ch 6)

When to use: Preparing any high-stakes talk.

How: Four separate rehearsal passes, one per intent — be open (imagine speaking to a close friend), connect (imagine a distracted child, then a teenager), be passionate (ask what is at stake and what result you want), listen (predict the audience's emotional state, then adapt live).

Trade-offs: Rehearsed gestures lag the words, and audiences read that lag as fake. Live adaptation requires knowing the material cold.

Springboard Story (Ch 7)

When to use: Driving adoption of a change after data and slides have failed.

How: A true, recent event with one identifiable protagonist and an authentically happy ending. Strip detail aggressively — seconds, not minutes. Close with "imagine if we did this everywhere."

Trade-offs: Less memorable than a fully told story. Without evidence of the positive outcome, jaded audiences generate an antistory.

Negative-Polarity Knowledge Story (Ch 7)

When to use: Transferring hard-won know-how.

How: Lead with the mistake, explain in detail why the fix worked, invite better alternatives. Often has to be teased out by first asking about successes.

Trade-offs: Boring, narrow audience, and cannot be compelled.

Engineered Yield Point (Ch 8)

When to use: Any pitch to a decision maker.

How: Pre-identify one element you will genuinely concede, surface it as early as possible, and invite the catcher's suggestions so they become a creative collaborator.

Trade-offs: Yield readily on everything and you become the pushover stereotype.

Compressed Reorg Announcement (Ch 9)

When to use: Restructuring.

How: Announce whole and fast, never preview. Frame as business necessity, show the chart on the spot, state the scope of change, give a bounded window to react and a stated time when work resumes.

Trade-offs: No consultation period, so the framing must be right the first time. Previewing cost HP roughly a full quarter.

Clarification Technique (Ch 10)

When to use: You are blindsided by a charged reaction you cannot explain.

How: Grant their perception, own the mismatch between your words and your intent, then return to the substance. Concede nothing about the facts.

Trade-offs: Unsatisfying if what you wanted was vindication.

Fight Tactics, Not People (Ch 10)

When to use: Facing shouting, accusation, distortion, or digression.

How: Name the behavior without attacking character — describe the difficulty the tactic creates for you rather than labeling the person.

Trade-offs: Makes the tactic the topic, delaying the substantive issue.

Rehearse With a Neutral Friend (Ch 10)

When to use: Before any conversation in a known danger zone.

How: Dump the content raw, restate it as if unloaded, fine-tune phrasing into temperate substitutes, check body language, write down hip-pocket phrases.

Trade-offs: Time cost; over-memorized scripts sound stiff.

HBR's 10 Must Reads on Public Speaking and Presenting

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules

Should you speak at all?

  • No compelling central idea → decline the invitation. Delivery can be coached out; the story cannot be coached in (Ch 1).
  • Idea indicts the audience's intelligence, judgment, or morality → expect to lose regardless of technique. Proceed only if it matters enough to your company and your identity (Ch 7).
  • You can't or won't change behavior → don't apologize. It will sound hollow (Ch 8).

Choosing your delivery mode (Ch 1)

SituationDo this
High stakes + weeks of rehearsal timeMemorize verbatim — but only if you can get past the valley of awkwardness
Limited prep timeBullet points on note cards; focus on the transitions
Any amount of prepNever read from script or teleprompter
Forced to readAt minimum, look up and make eye contact

Which persuasion frame? (Ch 7)

FrameVerdict
Business benefitsSafest and strongest — quantify, and find a second department that benefits
Opportunity ("don't miss this")Strong — gives audience control, inspires optimism
Threat ("here's what we lose")Coin flip — may produce fight or flight
Moral ("this is wrong")Weakest — reads as judgment of character

Which motivating language, how much? (Ch 6)

  • Unfamiliar task or unknown opponent → direction giving dominant.
  • Underdog, high stakes, or shaken confidence → empathy + meaning making dominant.
  • Veterans mid-operation → mostly direction; they're all business.
  • Purpose self-evident (e.g. staff who lost loved ones to the disease you treat) → dial meaning making down; it's already there.
  • Default sequence: direction → meaning → empathy → recap.

Warmth/competence diagnosis (Ch 4)

Emotion you elicitYour positionFix
Envy (respect + resentment)Competent, coldLead with warmth; validate feelings; share something personal
Pity (compassion + neglect)Warm, incompetentFull-height posture, deliberate movement, stillness; demonstrate track record
ContemptNeitherRebuild both, warmth first
TrustHappy warriorMaintain; stay a member of the group, not "them"
  • Threshold: a strongly disliked manager's odds of being rated a good leader ≈ 1 in 2,000.
  • Rule: stand up straight and smile — the only move that raises strength without costing warmth.

Should you apologize, and how hard? (Ch 8)

  1. Violation real or perceived? → perception counts; decide before the investigation finishes.
  2. Core (strikes the mission) → maximum apology on every dimension. Noncore → flexibility.
  3. Large/high-status org harming a low-power person → assume public outrage.
  4. Committed to change? → if no, don't apologize; if yes, name the specific change.
DimensionCore violation setting
WhoCEO or most senior leader available
WhatCandor + remorse + concrete change
WhereHigh profile; consider the site itself
WhenImmediately; placeholder if facts pending
HowSpoken, plain, self-implicating

Which visualization work am I doing? (Ch 10)

ConceptualData-driven
DeclarativeIdea illustration → editing + designEveryday dataviz → design + storytelling
ExploratoryIdea generation → facilitation, rapid sketchingVisual discovery → BI, programming
  • If it takes >3 seconds to read → it's a handout, not a slide.
  • If discussion is about the chart rather than the idea → the chart failed.
  • Exploring → iterate fast, ignore aesthetics. Declaring → aesthetics are the job.

Thresholds & defaults

  • Prep ratio: ~1 hour practice per minute of performance; ≥3 full trial runs (Ch 1).
  • Speech rate: reading ~300 wpm vs. listening ~150–160 wpm; 10 minutes ≈ 1,300 words (Ch 2).
  • Pauses: aim for 2–3 seconds at key moments; average speaker manages only ~3.5 pauses/minute (Ch 1).
  • Video clips: under 60 seconds or you lose the room (Ch 1).
  • Eye contact: pick 5–6 friendly faces spread across the room (Ch 1).
  • Power pose: 2 minutes before the encounter (Ch 4).
  • Finalize content: one month before the event (Ch 1).
  • Issue selling: all seven tactics combined ≈ 40% of the success/failure difference (Ch 7).
  • Warmth + competence: >90% of the variance in impressions (Ch 4).

Tells & smells

  • Audience calls a polished talk "calculated," "phoned in," or "not real" → you rehearsed gestures instead of intents (Ch 2).
  • You're describing your organization's achievements → you've lost them; switch to the problem you're solving (Ch 1, Ch 3).
  • Your draft has no antagonists → nobody will believe it; rosy pictures foment distrust (Ch 3).
  • You're arguing headquarters' logic to a skeptical field → reframe around their profit (Ch 5).
  • People comply but don't adopt → you led with strength, not warmth (Ch 4).
  • Your networking pitch is chronological → you're a fact teller; lead with where you're going (Ch 9).
  • Your presentation ends with a to-do list → add the new bliss (Ch 11).
  • Your chart shows two decades when the point is three years → subtract (Ch 10).
  • You feel defensive and unfairly blamed → that's the apology-delay reflex, not analysis (Ch 8).

Timing rules for selling upward (Ch 7)

  • Deadline far off, decision makers exploring → open-ended inquiry beats a specific proposal.
  • Imminent launch or release → propose now.
  • Priorities shifting, new players arriving, boss's preoccupations changing → window open.
  • Informal first to gauge interest → then formal to create pressure to respond.
  • Boss lacks power or interest → ask to accompany whoever pitches; if going direct, keep the boss in the loop.

glossary.md

Glossary

Accumulation of antagonists — Stacking successive obstacles in a story so the audience genuinely doubts a happy ending (Ch 3)

Apology Formula — The who/what/where/when/how framework for executing an organizational apology (Ch 8)

Apology rehearsal — Role-playing likely apology scenarios before they occur (Ch 8)

Battle exhortation — Precombat oratory; Keith Yellin identified 23 recurring "common topics" across history (Ch 6)

Board of advisers — A small designated circle who repeatedly hear and react to your evolving transition story (Ch 9)

Bundling — Attaching a small idea to a larger initiative to raise its prominence (Ch 7)

Catching the wave — Timing an issue to a trend more people are starting to care about (Ch 7)

Click and viz — Converting spreadsheet cells straight to a chart without thinking about purpose (Ch 10)

Coach out vs. coach in — Delivery flaws can be coached away; a missing central idea cannot be coached in (Ch 1)

Coherence — The quality of a life story in which past, present, and future link causally; the main generator of listener trust (Ch 9)

Companyspeak — PowerPoint, dry memos, and hyperbolic corporate communications that draw cynicism (Ch 3)

Core vs. noncore violation — Whether a failure strikes at the organization's central mission or a peripheral function (Ch 8)

Crutch words — Verbal fillers ("um," "ah," "like," "you know") that erode credibility; replace with pauses (Ch 1)

Declarative vs. exploratory — Communicating information vs. figuring something out; the second dataviz question (Ch 10)

Desire — The protagonist's core need, "the blood of a story"; not a shopping list (Ch 3)

Detective-story structure — Present a problem, describe the search, deliver an "aha" that shifts perspective (Ch 1)

Direction giving — Uncertainty-reducing language: exactly how to do the task and how performance will be judged (Ch 6)

Dread — Knowing what will happen and being unable to stop it; distinct from fear, which is not knowing (Ch 3)

Education plot — A transition story driven by growing insight and self-understanding (Ch 9)

Empathetic language — Praise, encouragement, gratitude, and acknowledgment of difficulty (Ch 6)

Everyday dataviz — Declarative + data-driven: simple charts for formal presentations (Ch 10)

Expertise — One of the two sources of credibility: track record and demonstrated knowledge (Ch 5)

Fact tellers — People who recite chronological credentials instead of telling a story; hard to help (Ch 9)

Four Aims (Intents) — Be open, connect, be passionate, listen; rehearse these instead of gestures (Ch 2)

Framing for common ground — Describing a position in terms of the listener's tangible benefits (Ch 5)

Happy Warrior — A leader combining high warmth with high strength; faces troubles without being troubled (Ch 4)

Idea generation — Exploratory + conceptual: whiteboard sketching to work through ambiguity (Ch 10)

Idea illustration — Declarative + conceptual: org charts, process diagrams, frameworks (Ch 10)

Inciting incident — The event that throws life out of balance and starts a story (Ch 3)

Inside-out vs. outside-in — Preparing by setting your emotional state vs. executing prescribed nonverbal cues (Ch 4)

Issue selling — Winning attention and resources from senior decision makers for an idea from below (Ch 7)

John Wayne approach — Stating a strong position up front and pushing to a close; gives opponents a target (Ch 5)

Lion tamer — Engaging the other party obliquely rather than presenting a clear target (Ch 5)

Mask — The persona individuals and institutions present; compelling stories live beneath it (Ch 3)

Maturation plot — A transition story about becoming your own person (Ch 9)

Meaning making — Language explaining why a task matters, linking mission to listeners' goals; the hardest MLT element (Ch 6)

Motivating Language Theory (MLT) — Mayfield framework: direction giving + empathy + meaning making (Ch 6)

New bliss — The closing depiction of how much better the audience's world becomes (Ch 11)

Persuasive story pattern — What is / what could be oscillation across beginning, middle, and end (Ch 11)

Placeholder apology — A fast interim apology issued while facts are still being gathered (Ch 8)

Poise — Stillness plus full-height posture; telegraphs equilibrium and stability (Ch 4)

Power poses — Open, expansive postures held two minutes; raise testosterone, lower cortisol (Ch 4)

Private conformity vs. outward compliance — Trust changes beliefs; fear changes only behavior (Ch 4)

Profluence of development — John Gardner's term for a story's felt sense of going somewhere (Ch 9)

Psychological contract — Stakeholders' unwritten expectations of an organization's responsibilities (Ch 8)

Pyramid search — Finding experts via adjacent-field experts who refer you onward (Ch 10)

Relationships — The second source of credibility: a history of listening and acting in others' interest (Ch 5)

Report–story continuum — Every presentation sits between data-rich report and engaging story (Ch 1)

Second conversation — Nick Morgan's term for the nonverbal channel, which fires before words (Ch 2)

Self-knowledge — The root of great storytelling; building characters by asking what you would do (Ch 3)

Seven issue-selling tactics — Tailor, frame, manage emotions, time, involve others, adhere to norms, suggest solutions (Ch 7)

Signposting — Explicit verbal markers ("to begin," "finally") essential in speech though inelegant in writing (Ch 2)

Skepticism — Believing nothing at face value; distinguishing text from subtext (Ch 3)

Spontaneous trait inferences — Snap judgments from brief exposure; warmth registers faster than competence (Ch 4)

Strategic unapologeticness — Deliberately refusing to apologize in order to affirm a value (Ch 8)

Talk as a journey — Framing a presentation by choosing where to start and where to end (Ch 1)

Turning point — The point of no return closing act two; usually made significant by the telling, not by the event (Ch 9)

Valley of awkwardness — The half-memorized stage where a talk sounds recited; rehearse past it or use notes (Ch 1)

Visual confirmation — Rapid prototyping of charts to test a hypothesis (Ch 10)

Visual discovery — Exploratory + data-driven: mining large data sets visually (Ch 10)

Visual exploration — Open-ended, inclusive plotting when you don't know what you're looking for (Ch 10)

Vivid evidence — Stories, metaphors, and analogies that make data emotionally memorable (Ch 5)

Warmth–competence matrix — The two dimensions of social judgment accounting for >90% of impressions (Ch 4)

What is / what could be — The two poles whose contrast generates presentation tension (Ch 11)

patterns.md

Patterns

Frame the Talk as a Journey

When to use: At the very first outline, before any slide exists (Ch 1).

How: Decide where to start (calibrated to what the audience already knows and cares about) and where to end (a changed view of the world). Limit scope to what you can explain and illustrate with examples in the available time. Go deeper, not broader — your unique contribution, not your whole field.

Trade-offs: Narrow framing means abandoning material you're proud of; overcorrecting into overexplanation insults an intelligent audience.

Detective-Story Structure

When to use: When the content is an insight or discovery (Ch 1, Ch 3).

How: Present a problem → describe the search for a solution → deliver the "aha" that shifts perspective.

Trade-offs: Requires you to genuinely have a problem worth solving; without one it becomes contrived suspense.

Rehearse the Four Intents

When to use: Any talk where credibility and buy-in matter more than information transfer (Ch 2).

How: Practice the speech four times, once per intent. Open: imagine speaking to someone you're totally relaxed with. Connect: imagine capturing an inattentive child's attention, then a distractible teenager's. Passionate: identify what's at stake and let the underlying emotion into every word. Listen: imagine what the audience will be feeling and watch for their signals.

Trade-offs: Slower than gesture drills and feels indirect, but rehearsed gestures fire late and read as fake.

Replace Fillers with Pauses

When to use: Whenever "um," "ah," "like," or "you know" recur (Ch 1).

How: Watch video or read a transcript of your last talk to identify your crutch words. Pair each with a physical action (tap your leg) or have a friend clap when you use one. Record yourself narrating your day using pauses instead of fillers. Prepare thoroughly — nervousness drives filler.

Trade-offs: Pauses feel far longer to the speaker than to the audience; great speakers pause two to three seconds.

The 1:60 Preparation Ratio

When to use: Sizing rehearsal for an important talk (Ch 1).

How: Roughly one hour of practice per minute of performance; minimum three full trial runs. Finalize content a month before the event; rehearse alone and in front of an audience. Be choosy about feedback givers — prefer experienced presenters.

Trade-offs: Not every presentation is worth that investment; if you can't get past the valley of awkwardness, use bullet points on note cards instead of memorizing.

Warmth Before Strength

When to use: First impressions, new teams, any stalled influence attempt (Ch 4).

How: Lower pitch and volume as if comforting a friend; validate what the room actually feels ("I know everybody's feeling a lot of uncertainty right now"); smile genuinely (eyes engaged, not just mouth); share one appropriately personal story. Then add strength: full-height posture, deliberate movement, stillness when finished.

Trade-offs: Amped-up enthusiasm reads as fawning; raised eyebrows while smiling signal anxiety and cost more strength than they gain warmth.

Power Pose Warm-Up

When to use: Two minutes before a high-stakes pitch or speech (Ch 1, Ch 4).

How: Adopt an open, expansive, space-occupying posture — standing tall, hands on hips, feet apart. Add deep breathing before going onstage.

Trade-offs: Builds personal agency and self-regulation, not dominance over others; it's an inside-out preparation, not a performance move.

Credibility Audit and Repair

When to use: Before beginning any persuasion campaign (Ch 5).

How: Score yourself separately on expertise (track record others know and respect) and relationships (seen as helpful, trustworthy, in sync). Test your self-assessment with trusted colleagues. Repair expertise by learning, hiring an outside expert, enlisting internal experts, citing independent research, or running a pilot. Repair relationships with one-on-one meetings that gather perspectives rather than pitch, and by involving allies who already have standing.

Trade-offs: Borrowed credibility works but takes time and can dilute your ownership of the idea.

Vivid Analogy Substitution

When to use: When your case rests on abstract projections the audience can't feel (Ch 5).
