Internal trigger — A cue from within (boredom, anxiety, loneliness) that prompts action (Ch 1).

Ironic process theory — Suppressing a thought makes it rebound more strongly ("don't think of a white bear," Wegner) (Ch 2).

Job strain — High expectations combined with low control; predicts workplace depression and distraction (Ch 6).

Liminal moments — Transitions between activities where "just a second" balloons into lost time (Ch 2).

Loss aversion — We're more motivated to avoid losses than to seek equal gains; the engine of price pacts (Ch 5).

Multichannel multitasking (cross-modal) — Pairing one attention-heavy channel with a low-demand one (audiobook + walking) (Ch 4).

Need density hypothesis — The more needs go unmet in real life, the more they're sought in virtual realities (Ryan) (Ch 7).

Negativity bias — Bad events demand attention more powerfully than good; one of four dissatisfaction factors (Ch 2).

Phubbing — Phone + snubbing: ignoring a person by attending to a device (Ch 8).

Precommitment — A choice made in advance that binds your future self (Ulysses pact) (Ch 5).

Price pact — A precommitment putting money on the line, forfeited if you get distracted (Ch 5).

Proximate vs. root cause — Devices are the proximate cause we blame; escaping discomfort is the root cause (Ch 2).

Pseudowork — Tasks that look like work but aren't aligned with top priorities (Ch 3).

Psychological safety — Belief that one won't be punished or humiliated for speaking up (Amy Edmondson) (Ch 6).

Relatedness — Psychological nutrient: feeling important to others and that others matter to you (Ch 7).

Reflect & Refine — Weekly 15-minute review of what worked in your schedule and what to change (Ch 3).

Residual beneficiary — The one who gets only leftover time; don't let loved ones become this (Ch 3).

Rumination — Repeatedly dwelling on bad experiences; one of four dissatisfaction factors (Ch 2).

Self-compassion — Talking to yourself like a friend after a slip; predicts resilience and well-being (Ch 2).

Self-determination theory — Ryan & Deci: the psyche needs autonomy, competence, and relatedness to thrive (Ch 7).

Social antibody — A group norm that blocks the spread of a harmful behavior (Paul Graham) (Ch 8).

Social contagion — The spread of behaviors (device use, overeating) through a social group (Ch 8).

Surf the urge — Riding a craving like a wave — observing, neither suppressing nor acting — until it subsides (Ch 2).

Sterile cockpit rule — Aviation rule banning non-essential activity below 10,000 ft; model for interruption-free zones (Ch 4).

Temptation bundling — Only allowing a tempting activity alongside one you should do (audiobooks only at the gym; Milkman) (Ch 4).

Ten-minute rule — When an urge hits, allow it — but wait ten minutes first (Ch 2).

Three life domains — You, Relationships, Work — the framework for allocating time (Ch 3).

Timeboxing — Deciding what to do and when; eliminating white space via implementation intentions (Ch 3).

TNT (T = n × t) — Total email time = number of messages × time per message; reduce both (Ch 4).

Traction — Any action that draws you toward what you planned to do (Ch 1).

Ulysses pact — A freely made decision designed to bind oneself in the future (Ch 5).

4 R's (smartphone) — Remove, Replace, Rearrange, Reclaim (Ch 4).

patterns.md

Indistractable — Patterns & Techniques

Reimagine the Internal Trigger (4 steps)

When to use: A recurring urge to distract (googling instead of writing, phone-checking).

How: (1) Look for the discomfort preceding it; (2) Write down the trigger — time, activity, feeling; (3) Explore the sensation with curiosity ("leaves on a stream"); (4) Beware liminal moments (transitions).

Trade-offs: Requires honest self-observation; takes trials to notice internal (vs. external) triggers.

The 10-Minute Rule / Surf the Urge

When to use: An in-the-moment craving for a pacifying distraction.

How: Tell yourself you can give in — but not for ten minutes. Ride the urge like a wave without suppressing or obeying it. Reassess after ten minutes (the urge usually passes).

Trade-offs: Not a hard "no," so it relies on the urge genuinely subsiding — works because most do.

Timeboxing the Three Life Domains

When to use: Whenever your days feel reactive or your calendar doesn't reflect your values.

How: Decide hours per week for You / Relationships / Work; build a "perfect week" template with zero white space; judge success by adherence, not output.

Trade-offs: Feels rigid at first, but constraints reduce decision fatigue and make distraction visible.

Reflect & Refine (weekly review)

When to use: Every week, ~15 minutes.

How: Reflect ("when did I do what I said vs. get distracted?"), then Refine ("what calendar change would help me live my values?"). Treat the week as an experiment.

Trade-offs: Only works if you commit to the schedule between reviews.

Schedule Syncing with Stakeholders

When to use: Any shared-time relationship — manager, partner, multiple bosses.

How: Share your timeboxed schedule; agree on it in regular increments (usually weekly; daily if it changes daily).

Trade-offs: Requires vulnerability/transparency; pays back in fewer imposed distractions.

The Critical Question

When to use: On any external trigger.

How: Ask "Is this trigger serving me, or am I serving it?" Keep triggers that lead to traction; hack back the rest.

Email TNT (T = n × t)

When to use: Email overload.

How: Cut n — office hours, delay-send, unsubscribe/black-hole. Cut t — batch; touch each email twice, tagging by when it needs a reply ("Today"/"This Week"), answer in scheduled blocks.

Trade-offs: Slower replies; usually a feature, not a bug (many issues self-resolve).

Smartphone 4 R's

When to use: Phone feels distracting (one-time, <1 hr).

How: Remove unused apps → Replace where/when you use tempting ones (desktop, wristwatch) → Rearrange home screen to Primary Tools + Aspirations → Reclaim notifications (sound/sight per app; Do Not Disturb).

Temptation Bundling + Multichannel Multitasking

When to use: To make a "should" (exercise) attractive or reclaim commute/chore time.

How: Only allow a tempting reward (audiobooks, saved articles) alongside the should. Pair one attention-heavy channel with a low-demand one (audio + walking).

Trade-offs: Only works across modalities — never two complex tasks at once.

Effort Pact

When to use: A distraction you can add friction to.

How: Make it physically harder — app blockers (Forest, SelfControl, Freedom), kSafe, co-working/Focusmate, iOS Downtime.

Trade-offs: Determined self can override; friction just has to exceed the impulse.

Price Pact

When to use: Short, well-defined task where you can remove the external trigger.

How: Put money on the line ("burn or burn"; forfeit to a friend). Exploits loss aversion.

Trade-offs: Four pitfalls — no escapable trigger, short tasks only, scary to start, not for the self-critical.

Identity Pact

When to use: Long-term behavior change.

How: Adopt a noun ("I'm indistractable"); say "I don't," not "I can't"; tell others to solidify it.

Trade-offs: Slower to take hold, but self-reinforcing once it does.

Create Psychological Safety (Edmondson's 3 steps)

When to use: Leading a team that overuses tech / can't raise concerns.

How: (1) Frame work as a learning problem; (2) Acknowledge your own fallibility; (3) Model curiosity, ask questions. Pilot small (one predictable night off, one team) and open a regular forum.

Social Antibody Against Phubbing

When to use: Someone uses a device in a social setting.

How: Sincerely ask, "I see you're on your phone. Is everything OK?" — offering a graceful exit or a return to the group.

Keep Sharp: Build a Better Brain at Any Age

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Keep Sharp — Cheatsheet

The one-line thesis

Cognitive decline is NOT inevitable. Lifestyle > genes (>90% of longevity is in your hands). Build the brain with 5 pillars; motivate by running toward a sharp brain, not away from fear.

The 5 Pillars (memorize)

Move · Discover · Relax · Nourish · Connect

If you do only ONE thing: Move. Exercise is the only behavioral activity scientifically proven to help the brain.

Decision rules

When…Do…Because…
You can do only one brain-health thingExercise (break a sweat daily)Only proven behavioral intervention; boosts BDNF
Motivating behavior changeFrame as running toward a goalFear activates amygdala → intense but transient
Choosing a "brain game"Pick complex + novel + social learning you enjoyCrosswords flex only word-finding; games are over-hyped
Memory "fails" on namesFix attention (stop multitasking) or retrievalUsually not systemic failure — both are trainable
Deciding whether to napCap at 30 min, early afternoonLonger/later naps wreck night sleep
Tempted by a supplementBuy walking shoes or a pillow insteadNo supplement reliably prevents dementia; industry unregulated
Someone offers "gluten-free will help your brain"Ignore unless celiac/sensitivityNo evidence; low-gluten-low-whole-grain can raise heart risk
A relative gets a dementia diagnosisRule out mimics (NPH, meds, depression) firstMany "dementias" are treatable
Talking to someone with dementiaNever correct them; redirectForces impossible recall, causes distress
You're a caregiverPut yourself on your to-do listCaregivers are the "invisible second patient" (up to 6x risk)

Numbers & thresholds worth committing

MetricTarget
Exercise, minimum150 min/week; 30 min cardio × 5 days
Exercise, optimal longevity~450 min/week (~64 min/day, mostly walking)
Sitting break≥2 min every hour
Sleep7–8 hrs nightly (need is constant with age)
Caffeine cutoff2:00 p.m.
Last meal before bed~3 hours
Bedroom temp60–67°F
Warm light2700–3000K
Alcohol moderation≤2 drinks/day (men), ≤1 (women); prefer red wine
Colored foods/day7 different real-food colors
Purpose (ikigai) effect~20% lower future dementia risk
MIND diet adherence (top third)53% lower Alzheimer's risk (~7.5 yrs of aging)
Alzheimer's preclinical windowstarts 20–30 yrs before symptoms

S.H.A.R.P. eating (fast recall)

Slash sugar · Hydrate smartly (drink instead of eat) · Add omega-3s (from food) · Reduce portions · Plan ahead

Food ABCs

  • A (regularly): greens, berries, fish, healthy fats (EVOO/avocado/eggs), nuts/seeds
  • B (include): beans, whole fruits, low-fat dairy, poultry, whole grains
  • C (limit): fried, sweets, processed, red meat, high-fat dairy, salt

Tells & smells (recognize the situation)

  • "Sitting is the new smoking" → prolonged sitting (>8 hr) harms metabolically even if you're lean.
  • Sleep as a badge of honor → red flag; no data links success to less sleep; you can't "game" the body clock.
  • Excessive daytime napping → possible early Alzheimer's sign (tau in wakefulness centers).
  • Long-term anticholinergics (Benadryl, "PM" meds) → 54% higher dementia risk at 3+ years.
  • Amyloid-riddled brain, no symptoms → cognitive reserve at work; goal = "asymptomatic Alzheimer's."
  • Loneliness → treat as a vital sign; social pain = physical pain in the brain.

Daily productivity/rest toolkit (from Ch6)

  • Pomodoro: 25 min focus / 5 min break.
  • Don't multitask — single-task "like a surgeon"; guard mornings for creative work; no email first thing.
  • Marbles before sand: schedule big commitments first.
  • Gratitude journal + 15 min/day for yourself + daydream (neural reset).
  • Analytical meditation / deep breathing (exhale to count of 20) to lower cortisol.

12-week program in one line

Add one habit per pillar per week; never restart — accumulate. Get a baseline checkup, re-check at week 12. Set nonnegotiables. "Progress is better than perfection."

glossary.md

Glossary — Keep Sharp

ABCs of food — GCBH framework: A-list (eat regularly), B-list (include), C-list (limit) foods (Ch7).

ABCs of prevention (Isaacson) — Anthropometrics, Biomarkers, Cognitive performance; reassessed every 6 months (Ch7, Ch10).

Advance directive — Legal document stating treatment/end-of-life wishes; includes living will and durable power of attorney for health care (Ch11).

Alzheimer's disease — Most common dementia (>half of cases); hallmarks are amyloid plaques and tau tangles (Ch2, Ch10).

Amyloid (beta-amyloid) — Sticky protein plaques that accumulate between neurons; healthy in normal form, harmful when misfolded (Ch2).

Amyloid Cascade Hypothesis (ACH) — Theory that plaque accumulation causes Alzheimer's; repeatedly failed in drug trials (Ch2).

Analytical meditation — Placing a problem in a mental "bubble" to isolate it from emotion and find clarity; taught by the Dalai Lama (Ch6).

Anticholinergics — Drugs blocking acetylcholine (Benadryl, some antidepressants); 3+ years' use linked to 54% higher dementia risk (Ch6, Ch10).

APOE gene — Risk gene with alleles E2 (protective), E3 (neutral), E4 (raises risk); not deterministic (Ch2, Ch10).

BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) — "Miracle-Gro for the brain"; boosted by exercise, sleep, stress reduction, sunlight, fasting (Ch3, Ch7).

Blood-brain barrier — Semipermeable wall protecting the brain; when leaky, toxins enter and worsen decline (Ch2).

Blue Zone — Region with unusually long-lived people (e.g., Okinawa) (Ch8).

Chrono eating — Eating aligned to daylight/circadian rhythm; frontloading calories (Ch7, Ch9).

Circadian rhythm — ~24-hr cycle governing sleep-wake, hormones, temperature (Ch6).

Cognitive reserve (brain resiliency) — The brain's ability to improvise around damage via built-up networks; from education, work, lifelong learning (Ch2, Ch5).

Conservatorship / guardianship — Court-appointed control when families can't agree; costly and abuse-prone (Ch11).

Cortisol — Stress hormone; chronic excess shrinks the hippocampus (Ch4, Ch6).

CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy) — Degenerative disease from repeated head blows; linked to tau (Ch2).

Dementia — Group of symptoms (memory loss, poor judgment), not one disease; spectrum from mild to severe; some causes reversible (Ch0, Ch10).

Dendrite — Branched extension of a neuron that receives signals; grows with novelty, entrenches with repetition (Ch1).

Dirty Dozen (myths) — The 12 destructive myths about the aging brain (Ch3).

Encoding — First memory phase: perception → hippocampus; requires attention (Ch1).

Entourage effect — Nutrients work best within whole food, not isolated supplements (Ch7).

Flow — State of total, energized immersion in an activity; requires purpose (Csikszentmihalyi) (Ch5).

Ghrelin / leptin — Appetite hormones (hunger / satiety); disrupted by poor sleep (Ch6).

Glymphatic system — The brain's self-cleaning drainage; runs in overdrive during sleep, clears amyloid (Ch6).

Hippocampus — Seahorse-shaped memory center; integrates sensory input; shrinks with stress/decline (Ch1).

Hogeweyk — Dutch "dementia village"; person-centered care model (Ch11).

Ikigai — Japanese "reason for being"; sense of purpose (Ch5).

Inflammation — Common thread across all brain-decline theories and most illness (Ch2).

Intermittent fasting — Limiting eating windows (12–16 hr); boosts BDNF and insulin sensitivity (Ch7, Ch9).

Invisible second patient — The caregiver, up to 6x more likely to develop dementia (Ch11).

KAER process — Gerontological Society four-step tool for detecting cognitive impairment (Ch10).

MCI (mild cognitive impairment) — Often a precursor to dementia; sometimes reversible (Ch4, Ch10).

MIND diet — Mediterranean–DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay; up to 53% lower Alzheimer's risk (Ch7).

Moai — Okinawan lifelong social support group (Ch8).

Neurogenesis — Birth of new neurons throughout life (proven 1998) (Ch1, Ch3).

Neuroplasticity — The brain's ability to rewire and reorganize connections; a two-way street (Ch1).

Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) — Treatable dementia mimic; CSF buildup fixed with a shunt (Ch10).

Omega-3 fatty acids — Brain-nourishing fats (DHA, EPA, ALA); get from food, not supplements (Ch7).

Pomodoro technique — 25 min focused work + 5 min break; dopamine-reward productivity method (Ch6).

Preclinical time — 20–30 year window between brain changes and symptoms; prime intervention period (Ch10).

Prions — Proteins that trigger others (amyloid, tau) to misfold; universally fatal diseases (Ch2).

Pseudodementia — Dementia-like symptoms from severe depression; reversible when treated (Ch10).

Retrieval — Final memory phase: pulling info into conscious awareness (Ch1).

S.H.A.R.P. — Slash sugar, Hydrate smartly, Add omega-3s, Reduce portions, Plan ahead (Ch7).

Sleep spindles — Deep-sleep activity bursts moving memories from hippocampus to neocortex (Ch6).

Sundowning — Late-day confusion/agitation in ~20% of dementia patients (Ch11).

SuperAgers — 80+ people with memories as sharp as those decades younger (Ch3).

Synapse — Gap where neurons connect via neurotransmitters; strengthens with use (Ch1).

Tau / neurofibrillary tangles — Protein "railroad tracks" inside cells; knot up when damaged ("the bullet") (Ch2).

Triple threat (Gary Small) — Walk + friend + honest conversation (Ch8).

Type 3 diabetes — Nickname for Alzheimer's as an insulin-resistance disease of the brain (Ch2, Ch7).

VO2 max — Aerobic-fitness measure; higher fitness → healthier white matter → better cognition (Ch4).

White matter — Nerve-fiber bundles connecting gray-matter regions; health signals inter-region communication (Ch4).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Keep Sharp

The 5 Pillars (master framework)

When to use: any brain-health plan; the backbone of the whole book.

How: Move · Discover · Relax · Nourish · Connect. One chapter each (Ch4–8), assembled in the 12-week program (Ch9).

Trade-offs: Move has the strongest evidence; the others are synergistic and reinforce each other.

Exercise Prescription (Pillar: Move)

When to use: building or upgrading a fitness routine.

How: ≥150 min/week; 30 min cardio × 5 days (heart rate ≥50% above resting for ≥20 min); add interval + strength training; optimal-longevity dose ~450 min/week (much can be brisk walking). Sedentary start: 5–10 min burst (30 sec effort / 90 sec recovery) → 20 min × 3/week.

Trade-offs: weightlifting alone is insufficient — you must go aerobic. Break up sitting every hour (2-min moves).

S.H.A.R.P. Eating (Pillar: Nourish)

When to use: designing brain-healthy meals.

How: Slash sugar (+ ABCs of food) · Hydrate smartly (drink instead of eat) · Add omega-3s from food · Reduce portions (cook at home, smaller plates) · Plan ahead (avoid starving → junk).

Trade-offs: a style, not a rigid diet; moderation beats elimination of whole food groups.

The ABCs of Food

When to use: quick food triage at the store or on a menu.

How: A-list (regularly): leafy greens, berries, fish, healthy fats, nuts/seeds. B-list (include): beans, whole fruits, low-fat dairy, poultry, whole grains. C-list (limit): fried food, sweets, processed food, red meat, high-fat dairy, salt.

Memory Diagnosis: Encode → Store → Retrieve

When to use: figuring out why memory fails and where to fix it.

How: Encoding needs attention (stop multitasking); storage needs sleep + no alcohol for short→long transfer; retrieval is trainable. "Bad memory" for names is usually attention or retrieval, not systemic failure.

Analytical Meditation (Pillar: Relax)

When to use: solving a nagging problem; building focus; daily rest.

How: eyes closed, place the problem in a large clear bubble in front of you; rotate/flip it; let it disentangle from emotion until the answer illuminates. First 2 min are hardest, then flow.

Trade-offs: different from single-point meditation; better for problem-solvers/skeptics.

Deep Breathing / Relaxation Response

When to use: fast stress relief anywhere.

How: sit relaxed, inhale through nose filling the diaphragm, take in a bit more at the top, exhale slowly to a count of 20; ≥5 rounds. Triggers parasympathetic response, lowers cortisol.

Pomodoro Technique (productivity)

When to use: focused work, beating procrastination.

How: pick your most important task, 25 min no-distraction work, 5 min break (dopamine reward), repeat.

Don't Multitask — "Tackle Your Day Like a Surgeon"

When to use: any cognitively demanding work.

How: the brain only switches attention, it doesn't parallel-process. Single-task in focused sequences; guard mornings ("golden time") for creative work; avoid email first thing.

Marbles-and-Sand Planning

When to use: weekly/daily prioritization.

How: put the marbles (big commitments — exercise, sleep, key tasks) in the jar first; let sand (email, nonurgent items) fill gaps. Sunday-night check-in: "What must I accomplish this week to call it a success?"

The Triple Threat (Pillar: Connect)

When to use: combining social + physical + emotional benefit in one act.

How: take a walk + with a friend/neighbor + talk through what worries you. Add appropriate touch (hand-holding lowers cortisol).

Social Engagement + Challenge

When to use: maximizing the brain benefit of socializing.

How: socialize around a challenging shared activity (class, quilting, photography), not passive chit-chat; keep a large, cross-age network and ≥1 reliable confidante.

Cognitive Reserve Building (Pillar: Discover)

When to use: choosing genuinely brain-building activities.

How: pick complex + novel + effortful + ideally social learning you enjoy (language, instrument, real class). Avoid crosswords-only and hyped "brain games." Define your ikigai; seek flow.

Intermittent Fasting / Chrono Eating

When to use: reducing calories, boosting BDNF and insulin sensitivity (with doctor's OK).

How: gentle 12-hr overnight fast (stop 7–8 p.m., resume 9–10 a.m.); 16-hr version skips breakfast. Frontload calories: "breakfast like a king, dinner like a peasant."

Trade-offs: not for everyone (esp. diabetics — consult doctor).

Sleep Hygiene (Top 10 Secrets, Pillar: Relax)

When to use: fixing poor sleep.

How: fixed wake time; sleep before midnight; morning light; no caffeine after 2 p.m.; no food 3 hrs pre-bed; cool/dark/quiet (60–67°F); no screens/blue light; 30–60 min calming ritual; know the warning signs → sleep study.

Rule out Dementia Mimics

When to use: before accepting a dementia diagnosis.

How: evaluate NPH (treatable with shunt), medications (anticholinergics, opioids, benzos, steroids), and depression (pseudodementia). Tell the doctor every drug/supplement.

Post-Diagnosis Planning Checklist (caregivers)

When to use: immediately after a dementia diagnosis.

How: line up support/education programs, early-stage engagement, clinical trials, home safety, legal plan (will/trust/POA/advance directive), financial plan, and a care team. Communicate with family early to avoid conservatorship.

The Cardinal Caregiving Rule

When to use: interacting with someone who has dementia.

How: never correct them. Early phase: gently guide with questions. Later: don't deny their reality; redirect. Use music (longest-surviving faculty) and touch; break repetition with an activity. Put yourself on your own to-do list.

Never Split the Difference: Negotiating As If Your Life Depended On It

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Never Split the Difference

Decision rules (if → then → because)

  • If you're about to compromise → don't; hold out or walk → "No deal is better than a bad deal"; splitting = one black + one brown shoe.
  • If you want a "Yes" fast → ask a "No"-oriented question instead → pushing for "Yes" makes people defensive.
  • If you hear "You're right" / "I'll try" → keep going with calibrated "How" questions → no buy-in; nothing will get implemented.
  • If you hear "That's right" → you've reached a breakthrough; advance → they've embraced your framing as their own.
  • If they drop "Fair" on you ("We just want what's fair") → don't concede; say "I apologize — show me where I treated you unfairly" or mirror "Fair?" → it's a destabilizing move.
  • If you're attacked/insulted → pause, bite your tongue, ask a calibrated question → counterattacking triggers a showdown.
  • If you don't know market value → let them anchor first → their opening may beat your target.
  • If pushed to name a price first → cite a high number "someone else" charges, or a bolstering range → avoids over-anchoring yourself low.
  • If the deal seems done but only with the people on the call → ask "How does this affect the rest of your team?" → behind-the-table players kill more deals than table players make.
  • If the counterpart seems "crazy" → assume ill-informed, constrained, or hidden interest → and dig for the Black Swan.
  • If a deadline is pressuring you → remember it's usually imaginary and cuts both ways → revealing yours often gets a better deal.

Voice selection

ToneWhenEffect
Positive/playful (smile)defaultmental agility, collaboration
Late-night FM DJ (downward)selectively, to make a pointcalm authority, "I've got it covered"
Direct/assertiverarelytriggers pushback — avoid

The core verbal toolkit

ToolOpenerGoal
Mirror(repeat last 1–3 words)?elaborate, build rapport
Label"It seems like…"defuse/reinforce emotion
Calibrated Q"How…/What…"illusion of control, info
Summarylabel + paraphrasetrigger "That's right"
Accusation audit"You'll probably think I'm…"pre-empt negatives

"No" without the word (in order)

  1. "How am I supposed to do that?"
  2. "Your offer is very generous, I'm sorry, that just doesn't work for me."
  3. "I'm sorry, I just can't do that."
  4. "I'm sorry, no." → 5. "No."

Ackerman numbers (memorize)

65 → 85 → 95 → 100% of target · decreasing raises · non-round final number · + a token non-cash item at the limit.

Three leverage types

  • Positive — give/withhold what they want ("I want…").
  • Negative — make them suffer (use sparingly; label, don't shove).
  • Normative — use their own norms/beliefs; expose hypocrisy.

Negotiator types & their silence

TypeTime meansSilence meansApproach
Analystpreparationthinkingdata, warn early, give time
Accommodatorrelationshipangersociable + calibrated questions for action
Assertivemoney"talk more"let them be heard; mirrors, "that's right"

→ Black Swan rule: treat them as they need, not as you'd want.

Tells & smells

  • Lots of "I/me/my" → low decision power; "we/they/them" → the real decider.
  • More words + third-person pronouns → likely lying (Pinocchio Effect).
  • Tone/body ≠ words (7-38-55) → label the incongruence.
  • "You're right" / "I'll try" → not bought in.
  • Specific, escalating threats → real consequences approaching; vague threats → early stage.
  • Any response that isn't outright rejection → you have the edge.

Go-to calibrated questions

  • "What is the biggest challenge you face?"
  • "What are we trying to accomplish here?"
  • "How am I supposed to do that?"
  • "How will we know we're on track?" / "…if we're off track?"
  • "How on board are the people not on this call?"

One Sheet (prepare every time — ~7:1 ROI)

I high-end Goal · II Summary (→"That's right") · III 3–5 labels/accusation audit · IV 3–5 calibrated questions · V non-cash offers.

glossary.md

Glossary — Never Split the Difference

Accommodator — negotiator type who prizes the relationship and free-flowing exchange; friendly, win-win seeking; for them silence = anger (Ch 9).

Accusation Audit — listing every negative thing the counterpart could say about you, then voicing it first to "take the sting out" (Ch 3, Ch 6).

Ackerman Model — offer-counteroffer haggling system: target → 65% / 85% / 95% / 100%, non-round final number + a token non-cash item (Ch 9).

Active Listening — the foundation skill set: pauses, minimal encouragers, mirroring, labeling, paraphrasing, summarizing (Ch 2, Ch 5).

Amygdala — brain's fear center; labeling a fear shifts activity to rational areas and defuses it (Ch 3).

Analyst — methodical, data-driven negotiator type that hates surprises; silence = thinking (Ch 9).

Anchor (emotional) — setting low expectations via an accusation audit before an offer, to trigger loss aversion (Ch 6).

Anchor (extreme/price) — an aggressive first number that bends the counterpart's reference point (Ch 6, Ch 9).

Anchor-and-adjustment effect — tendency to extrapolate from the first number heard (Ch 6).

Assertive — direct, time-is-money negotiator type that must be heard first; silence = a chance to talk more; mirrors work well (Ch 9).

BATNA — Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement; critiqued for tricking negotiators into aiming low (Ch 1, Appendix).

Behavioral Change Stairway Model (BCSM) — five stages: active listening → empathy → rapport → influence → behavioral change (Ch 5).

Behind-the-table (Level II) players — parties not at the table who can kill or implement a deal (Ch 8, Appendix).

Black Swan — a hidden, game-changing piece of information (unknown unknown); ~3–5 exist per negotiation (Ch 10).

Bolstering range — citing a range whose low end is what you actually want (Ch 6).

Calibrated Question — open-ended "What"/"How" question with no fixed answer that directs the conversation while giving the illusion of control (Ch 1, Ch 7).

Certainty Effect — preferring sure things to better-odds gambles (Ch 6).

Chris Discount — using your own name to humanize yourself and gain concessions ("What's the Chris discount?") (Ch 8).

Cognitive Bias — unconscious, irrational mental processes distorting perception (Ch 1).

Counterfeit Yes — a "yes" meant to stall or escape, with no commitment (Ch 4, Ch 8).

Forced Empathy — asking for help (e.g. "How am I supposed to…?") so the counterpart engages with your problem via reciprocity (Ch 7, Ch 8).

FM DJ Voice — late-night, deep, slow, downward-inflecting voice conveying calm authority (Ch 2).

Fairness ("the F-word") — emotionally loaded term; used defensively, distractingly, or positively ("stop me if I'm being unfair") (Ch 6).

Illusion of Control — making the counterpart feel in charge while you frame the conversation (Ch 7).

Known knowns / known unknowns / unknown unknowns — info you have / gaps you're aware of / Black Swans (Ch 10).

Labeling — naming an emotion aloud ("It seems like…") to validate and defuse/reinforce it (Ch 3).

Leverage (Positive / Negative / Normative) — ability to give what they want / make them suffer / use their own norms against them (Ch 10).

Loss Aversion — acting more strongly to avoid a loss than to gain an equal amount (Ch 1, Ch 6, Ch 10).

Minimal Encouragers — short cues ("uh-huh," "I see") signaling full attention (Ch 5).

Mirroring (isopraxism) — repeating the last 1–3 words to prompt elaboration and build rapport (Ch 2).

Multi-step "No" — four soft ways to say no before the word, to get the counterpart bidding against themselves (Ch 8).

Neural resonance — brains aligning during good listening, enabling anticipation (Ch 3).

"No"-oriented question — a question inviting a "No" ("Is now a bad time?") to give safety/control (Ch 4).

Pinocchio Effect — liars use more words and more third-person pronouns (Ch 8).

Pivot to nonmonetary terms — offering items cheap to you but valuable to them (Ch 6, Ch 9).

Prospect Theory — Kahneman/Tversky theory of choice under risk (Ch 6).

Religion (knowing their) — the worldview/values that hold authority over the counterpart; where Black Swans live (Ch 10).

Rule of Three — getting agreement to the same thing three times to test genuine commitment (Ch 8).

Similarity Principle — we trust those we see as similar/in-group (Ch 10).

Strategic Umbrage — well-timed, controlled offense-taking to wake the counterpart to a problem (Ch 9).

Summary — paraphrasing + labeling; reflecting "the world according to them" to trigger "That's right" (Ch 5).

System 1 / System 2 — fast emotional mind / slow logical mind; System 1 steers System 2 (Ch 1).

Tactical Empathy — recognizing and vocalizing the counterpart's perspective and what's behind it, to influence (Ch 1, Ch 3).

"That's right" — the breakthrough phrase signaling genuine understanding and buy-in (better than "Yes") (Ch 5).

"You're right" — a brush-off signaling no buy-in; nothing changes (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Wants vs. Needs — aspirations vs. the bare minimum/survival floor (Ch 2).

Wimp-win — settling low to protect self-esteem, dressed up as "win-win" (Ch 9, Appendix).

7-38-55 Rule — 7% words, 38% tone, 55% body language (Mehrabian) (Ch 8).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Never Split the Difference

Mirroring

When to use: build rapport, keep them talking, buy time, disagree without being disagreeable.

How: repeat the last 1–3 (or critical) words with an inquisitive upward inflection → then stay silent. Sequence: FM DJ voice → "I'm sorry…" → mirror → silence (≥4s) → repeat.

Trade-offs: feels awkward at first; stepping on it with a follow-up question kills its power.

Labeling

When to use: defuse a negative emotion or reinforce a positive one; whenever the counterpart is tense.

How: detect the emotion, then "It seems like… / It sounds like… / It looks like…" (never "I…"), then go silent. If they reject it: "I didn't say that's what it was. I just said it seems like that."

Trade-offs: must be neutral; "I"-framing raises guard.

Accusation Audit

When to use: before a confrontation likely to surface accusations against you.

How: list the worst things they could say → convert to anticipatory labels → role-play pacing/pauses → voice them first in the meeting.

Trade-offs: feels self-loathing; said aloud, accusations sound exaggerated and the counterpart often denies them.

Triggering "No"

When to use: openings, stalls, unresponsive counterparts.

How: "Is now a bad time to talk?"; ask what they don't want; mislabel to provoke correction ("It seems like you want this project to fail"); the "No"-oriented email "Have you given up on this project?"

Trade-offs: counterintuitive; goes against the "be nice / get to yes" instinct.

Summary → "That's right"

When to use: break deadlock; confirm genuine buy-in.

How: paraphrase + label = summary. Reflect "the world according to them" fully enough that the only reply is "That's right." (If you get "You're right," you've failed — no buy-in.)

Trade-offs: requires real listening; slow but durable.

Calibrated "How"/"What" Questions

When to use: nudge without pushiness, gather info, defuse confrontation, force empathy, guarantee execution.

How: avoid closed verbs (can/is/are/do/does). Start with What/How (rarely Why). Go-tos: "What's the biggest challenge you face?", "How am I supposed to do that?", "What are we trying to accomplish here?", "How will we know we're on track?"

Trade-offs: useless without emotional self-control; "Why" is accusatory unless aimed to serve you.

Multi-step "No" (bidding against themselves)

When to use: bargaining, getting concessions without counteroffering.

How: (1) "How am I supposed to do that?" → (2) "Your offer is very generous, I'm sorry, that just doesn't work for me" → (3) "I'm sorry, I just can't do that" → (4) "I'm sorry, no" → (5) "No."

Trade-offs: best when the counterpart has no other buyer.

Emotional Anchoring + Loss Aversion

When to use: before delivering a lowball or unwelcome offer.

How: accusation audit to anchor expectations low ("you're going to think I'm a lousy businessman…"), then frame the offer as something they'll lose to someone else.

Trade-offs: manipulative if misused; pairs with empathy.

Anchoring, Ranges & Odd Numbers

When to use: price discussions.

How: usually let them anchor first (you lack market info). When you must speak, use a bolstering range (low end = your goal). Use precise non-round numbers ($37,263) for credibility. Surprise with an unrelated gift to trigger reciprocity.

Trade-offs: brace for an extreme anchor from a pro; never open if you don't know market value.

Ackerman Bargaining

When to use: brass-tacks haggling toward a target price.

How: target → first offer 65% → raises to 85%, 95%, 100% (decreasing increments) → empathy + many "No"s to make them counter before each raise → non-round final number → toss in a token non-cash item at the limit.

Trade-offs: mechanical but powerful; the diminishing raises make them feel they squeezed you dry.

Reading People (verify & detect)

When to use: testing commitment and honesty.

How: Rule of Three (agree 3× via varied tactics); 7-38-55 (watch tone/body vs. words, label incongruence); pronoun analysis (lots of "I" = low power; "we/they" = real decider); Pinocchio Effect (liars use more words / third-person).

Trade-offs: heuristics, not proof; confirm with follow-up.

Black Swan Hunting

When to use: high-stakes or stuck negotiations; whenever the counterpart seems "crazy."

How: get face time; mine unguarded moments (start/end of meetings, interruptions); understand their "religion"/worldview; use the similarity principle; diagnose "crazy" as ill-informed / constrained / hidden interests; deploy positive, negative (sparingly), and normative leverage.

Trade-offs: hard to find over email; threats (negative leverage) leave toxic residue.

Three Negotiator Types (the Black Swan rule: treat them as they need)

Analyst — prepared data, warn early, give silence/time; apologies have little value.

Accommodator — be sociable but use calibrated questions to convert talk into action; uncover hidden objections.

Assertive — let them be heard first; mirrors, labels, summaries; aim for "that's right."

The Negotiation One Sheet (preparation)

When to use: before any significant negotiation (≈7:1 return on time).

How: 5 sections — (I) optimistic high-end Goal; (II) Summary the counterpart will answer "That's right" to; (III) 3–5 labels / accusation audit; (IV) 3–5 calibrated questions (incl. behind-the-table & deal-killer questions); (V) non-cash offers.

Trade-offs: don't over-script; stay agile.

Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Changing World Order (Dalio's judgment, distilled)

Decision Rules (if X → do/expect Y, because Z)

  • If all three big cycles are in good phases → country is strong and rising; if all three are bad → weak and declining. (The 3: debt/money, internal order, external order.)
  • If a government has bankrupt finances AND big wealth gaps → treat civil war/revolution as the single most likely lead outcome — a broke government can't save the system.
  • If a country runs big deficits producing more debt than non-central-bank buyers will absorb → it's the Stage-5 trigger toward Stage 6 (must raise taxes/cut spending, or print heavily).
  • If debt is in your own currency → expect devaluation, not default (repay 50–70% in real terms). If in a currency you can't print → expect true default.
  • If real interest rates are deeply negative late in the debt cycle → don't hold cash/bonds; buy "any stuff" that keeps pace with inflation (the payback period is the longest ever).
  • If you see capital controls on a currency during a domestic debt problem → run from that currency.
  • If money/credit is being printed cheaply → own assets (asset value is the reciprocal of money's value; money's value is the reciprocal of its quantity).
  • If a rival's power ≈ yours AND differences are existential/irreconcilable → highest war risk; trade red lines to avoid it.
  • If your relative power is declining → fight/negotiate EARLY; if rising → LATER.
  • If you don't want to be in a civil war → get out late in Stage 5, while the doors (and capital) are still open.
  • If a great power cuts off a rival's ESSENTIAL imports (oil, chips, rare earths) → major escalation toward a shooting war.

Cycle Clocks (rough durations — read conditions, not the calendar)

CycleTypical length
Short-term debt ("business") cycle~8 years
Long-term debt cycle~50–75 years (6–10 short cycles)
Internal order cycle~100 years
Big Cycle of an empire~250 years (±150)
Bad destruction/restructuring period~10–20 years
Peaceful prosperous period~40–80 years
Left/right political swings~10 years

The 6 Internal-Order Stages → the leader each needs

StageConditionBest leader
1New order, consolidate powerConsolidator of power
2Build systems/bureaucracyCivil engineer
3Peace & prosperity (sweet spot)Inspirational visionary
4Excess / bubbleDisciplined restrainer (rare)
5Bad finances + conflictStrong peacemaker (ideal) or fighter
6Civil war / revolutionInspirational general

Stage-5 → Stage-6 Tells (watch these on any country, esp. the US)

Decadence · high bureaucracy blocking good decisions · populism & polarization (moderates vanish) · class warfare + scapegoating · loss of truth in media · rules disregarded · blood spilled = Stage 6 has begun.

The 4 Debt-Reduction Levers (order of use)

  1. Austerity (deflationary, brief) → 2. Defaults/restructurings (deflationary, painful) → 3. Transfers/taxes (political) → 4. Print & devalue (most expedient, most common).

The Rise Sequence (and it reverses in the same order)

Education → innovation/tech → competitiveness → output & trade share → military → financial center → reserve currency (last to rise, last to fall).

Reserve-Currency Reserves Snapshot (~2019)

USD 51% · EUR 20% · Gold 12% · JPY 6% · GBP 5% · CNY 2%. No attractive alternative to the dollar — but a currency devalues anyway as capital flees to gold/commodities/stocks/property.

Current Readings (as of the book, 2021)

  • US: ~70% (±10%) through its Big Cycle; internal order Stage 5; ~30% civil-war-dynamic odds in 10 yrs.
  • China: internal order Stage 3 (peace/prosperity); rising fast; roughly tied with US in trade/output/innovation.
  • US-China: in 4 of 5 wars (trade/tech/capital/geopolitical), not military; ~35% odds of a big war in 10 yrs; MAD holds it down.
  • Biggest long-run risk: currency-value-of-money (creditors' assets devalued below inflation), not debtor default.

Portfolio Rules of Thumb

  • Risk = failing to meet your needs (unmet-needs, ruin, confiscation) — not volatility.
  • All markets driven by: growth, inflation, risk premiums, discount rates.
  • Diversify so no environmental bias; tilt tactically. Beware survivorship bias (don't extrapolate US/UK only).
  • In war: sell debt, buy gold (printing devalues money/debt; credit isn't accepted).
  • Ask constantly: does the interest compensate for the devaluation risk?

One-Line Principles

  • "Peace is profitable and war is costly." · "Power rules; tests of power reveal who rules."
  • "All currencies devalue or die." · "Debt eats equity — but central banks feed debt by printing."
  • "Bet on evolution's upside, but not so much that a bump knocks you out."
  • "In war, the ability to withstand pain matters more than the ability to inflict it."
  • The best way to win a war: get strong and show it, so the opponent won't fight. "Deserve Victory!"

glossary.md

Glossary — Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order

Acts of Nature — Droughts, floods, pandemics; historically bigger killers than wars/depressions and a determinant of decline (Ch 2, 14).

Anti-capitalist phase — Decline-era backlash blaming capitalism, capitalists, and elites; drives redistribution and populism (Ch 1, 5).

Balance of Power Cycle — The timeless allies-and-enemies dynamic driving struggles for power, internal and external (Ch 2, 6).

Beautiful deleveraging — Creating enough money/devaluation to offset a deflationary depression without triggering an inflationary spiral (Ch 3).

Big Cycle — The self-reinforcing rise-and-decline arc of an empire (~250 yrs), composed of the three cycles + 18 determinants (Ch 1).

Big Five — The five most important forces: the 3 cycles + innovation/technology + acts of nature (Ch 2).

Bretton Woods (1944/45) — The post-WWII monetary system linking the dollar to gold and other currencies to the dollar; start of the current long-term debt cycle (Ch 3, 11).

Capital war — Conflict via sanctions, asset freezes, and blocking capital-market access ("no money = no power") (Ch 6, 13).

Classic Toxic Mix — Bad finances + large wealth/values gaps + a severe negative economic shock; ignites big internal conflict (Ch 5).

Culture is destiny — Cultural differences in how people believe they should treat each other matter enormously (Ch 2).

Debt eats equity — Debt is senior and must be paid first, forcing asset sales — "but central banks can feed debt by printing money" (Ch 3).

Decadence — Late-cycle shift of time/money from productive investment to luxury/consumption; reduces productivity, breeds resentment (Ch 5).

Determinant — A single causal factor (e.g., money supply); a cycle is a self-reinforcing chain of determinants (Ch 2).

Determinants (18) — The measurable + qualitative forces explaining rises/declines; 8 headline powers + inherited + human/cultural factors (Ch 2).

Eight measures of power — Education, competitiveness, innovation/technology, economic output, share of world trade, military, financial-center, reserve-currency status (Ch 1).

Evolution + cycles (the upward corkscrew) — Steady productivity uptrend with pendulum cycles around it (Ch 1).

Exorbitant/extraordinary privilege — A reserve-currency issuer's ability to borrow cheaply and abundantly — which sows the seeds of its decline (Ch 1, 3).

Fiat money (Type 3) — Money not linked to anything of intrinsic value; printable without restriction (Ch 3).

Financial economy vs. real economy — Two systems with separate supply/demand; central banks move money/credit to steer the real economy imperfectly (Ch 3).

Financial wealth — Promises to deliver money (cash, bonds, stocks); no intrinsic value — only what it buys is useful. Invented ~1350 in Italy (Ch 2, 7).

Guns and butter — A country must fund both military strength and domestic living standards without excess (Ch 6, 11).

Hard money (Type 1) — Money with intrinsic value (gold, silver, copper coins) (Ch 3).

Human capital / "self-sufficient plus" — People (or countries) who produce more than they spend; the most sustainable capital (Ch 2).

Inflationary depression — Monetary inflation (currency devaluation) coexisting with real-economy deflation (Ch 3).

Internal order cycle (6 stages) — New order → build systems → peace/prosperity → excess → bad finances/conflict → civil war → repeat (~100 yrs) (Ch 5).

Legalism — Chinese philosophy favoring autocratic conquest and strict obedience; Western equivalent = fascism (Ch 12).

Linked currency system (Type 2) — Paper notes convertible to hard money at a fixed rate (Ch 3).

Long-term debt cycle — ~50–75 yr arc across 6 stages ending in debt/monetary restructuring; contains 6–10 short-term (~8 yr) cycles (Ch 3).

Mandate of heaven — The Chinese conception of legitimate rule that persists while the dynasty's approach works (Ch 12).

Monetary Policy 1/2/3 (MP1/MP2/MP3) — MP1 = interest rates; MP2 = printing to buy assets (QE); MP3 = fiscal-monetary coordination (govt spends, central bank buys the debt) (Ch 4, 11).

Monetary systems (Type 1/2/3) — Hard money → paper claims on hard money → fiat; countries rotate 1→2→3 then back (Ch 3).

New world order — The system of power set by the winners after a big war (Westphalia 1648, Vienna 1815, Versailles 1919, 1945) (Ch 6, 8).

Populism — Anti-elite politics of ordinary people; of the left or right; a Stage-5 marker (Ch 5).

Prisoner's dilemma — Game-theory reason rivals attack first; peace requires mutually assured protections (Ch 2, 6).

Real wealth — Goods with intrinsic value (house, car) — distinct from financial wealth (Ch 2).

Reserve currency — A widely saved/traded currency; grants cheap borrowing; the last strength to fade in a decline (Ch 1, 3).

Resulting / survivorship bias — Judging by (limited, winner-only) samples; using US/UK returns as "representative" distorts perspective (Ch 7).

Run (on the bank) — More claims on hard currency than the bank can satisfy; forces default or devaluation (Ch 3, 4).

Short-term debt cycle — "The business cycle," ~8 years (Ch 3).

Systemically beneficial vs. destructive devaluation — Debt relief that flows into productivity (beneficial) vs. one that wrecks the credit system but wipes out debt (destructive) (Ch 4).

Three big cycles — Money/credit/debt; internal order/disorder; external order/disorder (Ch 2).

Win-win vs. lose-lose — Relationship types both parties choose; win-win (grow and divide the pie) beats fighting (Ch 2, 6).

World order — The prevailing system of power domestically and internationally; changes when leading powers change (Ch 1).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Changing World Order

Concrete, reusable methods from the book for diagnosing and acting on Big Cycle conditions.

Rate a Country on the 18 Determinants (1–10 Scorecard)

When to use: To gauge whether a country is likely to rise or decline on a relative basis.

How: Score the country 1–10 on each of the 8 headline powers (education, competitiveness, innovation/tech, output, trade share, military, financial center, reserve currency) plus the other determinants. Sum them. Higher total → higher probability of relative rise; lower → decline. The average reading, not any single one, defines the Big Cycle stage.

Trade-offs: Approximate, not precise; strengths are mutually reinforcing so they move together.

Locate the Internal-Order Stage (Disease-Diagnosis Method)

When to use: To assess civil-conflict risk and the right policy response.

How: Match symptoms to Stage 1–6 (new order → build → peace → excess → bad finances/conflict → civil war). Watch the Stage-5 markers: decadence, bureaucracy, populism/polarization, class warfare/scapegoating, loss of truth in media, rule-following fading into raw fighting. Stage 6 begins when people die in the fighting.

Trade-offs: Being in a stage doesn't make the next inevitable — but it sets the risk profile.

Red-Flag Count → Civil-War Probability

When to use: Quantifying internal-conflict risk.

How: Count economic red flags (high inequality, high debt/deficits, inflation, bad growth). 60–80% present → ~1-in-6 chance of severe internal conflict; >80% → ~1-in-3.

Trade-offs: Base rates from ~2,200 yrs of nine powers; probabilistic, not deterministic.

The Financial Safety-Margin Projection

When to use: Assessing any entity's (your own, a company's, a country's) true financial health.

How: Project income vs. expenses and assets vs. liabilities forward. Ask: if income disappeared and assets fell by half, how long would you last? Distinguish "looks rich" (high spending on borrowed money) from "is rich." For countries, check surplus/deficit, assets/liabilities, own-vs-foreign-currency debt, and who funds it.

The 4 Levers to Reduce Debt Burdens

When to use: Diagnosing how a debt crisis will be resolved.

How: Expect the progression — (1) austerity (deflationary, brief), (2) defaults/restructurings (deflationary, painful both sides), (3) transfers/taxes (politically hard, part of the mix), (4) print & devalue (most expedient, most common). Aim for a "beautiful deleveraging" (enough printing to offset deflation, not enough to spiral into inflation).

Read the Monetary System Type (1/2/3) and Its Transition

When to use: Judging currency/devaluation risk.

How: Identify Type 1 (hard money), 2 (paper claims on hard money), or 3 (fiat). Countries move 1→2→3 for printing flexibility under stress/war, then back to 1 after hyperinflation. Transitions happen under financial stress + military conflict and precede runs and devaluations.

Spot a Reserve-Currency Decline

When to use: Anticipating a currency's fall.

How: Watch for chronic devaluations, falling net central-bank reserves (often years ahead), suspended convertibility, claims-on-gold exceeding reserves, and a war/defeat with large debts. Reserve status lags all other strengths, then plunges "slowly then suddenly" once the interest rate can't offset the decline.

The Win-Win Point-Allocation Negotiation

When to use: Resolving conflicts (personal to geopolitical) without a lose-lose fight.

How: Each party ranks its top-10 wants, allocating 100 points. Identify and trade items that are low-priority for you but high for them (and vice versa). Know and respect each other's existential red lines. Winning = getting what's most important without losing what's most important.

Power Timing (When to Fight vs. Negotiate)

When to use: Deciding whether to press a conflict now or later.

How: Use power when it's greatest. Fight early if your relative power is declining; fight later if rising. Have power, respect power (don't fight a war you'll lose), use power wisely (soft power/generosity often beats bullying; hide the knife until needed).

Watch the Escalation Ladder of the 5 (+2) Wars

When to use: Tracking how a great-power rivalry could turn hot.

How: Trade → technology → capital → geopolitical wars typically precede military war by ~5–10 years. The escalation marker is cutting off essential imports (oil, tech, rare earths). Also add culture war (what each will die for) and the war with ourselves (internal strength). Identify each side's red lines and trip wires.

The "Dropped into 1900" Portfolio Stress Test

When to use: Testing an investment strategy against tail risk.

How: Simulate your strategy across every decade and many countries since 1900, not just US/UK since the 1950s. Because 7 of 10 great powers of 1900 saw wealth wiped out at least once, always hold protections against big adverse moves and against being wrong. Define risk as failing to meet your needs — not volatility.

The 4-Determinant Market Read

When to use: Connecting the world to the markets.

How: All markets are driven by growth, inflation, risk premiums, discount rates. Forecast how each will move (given fiscal/monetary policy) and balance assets as building blocks so the portfolio has no environmental bias, then tactically tilt. When money/credit is printed cheaply, assets rise — own them; ask always whether interest compensates for devaluation risk.

Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Radical Candor — Cheatsheet

The quadrant: where is your guidance landing?

Challenge Directly = NOChallenge Directly = YES
Care Personally = YESRuinous Empathy (most common mistake)RADICAL CANDOR (goal)
Care Personally = NOManipulative Insincerity (worst)Obnoxious Aggression (2nd best)

Decision rule: If you're withholding criticism to avoid discomfort → you're in Ruinous Empathy; just say it. If you're being harsh without showing care → add care, don't stop challenging. Prefer Obnoxious Aggression to silence, but aim top-right.

Tells you're in the wrong quadrant

  • You say "good job" with no specifics → Ruinous Empathy praise.
  • You're rehearsing how to soften it until you say nothing → Ruinous Empathy.
  • You're thinking "you're stupid/lazy/greedy" → Obnoxious Aggression / personalizing.
  • You reversed your position to be liked / avoid conflict → Manipulative Insincerity.
  • Nobody is ever mad at you → you're not challenging enough.
  • All praise, no criticism coming back at you → you're not soliciting well.

Order of operations (rollout sequence)

  1. Share your stories — explain Radical Candor in your own words; show vulnerability.
  2. Get criticism first — prove you can take it before dishing it out (go-to question + silence).
  3. Career conversations — start with longest-tenured reports (life story → dreams → 18-mo plan).
  4. Perfect 1:1s in parallel (report owns agenda; you listen).
  5. Give impromptu guidance — and gauge it.
  6. Assess — don't add more until guidance + relationships + 1:1s feel solid.
  7. Staff / big-debate / big-decision meetings.
  8. Encourage guidance between people; prevent backstabbing.
  9. Fight meeting proliferation; think time.
  10. Growth-management plans; reward rock stars.
  11. Peer gauging; walk around; skip-levels (if manager of managers).
  12. Radically Candid hiring, firing, promoting, reviews.

Giving guidance — HHIPP

Humble · Helpful · Immediate · In person · Praise in public / criticize in private · don't Personalize.

  • Say it in 2–3 minutes between meetings; don't save it for a 1:1/review.
  • Use SBI: Situation → Behavior → Impact.
  • Say "that's wrong," not "you're wrong." Never Reply-All criticism.
  • Worry more about praise (make it specific/sincere); for criticism, "just say it."

Rock star vs. superstar

Rock Star (gradual growth)Superstar (steep growth)
Wantsmastery, stabilitynew challenge, learning
Reward withrecognition, top ratings, guru/teaching roles, tenure honorsnew opportunities, stretch projects, mentors
Don'tpromote out of a loved roleblock or squash ambition

Both essential. No permanent labels — trajectories change with life.

When to fire (three questions)

  1. Have I given Radically Candid guidance, repeatedly, over time?
  2. Do I understand the impact on the rest of the team?
  3. Have I sought a second opinion?

→ Yes + no improvement = it's time. The 4 lies that delay it: "it'll get better," "somebody > nobody," "a transfer is the answer," "it's bad for morale." Firing rules: don't wait too long · don't decide alone · give a damn · follow up.

GSD wheel (drive results)

Listen → Clarify → Debate → Decide → Persuade → Execute → Learn. Don't skip a step; don't get stuck on one. You're usually not the decider — push it to whoever's closest to the facts; get facts, not recommendations.

Persuade = Aristotle

Pathos (the listener's emotions — most neglected) · Ethos (expertise + humility, "we" not "I") · Logos (show your work).

Meeting rhythm

MeetingPurposeRule
1:1listen/clarifyreport sets agenda; never cancel
Stafflearn (metrics) / listen (snippets) / clarify (name debates)no decisions here
Big Debatewrestlenot deciding; decide-by date
Big Decisiondecidedecider named; decision is final
All-Handspersuade + hear dissentQ&A > presentation
Think Timethinksacred; no one schedules over it

Emotion first-aid (in a 1:1)

Acknowledge ("I can see you're upset") · ask questions · don't add your guilt · tissues a walk away · closed water bottles at hand · walk, don't sit · forgive yourself and step out if needed. Never say "don't take it personally / don't be sad."

Core self-check (when lost)

"Am I showing I care personally?" and "Am I challenging each person directly?" If both yes, you're doing fine.

glossary.md

Glossary — Radical Candor

Abrasive Trap — Gender bias whereby women who challenge directly get penalized as "abrasive/shrill/bossy"; a small rating bias compounds into far fewer female leaders (Ch 6).

Absentee Management — Hands-off, ears-off, mouth-off: no curiosity, no goals, unaware of problems. One failure mode opposite micromanagement (Ch 7).

All-Hands Meeting — Company/team-wide meeting to persuade people of decisions and hear/address dissent via Q&A (e.g., Google TGIF, Apple Town Hall) (Ch 8).

Big Debate Meeting — Meeting reserved for debating major issues, explicitly not deciding; lowers tension and builds a debate culture (Ch 8).

Big Decision Meeting — Meeting to make (final) decisions, usually following a big debate; led by the appointed "decider" (Ch 8).

Care Personally — First dimension of Radical Candor: giving a damn about people as whole human beings, not just their work (Ch 1).

Career Conversations — Russ Laraway's three 45-min conversations (life story → dreams → 18-month plan) to understand motivation and help people grow (Ch 7).

Challenge Directly — Second dimension of Radical Candor: telling people clearly when work isn't good enough (and when it is); often the best way to show you care (Ch 1).

Collaboration Tax vs. Investment — When GSD steps drag, collaboration feels like a tax; run well, it's an investment. The boss absorbs much of the tax (Ch 4).

Fundamental Attribution Error — Explaining behavior by personality traits ("you're lazy") instead of situation/behavior; inaccurate and unfixable (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Free at Work — The state people reach when the boss relinquishes unilateral authority and builds trust, so they bring their best selves (Ch 5).

Get Stuff Done (GSD) Wheel — Seven-step results process: Listen → Clarify → Debate → Decide → Persuade → Execute → Learn (Ch 4).

"Get it right" vs. "be right" — Great bosses care about reaching the right answer, not being right; they insist people tell them when they're wrong (Ch 4).

Gauge (guidance) — Having your team tag where your guidance lands on the quadrant, since Radical Candor is measured at the listener's ear (Ch 6).

Growth Management — Reframing "talent management/potential" as helping each person move along the growth trajectory they want (Scott Forstall's "growth" not "potential") (Ch 3, Ch 7).

Growth Trajectory — Whether someone is in a steep (rapid-change) or gradual (stability/mastery) growth phase right now; not permanent (Ch 3).

HHIPP — Principles for giving impromptu guidance: Humble, Helpful, Immediate, In person (Praise in public, criticize in private), don't Personalize (Ch 6).

Kanban Board — To Do / In Progress / Done board (Toyota/Ohno) making workflows and bottlenecks visible; measures activities, not just results (Ch 8).

Left-Hand Column — Argyris/Schön exercise: write what you said (right) vs. what you thought (left) to surface arrogant snap judgments (Ch 6).

Listen, Challenge, Commit — Andy Grove's mantra: humility to listen, confidence to challenge, wisdom to stop arguing and get on board (Ch 6).

Loud Listening — Stating a strong point of view and insisting people challenge it back ("strong opinions, weakly held") — Steve Jobs's style (Ch 4).

Manipulative Insincerity — Worst quadrant: neither caring nor challenging; fake praise/criticism for advantage or ease (Ch 2).

Micromanagement — Hands-on, ears-off, mouth-on: tells "how" without understanding, gets lost in details, hoards information (Ch 7).

Obnoxious Aggression — Challenging without caring ("front-stabbing"); the second-best quadrant — at least people know where they stand (Ch 2).

Partnership — The management target: hands-on, ears-on, mouth-off — curious, listens, asks why, removes obstacles (Ch 7).

Pathos / Ethos / Logos — Aristotle's persuasion elements: the listener's emotion, credibility (expertise + humility), and logic ("show your work") (Ch 4).

Personalizing — Making guidance about character/essence instead of a specific behavior; corrodes accuracy and the relationship (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Platinum Rule — Do unto others as they would have done to them (figure out their comfort), vs. the Golden Rule's own-preference default (Ch 5).

Radical Candor — Caring personally and challenging directly at the same time; also the top-right quadrant (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Rock Star — Person on a gradual growth trajectory; solid, has mastered and loves the craft, doesn't want the next job; reward, don't promote out (Ch 3).

Ruinous Empathy — Caring without challenging; withholding criticism to avoid discomfort; responsible for most management mistakes (Ch 2).

Situation–Behavior–Impact (SBI) — Feedback technique: describe the situation, the behavior, and the impact — keeps guidance humble and specific (Ch 6).

Skip-Level Meeting — Annual meeting with your reports' reports (without those managers) to help managers improve; "not for attribution" (Ch 6).

Snippets — Short written weekly updates in a shared doc, read in a staff-meeting "study hall" to avoid interminable verbal updates (Ch 8).

Spelunking — A boss occasionally diving deep into details / going straight to the source of facts to stay grounded (Ch 4).

Superstar — Person on a steep growth trajectory; needs constant new challenge; the source of a team's growth (Ch 3).

Think Time — Sacred blocked calendar time to think that no one may schedule over (Ch 8).

Whoops the Monkey — Dan Woods's stuffed-animal ritual: people self-report mistakes at all-hands for automatic forgiveness and shared learning (with a "Killer Whale" for peer praise) (Ch 6).

Work-Life Integration — Reframing "work-life balance" (zero-sum) so work and life give each other a "double bounce" (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Radical Candor

Concrete, reusable techniques from the book, with when/how/trade-offs.

Solicit criticism with a go-to question

When: Building a guidance culture; you get too little criticism.

How: Ask "Is there anything I could do or stop doing that would make it easier to work with me?" Then embrace the discomfort — count to six of silence, don't fill it, don't reassure. Ask again if needed. Reward whatever you get; never critique the criticism.

Trade-offs: Feels awkward at first; requires you to genuinely act on what you hear or trust evaporates.

Situation–Behavior–Impact (SBI)

When: Giving any praise or criticism.

How: State the situation you saw, the behavior, and the impact. ("In this morning's meeting (S), the way you talked through the objection (B) was persuasive because it showed you'd heard the other side (I).")

Trade-offs: Requires you to have observed specifics — a reason to give guidance immediately, before details fade.

Left-hand column

When: A frustrating conversation where judgment leaked out.

How: Draw a line down a page; right = what you said, left = what you thought. Question the left column's assumptions.

Trade-offs: Reflective, not in-the-moment; best as prep or debrief.

Gauge your guidance

When: You want to know how your guidance actually lands.

How: Explain the quadrant to the team; have them tag your praise/criticism by quadrant (stickers, or the Candor Gauge app). Track over time.

Trade-offs: Stickers cause pile-on/anonymity issues; anonymous tags signal low trust you must rebuild.

Reward candor visibly

When: Someone gives you hard, valid criticism.

How: Make a visible change (Kim's "radical bander" rubber band others could snap when she interrupted). If you can't change fast, show effort; if you disagree, agree with something, check understanding, then explain why.

Trade-offs: Gimmicks lose novelty; the point is the signal, not the prop.

Career conversations (3 conversations)

When: First thing to roll out on a team; yearly per report, in 1:1 slots.

How: (1) Life story — "from kindergarten, tell me about your life," note motivators at moments of change; (2) Dreams — ask for 3–5 dreams incl. a "crazy-ass dream," map dreams × skills × competence; (3) 18-month plan — what to learn, from whom, how the role can change, with action items.

Trade-offs: ~2.25 hrs/person over 3–6 weeks; respect discomfort and don't press personal topics.

Growth-management plan

When: Annually, to balance the team.

How: Put names in the growth 2×2 boxes fast (≤20 min), get an outside/peer check for bias, write 3–5 bullets per person. Calibrate with peers; ensure fairness by level.

Trade-offs: Boxes are temporary snapshots — never permanent labels.

Hiring process

When: Any hire.

How: Hiring manager (not recruiter) writes the job description defining fit as rigorously as skills; use blind skills assessments; a consistent 4-person diverse committee incl. someone off-team; casual moments reveal fit; write feedback within 15 min; bias toward "no" — if not dying to hire, don't.

Trade-offs: Slower; the cost of a bad hire (and firing) is far higher.

Firing well

When: Repeated Radically Candid guidance hasn't produced improvement.

How: Don't wait too long; don't decide unilaterally (boss/peers/HR, get documents edited); give a damn (follow gut over rigid legal advice when it reduces harm); follow up ~a month later.

Trade-offs: Emotionally and legally hard; reframe as freeing the person ("the job sucks for them").

GSD wheel

When: Any significant team decision/initiative.

How: Listen → Clarify → Debate → Decide → Persuade → Execute → Learn. Ensure each step happens; don't skip or stall. Push decisions to the person closest to the facts; collect facts, not recommendations.

Trade-offs: Feels slow, but skipping steps costs more later; you needn't be in every step.

Two listening styles

When: You want everyone heard.

How: Quiet (silence, neutral face — reassure sometimes) or Loud (state strong opinions weakly held, insist people push back). Pick the one natural to you.

Trade-offs: Quiet → people guess your view; loud → intimidates the marginal, so build their confidence.

Persuade with pathos/ethos/logos

When: Bringing along people who weren't in the decision.

How: Address the listener's emotions, establish credibility (expertise + humility, "we" not "I"), and show your logic ("show your work").

Trade-offs: The neglected one is usually the listener's emotion.

1:1 meetings

When: Weekly (5 reports) → biweekly (10–20); never cancel.

How: Direct report sets the agenda; you listen and clarify (not dump criticism). Use follow-up questions ("Why?", "How can I help?", "What wakes you up at night?", "What are you working on that you don't want to?").

Trade-offs: 1:1 time is the natural bottleneck on how many reports you can have.

Staff meeting (learn/listen/clarify)

When: Weekly.

How: Review key metrics (~20 min) → silent study-hall snippets in a shared doc (~15 min, no side chatter) → identify (don't make) key decisions/debates (~30 min), assigning owners to separate big-debate/big-decision meetings.

Trade-offs: Not the place for debates/decisions — split those out.

Split debate and decision meetings

When: Team > ~20; contentious topics.

How: Big Debate = wrestle, no decision, set decide-by date, switch roles halfway. Big Decision = decider (appointed) makes final call. Both: egos at the door, notes shared, anyone may attend.

Trade-offs: Looks like meeting proliferation but actually reduces it via self-selection.

Kanban board / measure activities

When: Making work visible; ensuring fair recognition.

How: To Do / In Progress / Done with color-coded Post-its; measure activities not just results.

Trade-offs: Visibility itself reduces bias and routes help to bottlenecks.

Walk around

When: ~1 hr/week, esp. as a manager of managers.

How: Talk to people you haven't seen lately; find and sometimes fix small problems yourself.

Trade-offs: Office hours attract the same cranks; walking reaches the quiet ones.

Prevent backstabbing / clean escalation

When: One person wants to complain to you about another.

How: Refuse; insist they talk directly. If unresolved, host a live three-way conversation (not email) and help them find a workable solution.

Trade-offs: Adds occasional mediation meetings but prevents political blowups.

Skip-level meetings

When: Once a year per direct report (manager of managers).

How: Meet reports' reports without the manager; explain-show-explain; get consent; do it for everyone; not-for-attribution; take & project notes yourself; share with the manager within ~8 min; ensure 1–2 concrete changes.

Trade-offs: Energy-intensive; guard against proliferation and gripe sessions.

Peer guidance: "Whoops the Monkey"

When: Building peer-to-peer candor.

How: At all-hands, people self-report mistakes (auto-forgiveness, shared learning) via a stuffed monkey; peers award a "Killer Whale" for great work.

Trade-offs: Culturally specific — inappropriate where mistakes are safety-critical or the design ethos is formal.

Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Range — Decision Cheatsheet

Decision Tree: Is this a KIND or WICKED environment?

1. Do the same patterns recur reliably?        no -> WICKED
2. Are the rules stable, complete, and known?  no -> WICKED
3. Is feedback fast (within the decision)?     no -> WICKED
4. Is feedback accurate and unambiguous?       no -> WICKED  <- most decisive
   all four yes -> KIND

Then:

  • KIND → repetition builds real intuition. Specialize, drill, trust the veteran, trust your gut, automate.
  • WICKED → experience builds confidence faster than accuracy. Prefer breadth, outside views, explicit probability, aggressive belief updating. Distrust the confident veteran — including yourself.
  • MIXED / SHIFTING → the common case. Re-score whenever rules change; expertise built under old rules becomes cognitive entrenchment under new ones.

Core Decision Rules

  • When feedback is delayed or ambiguous, do not trust pattern-matching intuition — because the environment never taught you the pattern, only that you had one.
  • When you're early in anything, sample rather than commit — because match quality information is the scarce resource, and head-start advantages fade out.
  • When deciding whether to quit, ask "what have I learned about myself since I chose this?" — because informed switching beats persistence, and grit research was measured on already-selected populations (restriction of range).
  • When practice feels smooth and fast, you are probably learning less — because desirable difficulties depress in-session performance and raise retention.
  • When estimating a project, build a reference class first — because your case's vivid details are exactly what corrupts the estimate.
  • When specialists are stuck, broadcast outward — because winners come from the margins, and the answer may already be published in a literature they don't read.
  • When you can't win on frontier tech, win on application of withered tech — because reach and reliability beat specs in most markets.
  • When the situation stops matching your training, drop the tool, don't grip it harder — because overlearned routines are lethal once conditions change.
  • When a forecaster is famous and certain, discount them — because fame correlates inversely with accuracy (hedgehogs make better television).
  • When your culture feels perfectly aligned, add cross-pressure — because congruence suppresses the dissent that prevents catastrophe.

Specialize vs. Sample

SignalSpecialize nowKeep sampling
EnvironmentKind, stable rulesWicked or shifting
Skill ceilingAge-limited (elite sport, music virtuosity)No hard age ceiling
Self-knowledgeYou've tested the fit against alternativesFit untested or inherited
FeedbackFast and unambiguousDelayed or noisy
Cost of switchingRising steeplyStill low
Your evidence"I tried others; this fits""I never tried anything else"

Breadth vs. Depth

Depth (I-shaped)Breadth (foxes, T/π-shaped)
Wins atRepeating problems, tactics, executionNovel problems, strategy, transfer
Fails atRule changes, novel structureRoutine technical mastery
LearningBlocked practice, fast gainsInterleaving, slow gains, far transfer
Best useKind domains, near-term outputWicked domains, breakthroughs
IdealNot either — breadth plus at least one depth

Thresholds & Defaults Epstein Commits To

  • Default to delayed specialization. Early specialization is the exception, justified only by a kind environment with a hard age ceiling.
  • The sampling period is integral, not a delay. Late specializers catch up fast and match better; they trade a head start for fit.
  • Judge learning on delayed tests and novel problems, never on in-session fluency or current test scores.
  • Use multiple, distant analogies — one near analogy is worse than none.
  • Belief updating frequency is the single best predictor of forecast accuracy — more than intelligence or subject expertise.
  • Plan experiments, not plans. Short-term steps from present interests; revise on results.
  • Breakthroughs are high variance — judge the portfolio and the process, not any single attempt.
  • Don't feel behind. There is no universal timeline; comparison to the Tiger path is the error.

Tells & Smells

A wicked environment is masquerading as kind when: success stories are told retrospectively as if the path were plannable; confident experts disagree with each other; feedback arrives long after the decision, or only via outcomes you can't attribute; "best practice" is defined by what current elites do now.

Specialization is premature when: the choice was made before any alternative was tried; the credential was committed to before the fit was known; interests are described in inherited language ("I've always been a X person"); the main argument for staying is time already invested.

The match is bad when: you're optimizing to survive the role rather than to do it; persistence is motivated by sunk cost, identity, or others' expectations; the "grit" you're exercising is consistency of interests you never chose.

You're stuck in local search when: everyone consulted shares your training; the problem is stated in terms that presuppose the solution's form; confidentiality reflex blocks asking outsiders; the first familiar approach keeps recurring (Einstellung).

You're gripping a familiar tool when: you demand quantification for a concern that can't be quantified; you defend the process rather than the outcome; dissent went to an offline caucus and came back unanimous; silence is being read as consent.

glossary.md

Range — Glossary

Action at a distance — A force operating without contact; the deep-structure idea Kepler reached only by analogy from light and magnets. (Ch 5)

Active open-mindedness — Jonathan Baron's disposition of treating your own beliefs as hypotheses to be tested rather than treasures to be defended; the strongest correlate of forecasting accuracy. (Ch 10)

Altered gospel — The popularized, truncated version of grit research that drops its caveats and turns "don't quit" into universal advice. (Ch 6)

Ambiguous Sorting Task — A test where problems can be grouped by surface features or by deep structure; people trained across domains sort by deep structure. (Ch 5)

Bansho — Japanese teaching practice of arraying multiple student-generated solutions on the board for comparison, forcing making-connections work. (Ch 4)

Birds and frogs — Freeman Dyson's division: frogs delve into the mud of specific problems; birds survey broadly and connect. Both are needed; ecosystems fail when only frogs are funded. (Ch 9)

Blocked practice — Drilling one skill type repeatedly before moving on. Feels effective, produces fast gains and poor retention. (Ch 4)

Career streams — Viewing a career as a path of experiences and learning rather than a ladder of titles. (Ch 1)

Centaurs — Human-computer teams; in freestyle chess, amateurs with good process beat both grandmasters and standalone engines. (Ch 1)

Chunking — Perceiving meaningful recurring patterns as single units; the mechanism of expertise in kind domains, and useless when patterns don't recur. (Ch 1)

Cognitive entrenchment — Ryan Dane's term for expertise that becomes inflexible: the deeper the specialization, the harder it is to adapt when the environment changes. (Ch 1)

Conceptual Swiss Army knife — Broad, transferable reasoning tools (Fermi-izing, economics, statistics) usable on unfamiliar problems. (Ch 2)

Congruence / Incongruence — Congruence is cultural "fit" among an institution's values, goals, and norms; Epstein argues incongruence (deliberate internal cross-pressure) protects organizations from conformity failures. (Ch 11)

Consistency of interests — The Grit Scale subcomponent measuring how long you stick with the same goals; high scores can indicate a good match or an unexamined one. (Ch 6)

Context principle — Dark Horse Project finding that motivation and performance are situation-specific, not fixed traits. (Ch 7)

Dark Horse Project — Harvard study of unconventionally successful people; nearly all used short-term planning from present interests rather than long-term destination plans. (Ch 7)

Deliberate amateur — Arturo Casadevall's ideal: a trained expert who deliberately works at the edge of their competence, where naivety enables questions insiders won't ask. (Ch 12)

Deliberate practice — Ericsson's narrow construct: effortful repetition with immediate feedback on well-defined tasks. Valid in kind domains; overextended everywhere else. (Intro, Ch 3)

Desirable difficulties — Robert Bjork's term for obstacles that slow learning down and make it stick: spacing, testing, interleaving, generation. (Ch 4)

Dropping your familiar tools — Karl Weick's concept: under pressure, experts cling to overlearned routines even when those routines are killing them; survival requires letting them go. (Ch 11)
