Eduction — Raven's term for making meaning out of confusion — solving novel abstract problems without prior instruction. (Ch 2)

Einstellung effect — A fixed mental set: the first familiar approach that comes to mind blocks better alternatives. (Ch 8)

Empowering innovation — Technology that makes an existing capability available to far more people, rather than pushing the frontier for a few. (Ch 9)

End of history illusion — Quoidbach/Gilbert finding that people at every age know they've changed but predict they won't change further. (Ch 7)

Fadeout — The pattern where early head-start advantages evaporate, and sometimes reverse, over time. (Ch 4)

Far transfer — Applying knowledge to a genuinely novel context; the rare, valuable form of transfer that breadth enables. (Ch 4)

Fermi-izing — Decomposing an unanswerable question into estimable parts to get a defensible order-of-magnitude answer. (Ch 2)

Figlie del coro — The all-female musicians of Venice's ospedali, Europe's finest, trained by wide instrument sampling rather than early specialization. (Ch 3)

Flynn effect — The steady rise in abstract-reasoning IQ scores across the 20th century, reflecting modern "scientific spectacles." (Ch 2)

Foxes vs. Hedgehogs — Berlin's distinction, tested by Tetlock: hedgehogs know one big thing and forecast worse the more famous they are; foxes know many small things and forecast better. (Ch 10)

Functional fixedness — Seeing an object or idea only in terms of its conventional use. (Ch 9)

Generation effect — Struggling to produce an answer before being shown it produces far better retention than being given the answer. (Ch 4)

Good Judgment Project — Tetlock's forecasting tournament; superforecasters were broad, numerate, and above all frequent belief-updaters. (Ch 10)

Hypercorrection effect — The more confident you were in a wrong answer, the more durably you remember the correction. (Ch 4)

Interleaving — Mixing problem types within practice so the learner must first identify which strategy applies. Feels worse, transfers far better. (Ch 4)

Kind learning environment — Hogarth's term: patterns repeat, rules are clear, feedback is fast, accurate, and unambiguous. Chess, golf, firefighting. (Ch 1)

Knowledge as a double-edged sword — Expertise that supplies solutions also constrains which solutions get considered. (Ch 8)

Lateral thinking with withered technology — Gunpei Yokoi's doctrine: take cheap, mature, well-understood technology and deploy it in a radically new use, rather than competing on the frontier. (Ch 9)

Local search — Solving a problem by looking only in the domain where it arose; the default that outsider searches beat. (Ch 8)

Match quality — The degree of fit between a person's abilities and interests and the work they do. Epstein's central optimization target — it is found, not planned. (Ch 6, Ch 7)

Moravec's paradox — Machines excel at what humans find hard (calculation) and fail at what humans find easy (perception, judgment in open situations). (Ch 1)

Multi-armed bandit process — The formal explore/exploit trade-off; sampling widely early has informational value that justifies its short-term cost. (Ch 6)

Naturalistic decision making (NDM) — Klein's research program on expert intuition; valid where environments are kind. (Ch 1)

Network of enterprise — Howard Gruber's term for creative people running many loosely connected projects at once. (Ch 9)

Oculostenotic reflex — The cardiologist's impulse to stent a visible blockage because it's visible, regardless of whether it helps. (Ch 11)

Outside view — Kahneman/Tversky: estimating by finding structurally analogous cases (a reference class) rather than reasoning from your case's vivid details. (Ch 5)

Overlearned behavior — A routine practiced to automaticity; efficient in kind conditions, lethal when conditions change. (Ch 11)

Possible selves — The range of future identities you might become; discovered by trying, not introspection. (Ch 7)

Principle of limited sloppiness — Max Delbrück's rule: be sloppy enough that unexpected things can happen, not so sloppy you can't tell what happened. (Ch 12)

Process vs. outcome accountability — Being answerable for following procedure vs. for results; process accountability alone breeds conformity and suppresses dissent. (Ch 11)

Range — Breadth of experience, training, and perspective; the book's title virtue. (Intro)

Restriction of range — The statistical artifact where studying an already-selected population (e.g. West Point cadets) hides how much a trait actually varies. (Ch 6)

Sampling period — The early phase in which future elite performers try many activities, learn their own abilities and interests, then narrow. Integral, not a delay. (Intro, Ch 3)

Scientific spectacles — Luria's finding that modern schooling teaches people to classify abstractly rather than reason from concrete experience. (Ch 2)

Sensemaking — Weick's alternative to decision making: figuring out what situation you are actually in, especially when the familiar frame has broken. (Ch 11)

Serial innovators — Employees who repeatedly create breakthroughs; characteristically broad, high in "systems thinking," and poorly served by narrow hiring rubrics. (Ch 9)

Single-loop learning — Argyris: responding to feedback by refining the existing approach rather than questioning the goal or model. (Ch 1)

Superforecasters — Good Judgment Project's top performers; distinguished by granular probability estimates and aggressive belief updating. (Ch 10)

Surface analogy — A match based on visible similarity rather than causal structure; the failure mode of analogical reasoning. (Ch 5)

T-shaped / I-shaped / π-shaped — Breadth-plus-one-depth, single narrow depth, and breadth-plus-two-depths skill profiles. (Ch 9)

Test-and-learn (vs. plan-and-implement) — Choose a promising next step, try it, learn from the result, revise. The Dark Horse strategy. (Ch 7)

Undiscovered public knowledge — Don Swanson's insight that answers already exist in the literature, unlinked across specialties nobody reads together. (Ch 8)

Whole Candidate Score — West Point's admissions composite; predicted who got in, not who stayed. (Ch 6)

Wicked learning environment — Hogarth's term: rules are unclear or incomplete, patterns don't reliably repeat, feedback is delayed, inaccurate, or absent. Most of the modern world. (Ch 1)

Withered technology — Mature, cheap, thoroughly understood technology — the raw material of lateral innovation. (Ch 9, Ch 12)

patterns.md

Range — Patterns & Techniques

Diagnose the Learning Environment Before Choosing a Strategy

When to use: Before deciding whether to specialize, trust an expert, or trust your own intuition in any domain.

How: Score the domain on Hogarth's four criteria — (1) Do patterns repeat? (2) Are the rules stable and known? (3) Is feedback fast? (4) Is feedback accurate and unambiguous? Four yeses = kind; any no, especially on feedback, = wicked. In kind environments, repetition builds real intuition — specialize, drill, trust the expert. In wicked ones, experience can build confident wrongness — favor breadth, outside views, and explicit belief updating.

Trade-offs: Most real domains are mixed and shift over time. Re-score when the environment changes; expertise built in a formerly kind environment becomes a liability (cognitive entrenchment) when the rules move.

Run a Sampling Period

When to use: Early in any career, skill, or field — and again after any major change in circumstances or interests.

How: Deliberately try several adjacent activities at low commitment. Judge each on two axes: what you're good at, and what you actually want to keep doing. Keep the period lightly structured; the goal is information about yourself, not accumulated hours. Narrow only when a clear match emerges, and expect the eventual specialist phase to be shorter and steeper than a head start would have been.

Trade-offs: You lose early technical head start and will trail the precocious for a while. In genuinely kind domains with fixed early ceilings (elite gymnastics, chess prodigies), that cost is real. Everywhere else, fadeout means the head start wasn't worth much.

Optimize for Match Quality, Not Persistence

When to use: Any decision to stay in or leave a job, field, degree, or project.

How: Treat the choice as a multi-armed bandit — weigh the informational value of switching against the value of continuing. Ask "is this the best fit I know of, given what I have learned about myself since I chose it?" not "am I a quitter?" Enumerate quit conditions in advance, while calm, so the decision isn't made under sunk-cost pressure. Distinguish informed switching (you learned something that changed the calculus) from avoidance (you hit an expected difficulty).

Trade-offs: Switching resets accumulated domain capital and looks like flightiness on a résumé. The cost falls over time as you learn more about yourself, so switch earlier rather than agonizing longer.

Make Practice Deliberately Harder (Desirable Difficulties)

When to use: Any time you want durable learning and transfer rather than a good feeling during the session.

How: Stack four moves. Generation — attempt the answer before seeing it, even wrongly; being confidently wrong then corrected sticks best (hypercorrection). Spacing — leave enough gap that recall is effortful. Testing — retrieve rather than reread. Interleaving — mix problem types so you must first identify which strategy applies, instead of blocking one type at a time.

Trade-offs: Performance during practice drops and learners feel they're learning less — so learners, teachers, and managers all reliably prefer the worse method. Measure on delayed tests and novel problems, never on in-session fluency.

Take the Outside View

When to use: Estimating cost, duration, or success odds for a project — especially one that feels distinctive.

How: Ignore your case's specifics first. Strip it to its structural bones, build a reference class of superficially unrelated situations that share that deep structure, and take the base rate. Only then adjust for genuine particulars. Use multiple, distant analogies rather than one near one — a single surface analogy is worse than none.

Trade-offs: Feels dismissive of hard-won detail, and insiders will object that their case is different. That objection is the inside view talking.

Run an Outsider Search

When to use: A problem has resisted the specialists who own it, or progress has stalled inside a single domain.

How: Write the problem abstractly enough that a non-specialist can grasp it — strip jargon and stated assumptions about the solution's form. Broadcast it outside the field (the InnoCentive model). Expect winners from the margins of the field, whose home domain differs from the problem's. Look for undiscovered public knowledge: answers already published in a literature nobody reads alongside yours.

Trade-offs: Requires disclosing the problem, which cuts against confidentiality reflexes and insider status. Most outside submissions are useless; the value is in the tail.

Lateral Thinking with Withered Technology

When to use: You cannot win a frontier-technology arms race, or you want reach and reliability over specification.

How: Pick technology that is cheap, mature, and thoroughly understood. Invest the creativity in the application, not the components. Ask "what could this well-worn thing do that nobody has tried?" Be a producer who spans domains, not an engineer optimizing one.

Trade-offs: Reads as unambitious, and specialists will mock the specs. The reverse failure is real too — abandoning the doctrine for novel technology you don't fully understand.

Build Incongruence Into a Team or Organization

When to use: Designing a culture where conformity failures would be catastrophic, or diagnosing why dissent isn't surfacing.

How: Deliberately cross-pressure the culture — pair process accountability with outcome accountability, individualist norms with collective ones. Create channels that bypass hierarchy (Monday Notes-style: chain of command is not the chain of communication). Actively prospect for doubts rather than waiting for objections. Never require dissent to be quantified before it counts.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable, slower, and less "aligned." Strongly congruent cultures are easier to describe and feel better from inside — which is exactly the trap.

Practice Sensemaking Under Pressure

When to use: The situation has stopped matching your training and you feel the pull to execute the familiar routine harder.

How: Name that you are in an unfamiliar situation before choosing an action. Ask what kind of situation this is, not what the procedure says. Identify your overlearned tools — the credential, the model, the standard process — and ask explicitly which to drop. Hold hunches lightly and say them out loud even without data.

Trade-offs: Dropping familiar tools feels like abandoning competence and identity, and is hardest exactly when it matters most.

Protect Deliberate-Amateur Time

When to use: Sustaining creative output over a career; running a research or product group.

How: Reserve recurring unstructured time for work outside your specialty and outside your obligations (Friday night / Saturday morning experiments; dabble time). Deliberately work at the edge of your competence where you can still ask naive questions. Maintain a network of enterprise — several loosely connected projects — and porous boundaries with other fields, importing methods from one to another.

Trade-offs: Unfundable by proposal (you must say what you'll find before you look), invisible on short-term metrics, and mostly unproductive — breakthroughs are high variance, so judge the portfolio, not the session.

Reshuffle: Who Wins When AI Restacks the Knowledge Economy

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Reshuffle — Decision Cheatsheet

The one reframe

When you catch yourself asking "How smart is the AI?" or "What can we automate?", stop. Ask "What does this system look like once it adopts the machine's logic?" — because AI's economic impact comes from restructuring the system around a task, not from performing the task.

Diagnostic order (never invert)

  1. Has the playing field (system/ecosystem) changed?
  2. Has the basis of value creation moved?
  3. Does the business model still hold?
  4. What capabilities does the new game need?
  5. Which roles and workflows still matter?
  6. Only now — where does AI apply?

Starting at step 6 is the framing error. It produces motion, not direction.

Constraint router — where does my value come from?

Your value rests onAI's effectDo this
Scarcity (rare knowledge, gated access)Collapses fastest — expertise commoditizesExit; rebundle around risk or coordination
Risk (errors are costly, someone must be accountable)Grows — probabilistic outputs create accountability gapsOwn judgment, liability, and trust
Coordination (many misaligned moving parts)Grows most — AI extends coordination into new domainsOwn representation, decision, and execution

Is this task safe? — displacement test

  • Did it get cheaper? → economic displacement.
  • Did it stop mattering in the workflow? → contextual displacement.
  • Either one devalues the job. A task can feel meaningful (intrinsic value), still be done, and command nothing.
  • Typist effect tell: the task still exists but no one needs a person whose job is that task.

Reskilling: when it actually works

  • Works when the system still needs a human to execute that work.
  • Fails when the system has removed the need. Then only rebundling around the new constraint works.
  • Default: stop asking "what skill next?" and ask "where has friction moved?"

Tool vs. Engine

AI as a ToolAI as an Engine
RoleOptimizes tasks in the current modelDetermines core system performance
EffectCompetes better at the old gameChanges the rules of competition
Replaceable?YesNot without re-architecting

If your AI could be swapped out without redesigning the business, it's a tool — expect no durable advantage.

Am I becoming a wrapper? — the integration trap, 3 stages

  1. Tools commoditize execution.
  2. Tools absorb expertise.
  3. You reorganize around the engine → performance-based lock-in.

Tells: you dropped internal processes because they "just add complexity"; your performance gains now arrive from the vendor's release notes; customers can't name what's yours.

Move: keep a layer the engine can't see — proprietary field data, risk absorption, decision rights, integrated delivery.

How far to climb the solutioning stack

ModelPaid forRequires
Work-as-a-serviceOperational delivery (hours, cycles)Tool performance ownership
Results-as-a-serviceMeasurable results to specDomain depth + deeper integration
Outcomes-as-a-serviceCustomer-specific strategic outcomesEnd-to-end control, liability, monitoring

Rule: climb only as far as you can absorb the risk. Liability without visibility, integration, and execution control is a loss engine.

Consensus or interpretation?

  • Participants can be made to adopt shared standards → coordination with consensus (CCC model): auditable, enforceable, slow to spread.
  • Participants won't ever agree on formats → coordination without consensus (Tractable model): AI interprets each actor's native inputs; standards become implicit. This is the domain AI newly opens.
  • Tell that you need the latter: repeated failed attempts to get everyone onto one platform.

Control point checklist (all three, or you don't have one)

  • Unified representation — shared source of truth everyone acts on
  • Unified decision — you resolve the decision they'd otherwise negotiate
  • Unified execution — workflows integrated so the decision actually happens

UI simplification alone never earns the right to coordinate. Power comes from dependence, not dominance.

Where the control point sits

  • Customers stuck on a hard choice → demand-side control point (own the decision moment).
  • Partners can't align on delivery → supply-side control point (own the coordination anchor).

Four strategic postures — pick one out loud

PostureMoveAdvantage
Reactive optimizerSpeed up today's tasksNone that compounds
Anticipator ("Gretzky")Spot value migration earlyIncremental; still the old game
Logic shifter ("Curry")Change where/how decisions are madeStructural, within the industry
Field reshaper ("Tiger")Restructure the ecosystemMost durable; you set others' rules

Rule: the deeper the reimagining of coordination, the greater the power shift and the more enduring the advantage.

Three traps when the ground keeps shifting

  • Chase transient advantage → wins evaporate, never compound (Chegg).
  • Build executional agility → faster at solving the wrong problem (Yahoo).
  • Perpetual experimentation → motion without commitment.

All three optimize within the old system and tether you to it.

Smells

  • "We need an AI strategy." → You need a strategy for the conditions AI creates.
  • AI pilots proliferating with no system thesis → execution bias.
  • Outputs that look impressive but lack rigor → vibe coding.
  • Task-level speedups + rising cross-team friction → coordination paradox; you fragmented the org.
  • "Humans stay in the loop, so we're fine." → human-in-the-loop illusion; check who actually decides.
  • Everyone's output suddenly looks alike → collapse of differentiation; the skill premium is gone.

glossary.md

Glossary — Reshuffle (Sangeet Paul Choudary)

Terms as the author defines them. Chapter attribution in parentheses.

A

Above-the-Algorithm vs. Below-the-Algorithm — Above: workers who use or build algorithmic systems for leverage. Below: workers managed by them, with little autonomy or differentiation. (Ch 3)

Accessibility — How easy it is for a customer to adopt and pay for a solution. (Ch 9)

Agentic Execution — Autonomous goal-driven agents that monitor systems, detect intent, and act across workflows without human prompting. (Ch 6)

AI as a Tool vs. AI as an Engine — Tool: optimizes tasks inside the existing model; doesn't change the basis of competition. Engine: drives core system performance and defines how the business operates. (Ch 12)

AI as Coordination Infrastructure — AI's transformational role is not automation but extending coordination into previously uncoordinated domains by structuring ambiguity and translating tacit cues. (Ch 6)

AI-Native Firm — An organization designed from the ground up around AI in core workflows and knowledge distribution, unlike incumbents layering AI on old systems. (Ch 6)

Algorithmic Management — Using algorithms to allocate, supervise, and evaluate work; compresses wages, standardizes output, strips decision control from workers. (Ch 3)

Assistive Execution — AI-supported workflows where humans still decide; the bridge to agentic workflows. (Ch 6)

Autonomy-Coordination Trade-off — The assumption that more team autonomy means less alignment. AI dissolves the trade-off. (Ch 6)

B

Barcode-Native Architecture — An organization built to fully exploit a coordination technology's data (Walmart with barcodes), not merely to adopt it. (Ch 1)

Behavior Graph — Preferences inferred from observed actions; replaces the social graph in AI-native experiences (TikTok). (Ch 10, 12)

Building Block — A discrete, modular capability that can be rented, reused, and recombined into a larger system. (Ch 7)

Building Block Economy — An economy of rentable modular capabilities; success depends on how well you rebundle them and manage constraints between them. (Ch 7)

C

Clockspeed — The relative pace of innovation across parts of a value chain; AI tools evolve faster than the businesses adopting them. (Ch 8)

Cold Start Problem — Participants won't join until value is visible, but value needs participants. (Ch 11, 12)

Collapse of Differentiation — When AI makes everyone's output look alike, expertise stops commanding a premium. (Ch 4)

Composable Business — A business that assembles third-party capabilities rather than building them. (Ch 7)

Composition Power — Control over how components and actors plug into a system. (Ch 1)

Constraints — System bottlenecks limiting performance: scarcity-based, risk-based, or coordination-based. (Ch 5)

Constraint Management — Identifying and designing around system limits to secure consistent performance and defensibility. (Ch 9, 12)

Contextual Value — The value a role holds because it resolves a critical constraint in a specific system — not because the skill is rare. (Ch 5)

Control Point — A chokehold others must operate through to create or deliver value; power by indispensability, not ownership. (Ch 11, 12)

Coordination — Aligning independent agents toward a shared outcome under fragmentation, ambiguity, or misaligned incentives. (Ch 1)

Coordination Gap — The space between what algorithms can coordinate (codified workflows) and what economic activity actually requires (judgment, context, tacit knowledge). (Ch 1)

Coordination Paradox — Narrow local automation fragments the organization and raises, not lowers, coordination costs. (Ch 6)

Coordination Tax — The hidden, exponentially scaling cost of keeping teams aligned: meetings, messaging, searching, manual handoffs. (Ch 6)

Coordination Technology — Technology that aligns fragmented system parts — barcodes, containers, and now AI. (Ch 1)

Coordination Without Consensus — AI-enabled coordination where actors need no prior agreement on formats or rules; AI interprets diverse inputs into shared understanding. (Ch 11)

Curation — Elevating relevant signal from noise and shaping context and narrative; rises in value as information commoditizes. (Ch 5)

Curiosity — The disciplined ability to frame high-leverage questions; an economic asset when answers are cheap. (Ch 5)

D

Data Flywheel — More usage → more data → better system → more usage. (Ch 11)

Decision Friction — The cognitive burden or uncertainty that stops customers choosing confidently. (Ch 10)

Dependence vs. Dominance — Ecosystem control now comes from being depended on, not from ownership or lock-in. (Ch 11)

Demand-Side / Supply-Side Control Point — Power from controlling customer decisions vs. power from coordinating how participants deliver. (Ch 10, 11)

E

Economic Collapse of the Task — A task still gets done but no longer commands a premium because AI made it cheap. (Ch 2, 4)

Economic vs. Contextual Displacement — A task can become cheaper (economic) or lose importance in the workflow (contextual). Either devalues the job. (Ch 4)

Economic Visibility — Whether the system recognizes and rewards a role's contribution; contextual value must be made visible to be captured. (Ch 5)

Ecosystem Flywheel — AI coordination attracts participants → more data → better coordination → more participants. (Ch 11)

Engine — The component that determines system performance; not replaceable without re-architecting. (Ch 8)

Execution Bias — Acting fast because execution is cheap, at the expense of strategic intent. (Ch 12)

Exponential Systems — One coordination breakthrough (containers, APIs) triggers layers of new capabilities, restructuring industries rather than just speeding outputs. (Ch 1)

F–H

Framing Error — Solving a problem with an obsolete mental model while the underlying structure has changed. (Ch 2)

Governance Power — The ability to set and enforce rules of participation. (Ch 3, 11)

Human-in-the-Loop Illusion — Believing humans stay central by supervising AI, while in fact being reduced to support roles in systems that make the decisions. (Ch 3)

I–L

Intrinsic / Economic / Contextual Value — A task can be meaningful, paid for, or workflow-critical; these come apart. (Ch 4)

Judgment — Making accountable decisions under uncertainty; gains value as AI outputs turn probabilistic. (Ch 5)

Knowledge as Capital — Knowledge as a rentable, scalable, recombinable asset rather than labor. (Ch 4, 7)

Learning Loop — AI improves from use, so unlike barcodes it changes the system as it learns from it. (Ch 1)

Leverage — Amplifying output without proportional input, via rented capabilities, AI, and platform orchestration. (Ch 7)

Local Optimization, Systemic Fragility — Isolated improvements in one part increase misalignment with the rest. (Ch 8)

M–P

Modularity — Discrete interchangeable components combinable into larger systems. (Ch 7)

Narrative Control — Power to shape meaning and action through framing and curation. (Ch 3, 5)

Network Capital — Distributed audience reach that enables outsized impact without infrastructure. (Ch 5)

Ownership of Outcomes — Accepting liability, which demands representation (visibility), integration (decision-making), and execution (delivery). (Ch 9)

Performance Leverage — Leverage from owning a superior critical component (engine). (Ch 8)

Performance-Based Lock-In — Dependence created by superior component performance, not contracts. (Ch 8)

Pie-Slicing vs. Pie-Growing — Technology grows the pie but also reshapes who slices it; AI concentrates coordination power. (Ch 3)

Platform Tax — Fees or concessions an orchestrator extracts for access to decision moments or customers. (Ch 10)

Positive Constraint — A deliberately chosen boundary or design rule that improves coordination and creates differentiation, preserving judgment or diversity that pure speed would sacrifice. (Ch 9, 12)

R

Rebundling — Reassembling unbundled tasks and capabilities into new roles, workflows, organizations, or industry architectures around new constraints. (Ch 5, 6, 7)

Reliability — How consistently a solution performs in the field under real-world constraints. (Ch 9)

Reliability Leverage — Leverage from taking responsibility for consistent outcomes in unpredictable environments. (Ch 8, 9)

Representation Power — The power to define what is visible and measurable, and thus to set the frame for decisions. (Ch 3, 11)

Reskilling Fallacy — Believing new skills alone protect you when the system no longer needs human execution of the task. (Ch 4, 5)

Right to Coordinate — The earned ability to organize an ecosystem by removing friction in both decisions and execution; requires deep integration, not a nicer UI. (Ch 11)

Risk Absorption — Internalizing technical, financial, or operational failure risk so the customer doesn't bear it. (Ch 9)

S

Scarcity- / Risk- / Coordination-Based Constraints — The three constraint types that generate role value: limited access; high-consequence errors; misaligned moving parts. (Ch 5)

Showrooming — Customers explore in-store and buy online. (Ch 10)

Skill Premium — Extra income from a rare or difficult skill; shrinks when AI lets less-skilled workers match output. (Ch 4)

Skill-Biased Technological Change — The claim that technology rewards the highly skilled; breaks down when AI narrows the high/low performance gap. (Ch 4)

Solution — A complete offering delivering reliable outcomes by managing constraints, integrating complements, and absorbing risk. (Ch 8, 9)

Solution Bundle — Tools, services, financing, and guarantees that together make performance predictable. (Ch 9)

Standardization Risk — The more standardized and measurable the work, the easier for tools and insurers to absorb its performance and liability. (Ch 9)

System Builder — A firm that reengineers the system around a tool — financing, operations, integration, risk — not just the tool. (Ch 9)

System-Aware Adaptation — Tracking where constraints move as systems evolve and repositioning to solve new frictions, instead of chasing skills. (Ch 5)

System-Centric vs. Task-Centric View — Analyzing how technology reshapes the architecture of work systems vs. evaluating task-by-task substitution. (Ch 2)

T–W

Tacit Knowledge — Expertise in intuition and experience, hard to codify but essential under uncertainty. (Ch 5, 6)

Three-Circle Model — The task-level job nested inside the organizational system, nested inside the competitive ecosystem — AI reshapes all three. (Ch 2)

Tool Provider vs. Solution Provider — Supplies functional components vs. integrates and is accountable for outcomes. (Ch 8)

Typist Effect — Job obsolescence caused by system redesign rather than task automation: the task survives, the logic that justified the job does not. (Ch 2)

Unbundling — Breaking a job, product, or workflow into components once old constraints are removed; separates expertise from labor. (Ch 4)

Unified Representation / Decision / Execution — AI produces a shared view, aligned decisions, and coordinated follow-through across actors using different tools. (Ch 6, 11)

Vertical Encroachment — A tool provider moving into the solution layer and absorbing the customer experience. (Ch 8)

Vibe Coding — Karpathy's term for outputs that look impressive but lack rigor; symptom of performative execution. (Ch 12)

Wrapper — A solution provider reduced to an interface over someone else's engine: controls appearance, not substance. (Ch 8)

Work- / Results- / Outcomes-as-a-Service — Paid for operational delivery, for measurable results, or for customer-specific strategic outcomes — each step deepens integration and liability. (Ch 9)

patterns.md

Patterns — Reshuffle (Sangeet Paul Choudary)

System-First Diagnosis

When to use: Before any AI initiative, roadmap, or "AI strategy" request.

How: Work outside-in, not inside-out. (1) Has the competitive landscape changed? (2) Has the basis of value creation moved? (3) Does the business model still make sense? (4) What capabilities does the new game require? (5) Which roles and workflows still matter? Only then ask what AI should do. Never start from "what can we automate?"

Trade-offs: Slower to first visible win; leadership impatient for demos. But task-first programs produce motion without direction — Yahoo was agile in the wrong direction.

Three-Circle Analysis

When to use: Assessing exposure of a job, product, or firm to AI.

How: Analyze at three nested levels — the task-level job, the organizational system it sits in, the competitive ecosystem that system sits in. A task can survive at level 1 and still be eliminated at level 2 (typist effect) or level 3.

Trade-offs: Requires information about the ecosystem you may not own; but skipping it produces the framing error of defending tasks in a system that no longer needs the role.

Locate the Moving Constraint

When to use: Repositioning a role, team, or firm when AI erodes existing value.

How: Classify what your value currently rests on — scarcity-based (rare access/knowledge), risk-based (high-consequence errors), or coordination-based (aligning many moving parts). AI collapses scarcity fastest. Ask where friction has moved to in the new system, then rebundle capabilities around that new constraint. Re-run periodically: constraints move.

Trade-offs: You may have to abandon the skill that earned your reputation. Reskilling into an adjacent scarce skill is the trap this pattern replaces.

Unbundle-Then-Rebundle a Role

When to use: A job whose core task has been economically collapsed by AI.

How: (1) Decompose the role into tasks. (2) Mark each task by whether it lost economic value (cheap now) or contextual value (no longer matters in the workflow). (3) Identify the new constraint the workflow now has. (4) Assemble a new bundle of complements around that constraint. (5) Make the contribution economically visible so the system pays for it.

Trade-offs: Rebundled roles (RevOps manager, nurse navigator) often lack a title or budget line at first — visibility must be created, not assumed.

Audit the Coordination Tax

When to use: When local AI deployments are delivering task speedups without organizational gains.

How: Measure the friction between teams — meetings, status chasing, document search, rework from handoffs — not the time inside tasks. Then apply AI to the seams. Watch for the coordination paradox: automating locally while leaving seams manual makes fragmentation worse.

Trade-offs: Coordination cost is invisible in most metrics, so the business case is harder to build than a task-automation ROI case.

Unified Representation → Decision → Execution

When to use: Building coordination advantage across fragmented teams or ecosystem actors.

How: Layer 1 — build a shared, live representation (a digital twin / source of truth) all actors can align on. Layer 2 — use it to drive a unified decision the actors would otherwise negotiate over. Layer 3 — integrate workflows so the decision is executed reliably across tools. Own all three layers and you own the control point.

Trade-offs: Deep integration is slow and expensive; a UI layer is fast but earns no right to coordinate.

Coordination Without Consensus

When to use: Ecosystems too fragmented to ever agree on shared standards (construction, healthcare, multi-vendor supply chains) — exactly where consensus-based platforms have repeatedly failed.

How: Don't force participants onto a shared vocabulary. Let each keep its own tools and formats, and use AI to interpret unstructured inputs into structured, shared meaning. Standards become implicit (learned from data) rather than explicit (agreed in advance).

Trade-offs: Consensus models (CCC) are more auditable and defensible once established; interpretation models (Tractable) scale into new geographies and insurers without new integrations but depend on data volume and stay probabilistic.

Escape the Tool Integration Trap

When to use: Your differentiation increasingly comes from an AI engine you don't own.

How: Watch the three stages — tools commoditize execution, then absorb expertise, then become the gravitational center you reorganize around. Counter by keeping a proprietary layer the engine cannot see: field data, risk absorption, customer decision rights, or an integrated delivery system. Diversify engines before performance-based lock-in sets in.

Trade-offs: Refusing maximum engine performance costs short-term competitiveness. The alternative is becoming a wrapper.

Climb the Solutioning Stack

When to use: Deciding how much outcome liability to take on as a tool or solution provider.

How: Move deliberately along work-as-a-service (paid for operational delivery) → results-as-a-service (paid for measurable results) → outcomes-as-a-service (paid for customer-specific strategic outcomes). Each step requires more visibility (representation), more decision integration, and more execution control. Only climb as far as you can absorb the risk.

Trade-offs: Higher rungs earn more pricing power but demand liability, monitoring, and domain depth; climbing without them turns a margin story into a loss story.

Design for Indecision

When to use: Customers face abundant options and low confidence — where AI has made supply cheap and choice overwhelming.

How: Find the highest-friction decision in the customer journey, take responsibility for it, and rebundle the fragmented steps around it into a trusted path. Owning the decision moment is a demand-side control point; you can then charge a platform tax for access to it.

Trade-offs: Owning decisions means owning blame for bad ones; trust is slow to build and fast to lose.

Choose Your Strategic Posture Deliberately

When to use: Setting the ambition level of an AI program.

How: Name which of the four you are: reactive optimizer (speed up today's tasks), anticipator (spot value migration early but keep the old game), logic shifter (change where and how decisions get made), field reshaper (restructure the ecosystem itself). Deeper reimagining of coordination = more enduring advantage.

Trade-offs: Reshaping requires ecosystem access and patience; optimizing is safe, cheap, and non-compounding.

Set Positive Constraints

When to use: Designing an AI-native product or workflow where unbounded capability produces mush.

How: Choose a deliberate boundary that structures behavior and generates data — TikTok's 60-second limit forced fast signal for the behavior graph. Retire the constraint once it has done its job.

Trade-offs: Constraints look like self-imposed handicaps to competitors and internal stakeholders until the flywheel they enable becomes visible.

Say It Well: Find Your Voice, Speak Your Mind, Inspire Any Audience

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Say It Well (Decision Rules)

Time Budget (the 50–25–25 Rule)

  • Rule: Spend 50% thinking/researching/organizing, 25% writing, 25% editing + practicing — because prep, not podium performance, predicts a good talk.
DeadlineThink/organizeWriteEdit + practice
1 month2 weeks1 week1 week
1 week3 days2 days2 days
Tonight1 hour30 min30 min

Length & Word Count (~150 words/minute)

FormatTimeWords
Speech / keynote15-20 min2,250-3,000
Eulogy5-7 min750-1,050
Toast / public comment3-5 min450-750
  • When time is tight, cut: right before a meal (short), right after a meal (shorter), during a reception (shortest), audience standing/outdoors (short). Cut ~15% of any draft no matter what.

Audience-Size Rule

  • <30-40 people → don't give a big formal scripted speech; convert to notes/talking points and speak conversationally.

Structure Defaults

  • Every speech = Beginning (hook + unite + values) / Middle (heart + human language + cadence) / End (ask + hope).
  • Number and count your pages before you speak; carry the script even if memorized.

Opening — do / don't

  • Do: say hello, shout out the crowd, introduce yourself with authority, start a story in medias res, drop a shocking fact, greet in the local language.
  • Don't: open with a long acknowledgments list (Death by Acknowledgments); chase a "perfect line" before getting the story right; tell canned or inside jokes.
  • Acknowledgments: 5-6 names max, or weave them in later; deliver as a celebration.

Persuasion Rules

  • Frame in the audience's values, not yours (Values-Based Public Speaking). Match to moral foundations: Care, Fairness (progressive-leaning); Authority, Loyalty, Sanctity (conservative-leaning); Liberty (universal).
  • Statistics test: keep a number only if it (a) clarifies, (b) increases action, or (c) tells a story — else cut. Pathos beats logos.
  • To motivate giving/action: "look at the one" — one identifiable person beats mass statistics (psychic numbing).

Demagogue Smells (avoid / detect)

  • Otherizes ("us" vs. "them"), demonizes ("evil/sinister"), dehumanizes ("vermin/animals"), or brands opponents "virus/poison" to "eradicate."
  • Questions motives, attacks character, uses Polarization-Dictionary labels (idiots, liars, fascists, elites), or threatens/incites violence ("fight," "take back," "enemies to destroy").
  • Rule: attack the problem/ideas, not the people. Watch your buts ("no violence, but…" negates everything before).

Plain-Language Tells & Fixes (BBQ Rule)

  • Aim ~8th-grade level. Swap: utilize→use, leverage→harness, align→coordinate, incentivize→motivate, "paradigm shift"→change.
  • Talk people/outcomes, not programs/inputs. SWAP: cut perplexing acronyms ("if you have to explain it, don't say it").
  • Avoid negative contractions ("can't"→"cannot"), double negatives, legalese, and loftiness ("Let's" not "Let us," except solemn occasions).

Make-It-Sing Rules

  • Be unpredictable: if the audience can finish your sentence, it's a cliché — replace it.
  • Write like a script (left-margin sentences, blank lines) or a song (verse breaks) to build in breaths and pauses.
  • Vary sentence length; don't keep everything at a "ten" — aim some sixes/sevens.
  • Alliteration cap: ≤3 alliterative words per sentence; never sentence after sentence.
  • Rule of Three pleases the ear — but use four if you have four.

Truth Checklist (verify before delivery)

  • Circle every fact, figure, quote; verify against ≥2 reputable sources (primary sources, Britannica, FactCheck/PolitiFact, Pew, AP/Reuters; quotes via Bartlett's/QuoteInvestigator).
  • Face the elephant in the room early, not as an afterthought.
  • Quantifiers: "some" <50% · "most" >50% · "vast majority" ≥70% · "nearly/almost all" ≥90% · beware "many" (true but misleading).
  • Prefer most/often/rarely over all/always/never.

Ending Rules

  • Always end with hope — the finale is what they remember; ~80% of people are wired for optimism, and hope motivates better than fear.
  • Hope must be realistic (Stockdale Paradox: confront brutal facts) and action-bound (hope without deeds = false hope).
  • Fearmonger test: if the audience leaves more afraid/angry/vengeful/violent, you've gone dark.
  • Ending options: recap · best hopeful story · bookend · a question ("What will you do?") · vision realized.
  • Have a specific ask; list demands one by one. Close with four words: "Thank you very much."

Nerves & Delivery

  • Nerves are natural (fight/flight/freeze/appease) — the audience can't see them (illusion of transparency); you'll be better than you think (98% rated themselves better on video).
  • Reframe: say "I am excited" (not "I am calm"); box-breathe (4-4-4-4); play a hype song; "the more I sweat, the more I'll succeed."
  • Rehearse aloud; don't memorize; feel your fears (rehearse with heart pounding); do a dry run in the room.
  • At the podium: SMILE (write it atop the draft), eye contact person-to-person, ~150 wpm, lower voice to pull in / raise to stress / slow to emphasize / pause for effect, silence beats "ums."
  • Body language: don't overthink it (the 7-38-55 "93% nonverbal" claim is a myth). Two rules: relax; let body match words. What you say matters more than how you say it.

Print Format for Delivery

  • 24pt, bold, 1.5 spacing, each page ends on a period, bottom third left blank (chin stays up), binder + plastic sleeves outdoors.

AI / Chatbot Rules

  • Don't use bots to write personal remarks (collator = unoriginal; no humanity/voice).
  • Do use bots to: brainstorm topics/outlines, find surprising quotes (with sources), simplify jargon ("10 simpler words for ___"), and edit ("remove 50 words"). Verify facts — bots hallucinate.

glossary.md

Glossary — Say It Well

100% Situational Awareness — Knowing everything about the event and audience before you speak; "assume nothing, know everything, ask lots of questions" (Ch 4).

7-38-55 rule (myth) — The debunked claim that 93% of communication is nonverbal; the source study addressed only how listeners identify emotions (Ch 15).

Anaphora — Starting several successive sentences with the same word or phrase ("We, the people, still believe…") (Ch 10).

Absolutes — All/always/everyone/never; use sparingly because most issues aren't black and white (Ch 11).

BBQ Rule — If you wouldn't say it at a BBQ with family (including your 13-year-old niece), don't say it in a speech; use everyday words (Ch 9).

Blemishing effect — Sharing a little negative information can strengthen a positive overall impression (Ch 11).

Bookending — Opening with a story and saving its ending for the close of the speech (Ch 5, Ch 13).

Box breathing — Calming technique: inhale 4s, hold 4s, exhale 4s, hold 4s, repeat (Ch 15).

Cadence — The rhythmic flow, beat, and tempo of spoken words; the mark of writing for the ear (Ch 10).

Call to action / the Ask — The specific thing you want the audience to do; every good speech has one (Ch 12).

Collator (bots) — A chatbot's content is by design an unoriginal amalgamation of existing material (Ch 2).

Curse of Knowledge — Assuming your audience shares your knowledge and vocabulary (Ch 9).

Death by Acknowledgments — Opening with a long recited list of names/titles; one of the worst ways to start (Ch 5).

Demagogue — A speaker who villainizes whole groups by appealing to prejudice; otherizes, demonizes, dehumanizes (Ch 6).

The Download — Obama's pre-speech meeting to set purpose; also the recap section ending each chapter (Ch 1, Ch 4).

Earbashing — Australian term for too much talking; the sin every speaker should swear off (Ch 14).

Elephant in the room — A controversy/crisis; make it the main event early rather than hiding from it (Ch 11).

Emotional reappraisal — Relabeling identical physical arousal from "anxiety" to "excitement" ("I am excited") (Ch 15).

Emotions Wheel / Feelings Wheel — A tool of emotion words to convey precise feelings ("indignant" not just "angry") (Ch 8).

Ethos — Aristotle's element of rhetoric: persuading through your character/authority ("As a resident of 30 years…") (Ch 5).

Fired Up! Ready to Go! — Edith Childs's chant; example of ad-libbing to re-energize a flat crowd (Intro, Ch 15).

Fifty-Twenty-Five-Twenty-Five (50-25-25) Rule — 50% thinking/researching/organizing, 25% writing, 25% editing + practicing (Ch 4).

Find the Gold — Researching by sifting a ton of material for the interesting nuggets — quotes, details, stories (Ch 4).

Golden Rule of Public Speaking — Be yourself; speak in a way natural to you (Ch 3).

Happy talk — One-sided positivity that ignores the negatives; erodes credibility (Ch 11).

Hope-monger — Obama's reclaimed label for an optimistic speaker; be one (Ch 13).

Identifiable victim effect — Greater empathy for one specific person than for a large group or statistics (Ch 8).

Illusion of transparency — The audience usually can't see your nerves (Ch 14, Ch 15).

Illusory truth effect — The more we hear something, even if false, the more we believe it (Ch 11).

In medias res — Starting a story "in the midst of things," at the moment of maximum emotion (Ch 5).

Interoceptive exposure — Rehearsing while your heart is pounding to build tolerance to anxiety (Ch 14).

Look at the one — Motivate by telling the story of a single person rather than citing mass statistics (Ch 8).

Loosen it up — Turning tight, intense lines conversational so the speech can breathe (sixes and sevens, not all tens) (Ch 10).

Mellifluous words — Elegant, pleasant-sounding words used sparingly for surprise and memorability (Ch 10).

Moral empathy gap — Failing to appreciate that others hold a different moral worldview (Ch 7).

Moral foundations — Six value prisms: Care, Fairness, Authority, Loyalty, Sanctity, Liberty (Ch 7).

Moral framing — Presenting an argument in the value language of the person you're persuading (Ch 7).

Muscle memory — Ease and naturalness gained by saying the words many times in rehearsal (Ch 14).

Neural coupling — Alignment of speaker's and listeners' brain waves during a speech (Ch 3).

Omit needless words — Sorensen's "Fish" lesson; the core of editing (Ch 14).

Only You Test — If someone else could deliver your script and it still makes sense, it's generic — rewrite it (Ch 2).

Optimism bias — ~80% of people believe the future will be better than the present; "hardwired for hope" (Ch 13).

Pathos / logos / ethos — Aristotle's three elements: emotion, logic, character; pathos beats logos for moving people (Ch 8).

Polarization Dictionary — ~200 words used by the most partisan accounts; avoid them when persuading (Ch 6).

Power of You / We / What We Do — Three ways to evoke shared identity (Ch 6).

Power pose (caveat) — Popular claim its original author later called "flimsy"; use only if it helps you feel confident (Ch 15).

Psychic numbing — The larger the suffering, the more overwhelmed and less helpful people become (Ch 8).

Reps — Repeated practice under real conditions; Obama's word for what he lacked early on (Ch 1).

Rule of Three — Ideas/phrases in threes please the ear ("of the people, by the people, for the people") (Ch 10).

Sacred story — Everyone's essential personal narrative; listening to others' helps you find your own (Ch 1).

Science of Hope — Hope = goals + willpower + pathways; a leading predictor of success (Ch 13).

Speak for the ear — Writing so every word is clear to a listener who cannot re-read (Ch 3, Ch 10).

Stockdale Paradox — Keep faith you'll prevail and confront the brutal facts of current reality (Ch 13).

SWAP — Stop With Acronyms that Perplex (Ch 9).

Ten Commandments for Telling the Truth — Szuplat's checklist for honest speaking (Ch 11).

Ten Questions of Self-Knowledge — Written self-inventory to find your voice before your words (Ch 1).

Ten Words / North Star — Your core message boiled to one sentence, ten words or less (Ch 4).

Threat Dictionary — ~240 vivid words (attack, chaos, collapse, suffering…) that rally collective action (Ch 6).

Three Fs — Firsts, foods, fans — the things an audience is proud of (Ch 5).

Three-Act Structure — Beginning (setting/characters), Middle (problem), End (solution) (Ch 4).

Turning actions into identities — Fewer verbs, more nouns ("be a voter" beats "plan to vote") (Ch 6).

Uncle Dan — Szuplat's device: write for one real, specific person you want to reach (Ch 8).

Values-Based Public Speaking — Framing arguments in the audience's values, not your own (Ch 7).

Venn diagram of connection — Your best speech lives in the overlap between you and your audience (Ch 4).

Voice of Doubt — The inner narrator that makes us reject ourselves to preempt others' rejection (Ch 1).

patterns.md

Patterns — Concrete Techniques from Say It Well

The 50–25–25 Rule

When to use: Every presentation, from a keynote to a tonight-only toast.

How: Split prep into 50% thinking/researching/organizing, 25% writing, 25% editing + practicing. Scale to deadline (1 month = 2wk/1wk/1wk; 1 week = 3d/2d/2d; tonight = 1hr/30min/30min).

Trade-offs: Front-loads work before any words exist, which feels unproductive to anxious speakers — but it's the strongest predictor of a good talk and reduces nerves.

The Ten Questions (Self-Knowledge)

When to use: Before developing any talk; revisit as life changes.

How: Answer in writing — who am I, where from, working toward what, what's important, what values, what do I believe, why this work, my fears, my hopes, how is my life part of a larger uniting story.

Trade-offs: Introspective and slow; but without it you can't say what only you can say.

The Only You Test

When to use: After drafting, to check for generic content.

How: Imagine someone else delivering your script. If it still makes perfect sense, it's generic — rewrite around your unique stories.

Trade-offs: Personal material can feel exposing, but it's more memorable and less scary to deliver.

Ten Words / North Star

When to use: In the "Think It Out" phase, before writing.

How: Boil your message to one sentence, ten words or fewer; print it, keep it visible, ask "Am I on message?" Then find 3-4 (max 5) supporting points.

Trade-offs: Forces you to sacrifice secondary points for focus.

Scope It Out — 10 Questions / 100% Situational Awareness

When to use: As soon as you're asked to speak.

How: Ask who's the audience, what do we share, when/what/why is it, why me, where do I fit in the run of show, where is it, what's the staging, is there a podium, how long. Get name pronunciations and VIPs.

Trade-offs: Time up front; prevents surprises (e.g., attacking a plan whose author is in the front row).

Three-Act Structure

When to use: Structuring any speech.

How: Beginning (setting, characters, hook), Middle (the problem/argument), End (solution + hope). Add signposts ("First… Second… Finally…").

Trade-offs: Can feel formulaic; keeps a long, intimidating speech manageable.

Opening Menu (Have 'em at Hello)

When to use: Crafting your first words.

How: Choose from — say hello; shout out the home crowd; introduce yourself with authority (ethos); killer opening line; start with a story in medias res; invoke Scripture (audience-dependent); lift up the Three Fs; shock 'em with a fact; greet in the local language.

Trade-offs: Scripture/humor can misfire with the wrong audience — always know who you're addressing.

Weave the Acknowledgments

When to use: Whenever you'd otherwise open with a name list.

How: Keep to 5-6 names max, or move them later; deliver with feeling as a celebration so the crowd cheers along.

Trade-offs: Risk of omitting someone who expected a mention; brevity is worth it.

Add Humor (Not Jokes)

When to use: To warm an audience and reveal a shared connection.

How: Be self-deprecating, surprise them, crib a comedian's line (with credit), or pun. Aim for chuckles; give the humor a point.

Trade-offs: Inside jokes and canned jokes fall flat; humor without a point wastes time.

The Three Shareds (Be a Uniter)

When to use: Stating your purpose early in the talk.

How: Rally around a shared challenge (concrete, vivid, Threat-Dictionary language); evoke a shared identity (Power of You/We/What We Do); appeal to/challenge/defend a shared idea. Say what you believe.

Trade-offs: Requires resisting the easy path of attacking opponents.

Values-Based Public Speaking (Moral Framing)

When to use: Persuading across ideological or cultural difference.

How: Identify the audience's moral foundations (Care, Fairness, Authority, Loyalty, Sanctity, Liberty) and frame your argument in their value language (Kansas abortion vote framed as "freedom" and anti-government-interference).

Trade-offs: Requires setting aside your own preferred framing and truly understanding the other side.

Speak From the Heart / To Theirs

When to use: The middle, when making your case.

How: Feel it first; use emotional words (Emotions Wheel); get emotional; be vulnerable. Then speak to one person (your "Uncle Dan"), to their experience (empathy), and show a human face ("look at the one").

Trade-offs: Emotional exposure feels risky, especially for women and people of color who face bias — but audiences always want more emotion, not less.

Use Statistics Sparingly (Story Test)

When to use: Deciding whether a number belongs.

How: Keep a stat only if it clarifies, increases the chance of action, or tells a story; otherwise cut. Bundle stats into a narrative with a beginning/middle/end.

Trade-offs: Data feels authoritative but rarely persuades and can backfire (psychic numbing).

BBQ Rule + Get Real + SWAP

When to use: Editing for clarity.

How: Say only what you'd say at a family BBQ; talk about people and outcomes, not programs and inputs; cut perplexing acronyms; avoid negative contractions, double negatives, legalese, and loftiness.

Trade-offs: You lose the appearance of expertise/sophistication — which is the point.

Make It Sing

When to use: Polishing the language.

How: Be unpredictable (avoid finish-that-sentence clichés); swap in mellifluous words sparingly; write like a script (left-margin sentences, blank lines) or a song (verse-like line breaks) to build in breaths, pauses, and varied sentence length; use refrains/anaphora, the Rule of Three, and light alliteration; loosen tight lines.

Trade-offs: Overdone (alliteration avalanche, everything at a "ten") it reads contrived.

Ten Commandments for Telling the Truth

When to use: Fact-checking and framing before delivery.

How: Don't steal (credit sources), don't fabricate, get facts right, find the original source, be honest about the past, avoid happy talk, face the elephant early, use absolutes sparingly, don't fear nuance, speak hard truths. Verify via primary sources, Britannica, FactCheck/PolitiFact, Pew, wire services; quotes via Bartlett's/QuoteInvestigator.

Trade-offs: Nuance takes more words and can be "less effective" politically, but protects credibility.

Have an Ask, Every Time

When to use: The end of every talk.

How: Make one specific, small request; for change, list demands one by one. Reinforce with lead-by-example (deeds, money) and a big, catchy vision.

Trade-offs: Specificity commits you publicly; vagueness would be safer but useless.

End With Hope

When to use: The finale — always.

How: Recap main points, end with your most hopeful story, bookend, end with a question, or paint the vision realized. Keep hope realistic (confront brutal facts) and action-bound.

Trade-offs: Must avoid false/blind optimism; honesty about roadblocks is required.

Cut 15 Percent + Omit Needless Words

When to use: The editing 25%.

How: Cut roughly 15% of any draft; interrogate every paragraph, sentence, adjective, and word ("Is it truly necessary?"). Use a bot to "remove 50 words." Get honest feedback from several people.

Trade-offs: Painful to cut carefully crafted lines; the result is sharper every time.

Rehearse Like a Performer

When to use: The practice 25% and day-of.

How: Print in 24pt, bold, 1.5 spacing, each page ending on a period, bottom third blank; don't memorize; practice aloud to time and de-tangle words; do interoceptive exposure (rehearse with heart pounding); visualize success; do a dry run in the room.

Trade-offs: Generates many pages (use a binder); time-intensive but builds calming muscle memory.

Delivery Toolkit (Stand and Deliver)

When to use: At the podium.

How: Smile; make eye contact person to person; ~150 wpm; lower voice to pull in, raise to stress, slow to emphasize, pause for effect; two body-language rules (relax; let body match words); keep water at hand; don't apologize for stumbles; own tech fails with humor; end with "Thank you very much."

Trade-offs: Many cues to track — treat them as goals, not marks you must hit; being natural beats being perfect.

Channel Anxiety into Excitement

When to use: Final minutes before speaking.

How: Say "I am excited" (emotional reappraisal), box-breathe, play a hype song; remember nerves are your body preparing you and the audience can't see them.

Trade-offs: Doesn't eliminate nerves; reframes them productively.
