  • Michael Johnson: astrophysicist whose work contributed to the first black hole image.
  • Concepts: Burden-Side Rule, Meet Him at the What, Caregiver-Labeled Signal; the autism binary; "neurotypical" over "normal"; Euler's disk ritual with tape rolls; "exposing your kids is exposing your heart."

Key numbers: ten-minute timer; none quantitative beyond that.

So what: Spend time with users before deciding the data; check which side you're taxing; cheap general tools often win; the research problem is transfer, not discovery; language is part of design.

Ch 26. David and Goliath

Argument: When your dataset can never reach modern AI scale, tether your small precise data to someone else's giant dataset rather than manufacturing abundance.

Stories & evidence

  • Kristy Johnson's choice: audio over sensors (smartphone, cheap mic, COVID-proof, caregiver-labelable). Picard warned messy nonscientist-labeled data would hurt her on tenure committees and "the nonverbal population is almost all edge cases"; the path cost a year as a $55,000 postdoc.
  • Comalla: six labels, confidence ratings, about 6,500 files. ROSCO: 18 months of design; standardized schedule with buffering-wheel interruptions at 40 seconds; funded by Boston Children's Hospital.
  • Siddhant Bikram Shah: converted on a Zoom he kept out of politeness; after 300 experiments (roughly five working) abandoned N-CORE synthetic expansion for LibriSpeech transfer plus gradient reversal; voice transfer into a RAVDESS actor's voice; stick figures via Video-LLaMA3 with CLIP as tutor.
  • Isaac Bevers recoded the Comalla app in days using Claude.
  • 2019 zero-shot study on 13 hours of Felix's vocalizations: 70% laughter, 69% negative emotion, chance for the rest.
  • Bonini's paradox; memorization like "a dog that's taught to sit, and keeps sitting when you ask it to fetch."
  • Funding: Johnson oversees the language component of a $27.7 million Yale grant, plus $700,000 from NIH to add 90 participants. Felix still has no translation device.

Key numbers: 13 hours; 70%/69%; 6,500 files; 73,728 combinations (24 actors x 8 emotions x 2 statements = 384 samples crossed with 1,536 frustration samples); $27.7M; $700,000.

So what: Diagnose the bottleneck (data, not models); inherit rather than manufacture data; suppress unwanted features; standardize structure, personalize content; budget for the career cost of interdisciplinary work; edge populations need labs, not companies.

Ch 27. Epilogue

Argument: What separates working AI projects from failing ones is not technical sophistication but an ordinary desire to be useful: someone picked one thing that mattered, learned the technology well enough to bend it, and treated it as their own. AI has no direction of its own; it takes its cues from whoever shows up with intent.

Stories & evidence

  • The executive at mile fourteen: a to-do list of more data centers, researchers, energy and funding; "a book about AI is a weather forecast for last week." Tyrangiel concedes obsolescence but rejects speed as the defining characteristic of knowledge.
  • The cast: Sal Khan, Peggy Buffington, Debbie Kwon, Chris Nguyen, Deacon Maddox, Cliff Walls, Kristy Johnson: extraordinary less than ordinarily useful.
  • Four-Step Civic Protocol, the Empowerment Test (teacher vs. company eliminating teachers; doctor vs. insurer denying claims), and "Follow the Money Back to Yourself."
  • Allocation scandal: ingenuity poured into ads and trippy images, hard problems left to small teams.
  • Cautions: AI for tasks where being wrong is cheap; know the swap (data or attention); read policies or have AI summarize them at an eighth-grade level.

Key numbers: none central; the evidence is the cast.

So what: Pair a specific problem with a specific capability; build hands-on intuition; judge deployments by who they empower; treat refusal as a vote; direct money through taxes, purchases and votes.

Recurring Stories & Figures

  • Operation Warp Speed (Perna, Maddox, Bush, Jaffe, Tiberius): Ch 1, 14, 15, 16; the "God view" and the sponsor-operator-translator triad.
  • Palantir: Ch 1, 12, 15, 16, 17; vendor test, ontology, FASA lawsuit, Hospital 360.
  • Khan Academy / Khanmigo (Khan, DiCerbo, Shieh, Zubovic): Ch 2-7.
  • Cleveland Clinic (Mihaljevic, Chandra, Kwon and Nguyen, Boose, Pappas, Morrison and Tallman, Saria): Ch 8-13.
  • Epic: the closed electronic health record shaping what hospital AI can do (Ch 11, 12, 13).
  • The frozen middle and Gall's Law: Ch 16 (exceptional to ordinary), 17, 18, 20, 21.
  • Hallucination, fluency over truth and sycophancy: Ch 2, 3, 4, 22.
  • Human-in-the-loop as safety, trust and legal cover: Ch 11, 12, 13, 20.
  • Small, quiet pilots (Buffington, Walls, Werfel's five-degree turns) versus DOGE's loud provocation: Ch 5, 19, 20, 21.
  • Kristy Johnson and Felix: Ch 22 (setup), 23, 25, 26, 27; with Picard's third mode and the translation parallel in Ch 24.
  • Ownership over expertise: the Epilogue's through-line for the whole cast.

Chaos Monkeys: Obscene Fortune and Random Failure in Silicon Valley

2 markdown files

Quiz

Chaos Monkeys Quiz Book

Chaos Monkeys: Obscene Fortune and Random Failure in Silicon Valley by Antonio García Martínez

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a chapter section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative 10-question final exam is at the end. Chapter numbering follows the study notes (14 chapters grouped from the book's sections), not the book's own 46 sections. Figures are period data (2007-2016) as given in the notes.

Chapter 1: The Undertakers of Capitalism / The Human Attention Exchange (Prologue, Part One)

Q1 (SA). What does "price on perception" mean, and how does it link Goldman Sachs to ad tech?

A: A credit-default swap prices the perceived probability that a corporation won't pay; an ad prices the perceived value of a slice of attention. "The same difference either way; only the scale of the money pile changes." The same quant skills and price-making dynamics apply to both.

Q2 (MC). Why did Goldman decline to move CDS onto exchanges?

a) Regulators forbade it b) With few players, total information asymmetry and price-making power, transparency only invites competition c) The technology wasn't ready d) Clients preferred it

A: b. "Goldman felt more comfortable owning a small market than merely participating in a larger one," a pattern Martínez says he saw again at Facebook.

Q3 (SA). What was the SLK lesson?

A: Goldman's acquired broker went from hundreds of traders and two programmers (2000) to two traders and twenty quants with fast machines (2007). Generalized (via Andreessen): two future job types, people who tell computers what to do and people told by computers what to do. Finance saw it first; ad tech (RTB) followed, then Uber/Airbnb/Instacart.

Q4 (SA). Distinguish direct response from brand advertising.

A: Direct response has a short, trackable attention-to-action window. Brand has a long window, offline conversion, and huge budgets spent in "embarrassingly large broadsides."

Q5 (T/F). By 2011 Facebook's rich store of user data had already transformed its monetization. A: False. A year of ingesting posts, check-ins, Likes and friends barely moved monetization; advertiser first-party data (what you bought and browsed) outranks publisher demographics, which is the thesis the rest of the book proves.

Q6 (SA). What was the outcome of the April 13, 2012 Zuck meeting?

A: Three proposals were on the table: Like-button browsing data (Zuck: no) and two ways to join external data. The quoted result: "yes to retargeting, but no to using social plugins."

Q7 (SA). What advice does the DUI gambit illustrate?

A: Negotiate from weakness by reframing the encounter from judgment to haggling (he offered the officer a taxi under observation instead of a station blood test). "If you want to be a startup entrepreneur, get used to negotiating from positions of weakness."

Chapter 2: Knowing How to Swim / Abandoning the Shipwreck

Q1 (SA). List the four signs of a doomed startup.

A: (1) Only the founder survives (the Team page has been purged). (2) It makes lots of money from something other than the product. (3) No clients for the actual product (rotating beta-customer logos). (4) Loyal employees despite mistreatment (Stockholm-syndrome retention).

Q2 (MC). Under the miracle count, a startup idea that needs zero miracles is:

a) a startup b) a laundromat, not a startup c) a bad idea d) a unicorn

A: b. One miracle is a startup (Airbnb: user behavior; Google: technical; Uber/Instacart: consumer workflow; Slack: business workflow). Two or more is "the classic sign of a shitty startup idea."

Q3 (SA). How many miracles did the team's bar-code-to-local-ad idea need, and how does the book define a "pivot"?

A: Five. A pivot is not a ballerina's turn but "a panicked sprint" for the last life raft; their product ended as "Plan J."

Q4 (T/F). Y Combinator judges the idea first and the team second. A: False. YC judges the team and uses the idea only as a probe. Claiming "stealth" or demanding an NDA is a "LOSER" tattoo.

Q5 (SA). Why is Adchemy's roughly $6M/month of lead-gen revenue described as a sedative rather than a runway?

A: It was money from something other than the product; like a trust fund it made "a drug addict's spiral more long lasting" and masked the product's failure.

Q6 (SA). What does H-1B "peonage" mean in the chapter, and how did Adchemy use it?

A: Visa holders can't quit without risking deportation, giving employers retention leverage. Adchemy's immigrant executives threatened to report a former employee to ICE for planning to work on an F-2 ("former slaves turned slave owners").

Q7 (SA). What was the "wrong answer" when Paul Graham called with the YC acceptance, and what is the lesson?

A: "I should probably ask him first" (about the cofounder). Decide commitment among cofounders before the offer arrives.

Chapter 3: War Face / Like Marriage / Speed Is a Feature / D-Day

Q1 (SA). What does YC actually sell, according to the chapter?

A: (1) Access to partners, (2) the YC-founder network (a private microcosm where you can rebuild ~80% of the stack from YC companies, with discounts, preferential adoption and logos), (3) bankable prestige, (4) Demo Day.

Q2 (SA). How does Google's auction work, and what is ROAS?

A: An auction on every query: bid x estimated click probability, highest product wins. ROAS = revenue / cost - 1, the universal marketer metric (the "nevada cheap divorce" example: 47%).

Q3 (MC). Why did Clickable, Lexity and Trada fail?

a) Bad engineering b) They tried the small-business last mile, where high-touch sales at $50-100/month can't scale and SMBs cancel as fast as they join c) Google sued them d) No demand for search ads

A: b. "Not every problem has an engineering solution. That doesn't mean you can't sell one."

Q4 (SA). What does "Have a leader" mean, and what went wrong with equal thirds?

A: Either a "Vulcan mind-meld" forged by shared hard experience or one person with 51%+; the only early title that matters is CEO. Equal thirds produced decision paralysis and rotating two-against-one factions. About six of thirty batch companies had disputed leadership and crumbled or had coups.

Q5 (SA). Describe the content-marketing launch recipe.

A: Pick the biggest nerve (New York's self-regard, then Goldman Sachs); post Tuesday morning (Monday too groggy, Thursday drifting, Friday for burying news); seed upvotes on Hacker News; reply to fans, egg on trolls; double down when it works; have servers ready (the single-server blog melted).

Q6 (T/F). In the book, "chaos monkey" originally refers to a tool that randomly kills servers to test resilience, and is used metaphorically for entrepreneurs who pull the plug on industries. A: True (Netflix's tool; Uber vs. medallions, Airbnb vs. hotels, Tinder vs. dating).

Q7 (SA). What lesson did Rapportive teach about comparing yourself to peers?

A: "This too shall pass." Its polished Prototype Day pitch dismayed him, but two years later both companies had the same acqui-hire exit.

Chapter 4: Conclave of Angels / Hill of Sand / Widening Gyre / ¡No Pasarán!

Q1 (SA). Contrast the old-school angel (Russ Siegelman) with the micro-VC (Chris Sacca).

A: Russ invests his own money, wants 2-4x, wants it back if you're imploding, does haphazard diligence through friends. Sacca runs a $20-40M fund ("a fund of bosses"), needs outsized wins, and supplies a gold-plated name that makes weak-kneed investors follow.

Q2 (SA). A $100K note has a $3M cap and the Series A prices at $10M. What does the angel own?

A: About 3.3%, regardless of the A's price. Without a cap, the angel's stake would shrink as the company does better (1% at a $10M A, 0.1% at $100M).

Q3 (MC). The best test to cut through VC titles is to ask:

a) "What is your fund size?" b) "Do you have decision-making power?" c) "Who else is investing?" d) "What is your carry?"

A: b. Any hedge means a lackey; route around them. What matters is carry and whether the person can present and defend a deal at the Monday partner meeting.

Q4 (SA). What was the Death Clock, and what did the author do with it?

A: A cash-burn spreadsheet with legal costs (Fenwick's estimate: ~$500K to reach trial, ~$1.5M total over 18 months, ~$20K/month); every version crashed. He hid it from cofounders and investors and "cooked the books" (lower legal costs, impossible launch date, "unconscionable" growth rate).

Q5 (SA). Explain the Fenwick deal as a "mispriced option."

A: Fenwick fronted $250K of fees as a loan for a small equity slice plus options. If AdGrok died, nothing was repaid; if it won, it could buy the equity back at the seed price with no prepayment penalty: "a one-in-a-million lottery ticket to win $250,000... for $250,000."

Q6 (T/F). After the lawsuit, Russ stayed in but cut the cap from $4M to $2M. A: True. About 22% was sold in the seed for ~$500K, roughly double typical seed dilution, accepted because the alternative was death.

Q7 (SA). What are "forgotten crimes"?

A: Balzac: "The secret of great fortunes without apparent cause is a forgotten crime." Examples: Gates cloned Kildall's QDOS and kept the copyright; Jobs pocketed the Atari bonus and paid Wozniak $350; Zuckerberg ran with the idea he was hired to build.

Chapter 5: Dog Shit Sandwich / Victory / Launching!

Q1 (SA). What are the two weak points of any tech company, and why?

A: Investors (board votes and personal sway; a CEO serves at the board's pleasure) and potential business partners (enterprise deals are lifeblood and even large companies fear public shaming and legal quagmires).

Q2 (SA). How was Adchemy's lawsuit actually defeated?

A: Paul Graham planned to anathematize Adchemy's VCs (August, Mayfield) by disinviting them from Demo Day; Sam Altman got Microsoft's BD to tell Adchemy the litigation was "problematic" for a Bing deal; the lawyers filed rebuttals and started hostile depositions. Adchemy offered to dismiss in late October; settled February 2011.

Q3 (MC). PG's instruction on handling the crisis inside the company was:

a) Tell the team everything b) "Come alone... keep them out of it" c) Hire more lawyers d) Go public with it

A: b. The team adds no value and loses productivity if the crisis becomes the internal narrative.

Q4 (SA). What two traits do founders actually need?

A: Monomaniacal focus on one thing at the expense of all else, and endurance of endless shit (learnable via hardship: cross the US by bicycle, sail an ocean, or join the Marines). Intelligence, technical skill and vision are not the scarce inputs. "It helps to have enemies."

Q5 (T/F). The Trough of Despair is a dip in the middle of fund-raising. A: False. It is the post-launch curve (spike, crash, long flatline, slight rise) that kills 90%+ of startups that survived founder fights, shipping and fund-raising.

Q6 (SA). How does the chapter define product-market fit?

A: Iterating from an approximately correct starting point, each iteration costing wages, servers and time, with a hard deadline when cash hits zero; fit means users pay more than they cost to serve and acquire.

Q7 (T/F). The tech press covers launches, so a launch spike is a reliable signal of success. A: False. A "launch" is a PR event (embargoed, timed Monday); the anti-pattern is "believing the launch spike."

Chapter 6: Dates @Twitter / Acquisition Chicken / Getting Liked / Getting Poked

Q1 (SA). What does "know them better than their mothers do" prescribe?

A: A Facebook-Twitter-LinkedIn stalk before any meeting: read CV tenure (<1 year = didn't vest; exactly 4 years = a plodder), mutual connections, where they eat, origin. "Know what they want... and you can predict 90 percent of what they eventually do."

Q2 (SA). What are the two channels in a deal, and what does email signal?

A: A formal channel (email, documents) and a clandestine one (phone, in person; the "dragoman" layer). "If you're still emailing about it, there's actually nothing real going on."

Q3 (MC). The right time to create an auction is:

a) After the no-shop is signed b) Before the no-shop lands (typically 60 days, enforceable) c) After the term sheet closes d) Never

A: b. "In play" was the phrase used to get a rival's product team to engage.

Q4 (SA). Why did the Google bluff work at Facebook?

A: Corp-dev chief Amin Zoufonoun, three days out of Google, had no back channel there to verify; "everybody in tech feared Google." A bluff works when the target can't check it.

Q5 (SA). Why do angels and fund-manager VCs differ on a good-enough offer?

A: Angels investing their own money (Russ) take 2x happily; fund managers (Sacca) need outsized multiples because funds are fire-and-forget, so VCs push you to swing for the fences. Use the VC as the cudgel when you want to reject a low offer.

Q6 (SA). How are acqui-hires priced and how should you approach the interview day?

A: Valley engineers fetched $0.5-2M each in four-year vesting equity; Twitter's "$5 million thing" for three hires was "way too cheap." Every wanted employee passes the standard hiring screen; the bundle is your union ("don't like the price, we're all off the table"). Get the interviewer list a day early and stalk each one.

Q7 (T/F). "Cultural fit" is a reliable measure of whether someone will succeed. A: False. The notes call it a license that in practice excludes the happy-hour buzzkill, the quiet Indian or Chinese engineer, and the self-taught kid from a no-name college.

Chapter 7: Forking Paths / Retweets / The Dotted Line / Endgame

Q1 (SA). What did Facebook want from AdGrok, and what did Twitter do after the walkout?

A: Facebook rejected the engineers but wanted the CEO. Twitter, expected to go silent, called back within an hour with $5M+ for the two engineers.

Q2 (SA). What does a fast callback reveal, and what is a "call station"?

A: A weak hand. Twitter should have gone silent for days and bought AdGrok "for a twenty-dollar Starbucks gift card"; instead its reflex was to call back above the original price.

Q3 (MC). In an acqui-hire, the acquirer is:

a) Careful to preserve the investors' pro rata b) Targeting a price per high-value person and indifferent to the founder/investor split c) Paying for the product d) Paying mostly cash

A: b. The headline "sold for $X million" may be ~10% company price and 90% signing bonuses and vesting; Twitter's default gave investors ~$1M of ~$10M instead of ~$2M pro rata.

Q4 (SA). What is a "replicating portfolio" and how was it used?

A: Demanding that the new employer match your slice of the other deal. Facebook's offer at ~$32/share pre-IPO came to ~$2.3M, about a 25% AdGrok stake after the split.

Q5 (T/F). Founders own their equity from day one, so they can walk away mid-deal. A: False. Founders' 20-40% stakes vest like employees' so a departing founder can't hold a gun to the company; "nobody at AdGrok actually owned anything."

Q6 (SA). What does "resign before you sign" mean?

A: Per the employment lawyer: accept immediately and resign first, or breach both noncompetes. He sent the resignation email as corp dev opened the door (the 3:07 Caltrain).

Q7 (SA). What was the "master play" he did not make, and why?

A: Negotiate both deals in secret, front-load Twitter with single-trigger acceleration or up-front cash, accept, quit day one, and walk to Facebook. It required deceiving cofounders, "a step too far out on the prick spectrum." His rule: lie to investors and acquirers if you must; deceiving cofounders is the line.

Chapter 8: Boot Camp / Product Masseur / Google Delenda Est / Leaping Headlong

Q1 (SA). How does the chapter describe Facebook's onboarding?

A: As a citizenship oath ("Ellis Island"): shed your prior culture; truth, selfless collaboration, ownership; posters (MAKE AN IMPACT, DONE IS BETTER THAN PERFECT, FORTUNE FAVORS THE BOLD); the blue T-shirt. "Think of onboarding as conversion, not orientation."

Q2 (SA). What is the PM as "shit umbrella / pirate captain"?

A: Internally, the PM does everything but coding (legal, sales pitches, horse-trading, fronting for management) and is "golden" only if engineers build what they stipulate; externally, a two-line email summons any company's leadership, and the craven mistake Facebook's power for the PM's own.

Q3 (MC). What was the "monetization = data per pixel" insight about 2011 Facebook?

a) Its CPMs were the highest in the industry b) The revenue dashboard's average CPM was bottom-of-the-barrel; it made money on volume while usage was "up there with heroin" c) It had no ads d) Mobile was its main revenue

A: b. The notes call the impression monetization "utter dog shit."

Q4 (SA). What was Project Chorizo and what was its result?

A: Systematic tests feeding every user action (posts, messages, links, check-ins) into topic targeting. Nothing improved advertiser performance: "A mile-long trainful of meat cows... one measly sausage."

Q5 (SA). What was the PM's first tiebreaker decision, and the reasoning?

A: Keep existing keywords (20% of revenue) and mark new topic segments with a Twitter-style "#"; no UI redesign (design was the bottleneck); launch fast. Kitten shipped in two months (launched August 1, 2011).

Q6 (T/F). The notes say "very few companies have died due to launching early... countless companies have died by losing the nerve to ship." A: True (bias for launching; knowing when to launch is "a subtle art at best, and a drunken coin toss at worst").

Q7 (SA). What triggered Lockdown, and what competitive intelligence did the author note?

A: Google Plus (June 2011, ad-free, subsidized by AdWords). Zuck invoked Cato's "Carthage must be destroyed." Google's engineering lot was empty on a Sunday; Facebook's was full.

Chapter 9: One Shot, One Kill / Twice Bitten / Ads Five-Oh / Narcissism of Privacy

Q1 (SA). What is the noisy-bar metaphor?

A: Facebook is every bar and cafe on earth; the targeting PM has a transcript of every conversation, but people rarely say anything a CMO cares about, sarcasm is unparseable, and it must work in Tigrinya. Social data is mostly commercially inert.

Q2 (MC). To "earn your beer money" at Facebook scale a new ads idea needed to move about:

a) 0.1% of revenue b) 1% c) 5% of revenue (~$100M/year then) d) 50%

A: c. Unsexy, programmatic, platform-wide changes (Kitten) beat niche ideas such as political-district or travel-intender targeting.

Q3 (SA). Why must a PM be technical?

A: To sniff-test engineers' claims, which may be accidental (wishful memory), passive-aggressive ("that'll eat up all our servers"), or lazy ("impossible"). A senior engineer's assurance about the Irish audit turned out wrong.

Q4 (SA). What happened on Christmas Eve 2011?

A: With the Irish discontinuation deadline hours away, the author ran an UPDATE on the live targeting tables behind ~$2B in spend, with one engineer watching, to verify what he'd vouched for; then he went for a beer. Lesson: verify the thing you personally vouched for, even in production.

Q5 (T/F). Facebook sells user data to advertisers. A: False. Facebook buys data: it provides services that incentivize advertisers to let it ingest their outside data, a "black hole of data that can never leave"; handing data out would be "suicidally stupid."

Q6 (SA). What was the 2011 data-policy referendum and its outcome?

A: Zuck's 2009 pledge to vote on policy changes with a 30% participation threshold (~300M people). About 90% of voters opposed the new policy but almost nobody voted, so the result was "taken under advisement." Without the new policy, the 2012-13 company-saving products would have been impossible.

Q7 (SA). Why is "embarrassing" not "valuable"?

A: No advertiser cares about your secrets, sex life or brownie recipe; they want last night's Netflix pick, your Amazon cart, Best Buy browsing, your car's age, your devices. Blaming Facebook for a creepy ad is like blaming Gmail for spam: Facebook is the telephone exchange, the advertiser addressed you.

Chapter 10: Are We Savages? / O Death / Barbaric Yawn / Going Public

Q1 (SA). Describe the blue-tape loop.

A: Bold experiment (employees paint the new campus) -> fast failure (two days of vandalism) -> prune (Zuck walked the halls with blue masking tape marking what came down) -> internalize ("bluetape" became a code-review macro meaning "remove this for sanity").

Q2 (SA). What is the corporate memento mori?

A: Sun logos deliberately left on doors and on the back of the Facebook sign, reminders that complacency (Sun ignored Linux on commodity hardware) leads to extinction. Death awareness as discipline, not fear.

Q3 (MC). The vesting math says to value a big-company offer at:

a) Its headline b) Half the headline (you'll leave in about two years), halved again if it is stock rather than options c) Double the headline d) Only the salary

A: b. Standard vesting is four years, 25% at one year, then quarterly.

Q4 (SA). What is "track racing vs. commuting"?

A: After a startup, a big company feels like crawling at 80 mph. Facebook was an autobahn (fast lane by Zuck's permission), Apple/Google the 101 at rush hour, Oracle a Delhi intersection. The itch to leave starts within months.

Q5 (SA). Why do big companies buy startups beyond recruiting?

A: Cultural hybridization: cross obedient-graduate DNA with founder wildness (the cattle-dog analogy). The product almost always vanishes; acquirees succeed only with Zuck-granted latitude (Instagram) or by reining themselves in. First rule: act like you belong.

Q6 (T/F). Haves and have-mores discuss money openly on Facebook's campus. A: False. Money was never discussed; the wealthy "furiously denied their very existence," and middle managers hired late knew the gap yet sided with the owners.

Q7 (SA). Why does Martínez call Facebook "the People's Republic"?

A: Mission cultures at scale resemble revolutionary regimes: endless toil for lapidary ideals from an unquestioned leader, a leadership caste chosen for adherence, a flattering media, foot soldiers who sacrifice family. Opting out is theoretical given Bay Area housing and tuition.

Chapter 11: Flying Saucers / Monetizing the Tumor

Q1 (SA). What did Festinger's flying-saucer cult teach about product organizations?

A: The cult grew stronger when the prophecy failed (1954); companies likewise "go temporarily mad" under market expectation and arrogance, ignoring contradicting data. Sponsored Stories persisted through this cognitive dissonance.

Q2 (SA). Why was Open Graph + Sponsored Stories a "two-miracle" plan?

A: It required every company to integrate and donate data at dubious benefit, and marketers to abandon proven workflows for an unprovable paradigm. Hence "almost certain to fail."

Q3 (MC). Social context lift of 40-60% matters little because:

a) It was a bad study b) It came from an abysmal base (~0.05% clickthrough vs. >=0.1% for the worst display ads and ~1% for well-targeted ads) c) It was only on mobile d) Advertisers hated it

A: b. A 60% lift on a 20x deficit is "piddly-boo." Judge lift against the best alternative, not your own baseline.

Q4 (SA). What did Sheryl declare in March 2012?

A: That no brand would keep paying ~$10M a year for Likes; the Like-buying party was over (in "Only Good News," the appellate court for Ads disputes).

Q5 (T/F). Ads and Growth are aligned, since both want a bigger Facebook. A: False. They are yin-yang and anticorrelated: Ads turns users into money; Growth turns money into users. "What makes a user use the product does not necessarily make money."

Q6 (SA). What was LOX and why did it show the Ads-Growth conflict?

A: The Logout Experience: selling the logout page to brand and movie marketers for a few hundred thousand dollars. Growth couldn't quantify the usage cost, so outrage and personal sway decided; LOX ran only where Facebook had won (the US), not where rivals like Orkut were "still warm" (Brazil).

Q7 (SA). What is "running out of humans"?

A: ~3B internet users minus ~600M in China and most of Russia, minus a 25% never-join haircut is ~1.8B addressable; at 1.44B (Q1 2015) and ~13% growth, roughly a year of growth left. Hence Internet.org and solar drones to create connectivity.

Chapter 12: Great Awakening / Barbarians at the Gates / IPA > IPO / IPO Reevaluation / Flash Boys

Q1 (SA). Explain "advertising is name-calling."

A: Direct mail uses a postal address, mobile a quasi-immutable device ID, the web a cookie. The dominant puzzle in marketing is joining these names and controlling the links; the platform war is over who controls the joins.

Q2 (SA). Who is the "real Big Brother" in the chapter?

A: Not Facebook, Google or the NSA but data brokers (Acxiom, Experian, Epsilon, Merkle, Neustar), who have tracked consumer America since the 1960s and sell segments no citizen can inspect.

Q3 (MC). Direct mail is a prize because it is:

a) Tiny and growing b) A $50B+ industry at ~$1,000 CPMs vs. ~$1 online c) Free d) Illegal

A: b. About $17B in postage; online can be a thousand times less effective and break even.

Q4 (SA). What is data on-boarding?

A: Firms (Datalogix, Neustar, LiveRamp) place invisible pixels where name/email meets a browser (newsletters, dating sites), drop or read a cookie, and store the join hashed. Facebook and Google out-on-board everyone; Custom Audiences match rates reach ~90%.

Q5 (SA). Describe the FBX build.

A: Five weeks to ship by June 15, 2012 to book Q3-Q4 revenue; three engineers; a parallel ads system with separate data stores, real-time global bidding hundreds of thousands of times per second, dynamic creative, separate stats and monitoring, partner docs; bought with a promise of $100M in 2012 revenue. First successful bid June 15 via TellApart.

Q6 (SA). Why is 120 ms significant?

A: It is the bound (a third of an eye-blink) to return a bid including network latency. North Carolina to Amsterdam is ~23 ms one way at light speed and ~60 ms in practice, so European requests timed out and FBX lost money there.

Q7 (SA). What was the "unforgivable sin" of FBX?

A: Its bids fed Facebook's own auction, making Facebook "merely one more DSP"; outside bidders who knew you'd just shopped for a handbag outbid Facebook's own data. Equality with outsiders was a feature to the author, a bug to management.

Chapter 13: Full Frontal Facebook / Microsoft Shrugged / Ad Majorem / Adiós, Facebook

Q1 (SA). What were the open and closed options, and what was decided on April 12, 2013?

A: Open: FBX (standard programmatic exchange, instant adoption, outside data on equal footing). Closed: Custom Audiences plus an in-house ad server (Atlas), years to build, total lock-in. Boz recommended to Sheryl no identity matching and no mobile on FBX; she said "if that's what you think... that's what we'll do."

Q2 (SA). Define incrementality and apply it.

A: New spend that would not otherwise have landed on Facebook. CA's dashboard dollars largely came from existing "Facebook" budget lines (discount them by half); FBX competed for budgets earmarked for Google's AdX, so it was 100% incremental.

Q3 (MC). Why does Google's ad server count clicks while Facebook wants viewthroughs?

a) Technical limitation b) Search exploits existing intent; Facebook must manufacture desire, so it wants credit for impressions, Likes, shares c) Legal requirement d) Advertisers demand it

A: b. The ad server is the oracle that counts delivery, frequency and geography; nobody in the chain trusts anyone.

Q4 (SA). What was Atlas and why was it a questionable acquisition?

A: Microsoft's creaky ad server (ran only on certain Internet Explorer versions; 20% share) bought for roughly the $0.1B left after Microsoft wrote down $6.1B of its $6.2B aQuantive purchase. "It's not what you pay, it's what they cost you": two-plus years of delays.

Q5 (SA). What does "do something vs. be someone" mean?

A: (Via Col. Boyd) One road is impact, truth to your vision and management's scorn; the other is plum products, facile praise and forgettable work. The author chose the first despite children's tuition riding on unvested stock.

Q6 (SA). Why are middle managers what they are?

A: Negative selection: the ambitious leave; the rest master managing up, acting visibly on feedback, championing reports, allying with sales, routing around incompetence, and banking the logo on the business card.

Q7 (SA). List the exit-playbook steps.

A: Don't quit before the vest; take vacation over the vesting date; clear your desk over the weekend; secure-erase personal files; expect a severance-for-non-disparagement offer ($30,000 for a year of silence) and decline to sign on the spot; keep the badge and phone "at home."

Chapter 14: Pandemonium Lost / Epilogue

Q1 (SA). How did the outsider's blog post work as an "insider's mouthpiece"?

A: Executives in an acquisition can't explain strategy publicly, but they can retweet a perceptive outsider. The Medium post on Twitter-MoPub was circulated by the deal's principals, reopening a door slammed two years earlier. Lesson in the meeting: "if in doubt, show more."

Q2 (SA). Give the two structural reasons mobile News Feed ads saved Facebook.

A: (1) Data: mobile browsers block third-party cookies and apps silo data, so even age/gender was valuable ("in the land of the mobile data blind, the one-eyed Facebook man was king"). (2) Inventory: mobile's savvy monetizers charged users directly, leaving exchanges with tiny bars, interstitials and Grindr; Facebook's in-feed units had no real competition.

Q3 (MC). "Which of the ten dice came up?" is the book's way to:

a) Pick a product b) Discount any founder's retrospective genius: try ten things, seven fail, two do OK, one transforms for reasons found afterward c) Measure risk d) Allocate headcount

A: b. The press then writes the narrative fallacy.

Q4 (SA). What happened to FBX?

A: About $500M by early 2014, all incremental, built by a handful and now costing nothing: a "perpetual motion machine of cash" and Facebook's window into programmatic competitors. Kept alive because too profitable to kill, starved of identity and mobile. Prediction: Facebook will eventually run a full exchange (even Goldman moved CDS clearing to ICE in 2013).

Q5 (T/F). The author profited hugely from his Facebook stock. A: False. Restricted stock was taxed as income at a $38 basis, then a lockout expired near $20, leaving "practically nothing" ("paying taxes on money I hadn't made"), while the AdGrok engineers' Twitter options made them rich.

Q6 (SA). Name the two acquisitions cited as Facebook "buying your way out."

A: Instagram (2012, $1B) and WhatsApp (2014, $19B).

Q7 (SA). What did the author do after finishing the book?

A: After his mother's death (summer 2014) he sold everything, finished the book, and outfitted Ayala, a forty-foot cutter, to sail around the world alone.

Cumulative Final Exam (10 questions)

F1 (SA). What do a credit-default swap and an ad have in common, and why did Goldman (and later Facebook) resist transparent markets?

A: Both price a perception (CDS: probability of non-payment; ad: a slice of attention). Incumbents with price-making power and information asymmetry prefer owning a small market to participating in a large transparent one, which only invites competition.

F2 (MC). Which idea needs the fewest miracles?

a) Sponsored Stories b) AdGrok's original bar-code idea c) A laundromat d) A one-miracle startup like Airbnb

A: c (zero). Sponsored Stories needed two, AdGrok's first plan five, Airbnb one.

F3 (SA). Compute: a $100K note has a $3M cap. What share does it convert to, and why do founders care about the number?

A: 3.3% regardless of the A's price. Dilution is the enemy; the higher the cap, the less you sell for the same cash.

F4 (SA). Name the two weak points used to beat Adchemy and the two people who activated them.

A: Investors (Paul Graham threatening to blacklist Adchemy's VCs from Demo Day) and potential partners (Sam Altman getting Microsoft's BD to flag the litigation).

F5 (T/F). In an acqui-hire, the acquirer cares how the money is split between founders and investors. A: False. It targets price per head and is indifferent; founders decide what investors get. Founders own nothing until they vest.

F6 (SA). Give two "tells" from the notes and what each signals.

A: Any two: "stealth"/NDA demand = naive founder; a counterpart calling back within an hour = weak hand; first-ever reminder of a one-on-one = HR is in the room; Google's parking lot empty on Sunday = they're not fighting; a prospect's hesitant headshake = will move if pushed.

F7 (SA). Why was Facebook's own social data worth less than outside data, and what evidence did the book use?

A: Noisy-bar metaphor (people rarely say anything of commercial intent); Project Chorizo (no user data improved performance); FBX outside bidders beat Facebook's own data in its own auction; what embarrasses you is worthless to advertisers, who want purchases and browsing.

F8 (MC). Which is the correct reading of a Facebook-style IPO?

a) A big first-day pop is a triumph b) A pop means bankers and their clients won; a flat open with ~1% fees is the real win c) IPOs are always underpriced for employees' benefit d) Fees were up to 7%

A: b.

F9 (SA). Contrast Custom Audiences and FBX on incrementality, openness and what happened on April 12, 2013.

A: CA: closed, creaky, roughly half its dashboard dollars non-incremental, paired with the Atlas ad server. FBX: open, standard, built in five weeks by three engineers, fully incremental. Facebook chose closed on April 12, 2013 (Boz's recommendation to Sheryl).

F10 (SA). What actually saved Facebook, and what general lesson does the author draw about narratives of success?

A: Mobile News Feed ads, for structural reasons (no third-party cookies, siloed apps, weak mobile inventory) nobody argued about at the time. Lesson: try ten things, one wins for reasons discovered afterward, and a narrative is written later ("Man plans and God laughs"); being right about the technology isn't the same as being right about what saves the quarter.

Arguments & Evidence

Chaos Monkeys: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Antonio García Martínez

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files in the martinez-chaos-monkeys skill (plus its glossary, patterns and cheatsheet), so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording. Chapter numbering follows the skill's 14 groupings. Figures are period data (2007-2016).

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Martínez, a Goldman quant turned ad-tech founder and Facebook product manager, argues that Wall Street and ad tech are one business, pricing human perception, in which incumbents prefer owned, inefficient markets to open ones (Ch 1). He tells a memoir in three parts: a doomed startup and the escape into Y Combinator (Ch 2-3), the founding of AdGrok, its survival of an incumbent's lawsuit, and its sale as an acqui-hire (Ch 4-7), and his years inside Facebook, where he sees the culture, the weak value of Facebook's own data, the "great folly" of Sponsored Stories, the awakening to identity joins, and the defeat of the open exchange (FBX) by the closed stack (Ch 8-13). The epilogue (Ch 14) shows that neither side of that fight saved Facebook: mobile News Feed ads did, for structural reasons nobody predicted, and success stories are narratives written afterward. Running throughout are practical playbooks: count miracles, have a leader, price per head, verify what you vouch for, measure incrementality, and vest before you leave.

Ch 1. The Undertakers of Capitalism / The Human Attention Exchange

Argument: Wall Street and ad tech are the same business, putting a price on human perception, and both are being taken over by machines. Markets are run by whoever makes prices; incumbents with information asymmetry keep markets inefficient; and quants and engineers are the enablers, not the stars.

Stories & evidence

  • The April 13, 2012 Zuck meeting: with the IPO imminent and revenue plateauing, three proposals; Zuck said no to Like-button browsing data and yes to retargeting ("but no to using social plugins"). Decisions made on "gut feel, the residue of whatever historical politics were in play."
  • Goldman and CDS: Goldman declined to move CDS to exchanges because transparency only invites competition; it preferred "owning a small market than merely participating in a larger one."
  • SLK: hundreds of traders and two programmers (2000) became two traders and twenty quants (2007), prefiguring ad tech's RTB and later Uber/Airbnb/Instacart.
  • The DUI gambit: offering the officer a taxi under observation to reframe encounter as haggling; the root of "negotiate from weakness."
  • The ID lottery: IDs in a $2,000 pot sold above the $200 fair value, with the premium rising as fewer remained; markets deviate predictably when payouts are large.
  • Facebook geography and Sheryl as gatekeeper: proximity to Zuck as status; the "Supreme Court of Sheryl."
  • The throwaway RTB engine built at Adchemy for the CEO's pitch later made him "light-years ahead" of Facebook's product team.

Key numbers: SLK 2000 vs. 2007 (hundreds of traders and 2 programmers vs. 2 traders and 20 quants); Goldman average pay 2005 $521K vs. grad stipend $19K (cheatsheet); IDs pot $2,000 / ten IDs = $200 fair value.

So what: Ask "who makes the price?" to find where power sits. Expect incumbents to resist transparency, advertiser first-party data to beat publisher data, and negotiate from weakness by reframing the encounter.

Ch 2. Knowing How to Swim / Abandoning the Shipwreck

Argument: You can diagnose a doomed startup from inside, you should leave it, and you get into Y Combinator by selling the team, not the idea. Counting the miracles an idea needs tells you whether it is a business, a startup, or a bad idea.

Stories & evidence

  • Adchemy's four symptoms: a purged Team page, ~$6M/month of lead-gen revenue acting as a sedative, rotating beta-customer logos, and staff who stayed despite abuse (Murthy broke the author's finger with a baseball and mocked him for months; employees still bought stock).
  • The five-miracle idea: a bar-code-to-local-ad product; the pivot ended at "Plan J."
  • The YC application and interview: a two-day deadline (March 1-29, 2010), four partners firing overlapping questions in ten minutes, no demo reached; the "Goldman Sachs of advertising" tagline and the Craigslist hack as answers.
  • PG's call: "I should probably ask him first" was the wrong answer.
  • The escape from Adchemy: harassment, retention bribes, and an ICE threat over an F-2 slip; H-1B visas as "indentured servitude."
  • The fourteen-line creed of Silicon Valley capitalism.
  • British Trader and Zoë: pregnant after weeks; Zoë born March 2010 during YC applications.

Key numbers: ~$6M/month Adchemy lead-gen revenue; five miracles for AdGrok's first plan; YC interview of ten minutes with four partners.

So what: Before any pitch, investment or job offer count miracles (zero = business, one = startup, two+ = pass). Treat retention pressure as confirmation to leave, and settle cofounder commitment before the offer.

Ch 3. War Face / Like Marriage / Speed Is a Feature / D-Day

Argument: Inside YC, success depends on network, prestige and leadership, not on the product; Google's auction prints money while the small-business last mile is a graveyard; and attention can be manufactured through provocation and timing. Every real startup problem is a people problem.

Stories & evidence

  • What YC sells: partners, the YC-founder network (rebuild ~80% of the stack from YC companies), prestige, Demo Day.
  • Google's auction: bid x click probability; ROAS = revenue / cost - 1; "nevada cheap divorce" at 47%; "mesothelioma" at ~$90/click; Google as "the bouncer at the door."
  • The graveyard: Clickable ($32M), Lexity ($6M), Trada ($19M) all died on the SMB last mile.
  • Equal thirds: decision paralysis and rotating two-against-one factions; PG diagnosed the leadership gap in ten minutes; ~six of thirty batch companies had disputed leadership.
  • The New York post: Tuesday-morning Hacker News post; #1 within minutes; Scoble tweet; the server melted; traffic jumped from ~a dozen views/day to 50,000; Business Insider and 20/20 called.
  • Rapportive: its Prototype Day pitch dismayed him, but two years later both companies had the same acqui-hire exit ("this too shall pass").
  • Demo Day mechanics: ~30 companies, 2.5 minutes each, no actual demos; the T-shirt arms race.
  • Chaos monkey: Netflix's random server-killer as metaphor for Uber, Airbnb, Tinder.

Key numbers: Google ~$70B; 47% ROAS example; ~$90/click; $32M/$6M/$19M raised by dead SMB-tools companies; 50,000 views; 30 companies at 2.5 minutes each.

So what: Pick one leader with 51%+ or a real mind-meld; avoid the Mom-and-Pop market unless you partner with someone who owns it; engineer attention (and have servers ready); don't overrate peers' triumphs or your troubles.

Ch 4. Conclave of Angels / Hill of Sand / Widening Gyre / ¡No Pasarán!

Argument: Seed fund-raising is about caps, dilution and finding the person with real decision-making power; and a larger, richer incumbent is not necessarily more dangerous than a small team with nothing to lose. The Valley's founding myths are "forgotten crimes."

Stories & evidence

  • Russ Siegelman vs. Chris Sacca: the old-school angel who wants 2-4x and invests his own money vs. a micro-VC with a "fund of bosses" and a gold-plated name.
  • Cap math: a $100K note at a $3M cap = 3.3% regardless of the A (vs. 1% at a $10M A and 0.1% at $100M without a cap).
  • Reading tells: Russ's headshake at a $4M cap; Sequoia's polite "white space" pass ("a truth that is also a polite lie"); Bill Tai's "would you sell for $50M?" and the wrong smirk.
  • The suit (Sept 10, 2010): filed by Wilson Sonsini personally against all three founders and the company, with ~$2,000 in AdGrok's bank.
  • The Death Clock: hidden and then "cooked."
  • The Fenwick deal: $250K fronted for a small equity slice plus options, a mispriced option ("a one-in-a-million lottery ticket to win $250,000... for $250,000"); Rodger Cole, "the Undertaker."
  • Forgotten crimes: Gates/Kildall, Jobs/Wozniak ($350), Zuckerberg and the idea he was hired to build; Balzac's line.
  • The round: four investors, ~$500K, at a $2M cap; cap cut from $4M after the suit.

Key numbers: YC 2010 caps: $3-4M middle, $6M good, ~$8M stellar (Hipmunk); AdGrok closed at $2M, ~22% sold, ~$500K; litigation ~$500K to trial, ~$1.5M total over 18 months, ~$20K/month, ~$800/hr (cheatsheet); solo lawyers at $400/hour vs. partners at $700/hour; Fenwick $250K.

So what: Negotiate the cap, ask "Do you have decision-making power?", groom your lead before Demo Day, fund-raise alone, and expect that the incumbent's employees are mercenaries while a cohesive, enraged small team can outlast them.

Ch 5. Dog Shit Sandwich / Victory / Launching!

Argument: A tiny startup can beat a funded incumbent's lawsuit by attacking the giant's dependencies (its investors and its prospective partners) rather than the legal claims. After surviving, the harder test is launch, the Trough of Despair and the search for product-market fit.

Stories & evidence

  • Knife to balls, October 2010: an Adchemy employee's drinks-fueled leak of a Bing deal; LinkedIn search for a two-hop connector; PG's threat to cut Adchemy's VCs (August, Mayfield) out of Demo Day; Sam Altman got Microsoft BD to call the litigation "problematic" ("the decapitated horse's head in Murthy's bed"); Dalal seen dressing down Murthy.
  • PG's principle: "reward your friends and punish your enemies"; his instruction to firewall the team ("Come alone... keep them out of it").
  • Deal flow: the 2010 shift (angel glut, micro-funds, YC, AWS) made YC the "water sluice" big VCs had to kowtow to.
  • Resolution: Adchemy offered to dismiss in late October; settled February 2011; Adchemy ended in 2014 after $130M+ raised with a fire-sale "acquisition" and employees who lost savings.
  • The launch (March 7, 2011): a paid PR agency, Internet Retailer and Direct Marketing News, a small sign-up wave.
  • Trough of Despair: the YC whiteboard curve.
  • British Trader: move-out December 2010; a second pregnancy.

Key numbers: Adchemy raised $130M+; dismissal late October 2010 / settled February 2011; 90%+ of surviving startups killed by the trough; launch March 7, 2011.

So what: Ask "who needs what from whom?"; keep existential crises out of the team's headspace; remember focus and endurance (and enemies) are the scarce inputs; and don't believe the launch spike.

Ch 6. Dates @Twitter / Acquisition Chicken / Getting Liked / Getting Poked

Argument: Acquisition talks are a seduction and negotiation manual: stalk everyone, be ready to demo, run formal and clandestine channels, and create an auction before the no-shop. The acquirer's interest and your VC's incentives both distort your judgment.

Stories & evidence

  • Twitter courtship (March 2011): lunch with @jess (Jessica Verrilli); the impromptu Bain demo saved by MRM's hosted demo; Kevin Weil's "Maybe you should join us... like in acquiring you"; the verbal $5M on March 29.
  • Deep Tweet: the composite insider source (Epicenter Café) who said "create an auction."
  • Orrick, not Kinko's: getting a first-rate corporate firm.
  • Sacca's reappearance: silent for months, then calling at all hours once Twitter was in play; "No fucking way should you engage on this offer"; the author hid Facebook from him.
  • Facebook, March 30: the Google bluff on Amin Zoufonoun; the parking-garage board call; interviews within 48 hours.
  • Facebook interview day (April 1): Alon Amit, Rohit Dhawan, Jared Morgenstern, Justin Shaffer, Gokul ("What's the first thing you would change?" -> "a conversion-tracking system").
  • Ads teams as future leaders at Twitter: Weil, Roetter, Bain, Verrilli.

Key numbers: Twitter's "$5 million thing" for three hires; engineers $0.5-2M each in four-year vesting equity; no-shop typically 60 days; ~400 Twitter employees; five PM archetypes.

So what: Preparation is stalking; phone calls mean yes and emails mean no; a bluff works when unverifiable; do not let the investor with a stake in the buyer run your process; and treat "cultural fit" with suspicion.

Ch 7. Forking Paths / Retweets / The Dotted Line / Endgame

Argument: Acquirers buy people at a target price per head and do not care how founders and investors split it; founders own nothing until they vest; and the whole startup may have been "a long, stressful job interview." The optimal play would have required deceiving cofounders.

Stories & evidence

  • Facebook as legalized crack: CityVille hit 100M users in a month; a Florida mother shook her baby to death over FarmVille notifications; the Cuban grandmother's dominoes now unused because his mother plays FarmVille.
  • The Whereoscope template (Mick Johnson) for shopping a company and forcing two partial bidders into one room.
  • The split deal: April 5, Twitter ~$10M; Facebook wanted only the CEO (Amin: "mixed" on Argyris and Matt, MRM a definite no); the lie to cofounders; the South Park reckoning; the desengaño (April 14); term sheets from both (April 15).
  • Sacca's last call (April 16): "You're going to fuck up this entire deal!"
  • April 18 walkout: Satya Patel; Twitter's callback within an hour for $5M+ for two engineers; the lawyer's "accept now, resign first"; the 3:07 Caltrain.
  • The Getaround race: Tesla Roadster vs. a Mini to Stinson Beach.
  • Consideration math: investors got ~$1M of ~$10M in Twitter's default term sheet.

Key numbers: Twitter ~$10M, then $5M+ for two engineers; investors ~$1M vs. ~$2M pro rata; Facebook offer at ~$32/share pre-IPO = ~$2.3M, about 25% AdGrok stake after split; founders' stakes 20-40% vesting; CityVille 100M users in a month.

So what: Think of an acqui-hire as N separate job offers; read the counterparty's hand from their tempo; resign before you sign; lie to investors and acquirers if you must but never deceive cofounders; and remember vesting governs every exit decision.

Ch 8. Boot Camp / Product Masseur / Google Delenda Est / Leaping Headlong

Argument: Facebook's onboarding is conversion to a belief system, producing true believers; the PM's real job is shit umbrella and tiebreaker; and early revelations (the cheap impressions and Project Chorizo) show Facebook's data had not yet been turned into money.

Stories & evidence

  • Onboarding: Cox's "New York Times of You"; Pedram's "leave your old culture behind"; Chamath's "just fucking do it"; posters on every wall; Faceversaries and Facebook "deaths."
  • Engineering boot camp: six weeks of bug-fixing in PHP; first act: changing the Like button text to an obscenity on a dev server.
  • Zuck as old-school genius: a Jefferson/Napoleon/Jim Jones figure whose vision converts followers ("true believers are scarier than the greedy because they can't be bought"); Chris Putnam's virus -> hired, not prosecuted.
  • Ads org 2011: a house "out of parts selected at random from a Home Depot."
  • Lockdown: Google Plus (June 2011, ad-free, subsidized by AdWords); the neon sign; Cato's "Carthage must be destroyed"; Google's lot empty on Sunday, Facebook's full; Google's instant counteroffers.
  • Kitten: the hashtag decision and the two-month launch (August 1, 2011).
  • Project Chorizo: "A mile-long trainful of meat cows... one measly sausage."

Key numbers: Ads 2011: ~30 engineers, 1 designer, ~a dozen products, 6 PMs; keywords = 20% of revenue; six-week boot camp; clickthrough ~0.05% (cheatsheet).

So what: Be the tiebreaker, layer new features on old paradigms, ship with a bias for action, build a dashboard you know to the decimal ("you make what you measure"), and measure commitment by who shows up on Sunday.

Ch 9. One Shot, One Kill / Twice Bitten / Ads Five-Oh / Narcissism of Privacy

Argument: Facebook's data was hard to monetize because social talk is commercially inert; at Facebook's scale only platform-wide ideas clear the revenue bar; and the privacy debate mistakes embarrassment for value. Advertisers want purchases and browsing from outside Facebook, and Facebook buys that data rather than selling its own.

Stories & evidence

  • The noisy bar: transcripts of every conversation with anonymous IDs; "Obama" in an Alabama bar preceded by an expletive; sarcasm; Tigrinya.
  • Failed niches: political-district targeting, a Hispanic cluster, travel-intender geodata.
  • Testing on slices of humanity: New Zealand as "Aotearoa... Facebook test set"; engineers horse-trading country-sized test populations.
  • Ireland: the audit, 4.5M people "wouldn't even fill a Facebook test set"; Christmas Eve 2011: the UPDATE on live targeting tables behind ~$2B in spend, Hong Ge watching, then beer.
  • Sheryl's ops meeting: the kitten-as-porn-placeholder demo; the author's up-and-to-the-right slide on ads reviewed vs. flat human hours.
  • The 2011 referendum: 30% participation threshold; ~90% opposed; almost nobody voted; taken "under advisement."
  • The 49ers-jersey anecdote explained by a game weekend and a broad campaign.
  • Scalps@Facebook and the safety work Facebook doesn't publicize.

Key numbers: new ads idea must move ~5% of revenue (~$100M/year then); ~$2B in spend behind the tables; 30% threshold = ~300M people; ~90% of voters opposed; Ireland 4.5M people; Noah born September 2011; $700/month sailboat.

So what: Use technical depth to detect engineer bullshit; verify what you vouched for even in production; prefer unsexy, programmatic, platform-wide ideas; and treat "Facebook is showing me X" as a category error (the advertiser addressed you).

Ch 10. Are We Savages? / O Death / Barbaric Yawn / Going Public

Argument: Facebook's culture is a loop of bold bets, fast failure, correction and ritualized memory; big companies decelerate founders and price offers through vesting math; and mission cultures at scale resemble revolutionary regimes with a hidden two-class wealth split.

Stories & evidence

  • The art experiment (Dec 2011): unlimited spray cans; two days of vandalism; Zuck's message ("I trusted you to make art and you vandalized the place"); blue tape; "bluetape" a code-review macro. David Choe commissioned (again).
  • The move-out riot: thirty minutes to vacate; the SPAIN plaque pried off with a rigging knife.
  • Memento mori: Sun logos left on doors and behind the Facebook sign; the red book (Facebook Was Not Originally Created to Be a Company) and posters like THIS JOURNEY 1% FINISHED.
  • Track racing vs. commuting: Facebook autobahn, Apple/Google the 101, Oracle a Delhi intersection.
  • The shuttle buses: protesters smashing windows; Google "spies" on the wrong bus.
  • IPO tent (Feb 1, 2012): an email from Zuck; "stay focused on our mission."
  • Haves and have-mores: the NR250 group; 401(k) matching arrived late because "the IPO was the pension"; the People's Republic comparison with his Cuban cousins' revolution.

Key numbers: four-year vesting, 25% at one year, then quarterly; halve the headline, halve again for stock vs. options; $2.4M Diamond Heights listings browsed during the speech.

So what: Build blue-tape loops (permission to experiment, ruthless pruning, an artifact that encodes the lesson); keep a memento mori; value acqui-hire offers at about a quarter of the headline; and read "we don't talk about money" as the tell of a two-class company.

Ch 11. Flying Saucers / Monetizing the Tumor

Argument: Facebook's pre-IPO monetization plan (Open Graph feeding Sponsored Stories) was a two-miracle idea sustained by cognitive dissonance until Sheryl said brands would not keep paying for Likes. The rush for revenue then collided with Growth, revealing that engagement and money are anticorrelated.

Stories & evidence

  • Festinger's 1954 flying-saucer cult: the cult grew stronger when the prophecy failed.
  • The two revenue streams c. 2010: brands (Starbucks, Burberry) buying page Likes; direct-response advertisers barely present except game developers (energy-drink Likes predicting mob-game conversions).
  • Social context lift: 40-60% on a ~0.05% base vs. >=0.1% for worst display and ~1% for well-targeted ads: "piddly-boo."
  • Gavage launching and partners reporting no difference.
  • Fog: a VP's magnum of champagne with a Post-it targeting 10% of revenue from Sponsored Stories by end-2011; never approached.
  • FMC (Feb 2012): Timeline Hallway; Paul Adams's Grouped thesis contradicted by Facebook research; Alicia Keys under the blue whale.
  • Growth team: retargeting on exchanges before Ads knew they existed; Risk-board map of countries yet to "tip."
  • LOX: the logout page for a few hundred thousand dollars; run only in the US, not Brazil.
  • Running out of humans: 1.8B addressable at 1.44B (Q1 2015).

Key numbers: ~$10M per brand Likes deal; 40-60% lift on a 20x deficit; 10% revenue target; ~3B internet users minus ~600M China, minus 25% = ~1.8B; 1.44B at ~13% growth.

So what: Count the miracles in your monetization plan; measure lift against the best alternative; listen when partners say it isn't working; and remember you can optimize for engagement or revenue in a given moment, not both.

Ch 12. Great Awakening / Barbarians at the Gates / IPA > IPO / IPO Reevaluation / Flash Boys

Argument: Advertising is name-calling, and the real war among platforms is over who controls the joins between names (postal address, device ID, cookie). Facebook's 2012 awakening produced Custom Audiences and FBX, and the supposedly "flat" IPO was the best in tech history because it screwed the bankers, not the employees.

Stories & evidence

  • Data brokers as the real Big Brother: Acxiom, Experian, Epsilon, Merkle, Neustar; Nielsen's PRIZM segments.
  • Direct mail economics: ~$17B postage, $50B+ industry, ~$1,000 CPMs vs. ~$1 online.
  • On-boarding: Datalogix, Neustar, LiveRamp; pixels on newsletters and dating sites; hashed joins as "privacy theater."
  • How Facebook learned: "mooched" from Turn, MediaMath, BlueKai, Acxiom, Epsilon; Experian sent a junior team with a box of cookies to a meeting about cookies.
  • Selling FBX internally (March 13, 2012): Zach Coelius of Triggit as the outside "voice of the market" for an hour; a written case within days.
  • The build: five weeks, three engineers, a parallel ads system; first bid June 15, 2012 via TellApart.
  • Flash Boys: 120 ms bid window; NC-Amsterdam ~23 ms one way at light speed, ~60 ms in practice.
  • The unforgivable sin: outside bidders beat Facebook's data in its own auction.
  • IPO night: a mandated hackathon, "IPO IPA," single malt at 5 a.m., Zuck: ring the bell, then get back to work.
  • Pay: 75,000 shares over four years, $175K salary, 5,000 shares cashed up front.

Key numbers: match rates up to ~90%; $100M promised 2012 revenue; open ~$42, close ~$38.37, ~1% fees vs. up to 7%; package ~$971K/year at the IPO price, ~$550K after tax.

So what: Think of every channel as an addressing scheme and every platform war as a fight over the join table; read any IPO with "who gets the pop?"; ship parallel systems fast with tiny teams; and expect an incumbent to protect asymmetry when outside data beats its own.

Ch 13. Full Frontal Facebook / Microsoft Shrugged / Ad Majorem / Adiós, Facebook

Argument: Facebook chose the closed stack (Custom Audiences plus the Atlas ad server) over the open exchange (FBX), repeating Goldman's choice of monopoly and information asymmetry over innovation. Incrementality is the honest measure of a new ads product, and the author chose "to do something" over "to be someone."

Stories & evidence

  • Great powers: no partners, only rivals and temporary allies; Amazon's A9 engineers "got it, instantly."
  • Google Plus's inflated usage: 400M registered / 100M active by counting anyone who clicked a Plus button; Larry Page's ultimatum; Vic Gundotra as the internal Emmanuel Goldstein.
  • The Omnicom meeting (Jan 2013): the suited retargeting executive and Gokul's non-answer.
  • "The Spartans lost at Thermopylae": a manager answers a resource plea with a movie reference.
  • LiveBoz (April 4) and April 12: Boz's recommendation; Sheryl: "that's what we'll do"; Gokul fled the room.
  • Atlas: Microsoft's aQuantive write-down; "it's not what you pay, it's what they cost you."
  • Ad servers: Google counts clicks, Facebook needs viewthroughs; IAB/MMA containers vs. native formats.
  • Court politics and negative selection of middle managers; the review "You're a very divisive figure."
  • Exit (April 15-16): vacation over vesting day, desk cleared, disk wiped, HR with a $30,000-for-silence document; Goodfellas "getting made."

Key numbers: April 12, 2013 decision; Atlas ~$0.1B of Microsoft's $6.2B aQuantive purchase after a $6.1B write-down; Atlas ~20% share; CA dollars discounted by half; $30,000 for a year of silence; Google Plus 400M/100M.

So what: Ask "is this dollar incremental?" before crediting any dashboard; treat the ad server (source of truth) as the strategic asset; expect middle management to side with power; and sequence your exit around the vest while assuming the company does the same.

Ch 14. Pandemonium Lost / Epilogue

Argument: Neither FBX nor Custom Audiences saved Facebook; mobile News Feed ads did, for structural reasons (data scarcity and weak inventory on mobile) nobody predicted. Success stories are post-hoc narratives ("ten dice, one winner"), and compensation form, tax timing and lockouts, not talent, decided who got rich.

Stories & evidence

  • Plantar fascia rupture and the MoPub essay: the Medium post circulated by the deal's principals, reopening a door; giving Twitter the full whiteboard ("if in doubt, show more"); the advisory offer (a thousand shares a quarter, ~$160K/year).
  • A grudge job: advising Twitter while employed by Nanigans, Facebook's largest ads partner.
  • Why mobile won: browsers block third-party cookies, apps silo data, Apple polices device IDs; mobile's savvy monetizers charge users directly, leaving exchanges with tiny bars, interstitials and Grindr; Audience Network proved "the one-eyed Facebook man was king."
  • Land rush: the Louisiana Purchase analogy; revenue kept growing after saturation.
  • Ten dice: seven fail, two do OK, one becomes transformational; the press writes the narrative fallacy.
  • Buying your way out: Instagram and WhatsApp.
  • FBX's fate: a "perpetual motion machine of cash," Facebook's periscope into programmatic competitors; Goldman moved CDS clearing to ICE in 2013.
  • Google's Punic defeat: Gundotra's April 2014 exit.
  • Compensation and karma: AdGrok engineers rich at Twitter; the author taxed at $38 on stock sold near $20.
  • The boat: after his mother's death (summer 2014), he outfitted Ayala, a forty-foot cutter.

Key numbers: MoPub ~$350M; FBX ~$500M by early 2014 (all incremental); Instagram $1B (2012), WhatsApp $19B (2014); Q2 2013 mobile actives up 50%+, mobile revenue roughly doubled; Twitter post-lockout price above $50; Facebook restricted stock taxed at $38 basis, lockout expiring near $20.

So what: Being right about the technology is not the same as being right about what saves the quarter; market structure (who can see what data) decides a dataset's value; discount any founder's retrospective genius; and "man plans and God laughs."

Recurring Stories & Threads

  • Goldman and the CDS exchange refusal, repeated at Facebook with FBX and Atlas (Ch 1, 12, 13, 14).
  • The miracle count: AdGrok's five-miracle idea (Ch 2) and Sponsored Stories' two (Ch 11).
  • Adchemy and Murthy: the doomed startup, the lawsuit and the fire-sale end (Ch 2, 4, 5).
  • Paul Graham and Sam Altman as loyal power brokers (Ch 2, 3, 5).
  • Sacca and Russ: the angel vs. micro-VC contrast, reappearing at the acqui-hire (Ch 4, 6, 7).
  • Twitter and the "call station": from the $5M courtship to the hour-long callback to the MoPub adviser role (Ch 6, 7, 14).
  • The Google bluff and Google's fear (Ch 6, 8, 13, 14).
  • Chorizo and the noisy bar: Facebook's data as commercially inert (Ch 8, 9, 12).
  • Sheryl's "Only Good News" as appellate court (Ch 1, 9, 11, 13).
  • Gokul, Boland and Boz: the Ads leadership through the open-vs-closed decision (Ch 6, 8, 12, 13).
  • Vesting: from founders owning nothing to halving offers to timing the exit (Ch 7, 10, 13).
  • British Trader, Zoë and Noah: the personal cost of the startup years (Ch 2, 5, 9).
  • The boat: the sailboat in Redwood City and Ayala at the end (Ch 9, 14).

Don't Believe Everything You Think: Why Your Thinking Is the Beginning & End of Suffering

2 markdown files

Quiz

Don't Believe Everything You Think Quiz Book

Don't Believe Everything You Think: Why Your Thinking Is the Beginning & End of Suffering by Joseph Nguyen

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. Questions are short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), or multiple-choice (MC). The book has 17 short chapters plus a guides appendix (Ch 18), so chapters are grouped two at a time, with six questions per group. A cumulative final exam is at the end.

Chapters 1-2: The Journey to the Root Cause / The Root Cause of All Suffering

Q1 (SA). What are the "two arrows," and which one is optional?

A: The first arrow is the event (pain), which is often unavoidable. The second arrow is your reaction to it (suffering), which is always optional.

Q2 (T/F). Nguyen claims that physical pain and bad events are not real. A: False. The book does not deny pain. "Suffering" is scoped strictly to psychological and emotional distress, produced by reaction rather than by the event.

Q3 (SA). Why did Nguyen's long list of self-improvement efforts (books, therapy, shadow work, meditation, retreats, diets, routines) fail to end his suffering?

A: Each gave incremental gains but treated symptoms, not the root. What changed things was an understanding of how experience is generated from thinking, not another technique.

Q4 (MC). Which sequence describes "inside-out" experience?

a) Feeling, then event, then thinking b) Event, then your thinking/meaning, then your feeling c) Event, then feeling, then thinking d) Thinking, then event, then feeling

A: b. Reality is the bare event with no meaning; every interpretation is added by you.

Q5 (SA). What two questions does Chapter 2 give you to test whether a situation is really "making" you feel something?

A: First, would every person in that situation feel identically? If not, the feeling comes from thinking. Second, "Who would you be without that thought?" (adapted from Byron Katie), which usually reveals something light, free, and peaceful underneath.

Q6 (SA). In the Zen story of the empty boat, what does the monk discover and what is the lesson?

A: After fleeing noise to the middle of a lake, a boat rams his. He yells at the pilot, then finds the boat empty and drifting, and his anger evaporates. Nothing external can anger you without your reaction; every disturbance is an empty boat.

Chapters 3-4: Why Do We Even Think? / Thoughts vs. Thinking

Q1 (SA). What is the "survive vs. thrive" split?

A: The mind's job is survival and safety; consciousness/the soul's job is fulfillment. Inner conflict arises from confusing the two, and from not realizing the mind is only doing its job.

Q2 (T/F). Chapter 3 recommends fighting and correcting your anxious mind. A: False. The practical stance is to relieve the mind of its duty (thank it, stop taking its alarms as truth). Getting angry at your mind adds a second layer of thinking.

Q3 (SA). Define "thought" and "thinking" as Nguyen uses them.

A: A thought (noun) is effortless raw material that arrives unbidden from beyond you; it is light, expansive, and creative. Thinking (verb) is your effortful engagement with a thought (judging, analyzing, criticizing); it costs willpower and is heavy, restrictive, and destructive.

Q4 (MC). In the 5x income experiment, which part is "thinking"?

a) The first answer to "what's your dream income?" b) The idea that pops up for how to make it c) The cascade of "no way," "nobody in my family earns that," and "that's greedy" d) The number itself

A: c. The first answers are thoughts; the doubt cascade is thinking, and it brings self-doubt, unworthiness, and guilt.

Q5 (SA). How do you use feelings as a "radar"?

A: Negative emotion or heaviness means you are thinking; lightness and aliveness mean you are receiving thoughts. Feelings are a dashboard, not facts about the world.

Q6 (T/F). According to Chapter 4, you can learn to control which thoughts arrive. A: False. Thoughts are not yours to control. You cannot stop thoughts, but you can stop thinking about them.

Chapters 5-6: Don't We Need to Think Positively? / The Three Principles

Q1 (SA). What is the refined principle of Chapter 5?

A: We only feel negative emotion when we are thinking. Peace, love, and joy are the natural default and need no thought to produce them.

Q2 (SA). Explain the thought-o-meter. Does content or quantity of thinking matter more?

A: It is a mental speedometer of thoughts per minute; the red zone is burnout, fury, panic. Negative emotion intensity rises with the volume of thinking, and positive emotion intensity rises as thinking volume falls. It is not what you think about but that you are thinking.

Q3 (SA). Describe the paired-recall exercise and what it is meant to show.

A: Recall 2-3 memories of extreme stress and note how much thinking was running, then recall 2-3 memories of peak joy or love and note the same. Typically thinking is heavy in the first set and near-silent in the second, which is the experiential proof the chapter relies on.

Q4 (MC). Name the Three Principles.

a) Mind, Body, Spirit b) Universal Mind, Universal Consciousness, Universal Thought c) Thought, Feeling, Action d) Past, Present, Future

A: b. They come from Sydney Banks.

Q5 (SA). Using the DVD analogy, what does each principle correspond to?

A: Thought is the DVD (the information), Consciousness is the TV and player (it brings the thought to life), and Universal Mind is the electricity (the invisible power connecting everything).

Q6 (T/F). Chapter 6 presents the Three Principles as techniques to practice. A: False. They are descriptions of how experience works, not practices to perform. Any felt separation from anything is an illusion produced by thinking.

Chapters 7-8: How Do We Stop Thinking? / Thriving Without Thinking

Q1 (SA). What is the only tool Chapter 7 says you need to reduce thinking?

A: Awareness: notice that you are thinking and that thinking is the cause of the feeling. That detaches you from it and it settles on its own.

Q2 (SA). Explain the murky water and quicksand images.

A: Murky water clears by being left alone, not by filtering or boiling it (analyzing, problem-solving, working on the thoughts). Fighting thinking is like struggling in quicksand: resistance tightens the grip, stillness lets you rise.

Q3 (T/F). The goal of non-thinking is to have no thoughts at all. A: False. Non-thinking means allowing thoughts to flow through without engaging them. Oscillation between thinking and non-thinking is normal, and making "never think" the goal creates more thinking.

Q4 (SA). In the Heaven and Hell parable, what is the point?

A: A Zen master insults a samurai, who draws his sword in rage. The master says "That's hell." The samurai sees that his own mind manufactured the rage and bows, and the master says "And that's heaven." The whole distance between the two states was one moment of awareness.

Q5 (MC). What is mushin?

a) A breathing technique b) "No mind": a mind free of random thoughts, anger, fear, and ego, acting from trained instinct c) A form of positive thinking d) The Japanese word for patience

A: b.

Q6 (SA). What is the guided inquiry of Chapter 8, and what does it demonstrate?

A: Ask, "When you're doing your absolute best work, fully captivated with time and space gone, what thoughts are running through your head?" Nearly everyone reports none, or thoughts flowing through without engagement. That first-person evidence is the argument. Practice is where learning belongs; performance is where thinking should stop.

Chapters 9-10: Goals, Dreams & Ambitions / Unconditional Love & Creation

Q1 (SA). Contrast desperation goals and inspiration goals.

A: Desperation goals come from thinking: scarcity, urgency, heaviness, "HAVE to," always a means to something else, built from analyzing the past; success brings emptiness and a bigger desperate goal. Inspiration goals come as thought: light, expansive, "WANT to," an end in themselves, from abundance, and feel like they come through you.

Q2 (SA). What three questions test the source of a goal?

A: Did it arrive as a thought or get built by thinking? Does it feel light or heavy? Is it a means or an end?

Q3 (SA). State the Infinite-Resources Question.

A: "If I had infinite money, had already traveled the world, had no fear, and would receive no recognition for what I do, what would I do or create?" It strips out fear, scarcity, and external motives. Act on the first answer, not the critique of it.

Q4 (T/F). Nguyen says that if you adopt non-thinking you should give up your ambitions. A: False. Keep your ambitions and change their source.

Q5 (SA). Why does listing reasons make love "conditional"? How does Nguyen test this in his own relationship?

A: Each reason is a condition under which love could be withdrawn. Nguyen listed fifty reasons for loving his partner Makenna and was bothered that she could not list reasons for loving him ("I don't know, I just do"). Asking whether he would stop loving her if she stopped laughing or helping people showed the reasons were never the cause; her inability to list reasons was the signature of unconditional love.

Q6 (MC). The paradox of unconditional creation is that:

a) it is only for professionals b) creating with no conditions delivers the feelings you were chasing immediately, while creating for a reason postpones them, possibly forever c) it guarantees money d) it removes the need for love

A: b. What you want is always a feeling (security, love, fulfillment), generated internally and never delivered by an object.

Chapters 11-12: What Do You Do After Experiencing Peace? / Nothing Is Either Good or Bad

Q1 (SA). Why do worry and doubt often return after a first taste of peace, and what does Chapter 11 recommend?

A: It is the ego reasserting itself plus a surplus of energy formerly spent on thinking. Recommendation: channel the energy into pre-written inspiration goals and shorten recovery time rather than try to prevent relapse.

Q2 (T/F). Progress is measured by how rarely you fall back into thinking. A: False. Success is faster remembering ("this is just thinking") and returning, measured by recovery speed, not zero relapse.

Q3 (SA). What is an activation ritual and what must it never include?

A: A morning routine that puts you into non-thinking/flow first thing so momentum carries through the day. Never start the day with phone or email, which launches fight-or-flight momentum.

Q4 (SA). Explain the 88 piano keys idea.

A: No key is inherently wrong; a key only seems wrong relative to a song someone assumes is being played. Likewise there are no wrong decisions, only more or less pleasant sequences. Replace "was that wrong?" with "what does this vantage point let me see?"

Q5 (SA). What is the Universal Truth Test?

A: If something is "true" for one person but not another, it is not truth, it is thinking. Truth is what holds for every conscious human regardless of origin.

Q6 (MC). According to Chapter 12, what does being gripped by negative emotion signal?

a) The situation is truly bad b) You have been wronged c) You currently believe your thinking and have forgotten where experience comes from d) You need a new plan

A: c. Treat it as a flag reading "misunderstanding here," not a verdict on the situation.

Chapters 13-14: Knowing What to Do / How to Follow Your Intuition

Q1 (SA). What is "know that you already know"?

A: You almost always already know what to do, and fear or self-doubt hides it. First check for fear masking a known answer; only if you are genuinely unsure with no fear present, trust that inner wisdom will supply the answer ("if you don't know, know that you can know").

Q2 (SA). What does the inner GPS analogy say about intuition?
