A: Intuition guarantees the destination, not the route. Detours and blockages are rerouted in real time, so trust the GPS for the destination and release the route.

Q3 (T/F). If your intuition is right, society will confirm it early. A: False. Society never confirms early; seeking outside validation produces backlash and conflicting opinions, which is expected and not a sign you are wrong. Regret is the signature of having overridden intuition with someone else's advice.

Q4 (SA). What does "what, not how" mean?

A: Hold the what you want (decided with imagination) and enter non-thinking; the how and when belong to the Universe/Infinite Intelligence. Trying to figure out the how is the source of "hard work and suffering."

Q5 (SA). List the identifying features of intuition and what to do when fear appears.

A: It arrives as a spontaneous thought with a sense of knowingness, rarely seems logical, points toward the unknown, and feels light despite the fear that follows. Fear signals you are at the edge of the unknown; recall that the fear is only thinking, it dissolves, courage surfaces, and you act.

Q6 (MC). Why does the path reveal itself only as you walk?

a) The Universe is playful b) Lighting the whole route in advance would negate faith, which is structurally required c) Planning is impossible d) Nobody can see the future

A: b. The unknown is also the only place new outcomes can come from ("to get what you don't have, do what you haven't done").

Chapters 15-16: Creating Space for Miracles / Potential Obstacles

Q1 (SA). What does "empty your cup" teach?

A: In the Zen story the master overfills the scholar's teacup; a mind full of its own opinions has no room for insight. Stop generating, surrender, and ask questions that challenge your current thinking.

Q2 (SA). State the three steps of the Divine Download Process.

A: (1) Become aware that your thinking is the root cause of the negative emotion. (2) Create space: surrender manual thinking, have complete faith inner wisdom will answer, and surrender the how and when. (3) Notice the feelings that arise as you surrender, magnify love, peace, and joy, and meet the problem with love. The answer comes.

Q3 (SA). What do the Edison steel-ball trick and Einstein's violin illustrate?

A: Deliberately engineered non-thinking. Edison dozed holding steel balls and the solution was there when they dropped and woke him; Einstein stopped working on the problem, played the violin, and let the answer arrive.

Q4 (SA). What is the unfamiliar-peace trap?

A: Sustained peace feels unfamiliar and the brain treats unfamiliar as unsafe, so the mind (the "greatest salesman") sells you the idea that something is wrong ("you've lost your edge," "you're lazy"). Label it as the mind trying to make you think again and choose the unknown.

Q5 (T/F). Relapsing into thinking calls for self-punishment so you learn. A: False. Guilt is more thinking. Falling back is human: notice, return, no guilt.

Q6 (MC). What is "the Choice" of Chapter 16?

a) Work or rest b) Free and happy in the unknown, or confined and suffering in the familiar c) Thought or feeling d) Plan or improvise

A: b. It is always this binary, and faith (the Universe works for you; no failures, only lessons) is the operating requirement.

Chapters 17-18: Now What? / Summary & Practical Guides

Q1 (SA). What is "one thought away" and what is the single thing to remember when life gets hard?

A: At any moment you are one thought, or one moment of non-thinking, from peace, love, and joy. Forgetting is normal and remembering is the whole practice.

Q2 (T/F). If the message seems too simple, that is a reason to doubt it. A: False. Chapter 17 treats that objection as the mind restarting thinking; simplicity is the truth-test and complexity moves away from truth.

Q3 (SA). Give the order of the four-category trigger removal and name the categories.

A: Audit what makes you prone to thinking/fight-or-flight, categorize into Physical Health, Physical Environment, Digital Environment, and Digital Consumption, rank within each category by impact, then pick the top items and write a removal action. Start small, because removing too much at once creates more stress.

Q4 (SA). Describe the work energy ledger and its target.

A: List draining and energizing work activities, rate each 1-10 (1 most draining, 10 most alive), eliminate 1-3 drainers each week and do more 9s and 10s. The target is 80% of work time on 9-10 activities.

Q5 (SA). What is the key move in the destructive-habit inquiry?

A: Surface the belief that makes you feel you HAVE to do it and ask what you think happens if you don't, then "Is it absolutely 100% true?" Habit change is inquiry into the belief, not willpower against the behavior; you know it worked if you feel physically lighter and see the habit differently.

Q6 (MC). Which are the two reflection prompts the guide offers?

a) "What did I accomplish?" and "Who let me down?" b) "1-10, how much did I think today?" and "What percent of today was fight-or-flight versus calm?" c) "What went wrong?" and "What next?" d) "Am I right?" and "Am I wrong?"

A: b.

Final Exam (cumulative, 10 questions)

Q1 (SA). State the book's central claim in one sentence.

A: Thinking is the root cause of all psychological suffering; the event (pain) is unavoidable, but you can only feel what you are thinking, and peace, love, and joy are the default when thinking settles.

Q2 (SA). Distinguish thoughts from thinking and give the fast tell.

A: Thoughts arrive effortlessly, are light and creative (thoughts create); thinking is effortful engagement that is heavy and restrictive (thinking destroys). Lightness signals thought, heaviness signals thinking.

Q3 (T/F). Nguyen's recommended remedy for a bad mood is to replace negative thoughts with positive ones. A: False. Positive states are the default; reduce thinking rather than add pleasant thinking, since stress tracks the volume of thinking, not its content.

Q4 (SA). What are the Three Principles and which analogy explains them?

A: Universal Mind, Universal Consciousness, Universal Thought; the DVD analogy (Thought = DVD, Consciousness = TV and player, Mind = electricity).

Q5 (SA). Why can't you just fight thinking, and what is the alternative?

A: Fighting is quicksand and filtering or boiling stirs the murky water. Awareness that "this is thinking" lets it settle; oscillation is normal and progress is measured by recovery speed.

Q6 (MC). A goal that feels heavy, urgent, "HAVE to," and aimed at something beyond itself is:

a) an inspiration goal b) a desperation (means) goal c) an unconditional creation d) a divine download

A: b.

Q7 (SA). Why does Nguyen say reasons make love and creation conditional, and what do you gain by dropping them?

A: Every reason is a condition under which love or creation could stop. Create or love with no reason and the feelings you were chasing (security, love, fulfillment) arrive immediately rather than being postponed.

Q8 (SA). Walk through the chain from deciding to acting on intuition.

A: Own the what, surrender the how and when, enter non-thinking, receive a thought with knowingness (usually irrational and pointing into the unknown), meet the fear by recalling it is only thinking, act, and take the next revealed step.

Q9 (SA). Name two Zen stories from the book and the point each makes.

A: The empty boat (nothing external angers you without your reaction) and Heaven and Hell (the distance between rage and peace is one moment of awareness). Also acceptable: empty your cup (a full mind has no room for insight).

Q10 (T/F). After first experiencing peace, doubts like "I've lost my edge" mean the approach is failing. A: False. This is the ego and the unfamiliar-peace trap; label it, stay, pre-load inspiration goals, and use an activation ritual. Remembering faster, not never relapsing, is the measure.

Arguments & Evidence

Don't Believe Everything You Think: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Joseph Nguyen

Each chapter (or group of closely related chapters) has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (the anecdotes, parables, and exercises used), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the chapter files in the nguyen-dont-believe-everything skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording. Note: the book's evidence is experiential and spiritual (the Three Principles tradition), not empirical; there are no studies, and numbers are few.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Ch 1-2 argue that suffering (as opposed to pain) is optional and that its root cause is our own thinking, since we live in a world of thought rather than reality. Ch 3-4 explain why the mind thinks (survival) and draw the book's central line between thoughts, which create, and thinking, which destroys. Ch 5-6 argue positive states are the default and ground it in the Three Principles. Ch 7-8 give the method (awareness, letting the water settle) and tie non-thinking to flow and peak performance. Ch 9-10 apply it to goals, love, and creation. Ch 11-12 deal with what comes after peace and with the idea that nothing is inherently good or bad. Ch 13-15 show how to decide, follow intuition, and create space for insight. Ch 16-17 cover obstacles and the closing message that you are always one thought away. Ch 18 turns it into practical guides.

Ch 1. The Journey to Finding the Root Cause of Suffering

Argument: Pain is unavoidable, but suffering (psychological and emotional distress) is optional, and no amount of external self-improvement stops it until you understand how the mind creates experience.

Stories & evidence

  • The two arrows (Buddhist teaching): the event is the first arrow; your reaction is the second.
  • Nguyen's own search: hundreds of books, a psychology study, therapy, shadow work, meditation, retreats, diet and schedule overhauls (including 4 a.m. routines and personality typing). He still had daily anxiety, irritation, and heaviness, and felt he had lost more than he began with. The turning point was a mentor pointing him to how experience is generated from thinking.
  • Thich Nhat Hanh epigraph: people prefer familiar suffering to unknown peace.

Key numbers: none in the notes ("hundreds of books" is the only quantity).

So what: Separate pain from suffering first. If you have "tried everything," the missing piece is likely understanding rather than effort, and stacking more techniques only adds effort.

Ch 2. The Root Cause of All Suffering

Argument: We live in a world of thought, not reality. Feelings come from our thinking about events, so the root cause of all psychological suffering is our own thinking.

Stories & evidence

  • Inside-out model: event, then your thinking/meaning, then your feeling. The same object (money, politics, a job) gets described 100 ways by 100 people, so the variance proves the feeling is generated internally.
  • The living-room test: fuming about work while relaxing at home shows the job is not the cause.
  • The coffee-shop pair: same room, same smell, one person in crisis and one at peace.
  • Sydney Banks: "Thought is not reality, yet it is through thought that our realities are created."
  • The Empty Boat (Zen story): a young monk flees noise, rows to the middle of a lake, and on day three a boat rams his. He yells, gets no reply, rises in fury, and finds the boat empty. The anger evaporates; he returns to the noisy monastery and meditates in peace.
  • "Who would you be without that thought?" (adapted from Byron Katie): a one-minute inquiry.

Key numbers: one minute for the inquiry; 100 people in the thought experiment (illustrative).

So what: Don't try to fix the outside to fix the inside. Test any "this makes me feel X" belief by asking whether everyone would feel the same, and remember you are always one thought away from a different experience.

Ch 3. Why Do We Even Think?

Argument: The mind evolved for survival, not fulfillment. Its threat-scanning and scenario-building were adaptive in the wild but leave modern humans in permanent fight-or-flight.

Stories & evidence

  • Threat scanning: the mind surveys surroundings and replays memories to forecast hypothetical dangers.
  • Smoke-detector image that also imagines future fires from past ones, and the "bush with a predator, or a thought about one?" check.
  • Innocent misunderstanding: inner conflict comes from not knowing the mind's only duty is survival.

Key numbers: none.

So what: Don't ask the mind for what it can't give. Thank it, relieve it of duty, and stop taking its alarms as truth; freedom comes from going beyond the mind, not perfecting it.

Ch 4. Thoughts vs. Thinking

Argument: Thoughts (nouns) are effortless raw material that arrives from beyond you; thinking (verb) is the effortful act of engaging with them. Thoughts create, thinking destroys, and thinking is the root of suffering.

Stories & evidence

  • The 5x income experiment: ask your dream yearly income and an answer surfaces in seconds (a thought). Multiply by 5 and sit with it for a minute: "no way," "nobody in my family earns that," "wanting that is greedy" (thinking), bringing self-doubt, unworthiness, and guilt. Repeat with "how could I make that?" and ideas pop in effortlessly until you start evaluating them.
  • Thought vs. Thinking chart: source (Universe vs. ego), weight (light vs. heavy), quality (infinite and creative vs. limited and destructive), emotion (love, alive vs. fear, stress), belief, sense (wholeness vs. separateness), effort (effortless vs. laborious).
  • Seeds and herbicide image.

Key numbers: multiply by 5; one minute of sitting with it.

So what: Keep the first spontaneous answer and drop the cascade that follows. Use heaviness versus lightness as radar; you cannot stop thoughts, but you can stop thinking about them.

Ch 5. Don't We Need to Think Positively to Feel Good?

Argument: No. We only feel negative emotion when we are thinking. Joy, love, and peace are the natural default, and the amount of thinking, not its content, sets stress intensity.

Stories & evidence

  • Paired-recall exercise: recall 2-3 memories of extreme stress and 2-3 of peak joy or love, noting how much thinking was running. Result: heavy thinking in the first set, near-silence in the second.
  • Thought-o-meter: a speedometer of thoughts per minute; red zone is burnout, fury, panic.
  • Unconditioned baby as the picture of the factory default; sun-and-clouds image.

Key numbers: 2-3 memories per set; negative intensity scales with thinking volume, positive intensity with its inverse (conceptual, not measured).

So what: Don't add positive thinking, since it keeps the meter high. Reduce thinking and let the natural state surface; use stress level as a gauge of how much you are thinking, whatever the topic.

Ch 6. How the Human Experience Is Created: The Three Principles

Argument: All human experience is generated by Universal Mind, Universal Consciousness, and Universal Thought (Sydney Banks). Understanding them is itself the intervention.

Stories & evidence

  • Universal Mind: the intelligence in all things (acorn to tree, heart beating, wound healing); also called God, Source, Infinite Intelligence, Quantum Field.
  • Universal Consciousness: the awareness that lets us know we exist and perceive thought.
  • Universal Thought: the raw material of creation, the object consciousness perceives.
  • DVD analogy: Thought = the DVD, Consciousness = the TV and player, Mind = the electricity.
  • Lineage: Banks, Neill, Bailey (Nguyen's mentors and sources).

Key numbers: three principles.

So what: Trace any experience back: Thought (content), Consciousness (brings it alive), Mind (powers it). Treat felt separation as an illusion of thinking, and don't treat the principles as techniques.

Ch 7. How Do We Stop Thinking?

Argument: You can't eliminate thinking, but you can shrink time spent in it, and awareness ("this is just thinking") is the only tool required.

Stories & evidence

  • Murky water: cloudy water clears when left alone, not when filtered or boiled.
  • Quicksand: struggling tightens the grip; stillness lets natural buoyancy lift you.
  • Heaven and Hell (Zen parable): a samurai demands the master explain them. The master insults him; the samurai draws his sword in rage. "That's hell." He freezes, sees his own mind manufactured the rage, and bows. "And that's heaven."
  • Sun behind the night: peace is obscured, not lost.

Key numbers: four steps (notice the feeling, recognize "I'm thinking," don't fight it, let it settle).

So what: Don't filter, boil, or fight. Notice and wait, expect oscillation, and drop guilt about relapse since guilt is more thinking.

Ch 8. How Can We Thrive Without Thinking?

Argument: Peak performance is the state of non-thinking. Flow, "the zone," and mushin describe doing your best work with no thinking present; thinking only adds hesitation, doubt, and fear after training is complete.

Stories & evidence

  • Guided inquiry: "When you're doing your absolute best work, what thoughts are running through your head?" Sit 30-60 seconds; nearly everyone reports none. The chapter relies on this first-person evidence more than on athlete anecdotes.
  • Mushin (no mind): free of random thoughts, anger, fear, and ego; action from trained instinct.
  • James Clear quote: "Anxiety is thought without control. Flow is control without thought."

Key numbers: 30-60 seconds of reflection.

So what: Train hard, then execute without thinking. Don't adopt it as a belief; test it in your next task.

Ch 9. What About Goals, Dreams & Ambitions?

Argument: Non-thinking doesn't end ambition; it changes its source. Goals come from inspiration (thought) or desperation (thinking), and the source determines whether pursuit is joyful or miserable.

Stories & evidence

  • The desperation loop: a "realistic" goal built from past data, then scarcity and urgency, then hunting for faster methods, then achievement and emptiness within days (the text says "within hours" in one place and "days" in another), then a bigger desperate goal after seeing others do the same.
  • Means vs. end goals: quit job to escape stress; $1M for freedom.
  • Children's wild ambitions as the unblocked default; painters paint, writers write, parents have kids to share overflow.
  • The Infinite-Resources Question: infinite money, already traveled the world, no fear, no recognition: what would you create?
  • The dam: thinking blocks the river of inspiration.

Key numbers: three tests (thought or thinking, light or heavy, means or end); four conditions in the question.

So what: Keep your ambitions, change their source. Act on the first answer to the question, not on the critique of it.

Ch 10. Unconditional Love & Creation

Argument: Love with reasons is conditional and has built-in conditions for withdrawal. Unconditional love and creation flow from inner abundance with no reason, and deliver immediately the feelings we chase through conditional goals.

Stories & evidence

  • Nguyen and Makenna: he asks why she loves him ("I don't know, I just do, a lot"). He lists fifty reasons for loving her and is bothered for years that she can't reciprocate. Asking whether he would stop loving her if she stopped laughing or helping people shows the reasons were never the cause.
  • Feelings are the real goal: money for security, family time for love, meaningful work for fulfillment; all feelings, generated internally.
  • Contract-clause image: each reason is a clause that could be breached.

Key numbers: fifty reasons (Nguyen's list).

So what: Drop the "because" in love and in work. Create for no reason and feel the feelings now rather than postponing them.

Ch 11. What Do You Do After Experiencing Peace?

Argument: After tasting peace, worry and doubt often return as the ego reasserts itself plus a surplus of freed energy. The remedy is to channel that energy into inspiration goals and shorten recovery time rather than prevent relapse.

Stories & evidence

  • Snake-and-rope reflex: the initial fear is unpreventable, but seeing through the illusion is always available.
  • "Lost my edge" as a common ego tactic.
  • Water under pressure: give it a channel or it floods the old riverbed.
  • Object in motion stays in motion: start the day in non-thinking.

Key numbers: none.

So what: Pre-write inspiration goals, build a morning activation ritual (not phone or email first), and measure success by how fast you remember.

Ch 12. Nothing Is Either Good or Bad

Argument: Right/wrong and good/bad are categories manufactured by thinking; they create duality and conditions that dictate how you feel. Look for what is universally true instead of who is right.

Stories & evidence

  • 88 piano keys: no key is wrong, only wrong relative to an assumed song.
  • Mountain trail vantage points: none wrong, each reveals a different view.
  • Opposing political parties as different keys, not wrong keys.
  • Universal truth test: if it holds for one person but not another, it is thinking.

Key numbers: 88 keys.

So what: Treat negative emotion as a flag for misunderstanding, not a verdict. When triggered, remember the cause is thinking, don't resist, let it pass.

Ch 13. How Do You Know What to Do Without Thinking?

Argument: You almost always already know what to do; fear and self-doubt make it feel otherwise. Decide from intuition, not pros/cons lists and external polling.

Stories & evidence

  • Know that you already know: recognize the known answer, or trust that it will come.
  • Weight-loss test: you already know the formula; not-knowing is really fear.
  • Inner GPS: guarantees the destination, reroutes in real time.
  • Henry Ford's line: "whether you think you can or can't, you're right."
  • Pros/cons lists and asking everyone (including the pets) as the anti-pattern.

Key numbers: none.

So what: Remove fear first, then ask whether you truly don't know. Expect society not to confirm early; be wary of mentors who don't point you inward.

Ch 14. How to Follow Your Intuition

Argument: Intuition is available only in the present moment and only in non-thinking. It arrives as thoughts, usually defies logic, and lives in the unknown, which is why it feels frightening and why it is the only place anything new can come from.

Stories & evidence

  • The manifesting loop: decide the what with imagination, enter non-thinking, receive a thought (talk to the stranger, call the friend, put your work out publicly), feel fear, recall it is only thinking, act, and then see the next step.
  • Highest achievers: Nguyen notes that the highest-achieving people he has asked attribute success to a higher power or luck, rather than sheer force.
  • Miracles: deals, people, money, and connections arriving "out of nowhere" in flow.
  • "To get what you don't have, do what you haven't done."

Key numbers: none.

So what: Own the what, surrender the how. Take one step at a time; faith is structurally required.

Ch 15. Creating Space for Miracles

Argument: Everything comes from nothing; new thoughts need empty space, and a mind full of old thinking can't receive them. Non-thinking makes the space and the answer arrives as a divine download.

Stories & evidence

  • Empty your cup: the Zen master overfilling the scholar's teacup.
  • Edison's steel balls: he dozed holding them; when they dropped and woke him, the solution was there.
  • Einstein's violin: stop working, play, let the answer arrive.
  • Rest as results: athletes gain strength in recovery, not during the workout.
  • Einstein-quote logic: old thinking can't solve the problems it created.

Key numbers: a 3-step process.

So what: When stuck, run the download process: aware of thinking, create space and surrender the how and when, meet it with love. Simple, not easy.

Ch 16. Potential Obstacles When Living in Non-Thinking

Argument: Sustained peace feels unfamiliar, and the brain treats unfamiliar as unsafe, so just when things go well the mind sells you the idea that something is wrong. Faith in the unknown is the counter.

Stories & evidence

  • Mind as greatest salesman: pitches like "you've lost your edge" and "you're lazy."
  • Phishing-email image for "something must be wrong, I feel too good."
  • Productivity claim: humans are most productive when happy and not thinking; tasks feel easier and people gravitate to you.
  • The Choice: free and happy in the unknown, or confined and suffering in the familiar.

Key numbers: none.

So what: Expect the attack when you feel best, label it, stay long enough to see results, and relapse without guilt.

Ch 17. Now What?

Argument: The end is the beginning: once an insight is seen it can't be unseen, and expanded consciousness doesn't contract. You will forget and think again; remembering is all that's required.

Stories & evidence

  • Irreversible insight and "read for insight, not information" (from the introduction).
  • The world's advertising: constant messaging that you're not enough; others' opinions are their innocent thinking.
  • Emanation: people ask why you've changed before you explain.

Key numbers: none.

So what: Remember you are one thought away, treat simplicity as the truth-test, embody rather than evangelize, and know that what you seek is already inside you.

Ch 18. Summary of Non-Thinking & Practical Guides (Appendix)

Argument: Philosophy becomes practice through environment-level and moment-level guides: remove triggers before adding practices, restructure work by energy, and treat habits as beliefs to inquire into.

Stories & evidence

  • Moment-level framework: realize thinking is the root, create space for persistent negative feeling (you are the sacred space holding it, not the feeling), acknowledge it and let it pass.
  • Obstacles: clinging to thinking ("what got you here won't get you there"), insufficient faith, fear.
  • Trigger audit across four categories: Physical Health, Physical Environment, Digital Environment, Digital Consumption.
  • Non-thinking environment guide and activation ritual; daily decompression space (walk, journal, nap, yoga, pets, meditation).
  • Work ledger: rate activities 1-10, eliminate drainers.
  • Destructive-habit inquiry: nine steps, centered on "Is it absolutely 100% true?"
  • Non-thinking tell: peace, love, joy, passion, inspiration; loss of time, space, self.

Key numbers: 80% of work time on 9-10 activities; cut 1-3 drainers per week; 1-10 scale; four trigger categories; nine habit-inquiry steps; 1-10 "how much did I think today" prompt.

So what: Start small, remove before adding, measure work by energy, and change habits by dismantling the belief rather than using willpower.

Recurring Stories & Images

  • The two arrows: pain versus suffering (Ch 1).
  • The empty boat: the monk on the lake (Ch 2).
  • Zen parables: Heaven and Hell (Ch 7), empty your cup (Ch 15).
  • Water images: murky water that clears when left alone, and quicksand (Ch 7); the dam on the river of inspiration (Ch 9); water under pressure (Ch 11).
  • The 5x income experiment (Ch 4) and the Infinite-Resources Question (Ch 9).
  • Nguyen and Makenna: fifty reasons for love (Ch 10).
  • 88 piano keys (Ch 12) and inner GPS (Ch 13).
  • Edison's steel balls and Einstein's violin (Ch 15).
  • Snake and rope (Ch 11) and the ego's phishing email (Ch 16).
  • The DVD analogy for the Three Principles (Ch 6).

Expect to Win: 10 Proven Strategies for Thriving in the Workplace

2 markdown files

Quiz

Expect to Win Quiz Book

Expect to Win: 10 Proven Strategies for Thriving in the Workplace by Carla A. Harris

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a chapter section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative 10-question final exam is at the end. Built only from the harris-expect-to-win skill notes, not the book's own wording.

Chapter 1: Authenticity — The Power Is You

Q1 (SA). Why does Harris call your authentic self your competitive advantage?

A: You were hired because your specific combination of skills, personality, and values beat every other candidate ("someone else didn't get the job that day because you were the best candidate"). Impersonating someone else gives that advantage away, and bringing the real you is the source of the confidence that makes clients buy, colleagues trust, and bosses promote.

Q2 (T/F). Authenticity means wearing whatever you like regardless of the firm's culture.

A: False. Authenticity transcends the personality: it means choosing an environment whose written and unwritten rules (attire, expected skill profile, persona) you can honestly satisfy, then owning that choice. If meeting them would be a constant struggle, you are in the wrong seat.

Q3 (SA). What is the elevator speech and what is it built from?

A: A ready-at-all-times statement of who you are, what you are good at, and what you want in the organization, deliverable in an elevator ride. It comes from your strengths/weaknesses list and your answer to why you are in this profession, firm, and seat.

Q4 (MC). When preparing for a client, Harris says to ask:

a) What will my colleagues think of my delivery? b) What does the client need, what would I worry about in their shoes, and do they need educating or convincing? c) How can I fit in more slides? d) How can I sound like the senior banker?

A: b. The aim is to turn a presentation into a conversation: "When you can turn a presentation into a conversation, you have won the battle of converting a client."

Q5 (SA). What did the stories of Marissa and Peter illustrate?

A: Marissa, a Spanish-speaking Latina, suppressed her identity so thoroughly that leadership never considered her for the Latin America role she was best qualified for. Peter was charismatic and influential outside the office but quiet and credit-avoiding inside; eighteen years in, he had no promotion in eight. Both show the cost of splitting or hiding yourself.

Q6 (SA). What is the "wrong building" diagnosis, and what did Anne do about it?

A: The ladder leaning against the wrong building: a fundamental mismatch between your inspirations and the firm's success model. Anne, a 17-year financial-marketing writer, kept her job, earned a journalism master's at night over 3.5 years, networked with publishers and editors, met an author needing a ghostwriter at an event hosted by her own firm, and became a freelance writer. The play: keep the paycheck, build transferable skills, network toward the new field, then jump.

Q7 (T/F). Preparing hard and then sitting silent in meetings is a safe way to avoid mistakes.

A: False. It reads as "does she even have a clue?" and stalls promotion; it was Carla's own early mistake.

Chapter 2: Be the Architect of Your Own Agenda

Q1 (SA). What goes into the personal career agenda?

A: A written plan with (a) broad macro career goals, (b) specific micro goals for the current seat (skills, experiences, people), (c) compensation and promotion targets, and (d) a timeline, including how long you want to stay.

Q2 (SA). What is the agenda's main function when a setback or an offer arrives?

A: It is a decision filter that takes the emotion out of decisions (stay or quit after a missed promotion) and lets you self-motivate. The agenda fixes the goals; the strategy stays flexible.

Q3 (MC). Harris says industry norms such as 3–4 years to VP and 8–12 to MD should be treated as:

a) law b) a guide, not law c) irrelevant d) a promise from HR

A: b. Comparative pay data should be used only to catch egregious inequality, not marginal differences.

Q4 (SA). What is the "they" syndrome and what replaces it?

A: Explaining a stalled career with "they did this, they won't…," which makes you a victim and gives away your power. Replace it with "What did I do to contribute?" (not enough exposure, too few supporting relationships, no homework on how the organization works, waiting for projects rather than pursuing them).

Q5 (SA). Walk through Sherry's mistake-recovery conversation.

A: After a costly naked-short error on an emerging-markets deal, with her boss repeatedly resurfacing it in meetings, she took him aside and (1) owned the mistake without hedging, (2) stated the lesson (never again make a solo judgment when she knew she needed help), (3) said she had learned it and it was time to move on, and (4) asked for his explicit support going forward. He affirmed her, offered coaching, and never mentioned it in a meeting again.

Q6 (SA). Explain "political maniac vs. workhorse" and the key rule about them.

A: Political maniacs work relationships and the system; workhorses follow rules, out-work everyone, and rise on merit. People value the opposite type but reward their own, so align with a boss of your type. "Being valued and being rewarded are two different things."

Q7 (T/F). An off-line role (no direct client contact or revenue) is generally a career dead end.

A: False. It can be the fastest route to senior exposure; Carla's operations-officer stint produced a future president of Morgan Stanley as her sponsor.

Chapter 3: You Are the Captain of Your Career — The Ninety-Day Rule

Q1 (SA). What three things does an organization assess, and which is most decisive?

A: Can do (ability), will do (motivation, teamwork, follow-through), and fit. Fit is the most subjective and most decisive.

Q2 (SA). What are the three deliverables of the ninety-day rule?

A: (1) Learn the basic skill needed to perform the job, (2) learn the unspoken rules of the game (the informal politics), (3) identify the pertinent players and the key relationships you must develop.

Q3 (T/F). "No one taught me" is an acceptable reason for a skills gap in your first year.

A: False. The organization never accepts it; it reads as lack of initiative. Training is offered, not pushed, so seek it internally, externally, or teach yourself.

Q4 (MC). Which is the best way to open a day-91 check-in?

a) "How am I doing?" b) "I've attained proficiency in A, B, C; next quarter I plan D, E, F. Is there anything you'd add or change?" c) Wait for the annual review. d) Ask for a raise.

A: b. Simply asking "How am I doing?" signals insecurity.

Q5 (SA). What is the halo effect and what is the flip side?

A: A strong first-quarter impression means your work is assumed right until proven otherwise and mistakes get the benefit of the doubt. A weak one means every assignment becomes an exercise in proving yourself and you are excluded from the meaty, developmental projects that create stars.

Q6 (SA). What did Carla do about the group's social rhythms and hours?

A: She adopted the group's hours (late nights in M&A, 7 a.m. starts in capital markets) because that is where rapport is built. When the group's conversation was sports, she phoned her sports-fan father every Sunday to learn enough to open Monday's conversation. If not invited to lunch or drinks, invite yourself.

Q7 (SA). What question should you ask the decision-maker, and why?

A: Ask your manager what, in their mind, is required for you to advance. It signals your intention to advance and gives you a concrete map from a decision-maker.

Chapter 4: Perception Is the Copilot to Reality

Q1 (SA). State Harris's perception formula and which half to change.

A: Perception = self-presentation + the baggage of the beholder. Change self-presentation (behavior, speech, dress), because it is infinitely easier to change.

Q2 (SA). What are the "three adjectives" and the two constraints on choosing them?

A: The words you want people to use to describe you when you are not in the room (because every major decision is made without you). They must be true of you and valued by the organization's business model.

Q3 (SA). How do you find which adjectives your firm values?

A: What recruiters said they were hiring for; the annual report, marketing literature, and website; and asking "How does my company make money? What skills does it value? Why am I relevant to the product/profit equation?"

Q4 (SA). Describe Carla's "tough" campaign.

A: After being told "I don't know if you're tough enough," she worked tough into nearly every sentence and acted congruently for about three months ("You'd better make sure it's right, because you know I'm tough!") until a VP was overheard warning his team to double-check assumptions because "Carla Harris is so tough."

Q5 (MC). The fan/non-fan feedback audit involves:

a) 1 fan b) 2–3 non-fans and 2–3 fans, with non-fans met over coffee as equals c) only your boss d) an anonymous survey

A: b. Whose perception to fix first: the boss's, because it is the hardest to change and the most influential.

Q6 (T/F). The associate who wanted VP was promoted mainly because she dressed like the women officers.

A: False, and Carla warns you can't dress your way to success. Her objective record was already strong; dressing like the officers and holding a pre-meeting with her boss before group meetings supplied the missing subjective evidence of officer-level behavior.

Q7 (SA). Name some behaviors that create a negative perception.

A: Always soliciting opinions before deciding (indecisive), always saying why things won't work (not commercial), belittling others in meetings (a bully), and running from people who don't like you (the misperception hardens).

Chapter 5: The Mentor, the Sponsor, the Adviser

Q1 (SA). Define adviser, mentor, and sponsor.

A: Adviser: answers isolated career questions without knowing your broader agenda. Mentor: gives tailored developmental advice in the context of your strengths, weaknesses, and agenda, and hears the good, bad, and ugly. Sponsor: uses internal political and social capital to move your career, arguing your case behind closed doors ("carry your paper into the room").

Q2 (SA). What is the test for whether someone is a mentor or only an adviser?

A: If you are not comfortable sharing all the facts with them, they are an adviser. A company-assigned "mentor" is really an adviser until trust is earned.

Q3 (MC). A good sponsor must have:

a) seniority only b) a seat at the decision table in your functional area, political and social capital, and willingness to spend it on you c) a friendly manner d) membership in the same ethnic group

A: b. Ideally it is your boss; if not, your boss can be a bridge to someone who is.

Q4 (SA). What is the sponsor ROI?

A: Sponsors spend capital and expect a return, chiefly the credit and expanded power base of being associated with a star. Reciprocate with information, relationships, and support, without compromising your integrity.

Q5 (SA). What did Carla do before her 1999 managing-director promotion?

A: She realized she could not name who would passionately argue her case on the committee. She asked a senior MD with a seat on the committee directly, saying she needed someone to argue for her, specifically him, and that she would give him the strongest package. He agreed. She also recruited a second advocate without a seat but with influence over those who had one. She was promoted.

Q6 (T/F). Asking someone directly to sponsor you has no real downside.

A: True per Harris: a yes gets you an advocate, and a no gets you the reason the organization might not back you.

Q7 (SA). What should you secure when joining a firm or switching divisions, and how many?

A: Explicit sponsor commitments from at least two people, asked of those selling you hardest ("Who will sponsor me? Will you be a member of my success team?"). Your old sponsorship stays behind when you change divisions.

Chapter 6: Leverage Your Voice

Q1 (SA). What are the three functions of voice?

A: (1) Creates perception, (2) creates a level of expectation of your contribution, (3) creates the mechanism to articulate your expectations of the organization.

Q2 (SA). Explain the 50/50 rule and the fix.

A: Before you speak, a first-time observer gives you 50/50 odds of being smart or not. Silence lets the coin land on "stupid." Say something in every meeting; if you have nothing to add, paraphrase what someone else said.

Q3 (SA). How should you answer when you're unsure in front of a client or senior?

A: Confidently, with room to adjust: "In my judgment the answer is X, Y, Z, but I'll double-check a couple of sources and get back to you." Speak audibly, since a drop in volume is the tell of uncertainty. Visible doubt destroys credibility.

Q4 (MC). The two-thirds evaluation rule says a review should be:

a) all about last year b) one-third lessons from last year and two-thirds next-year aspirations, needs, and timelines c) two-thirds complaints d) skipped

A: b. Goals carry timelines (3–6 months for most items), and you should ask for next year's promotion this year.

Q5 (SA). What was the "eureka year"?

A: In a tough year with cutbacks, Carla worked hard, said nothing about wanting promotion, and wasn't promoted. Her boss said peers had been pleading their cases for months and she had been silent. Lesson: in marginal decisions, the person who voiced expectations wins the tie.

Q6 (SA). What was the "yes, uh-huh" discipline and its result?

A: Told that her boss hated giving her feedback because "she has an answer for everything," she responded in the next review only with acknowledgments ("yes," "uh-huh," "oh really? okay"). The feedback became specific, and the relationship evolved from manager to adviser to sponsor.

Q7 (T/F). Keeping your head down is a safe strategy.

A: False: "Keeping your head down doesn't keep you from getting shot; it only increases the chances that you won't see the bullet coming."

Chapter 7: Have a Penchant for Taking Risks

Q1 (SA). State Harris's success equation.

A: Achieving success and moving ahead = performing extremely well + aligning with internal politics + taking risks.

Q2 (SA). Distinguish latent risk from forward risk.

A: Latent risk is out of your control and untied to your performance (takeover, division sold, sponsor leaving abruptly, a mismatched role). Forward risk is a chosen action with an uncertain outcome that leaves you better off regardless (skills, experience, finances, positioning). Stacking forward risks builds a platform to navigate latent shocks.

Q3 (MC). Which risk type fits "I know the outcome I want but not how I'll get there"?

a) Calculated b) Studied c) Step-out-on-faith d) Latent

A: c. Reserve it for when you are the primary person affected and repercussions on others are very small.

Q4 (SA). What are the three "test the waters" questions, and the decision rule?

A: (1) Will it give me skills and experience I wouldn't get staying in my seat for the next twelve months? (2) Will it expose me to people and relationships I wouldn't otherwise reach? (3) Will it create new branches on my decision tree? Three yeses means take it.

Q5 (SA). When should you take a studied risk?

A: When the action is clear but reactions can't all be anticipated, the upside must be markedly greater than the downside. (Example: Carla recommended postponing an oversubscribed Internet IPO; the next day NASDAQ fell over 100 points, and the client returned months later and priced successfully.)

Q6 (T/F). Declining an opportunity carries no risk.

A: False. Declining is also a risk (annoying the boss, losing an accelerator). Do it with a solid rationale ready and willingness to accept repercussions, as Carla did when she declined the new retail-distribution effort in her MD year and was promoted.

Q7 (SA). What does F-E-A-R stand for and what is the "predecessor rule"?

A: False Evidence Appearing Real. Predecessor rule: "If you're doing your job the way your predecessor was doing it, you, too, will likely soon find yourself a predecessor."

Chapter 8: Power in the Network

Q1 (SA). Name the four relationship types.

A: Upward (boss and higher), lateral (peers and the assistants of senior people), downward (junior people), and external (nonprofit boards, other-firm colleagues, entrepreneurs, headhunters, clergy, and so on).

Q2 (SA). Where does a network's power come from?

A: Relationship strength, how you manage it, and the role you play (connector, information gatherer, or helpful person), not the number of business cards.

Q3 (MC). The recommended cadence for your most important relationships is:

a) one e-mail a year b) one face-to-face plus four voice-to-voice contacts a year c) daily calls d) only at promotion time

A: b. Other relationships get e-mail updates that include what you are doing and your future goals.

Q4 (SA). Why does Harris emphasize assistants?

A: The assistant is closest to a CEO/CFO/COO, controls access, knows the mood and the best moment to approach, and can frame your request favorably. Ignoring or being rude to one is a career derailer. Honor everyone's power.

Q5 (SA). How did Carla produce her first CD through her network?

A: She took a banker-musician colleague to lunch; he mapped the steps and introduced a colleague with a recording studio, who introduced a Broadway musical director who agreed to produce after an audition. A senior internal sponsor walked her to a music-label CEO for distribution. Every link was a relationship she already had.

Q6 (T/F). You are competing with your peers, so you should avoid asking them for help.

A: False. Asking a peer for help starts a long-term relationship; you compete with yourself ("there is plenty of room at the top"); "don't hate, gravitate" toward the peer who is ahead.

Chapter 9: Balance Is a Necessity

Q1 (SA). How does Harris redefine balance?

A: Not work versus family, but integrating your passions and giving back into your professional life.

Q2 (SA). What happens without something outside the job that makes you feel alive?

A: "Your life becomes a function of somebody else's day" (the boss's mood, a deal's outcome, a Friday disagreement). Professional life will never consistently fulfill you.

Q3 (MC). To "calendarize," Harris suggests:

a) quitting email b) mapping a typical day, taking two lunches a week for something joyful, and batching reading and e-mail into fixed blocks c) working later d) delegating everything

A: b. This is "congregate like actions": e-mail only in several fixed half-hour slots.

Q4 (T/F). Honoring your passions at work is a distraction that hurts your career.

A: False. In Carla's case, the gospel CDs and Carnegie Hall concerts produced a Sunday New York Times Business feature (CD released 2000) and a half-page Wall Street Journal story (2006), raised her standing with clients, and opened new relationships.

Q5 (SA). Why is giving back part of the success equation?

A: It is a duty of gratitude and its own reward, but it also refuels you, keeps you humble, reminds you why you work hard, and unplanned builds client relationships and visibility ("You never know who may be sitting in the chair next to you at that nonprofit board meeting").

Chapter 10: Expect to Win

Q1 (SA). Contrast "know," "maybe," and "hope."

A: At eighteen Carla knew she'd get into Harvard, HBS, and a top Wall Street firm. After bad deals and disappointing pay, her language slid to maybe and hope: "mediocre thoughts, mediocre results." The fix is to tell yourself daily that you know it will happen, and act "as if" until you believe it.

Q2 (SA). List the five principles of the winner's lens.

A: (1) Identify the best outcome early and devise a strategy; (2) fearlessness: either the goal is achieved or a valuable lesson is learned; (3) assume everything works out for your good; (4) goals can't be reached alone, so engage in interdependent relationships; (5) acquire the skills to be the best, a positive outlier.

Q3 (SA). What are the four sheets of the annual reflection?

A: Who have I been this year? Who do I want to be? What lessons have I learned this year? What do I want to accomplish in the next year? Include weaknesses; write in third person if it's hard.

Q4 (MC). When you feel low, the lift-someone-up reset says to:

a) wait it out b) ask what you can do today for somebody else to lift them up c) quit d) vent to peers

A: b. Posture and attitude follow, and power is reclaimed.

Q5 (T/F). Winners are motivated mainly when things are going well.

A: False. "Selectively motivated" (working hard and smart only when things go well) is the trait Harris says winners lack.

Q6 (SA). What is the sign of complacency and the response?

A: Work has become rote and effortless. Time for a new challenge or a new place; return to the agenda and ask whether you are getting the experiences, people, and lifestyle you came for.

Chapter 11: My Most Precious Pearl

Q1 (SA). What is the "eleventh pearl"?

A: Know not only who you are but whose you are. For Harris it is her Christian faith ("I am a child of God"); for any reader, something over and above the job to turn to for strength, guidance, and comfort.

Q2 (SA). What is "lesson or blessing"?

A: Every career event is one or the other, and both are to be leveraged to keep moving forward and upward ("Consider it all good").

Q3 (SA). What should you do if you can't give your best?

A: Identify the problem (not challenged, not motivated, treated unfairly), apply your tools (intelligence, experience, faith, the pearls), find the solution, and hand the remainder over.

Q4 (MC). In Harris's mapping, Romans 8:28 stands for:

a) No challenge is insurmountable b) Even when things look bad, they will work out for my benefit c) I need not fight alone d) Don't worry about anything

A: b. (Philippians 4:13 is the insurmountable-challenge verse, Hebrews 13:5 is "no battle alone," and Philippians 4:6–8 is "don't worry.")

Q5 (SA). How did the faith practice begin?

A: As a second-year associate under an insecure manager uninterested in training her, she was told by a close friend's mother to read and pray Psalm 91 and Psalm 4 daily. These became a mantra, then "armor," and the start of using faith deliberately as a tool.

Q6 (T/F). Hard work guarantees the assignment, promotion, or platform on your timeline.

A: False. That is the belief her early career dismantled; things like timing and others' decisions are beyond control, so you need a resource for them.

Cumulative Final Exam (10 questions)

F1 (SA). Harris says no organization is a true meritocracy. Why, and what does she add to hard work and intelligence?

A: Because people evaluate people. She adds strategy, relationships, politics, tenacity, and faith.

F2 (SA). Give the success equation and say which chapter's ideas map onto each term (performance, politics, risk).

A: Moving ahead = performing extremely well + aligning with internal politics + taking risks. Performance is supported by Ch 3 (ninety days, skills); politics by Ch 2 (ecosystem), Ch 3 (unspoken rules), and Ch 5/8 (sponsors, network); risk is Ch 7.

F3 (MC). Which pair correctly names Ch 3's and Ch 4's key tools?

a) Ninety-day rule; three adjectives b) Four-sheet reflection; 50/50 rule c) Elevator speech; test-the-waters d) Calendarize; lens

A: a.

F4 (SA). Compare the "they" syndrome (Ch 2) with the "selectively motivated" trap (Ch 10). What do both give up?

A: Both forfeit power and agency: blaming others makes you passive and a victim; working hard only when things go well makes motivation conditional. The cure in each is to focus on what you control (what did I contribute; show up with your best self every day).

F5 (T/F). The three adjectives you choose should be whatever the firm values most, even if untrue of you.

A: False. They must be true of you and valued by the business model; untrue adjectives lead to burnout and an inconsistent perception.

F6 (SA). How do silence and the 50/50 rule (Ch 6) connect to the "smart or stupid?" perception (Ch 1 and 4)?

A: Submerging yourself out of fear creates the perception "I don't know if she's smart or stupid." Silence lets the 50/50 coin land on "stupid," so speaking in every meeting (even a paraphrase) shapes perception.

F7 (SA). What are the sponsor's three criteria and the two-commitment rule?

A: A seat at the decision table in your functional area, political and social capital, and willingness to spend it on you (ideally your boss, or a bridge to someone). Get explicit commitments from at least two people before joining or switching divisions.

F8 (MC). An offer pays the same as your current job but is bigger. Per the cheatsheet, you should:

a) refuse because pay is equal b) take it as a platform to argue for pay and authority later c) ask permission first d) consult no one

A: b. (Similarly, a better-paid move at another firm is compensated risk; take it.)

F9 (SA). Name three ways Carla's outside passions (singing, faith, giving back) helped her career, across Ch 1, 8, 9, and 11.

A: Passions are relationship bridges (Ch 1); her network helped produce her first CD, which became a conversation piece with clients (Ch 8); the CDs and Carnegie Hall concerts, with proceeds to two schools, earned New York Times and Wall Street Journal coverage and rising standing with clients (Ch 9); faith is her steady constant through uncontrollable events (Ch 11).

F10 (SA). Give four timing/number rules from the book.

A: Any four of: 90 days to prove value, with day 91 advertising points on the board; 3 adjectives; about 3 months to install or overwrite a perception; 2–3 fans plus 2–3 non-fans in an audit; one-third lessons and two-thirds aspirations in an evaluation; check-ins every 2 months, report card done by month 6; 8–10 mentor touches per year; 1 face-to-face plus 4 calls a year for key contacts; 2 sponsor commitments; 2 lunch hours a week for passions; perform at the next level 6–12 months before you want the title.

Arguments & Evidence

Expect to Win: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Carla A. Harris

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (the anecdotes and cases the book uses), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter, glossary, patterns, and cheatsheet files in the harris-expect-to-win skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording. The book is a practitioner's advice book: its evidence is mostly Harris's own stories and others' cases, not studies.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Harris's premise is that no organization is a true meritocracy, because people evaluate people, so hard work and intelligence are necessary but not sufficient. Ch 1–2 lay the foundation: be your authentic self and write your own career agenda. Ch 3–4 cover how you are judged: the first ninety days and the perceptions people form of you. Ch 5–6 cover the people and the voice that move you forward: sponsors, mentors, advisers, and speaking up and asking. Ch 7–8 add the other terms of the success equation (risk) and the network that carries you. Ch 9–11 turn inward: integrating passions and giving back, expecting to win, and knowing whose you are, the faith that steadies you when timing and others' decisions are out of your control.

Ch 1. Authenticity: The Power Is You

Argument: You were hired because your particular combination of skills, personality, and values beat every other candidate; that is your only durable competitive advantage. Impersonating others or staying silent to seem safe spends mental capacity, reads as lack of confidence, and costs promotions. Authenticity also means choosing an environment whose written and unwritten rules you can honestly meet.

Stories & evidence

  • Carla's turnaround pitch: after repeated "flat and rote" feedback, she prepared around the client (what do they need, what would I worry about in their shoes, educate or convince?) and held a conversation with a Fortune 500 CEO, CFO, COO, and head of HR, backed by a colleague who spent political capital to get her in. The CFO called the senior banker the next day with rave reviews. "The real Carla was my best competitive weapon."
  • Marissa: a Spanish-speaking Latina who suppressed her identity so fully that leadership never considered her for the Latin America role.
  • Peter: charismatic outside, quiet inside; eighteen years in, no promotion in eight.
  • Anne: 17 years writing financial marketing, good reviews, no passion; kept her job, earned a journalism master's at night over 3.5 years, networked, met an author needing a ghostwriter at an event hosted by her own firm, and became a freelance writer.
  • Carla's own early mistake: preparing hard and then sitting silent in meetings, and losing confidence under an insecure boss.

Key numbers: 12–24 months for a deliberate plan if you are in the wrong seat; 3.5 years for Anne's degree.

So what: Know your strengths, weaknesses, and why you are in this seat (the elevator speech). Prepare for clients around their needs and aim for conversation. Bring outside interests to work as relationship bridges. If the building is wrong, build a plan rather than just a complaint.

Ch 2. Be the Architect of Your Own Agenda

Argument: Write a career agenda (macro goals, micro goals, compensation and promotion targets, a timeline) and use it as the decision filter for every setback and offer. The goals are fixed; the strategy flexes. Own mistakes once and move on, stop blaming "they," and line up with your corporate-ecosystem type.

Stories & evidence

  • Sherry's naked short: a largely self-taught associate guessed on share allocation, the stock rose, and covering cost the firm revenue. Her boss kept raising it for weeks. One conversation (own it, state the lesson, say it is time to move on, ask for support) ended it and earned coaching.
  • Carla's operations-officer stint: an off-line role that produced a future president of Morgan Stanley as her sponsor.
  • Gina: rejected a small new product judged on current revenue; waited six more years while the person who took it was promoted in three.
  • Hazel vs. Curtis: resenting a peer's earlier promotion when he had made sacrifices (Hong Kong, uprooting family) she chose not to make.
  • Carla's demeaning manager: she worked for him repeatedly because she did not know she could decline projects.
  • Political maniacs vs. workhorses: people value the opposite type but reward their own.

Key numbers: industry norms of 3–4 years to VP and 8–12 to MD (a guide, not law).

So what: Measure yourself against your own agenda, not a peer's report card. Swap "they" for "What did I contribute?" Say yes to unglamorous roles that buy exposure. Ask for the pay you deserve and what the top bracket requires. Engage decision-makers when passed over to create an IOU rather than restarting political capital elsewhere.

Ch 3. You Are the Captain of Your Career: The Ninety-Day Rule

Argument: You have about a quarter in any new job to create the impression of your value. Organizations assess can do, will do, and fit, and fit is the most subjective and decisive. The first-quarter impression sets a halo (or its opposite) that shapes trajectory.

Stories & evidence

  • Presentation-skills sprint: two years into banking Carla realized she lacked the board-room presentation experience VP required. Quarter one: internal reps (campus recruiting presentations, shadowing strong presenters). Quarter two: external reps (finance/treasury committees at nonprofits). Presenting was no longer an impediment by the VP decision.
  • Social rhythm: she adopted M&A's late nights and capital markets' 7 a.m. starts; she phoned her sports-fan father every Sunday to open Monday's conversation.
  • Informal hazing: up-or-out groups may not invite the new person; the test is passed by inviting yourself.
  • Day-91 check-in template: lead with proficiency attained, whom you enjoyed learning from, and the plan for next quarter; ask what to add or change.

Key numbers: 90 days to prove value; day 91 to advertise; 6 months to be on par; one year on par or ahead; 3 deliverables; perform at the next level 6–12 months before wanting the title; days 91–180 to become the go-to person.

So what: Calendar the three deliverables (skill, unspoken rules, key relationships). Never say "no one taught me." Request the deals and seniors you need. Ask the decision-maker what advancement requires.

Ch 4. Perception Is the Copilot to Reality

Argument: People treat you as who they think you are, and because evaluation has a subjective component, perception decides assignments, pay, and promotion. Perception equals your self-presentation plus the beholder's baggage; change the first, deliberately.

Stories & evidence

  • The "tough" campaign: told "I don't know if you're tough enough," Carla worked tough into her speech and acted congruently for about three months, until a VP was overheard warning his team to double-check assumptions because "Carla Harris is so tough."
  • The associate who wanted VP: strong objectively, yet treated as an associate. Prescription: dress like the women officers and pre-meet her boss before group meetings. She was promoted, though Carla cautions you can't dress your way to success.
  • Perception noise is especially dangerous in small organizations where one vocal person's view becomes everyone's.
  • Adjectives by level: junior (eager, resourceful, analytical), mid-level (gets things done, mobilizes others, strategic potential), senior (visionary, commercial, client-focused, authority).

Key numbers: at least 3 adjectives; about 3 months to change a perception; 2–3 fans plus 2–3 non-fans in the audit.

So what: Pick adjectives true of you and valued by the firm's business model, behave consistently, audit your perception between annual reviews, meet non-fans over coffee, fix the boss's perception first, and refresh adjectives as you rise.

Ch 5. The Mentor, the Sponsor, the Adviser

Argument: Three different relationships power a career and most people conflate them. Advisers answer discrete questions, mentors give tailored advice and hear everything, sponsors spend political capital to carry your paper into the room. Long-term advancement without a sponsor is nearly impossible, and finding one is your responsibility.

Stories & evidence

  • Carla's 1999 MD promotion: unable to name who would argue her case, she asked a senior MD with a committee seat directly and promised him the strongest package; she added a second advocate with influence over seat-holders. Promoted.
  • Reciprocity: a former mentee, now close to a client firm's decision-maker, gave her team post-pitch feedback and vouched for their integrity; they were named a book runner.
  • Boss capital: a boss may have capital for one or two protégés and four or five who deserve it.
  • Women and women of color are less often chosen for mentoring because relationships form along lines of commonality.

Key numbers: 8–10 mentor contacts per year (Carla: every six to eight weeks); at least 2 explicit sponsor commitments before joining or switching divisions; 4 sponsor criteria.

So what: Ask "Who is carrying my paper into the room?" and go recruit one if you can't answer. Test mentors against your agenda alone. Build a diverse career board of directors. Follow through and follow up, and reciprocate.

Ch 6. Leverage Your Voice

Argument: Voice creates perception, sets the expectation of your contribution, and is the mechanism for stating what you expect in return. Silence and head-down hard work are not safe: in marginal decisions, those who voiced expectations win.

Stories & evidence

  • The eureka year: in a tough year, Carla worked hard, said nothing, and was not promoted. Her boss said peers had been pleading their cases for months.
  • The listening turnaround: told her boss hated giving her feedback because "she has an answer for everything," she replied only with "yes," "uh-huh," and "oh really? okay." Feedback became specific; the boss became adviser, then sponsor, and discounted false claims about her.
  • "Frequently wrong, but never in doubt", adapted: answer confidently with room to adjust.
  • Word-framing: "There are three reasons…" (analytical); "This called for creative thinking" (creative).
  • Strategic silence: once you have a voice, not speaking is noticed ("Carla, you're quiet").

Key numbers: 50/50 odds before you speak; evaluation one-third lessons, two-thirds aspirations; goal timelines of 3–6 months; check-in every 2 months; report card done by month 6.

So what: Say something in every meeting, ask for next year's promotion this year, run reviews forward-looking with explicit asks, listen without defending, and thank the giver of feedback.

Ch 7. Have a Penchant for Taking Risks

Argument: Playing it safe won't get you ahead; with knowledge widely available, willingness to take risk differentiates you. Success equals performance plus political alignment plus risk. You can't prevent latent risk but can offset it by stacking forward risks.

Stories & evidence

  • Carrie (calculated): two years past ready for SVP; she met her boss's boss first, then told her boss, having mapped the possible reactions and prepared to search externally. Promoted.
  • Carla's Internet IPO (studied): oversubscribed book, thin investor feedback; she recommended waiting. The next day NASDAQ fell over 100 points and most Internet IPOs priced that day traded below issue; the client returned months later and priced successfully.
  • Risk of saying no: in her MD year she declined her boss's request to launch a retail-distribution effort, with a rationale ready, and was promoted with his sponsorship intact.
  • Observation: nobody who took a well-thought-out risk regretted it; almost everyone regrets a risk not taken.

Key numbers: 3 risk types (calculated, studied, step-out-on-faith); 3 test-the-waters questions (all yes means go); 12-month comparison horizon.

So what: Prefer calculated risks, take studied risks only when upside markedly dominates, keep faith risks for when you alone bear consequences. Take same-pay bigger jobs as platforms and better-paid moves as compensated risk. Title doesn't limit risk, self-imposed limits do.

Ch 8. Power in the Network

Argument: No one moves up alone, and because many decisions aren't made on merit, who you know decides between equally qualified candidates. A network's power lies in relationship strength and your role, not card count.

Stories & evidence

  • The first CD (1999): a chain of existing relationships (banker-musician, studio-owning colleague, Broadway musical director/producer, senior sponsor walking her to a music-label CEO, PR contacts) produced and distributed a gospel album to raise money for two schools; it also became a conversation piece with clients.
  • Closing the information gap: surrounded by former analysts with a ready-made network, she targeted a classmate and a former analyst, invested in meals and drinks, asked for help, and offered her external network in return.
  • Recruiting as exposure: captaining a recruiting team gave her reasons to call senior people.
  • Town-hall play: front row, prepared question, introduce yourself afterward.

Key numbers: 4 relationship types; 4 roles of the lateral network; 1 face-to-face plus 4 calls a year for key contacts; 1–2 e-mails a year for others.

So what: Build all four rings, decide your role, honor everyone's power (especially assistants), ask peers for help, gravitate toward those ahead of you, and treat external service as investment time.

Ch 9. Balance Is a Necessity

Argument: Balance is integrating your passions and giving back into your professional life. Without something outside the job that makes you feel alive, your life becomes a function of somebody else's day.

Stories & evidence

  • Gospel CDs and Carnegie Hall: proceeds went to two schools (one in Harlem, one in Jacksonville). After twelve years with no press mention, the 2000 CD brought a Sunday New York Times Business feature and a 2006 Wall Street Journal half-page on her first Carnegie Hall concert. Colleagues congratulated her; clients called to thank her for speaking openly about her faith.
  • Calendarizing: map the day, take two lunches a week for joy, and batch reading and e-mail (continuous e-mail is the biggest time leak in her experience).
  • Community service as common ground with clients.

Key numbers: lunch is 5–10 hours a week; 2 lunches a week for passions; e-mail in several fixed half-hour slots; several hours a day recovered.

So what: Put something that brings joy in every day, give back out of gratitude (not in order to get), and talk about your passions and service at work.

Ch 10. Expect to Win

Argument: Approach your career expecting to succeed and you will; approach it with "maybe" and you get mediocre results. Expectation is a daily decision that shapes body language and speech, and competitive environments exploit doubt.

Stories & evidence

  • Know to maybe: at eighteen she knew she'd reach Harvard, HBS, and a top firm; after bad deals and disappointing pay her self-talk became maybe and hope.
  • The Cleveland hotel room: the night before her birthday on a business trip, she ran the reflection she first did at thirteen, wrote who she had been and who she wanted to be, and chose the agenda and a turnaround plan over dwelling on lost money and deals.
  • Syndicate desk: she often met a CEO and CFO only two hours before a road show she'd run over ten days; she walked in expecting to build trust and "in almost every case, it worked."

Key numbers: 5 principles of the winner's lens; 4 reflection sheets; age 13 (first reflection), age 18 (the "know").

So what: Decide each morning to be triumphant, act "as if," run the four-sheet reflection yearly, lift someone else when low, revisit the agenda when complacent, and welcome change without being wedded to specifics.

Ch 11. My Most Precious Pearl

Argument: The eleventh pearl is knowing whose you are as well as who you are. Faith (for Harris, Christian; for any reader, something above the job) is the platform for managing what preparation can't control: timing, other people's decisions, a sponsor's sudden exit, illness.

Stories & evidence

  • Second-year associate: working under an insecure manager uninterested in training her, she was told by a friend's mother to read Psalm 91 and Psalm 4 daily; they became mantra, armor, and comfort.
  • Scripture-to-principle mappings: Philippians 4:13 (no challenge is insurmountable); Philippians 4:6–8 (don't worry); Isaiah 54:17 (those who wish me ill won't prevail); Romans 8:28 (it will work out for my benefit); Isaiah 41:10 (nothing to fear); Hebrews 13:5 (no battle alone).
  • Lesson or blessing: every career event is one or the other.

Key numbers: none given beyond the two psalms and the verse mappings.

So what: Anchor identity outside the organization, expect some things to be beyond control, classify events as lesson or blessing, give your best daily, and diagnose when you can't.

Recurring Stories & Motifs

  • Carla's own career at Morgan Stanley (turnaround pitch, ops-officer stint and sponsor, 1999 MD promotion, eureka year, Internet IPO, Cleveland hotel room).
  • The gospel CDs and Carnegie Hall (Ch 8 and 9, plus the authentic-self theme in Ch 1 and faith in Ch 11).
  • Insecure bosses (Ch 1, 6, 11).
  • Sponsors carrying your paper into the room (Ch 2, 5, 6, 7).
  • Silence versus voice (Ch 1, 4, 6).
  • Women and women of color (Ch 3–6, 8: mentoring gaps, avoidance of non-fans, silence in meetings, underused networks).
  • Marginal decisions (Ch 6, 8): ties go to the person who is known or who asked.
  • Failure as experience, lesson or blessing (Ch 2, 7, 10, 11).

Inner Excellence Quiz Book

Inner Excellence: Train Your Mind for Extraordinary Performance and the Best Possible Life by Jim Murphy

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative final exam is at the end. Chapter numbering follows the murphy-inner-excellence skill (Ch 0 is the Preface, Presuppositions and Introduction; Ch 11 includes the Conclusion). The questions test the skill's summary of the book, not the book's own wording.

Chapter 0: Preface, Presuppositions & Introduction

Q1 (SA). What is Murphy's central claim about extraordinary performance and the best possible life?

A: They are the same path, and both run through the heart. The biggest obstacle on that path is self-centeredness. Order matters: heart first, performance second.

Q2 (SA). What does BFF stand for, and which resource produces each element (as mapped later in the book)?

A: Belief, Focus, Freedom, the three performance variables. Wisdom produces belief, courage produces focus, love produces freedom.

Q3 (SA). State the Inner Excellence mindset in Murphy's words.

A: "I compete to raise the level of excellence in my life, to learn and grow, in order to raise it in others."

Q4 (MC). Which is NOT one of the ten presuppositions?

a) The map is not the territory b) You are not your mind c) There is no failure, only feedback d) Winning is everything

A: d. Winning is everything is the world's mindset. The Inner Excellence view is that inner strength and growth last longer.

Q5 (SA). Presupposition 8 says "the problem is not the problem." What is the rest of it?

A: The problem is how you're thinking about it.

Q6 (T/F). In the Inner Excellence mindset, the opponent is an enemy to be beaten. A: False. The opponent is a partner in the dance. The world's mindset (opponent = enemy) is the contrast.

Q7 (SA). What did Murphy's great-great-grandfather Bunpachiro the samurai illustrate?

A: Identity built on a role that can be lost. When the role was lost he turned to alcoholism. Build identity on something no circumstance can remove.

Chapter 1: Maslow and the Maserati

Q1 (SA). What does PALMS stand for, and what is the actual problem with it?

A: Possessions, Achievements, Looks, Money, Status. The virus is not wanting or having them; it is placing trust and identity in them. Its engine is not "more" but "more than others."

Q2 (SA). What are the three diagnostic questions for finding what you love (worship) most?

A: What do I dream about? What do I worry about? What do I get upset about? Your life is built on the answer, and your stability equals its stability.

Q3 (MC). The two paths in this chapter are:

a) the wide road of praise and comfort vs. the narrow road of facing fears and connecting to your true self b) the road of work vs. the road of rest c) the road of goals vs. the road of dreams d) the road of ego vs. the road of money

A: a. The narrow road is difficult but leads to deep contentment, joy, confidence and an undivided heart.

Q4 (SA). What do the lollipop and the whole candy store stand for?

A: Gold medals and CEO titles are lollipops; fullness of life is the candy store.

Q5 (T/F). Murphy says it is wrong to have possessions, achievements or status. A: False. They are fine to have and fatal to build identity on.

Q6 (SA). Name at least four of the nine characteristics of the selfless-actualizer (Maslow, relabeled).

A: Any four of: total absorption; personal growth (the means is the end); self-awareness; Gemeinschaft (community); fresh gratitude; authenticity / resistance to enculturation; comfort in solitude; purpose beyond self; lack of ego defenses.

Q7 (SA). What did the Costa Rica observation (the dentist and the tow-truck driver) show?

A: A PALMS-free social world: a dentist invited the tow-truck driver in for dinner and got excited when the driver pointed out his hometown on a map. People who "needed little and appreciated much" seemed far happier than people in Murphy's own culture.

Chapter 2: Where the Wild Things Are

Q1 (SA). What is the root cause of fear of failure, according to this chapter?

A: Self-centeredness: the hard-wired preoccupation with self and attachment to the past. It breeds self-consciousness, feeds the ego and ends in self-rejection.

Q2 (SA). Walk through the Path to Fear.

A: Self-centeredness, attachment to past failures, self-consciousness, ego amplified, comparison (via PALMS), pride and fear. Doubts then escalate from external ("I won't achieve it") to personal ("I'm not able") to identity ("I'm a failure").

Q3 (T/F). Self-centeredness means being morally selfish. A: False. It is not selfishness or a moral flaw but a preoccupation with self that limits options and stunts growth. It has been the default since infancy.

Q4 (MC). C.S. Lewis described pride as:

a) a sense of superiority over rivals b) "unsmiling concentration on the self," taking pleasure only in having more than the next person c) joy in accomplishment d) fear of public speaking

A: b.

Q5 (SA). Contrast self-centeredness and self-awareness.

A: Self-centeredness is nearsightedness that can't see past failures and limits. Self-awareness observes thoughts unattached, sees the bigger picture and treats setbacks as feedback.

Q6 (SA). Describe the "Me, Myself and I" exercise and its purpose.

A: At a social event with strangers, go the whole evening without saying anything that puts you in a favorable light, without talking about yourself except to answer direct questions, and without using "me," "myself," or "I." It exposes how hard it is to be non-self-occupied and how acceptance-driven the ego is.

Q7 (SA). In the two-colleagues story, what differs between them after the same bad meeting?

A: Only the lens. The self-centered one concludes "I'm a poor speaker, they're being nice, they'll gossip." The self-aware one notices the well-prepared did better, accepts the compliment and prepares more.

Chapter 3: The Greatest Opponents You'll Ever Face

Q1 (SA). Name the three adversaries and what each does.

A: The Critic delivers a negative verdict and reacts emotionally. The Monkey Mind clutters and overanalyzes. The Trickster lies and accuses ("your worth depends on your results").

Q2 (SA). What are the Trickster's two tools, and why is it convincing?

A: Deception and accusation. It sounds logical because it cites real past failures.

Q3 (SA). What is the D-slide?

A: Failure going Disappointed, Devastated, Defeated, Defective (Dr. David Coppel). Many go straight from disappointed to defective.

Q4 (MC). The difference between judging and discerning is:

a) none b) judging delivers a negative verdict, discerning uses wisdom to choose the best course c) discerning is harsher d) judging is only about other people

A: b.

Q5 (T/F). Thoughts are facts if they feel true. A: False. Circumstances are facts free of opinion and emotion; thoughts are opinions with emotion attached; thoughts are not facts.

Q6 (SA). What is the first defense against all three adversaries?

A: Separate circumstances from thoughts before seeking a solution (for example, two columns; nobody can argue with the circumstances column).

Q7 (SA). According to the chapter, when does the Critic have power and when does the Monkey Mind thrive?

A: The Critic has power only when you are attached to an uncontrollable goal. The Monkey Mind thrives in a heart without one central devotion.

Chapter 4: The Daring and the Twilight (Three Pillars)

Q1 (SA). Name the three pillars with what each leads to.

A: Love: lead with your heart, brings freedom, becomes passion. Wisdom: expand your vision, brings belief, becomes purpose. Courage: be fully present, brings focus, becomes poise.

Q2 (SA). What are the three marks of self-mastery (mastering the ego)?

A: Unembarrassable, unoffendable, unirritatable.

Q3 (SA). Distinguish goals from dreams.

A: Goals are external outcomes not fully in your control (win, hit .300, become CEO). Dreams are the feelings you set goals in order to have. Live the dream daily while pursuing the goal.

Q4 (SA). List the Fearless Four.
