A: (1) Give my best (100% of what I have today); (2) be present; (3) be grateful; (4) focus on my routines and only what I can control.

Q5 (MC). Frosty Westering's three types of "best" are:

a) first, second, third b) the best, your best, your best shot c) good, better, best d) physical, mental, spiritual

A: b. Only the best shot (prepare, go out, love doing it even when it isn't good) is always available.

Q6 (T/F). Resonance is mainly a by-product of great results. A: False. It is the reverse: great results are the by-product of resonance, the effortless excitement of being fully engaged with a clear mind and unburdened heart.

Q7 (SA). What changed between Lewis Pugh's failed test swims and his successful North Pole swim?

A: His fear did not change. What changed was his connection to a purpose beyond himself (global warming, the coral reefs he'd seen) and his coach's chunking: a teammate's national flag every 100 m, thinking only about one nation at a time, never the kilometer.

Chapter 5: Code of the Samurai

Q1 (SA). What is the Samurai Paradox?

A: The samurai learned to fight to the death by focusing on love (honor, service) more than self. They prepared to die each day: "die anew every morning."

Q2 (SA). Name the five steps of Beauty Before Bed.

A: (1) Review the day; (2) recall three small, specific beautiful moments; (3) reprogram mistakes (see yourself doing it as you wish) and let go of the day; (4) preview tomorrow's routines; (5) visualize tomorrow's feelings.

Q3 (SA). Contrast happiness and joy.

A: Happiness is temporary and attached to circumstance. Joy is deep well-being, freedom and gratitude independent of circumstance, and possible in suffering. Chasing happiness is "The Great Mistake."

Q4 (SA). List the eight attachments.

A: How others see you; money and possessions; what you want (goals); comfort; your past; how things are (status quo); expectations; your self.

Q5 (T/F). Victory is the safest position for a competitor. A: False. Victory is the most dangerous position (it tempts pride and slack). Failure is dangerous too, because of self-rejection.

Q6 (SA). What is the Lollipop Exchange?

A: You can't take a lollipop from a kid without resistance unless you give a bigger one. Trade "winning" for "fullness of life" as the highest goal, and you get the best shot at the medal as a bonus.

Q7 (MC). According to the chapter, all addiction is ultimately:

a) weak willpower b) avoidance of emotional pain c) genetic d) a lack of discipline

A: b. The hardest are hidden, socially acceptable ones such as pride, needing recognition and comfort.

Chapter 6: Change Your State, Change Your Life

Q1 (SA). Give the Results Chain.

A: Circumstance, filtered through memories and beliefs, then thoughts, feelings, actions, results (which become new circumstances).

Q2 (SA). What are the steps of the Reset (Reboot)?

A: Stop what you're doing; pick a spot above the horizon and stare, stopping all thoughts; inhale through the nose (about 4); exhale longer (about 6), relaxing jaw and face and letting go of all desires and concerns; do it twice (once is fine).

Q3 (SA). What is box breathing?

A: Inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4 (jaw loose), hold 4.

Q4 (MC). "I expect... nothing" rests on which distinction?

a) Expectation is anticipation of circumstances (avoid); confidence is faith in the future (keep) b) Expectation is good, confidence is bad c) They are the same d) Expectation is physical, confidence is mental

A: a. The longer version is "I expect nothing... I can handle anything": expect abundance, attach to nothing.

Q5 (SA). What are soft/sharp focus and moderate/complete relaxation?

A: Focus softly between plays (relaxed readiness) and sharply at key moments; relax moderately (between sets, off-days) and completely (naps, sleep). The skill is moving back and forth, practiced with peripheral vision and Open Focus (Fehmi).

Q6 (T/F). Anchoring works best with a visual cue. A: False. Smell is the strongest cue (for example peppermint oil), paired with the peak feeling at its height; a fist clench or a song also works.

Q7 (SA). What does "what gets your attention gets you" imply, and what research supports it?

A: Attention leads to thoughts, feelings, actions and results, so organize your environment. Priming research (hot coffee leading to warmer judgments and more generosity) shows subtle cues steer behavior without awareness.

Chapter 7: The World Is Flat

Q1 (SA). Why does Murphy call beliefs a thermostat?

A: The subconscious keeps performance inside what you believe is right for you (homeostasis), dragging down over-performance and lifting under-performance.

Q2 (SA). How do beliefs form?

A: From repeated thoughts and especially feelings. An experience with strong feeling is filed by the brain to protect you, often in an instant and often for life. The stronger the negative feeling, the more likely a limiting belief.

Q3 (SA). What does "speak the truth about the past" mean? Give the example form.

A: Say everything you don't want to continue in past tense: not "I'm struggling with my putting" but "In the past I struggled with X and I'm getting better every day."

Q4 (T/F). You must believe an affirmation before you use it. A: False. You are not expected to believe them at first; that is why you affirm. Make them positive, short and present tense.

Q5 (MC). The One-Second Tingle asks you to:

a) visualize some aspect of your biggest dream daily until you feel excitement for at least one second b) meditate one second a day c) exercise one second d) write a goal once

A: a. Daily beats long.

Q6 (SA). What is the "final piece" congruence check?

A: Subconscious sabotage occurs when achieving the goal conflicts with a value or threatens something you'd lose (smokers' social bond; a wealthy outcome a strict upbringing distrusts). Ask what achieving the dream will give you and whether any of it is incongruent with who you want to be.

Q7 (SA). How did Callista Balko prepare for Cat Osterman, and what happened?

A: She had struck out 9-of-9 against Osterman. In preseason she wrote affirmations, scripted the post-championship interview and visualized the exact scenario daily for months. In the game they walked a batter to face her with the World Series on the line; she felt confidence, and the game-winning hit came as rehearsed.

Chapter 8: A Clear and Present Beauty

Q1 (SA). List the five ways to be fully present.

A: (1) Get out of your head (one devotion); (2) focus on routines and only what you can control; (3) be grateful; (4) focus on a mantra; (5) ruthlessly eliminate hurry.

Q2 (SA). What are the four parts of the GPS morning tool and their lengths?

A: 3 minutes Gratitude (small, specific, last 24-48 hours), 3 minutes Presence (eyes open, let go of desires), 3 minutes Showtime (visualize the big moment under pressure), 1 minute Funnel (outside, barefoot, arms in a Y, receive abundance with gratitude).

Q3 (T/F). Hurry sickness is mainly a scheduling problem. A: False. It is a disordered heart. Hurry is the cause of stress, not its cure, and it kills joy and compassion.

Q4 (SA). What rest rhythm does the chapter prescribe?

A: Gaps about every 90 minutes, one full day in seven, one year in seven.

Q5 (MC). Why is gratitude a route to presence?

a) it is polite b) you can't be anxious and grateful at once, or judgmental and grateful c) it makes you work harder d) it raises expectations

A: b. Gratitude and entitlement are opposite poles.

Q6 (SA). What does "perfection is the enemy of presence" mean, and which examples support it?

A: Wanting control and wanting perfection are the same fear; surrendering control is how you gain it. Reid Hoffman's embarrassing first version and Lamott's messy first drafts illustrate it.

Q7 (SA). What is the "simple mind" check?

A: Define the one basic element (get the sign, see the pitch, throw it, per Ronn Svetich) and between innings ask "did I keep a simple mind at least 80% of the time?"

Chapter 9: Unstoppable (Mental Blocks)

Q1 (SA). Why does Murphy say a mental block or phobia is the subconscious working perfectly?

A: The subconscious files emotional danger in the same folder as physical danger and protects you from the feeling it has filed as danger. The block is an anchored association between a context and that protection.

Q2 (SA). What are the subconscious's three jobs?

A: (1) Sift sensory input for physical or emotional danger; (2) run life in the background (shoes, driving); (3) line up circumstances and results with your beliefs.

Q3 (SA). State the four removal principles.

A: (1) Take the emotion out; (2) find the smallest change that would have made a difference; (3) insert a positive, high-energy feeling plus the small change into the block's context; (4) anchor that feeling to the original painful context for a new, stronger association (re-run first-person, in color, 5-7 times).

Q4 (SA). What is the Hollywood Helper?

A: A movie-theater dissociation: see a black-and-white still of yourself on screen, float up into the projection booth and watch yourself watching, run the event in black-and-white, replay at 2x, 4x, 8x, then step into the film at the end and run it backwards first-person at 2x, 4x, 8x, 16x.

Q5 (MC). On the pain-rating scale, the work is done when the memory rates:

a) 5 b) 3-4 c) 0-2 d) 10

A: c. Rate 1-10 before (look for 9s and 10s) and repeat if not near zero. No details of the memory need to be shared.

Q6 (T/F). The right response to a block is to work harder at the blocked skill. A: False. Sax threw perfectly blindfolded in an empty stadium; effort wasn't the problem. Analyzing and worrying about the block also convinces the subconscious the danger is real.

Q7 (SA). What is Power APP?

A: Anchor Peak Performance: place the painful memory on a floor spot, step in first-person, step out and shake off, build a peak state with countdown breathing (inhale counting 10 to 7, pause, exhale 6 to 1), walk to the spot only when calm, step in, turn a full circle, stay 3-4 minutes, step out.

Chapter 10: The Hero and the Goat

Q1 (SA). Name the four keys to resonance.

A: Share your heart, not your ego; pursue mastery, not the score; love your opponent; visualize presence, not perfection.

Q2 (SA). Give the six elements of performance and say which matter most.

A: Circumstances, beliefs, thoughts, state, performance, results. The three that matter most (beliefs, thoughts, state) are all unseen.

Q3 (SA). What are resonance's three characteristics and three obstacles?

A: Characteristics: clear mind; unburdened heart; non-judgmental awareness. Obstacles: overanalysis, self-consciousness, constant judging of circumstances and results.

Q4 (MC). In the visualization advice, the recommended split (from Georges St-Pierre) is roughly:

a) 50/50 b) 80% what he'll do, 20% overcoming adversity c) 20% execution, 80% adversity d) 100% perfection

A: b. Also exaggerate pressure beyond anything reality can bring.

Q5 (T/F). Visualizing a flawless performance is the best preparation. A: False. Visualizing perfection sets up judgment; visualize presence and readiness for anything.

Q6 (SA). What is the Scene of Success?

A: Visualize the 20 seconds and then the 20 minutes after the performance, not the performance itself.

Q7 (SA). How did Stewart Cink win the 2009 Open without confidence?

A: He said "nah, don't got it," but he had no fear of the feeling of failing and was grateful to be there. Resonance without confidence; he won.

Chapter 11: Three Hallmarks of Extraordinary Leaders (+ Conclusion)

Q1 (SA). Name the three hallmarks of extraordinary leaders.

A: Redefine success; connect individuals with a vision beyond themselves; seek self-mastery and help others do the same.

Q2 (SA). Distinguish purpose from vision.

A: Purpose is who you are (meaning, inspiration). Vision is a goal serving the greater good (direction, focus).

Q3 (SA). What does "pace, pace, pace, lead" mean, and what weights does the chapter give to rapport channels?

A: Match the person before leading them: posture/physiology (55%), tone (38%), words (7%). Example: walk with the angry employee, match volume, then guide them to sit.

Q4 (SA). Describe values elicitation.

A: Ask "What's most important to you about your job?", then "What does that give you?", and repeat until the answer stops changing (for example, security). Connect the group's vision to that root value.

Q5 (MC). The "pink elephant" lesson for coaching is:

a) praise often b) the brain doesn't picture "don't," so say "hold on to the ball," not "don't fumble" c) never give instructions d) yell at one player to teach all

A: b. Yelling at one player is yelling at everyone (Davey Johnson).

Q6 (T/F). Wooden scouted opponents heavily and recruited aggressively. A: False. Wooden neither scouted opponents nor recruited, an example of the view that visionary companies beat themselves, not the competition.

Q7 (SA). Why did Michael Jordan love practice, per the chapter?

A: It was "pure basketball": challenged in what he was good at, no crowd, no score. Practice and games became the same opportunity for resonance.

Final Exam (Cumulative)

Q1 (SA). State the book's thesis in one sentence.

A: Extraordinary performance and the best possible life are the same path, through the heart, and self-centeredness (the root of fear) is the chief obstacle to both.

Q2 (SA). Walk the chain from self-centeredness to the thought "I'm a failure."

A: Self-centeredness, attachment to past failures, self-consciousness, ego amplified, comparison (via PALMS), pride and fear, then doubts escalating external, personal, identity. The Trickster's D-slide (disappointed, devastated, defeated, defective) is the same slide in the mind.

Q3 (MC). Which pairing is correct?

a) Love, belief b) Wisdom, belief c) Courage, freedom d) Love, focus

A: b. Love brings freedom, wisdom brings belief, courage brings focus (BFF).

Q4 (SA). Why "goals are not dreams," and why does it matter under pressure?

A: Goals are outcomes not fully in your control; dreams are the feelings you set goals to have. Under pressure you can always share something beautiful and give your best shot (feelings and process are yours), while the score is past/future and uncontrollable.

Q5 (SA). What is the first thing to do when frustration or a "what if..." thought shows up, and which Ch 6 tool re-centers you when you are not present?

A: Separate circumstances (facts) from thoughts (opinions). To re-center, use the Reset: spot above the horizon, nose inhale about 4, longer exhale about 6 with jaw loose, release all desires, twice.

Q6 (T/F). The subconscious that produces a mental block is malfunctioning. A: False. It is working perfectly to protect you from a feeling it has filed as danger, which is why the fix is to update the association (remove emotion, smallest change, anchor a stacked confidence feeling) rather than fight it.

Q7 (SA). What are the two mechanisms of belief change in Ch 7, and how does the Ch 8 GPS tool relate?

A: Speak the truth about the past (past tense for what you don't want to continue) and affirm/model/act-as-if with a daily one-second feeling of the dream. The GPS tool (3 gratitude, 3 presence, 3 showtime visualization, 1 funnel) is a morning ritual that builds presence and rehearses the pressure moment.

Q8 (SA). Contrast happiness and joy, and the lollipop and the candy store. How do they connect?

A: Happiness is circumstance-dependent; joy is independent of circumstance and survives suffering. Winning is the lollipop; fullness of life (zoe) is the store. Trading the lollipop for the store makes joy the target and also gives the best shot at the medal.

Q9 (SA). Which two ideas from Ch 4 and Ch 10 produce "poise," and why does Murphy say to love the opponent?

A: Resonance (clear mind, unburdened heart) and the Fearless Four/best-shot mindset. The opponent is a partner in the dance; their best brings out yours, and wishing them to fail creates negative energy and bad strategy.

Q10 (SA). Give three leadership behaviors from Ch 11 and tie one back to an earlier chapter.

A: Redefine success (effort, growth, for the group); pace three times then lead, and elicit root values; coach in pictures of what you want rather than "don't"; renew daily and keep one day in seven. Tie-back examples: redefining success connects to Ch 1 (lollipop vs. candy store) and the double win in Ch 4; renewal connects to Beauty Before Bed in Ch 5.

Arguments & Evidence

Inner Excellence: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Jim Murphy

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files in the murphy-inner-excellence skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording. Murphy's evidence is mostly anecdotal (athlete and coaching case studies) and his framing is explicitly spiritual; the block-removal techniques come from coaching experience, not controlled trials.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Ch 0 sets the thesis (extraordinary performance and the best possible life are one path through the heart) and the ten presuppositions. Ch 1-3 diagnose the problem: the affluenza virus (identity in PALMS), self-centeredness as the root of fear, and the three inner adversaries (Critic, Monkey Mind, Trickster). Ch 4-5 give the answer: love, wisdom and courage as three pillars, self-mastery, and the samurai discipline of dropping attachments. Ch 6-9 supply the skills: controlling state, rewriting beliefs, being fully present, and removing mental blocks. Ch 10 applies them to poise under pressure and Ch 11 to leading others, ending with a call to develop the inner world first.

Ch 0. Preface, Presuppositions & Introduction

Argument: Pursuing extraordinary performance and pursuing the best possible life are the same path, and both run through the heart. The biggest obstacle is self-centeredness. Heart first, performance second.

Stories & evidence

  • Bunpachiro the samurai (Murphy's great-great-grandfather): his identity rested on a role that could be lost; when it was, he turned to alcoholism.
  • Ryan Dodd: same training volume before and after his skull fracture; what produced a world record was how he saw the world.
  • Magritte's pipe: the basis of the presupposition "the map is not the territory."
  • World's mindset vs. Inner Excellence mindset: winning is everything vs. inner strength lasts longer; you are your results vs. results are inconsistent (you can play well and lose); opponent as enemy vs. partner in the dance; failure not an option vs. failure is the key to growth; fierce competitors get mad vs. the best develop emotional control.
  • Finite vs. infinite game; "the lens": most play a zero-sum finite game; the extraordinary share an uncommon lens.

Key numbers: 10 presuppositions; 3 elements of quality of life (inner world, frame of reference, relationships); 3 performance variables (BFF: Belief, Focus, Freedom).

So what: Adopt the ten presuppositions as the lens for everything else, especially "the problem is not the problem, it's how you're thinking about it." Ask which game you are playing, and build identity on something no circumstance can remove.

Ch 1. Maslow and the Maserati

Argument: Real freedom is costly: it means the narrow path of facing fears and connecting with your true self rather than the wide road of comfort and symbols of success. Western culture's "affluenza virus" swaps the real dream (feeling fully alive) for its symbols.

Stories & evidence

  • Murphy's own Cubs experience: batting average as self-worth made life a roller coaster.
  • Michelangelo's David: the true self is revealed by removing what isn't you.
  • David Foster Wallace ("everybody worships"): the only choice is what; worship money, body, power or intellect and it "eats you alive."
  • Joe Ehrmann (ladder on the wrong building): outward NFL success, inner emptiness.
  • Dean Smith / Krzyzewski: winning as by-product of process; defining success by what you can't control undermines the process.
  • Costa Rica: a dentist invites the tow-truck driver to dinner and gets excited when the driver points out his hometown on a map; people who "needed little and appreciated much."
  • Augustine's ordered loves: we are shaped by what we love; discontent comes from loves out of order.
  • Thoreau: the price of anything is the amount of life you exchange for it.

Key numbers: 9 characteristics of the selfless-actualizer; 5 PALMS; 3 diagnostic questions (dream / worry / get upset about).

So what: Run the three questions to find what you really worship; your stability equals its stability. PALMS are fine to have and fatal to build identity on, and the fuel is "more than others." The person you become is the real prize.

Ch 2. Where the Wild Things Are

Argument: Fear of failure is the chief obstacle to freedom and performance, and its root cause is self-centeredness: the hard-wired preoccupation with self and attachment to the past that breeds self-consciousness, feeds the ego and ends in self-rejection.

Stories & evidence

  • The free throw: "I've gotta make this" replaces the routine; heart on one side, ego on the other.
  • C.S. Lewis on pride: "unsmiling concentration on the self"; pleasure only from having more than the next person. Competitiveness is at the heart of pride (Keller).
  • Dweck's fixed mindset: the ego's home; a failure can define you permanently.
  • Dean Smith: leaders must be able to handle losing.
  • The two colleagues after the same bad meeting: the self-centered one concludes "I'm a poor speaker, they're being nice, they'll gossip"; the self-aware one notices the well-prepared did better, accepts the compliment, prepares more.
  • "Me, Myself and I" exercise and the 3x5-card day (mark every time the mind is in past or future).

Key numbers: 7-link Path to Fear (self-centeredness through to doubts about identity); 3 levels of doubt (external, personal, identity).

So what: Fear is the symptom; self-centeredness is the disease. When upset, ask whether it was me or something mine that was threatened. Doubt is powered by your own thoughts; self-awareness (observing thoughts unattached) is the exit.

Ch 3. The Greatest Opponents You'll Ever Face

Argument: Three adversaries in your own mind sabotage focus and confidence: the Critic (judges and reacts), the Monkey Mind (clutters and overanalyzes) and the Trickster (lies and accuses). Each gains power from attachment to results; the first defense is separating circumstances from thoughts.

Stories & evidence

  • Cal Botterill: overanalysis is the number one obstacle for performers; caring too much is number two.
  • Dr. David Coppel's D-slide: Disappointed, Devastated, Defeated, Defective.
  • Henri Nouwen: self-rejection is the greatest trap in life, not success, popularity or power.
  • Charlie Maher (fusing with language): "What if...?" thoughts create a reality that isn't there; the real reality is a hitter, a catcher and runners.
  • The pandemic example: circumstances (schools closed, events cancelled, people ill), thoughts ("everything's falling apart"), truth (life is different; the real question is whether we'll fully live).
  • The lost-sale D-slide: a lost sale becomes "I am a failure"; fix by listing facts in one column and thoughts in another.

Key numbers: 3 adversaries; 4 stages of the D-slide; 2 Trickster tools (deception, accusation).

So what: Name the voice. Separate facts from opinions before solving anything. Judge = deliver a negative verdict; discern = choose the best course. Set an alarm ("Where's your mind right now?") and reset with two long breaths, exhale longer than inhale.

Ch 4. The Daring and the Twilight (Three Pillars)

Argument: Fear is overcome by the three most powerful resources, love, wisdom and courage, which become the three pillars: lead with your heart, expand your vision, be fully present. Together they produce resonance, and pursuing them directly is self-mastery.

Stories & evidence

  • Lewis Pugh's North Pole swim (2007): two failed test swims days before (cells in his hands burst; 600 m max in warmer water); scientists called it lethal and his doctor's hands shook. Fear did not change; what changed was purpose beyond himself (global warming, coral reefs) and his coach planting a national flag every 100 m with one team member's nation at a time.
  • Dawn Staley: gold medal is the goal; playing to win against the best is the dream.
  • Frosty Westering's three bests: the best, your best, your best shot.
  • Georges St-Pierre: fear never disappears; what changes is acceptance ("a suffering process I go through before a fight").
  • Unconditional love in traffic: let someone in with no attachment to a thank-you wave.
  • Why people risk death: purpose beyond self, feeling alive at full concentration, lack of self-concern.

Key numbers: 3 pillars; 3 marks of self-mastery (unembarrassable, unoffendable, unirritatable); 4 Fearless Four goals; ~90% of anything good was given to you (the humility point); 5 ego reality-check questions.

So what: Review the Fearless Four daily; giving 100% of today's 40% is success. Live the dream (a feeling) while pursuing the goal (an outcome). Fearlessness has two components: purpose beyond self and unconditional love.

Ch 5. Code of the Samurai

Argument: The samurai were fearless because they prepared to die each day, loving honor and service over self. Self-mastery is surrendering self-concern for a greater purpose, embracing suffering and dropping attachments: exchange the lollipop (winning) for the candy store (fullness of life).

Stories & evidence

  • Murphy's Scenario A vs. B: marching in the Sydney 2000 Opening Ceremony minutes after a talk from Nelson Mandela (elation on top of anxiety) vs. sitting broke and in debt in a friend's tiny LA apartment while he played a song of gratitude on guitar (deep sense of being fully known and loved). Extraordinary circumstances gave happiness-over-anxiety; nothing circumstances gave joy.
  • Kalanithi: "wouldn't it be great if it were more painful?" The pain of loss measures the size of the gift.
  • Apolo Ohno: at 3:30 a.m. in a parking lot with a miner's lamp, "I'm willing to do what nobody else is willing to do."
  • UBC golf team: "The score is for the fans, we play for the love of the game"; lost when attached, won two national titles when they let go.
  • Wim Hof lesson: focus on the cold rather than ignore it.
  • Suzuki's four horses: the best horse runs before the whip's shadow; the worst only when pain reaches the marrow.
  • 12-step groups: the illness is self-centeredness; the cure is dying to the old nature and vision beyond self.

Key numbers: 8 attachments; 5 steps of Beauty Before Bed; one full day in seven off.

So what: Renew the mind nightly (Beauty Before Bed) and weekly (a full day off). Target joy, not happiness; joy survives suffering. Name your addiction, especially the socially acceptable ones, and list your eight attachments. Live as if you'll die tomorrow; prepare as if you'll live forever.

Ch 6. Change Your State, Change Your Life

Argument: Everything pivots on how you feel, and your state comes almost entirely from what you think, directed by what your heart desires most and what you pay attention to. Direct attention, desires, focus/relaxation and breathing, and you control your state.

Stories & evidence

  • Priming research: hot coffee leads to warmer judgments and more generosity.
  • Gareth Bale: sleeps 9-10 hours plus a 1-2 hour nap, waking exactly four hours before kick-off (homeostasis of routines).
  • Freddie Roach: "I don't want him angry. We have a plan."
  • The kid on the bike staring at the rock: you move toward what you focus on.
  • The $10M ocean-house choice vs. an apartment with guaranteed deep contentment: go directly for what the house is supposed to give you.
  • Driving-to-an-event worked example: pull over, spot above the horizon, two long exhales, then "I expect nothing... I can handle anything."
  • Erica K., ballet dancer: stands at center stage hours early, breathes, imagines hugging the entire audience.
  • Juicy lemon drop: vividly imagined is processed as real.

Key numbers: Reset: inhale about 4, exhale about 6, twice; box breathing 4-4-4-4; 4 pattern processes (assumptions, generalizations, deletions, distortions).

So what: Control attention and environment. Practice soft/sharp focus and moderate/complete relaxation daily, not just on game day. Use the Reset, expect abundance while attaching to nothing, anchor the states you want (smell is strongest) and float up to release the ones you don't.

Ch 7. The World Is Flat

Argument: Beliefs, the subconscious ideas about who you are and what's possible, are the X factor behind every performance; they act as a thermostat pulling results back to your comfort level. They form from repeated thought and especially feeling, and can be rewritten deliberately.

Stories & evidence

  • The Super Bowl kick: decided less by form, wind or the snap than by the preceding months' beliefs, thoughts and feelings.
  • Callista Balko vs. Cat Osterman: struck out 9-of-9; wrote affirmations, scripted the post-championship interview, visualized the exact scenario daily for months; in the game they walked a batter to face her and she got the game-winning hit.
  • Andy Lopez / Pepperdine: played College World Series footage in the locker room all season; the small school won it all.
  • Muggsy Bogues: shot at five, 5'3", 14 NBA seasons, imagination fed daily.
  • Olympian and the hurdle in the living room: clearing a 42-inch hurdle 25 times a day to plant the image.
  • Delancey Street (ex-felons): stand tall, look up when you don't feel confident (act as if).
  • The "spider" that was a ball of yarn; the rejection when you sang: how a single feeling-laden experience becomes a lifelong belief.
  • Murphy's Achilles cast: a healing affirmation written on it.

Key numbers: 1 second of tingling excitement daily; 3 main beliefs in the belief audit; 42 inches and 25 times a day (hurdle).

So what: Put every unwanted pattern in past tense when you speak; feel the dream daily; affirm before you believe; model the best; act as if; and check congruence so the dream fits who you want to become.

Ch 8. A Clear and Present Beauty

Argument: Being fully present (no past or future, no needs, no thoughts of outcome) is one of the two decisive factors in peak performance, with belief. Five practices produce it: get out of your head, focus on routines and only what you control, be grateful, use a mantra, and ruthlessly eliminate hurry.

Stories & evidence

  • Bruce Lee: the great mistake is anticipating the outcome.
  • Bonhoeffer: room for only one all-embracing devotion; Phelps: "what could I remove from my life?"
  • Ronn Svetich's simple mind: get the sign, see the pitch, throw it.
  • Reid Hoffman's embarrassing first version; Lamott's messy first drafts: perfection is the enemy of presence.
  • Navy SEAL instructor: "humility can defeat any opponent; pride busts down the front door... humility sees the back door."
  • Harrington's "I'm going to win" in the Open playoff; Murphy's trail-riding trio (sing, visualize ESPN, "I am the best athlete in the world").
  • Wim Hof retreat: "My body is a sauna..." through a two-hour shirtless hike at -8 C.
  • Hurry sickness (Friedman & Rosenman): symptoms include passing cars for no reason and pressing the elevator close button; 95% of executives have it (Jolly). Willard to Ortberg: "ruthlessly eliminate hurry."
  • Monks and the mandala: days of sand painting, then destroyed; the process is what matters.
  • PGA Tour client (2019): reviewed the Fearless Four with his caddie before every round, then one silent minute of visualization; several weeks later he won, worth over $1M.
  • Haiti rubble: a single focus makes you selfless, therefore fearless, therefore present.

Key numbers: 5 ways; GPS tool 3+3+3+1 minutes; simple mind at least 80% of the time; gaps every ~90 minutes, one day in seven, one year in seven; 95% of executives (hurry sickness).

So what: One devotion, one basic element at a time. Be meticulous with routines but never attached ("that's how it's supposed to be today"). Gratitude on small specifics is the fastest exit from anxiety and judgment. Hurry is a heart problem, not a schedule problem.

Ch 9. Unstoppable

Argument: The yips, mental blocks and phobias are not malfunctions; they are the subconscious working perfectly to protect you from a feeling it has filed as danger. Because the block is an anchored association, it can be collapsed and replaced, often in one session, by removing the emotion, adding a small change and anchoring a positive state.

Stories & evidence

  • Steve Sax sequence: error, felt bad, looked at stats and projected the future, more errors, obsession (idee fixe), career-threatening block; threw perfectly blindfolded in an empty stadium; his dad's "one day you'll wake up and it's gone; it happened to me too" was the first crack; the smallest change was calling his dad immediately.
  • Rick Ankiel: wild pitches in the playoffs, nightmares, vodka before games, years in the minors, quit, returned as an outfielder throwing 300-foot lasers. Same arm, different anchored context; his smallest change was calling time after the first wild pitch and recalling a moment of perfect accuracy.
  • Easy-task blocks: extra points and two-foot putts, because of social pressure not to miss.
  • Top-10 golfer who hit into the water on a par 3: rated confidence "very low"; fifteen minutes by phone; played that hole effortlessly the rest of the week.
  • Pre-Masters client: 20 minutes on the holes he lacked confidence in; birdies or pars on them all tournament, top-10 finish.
  • Client abused as a child: four or five memories rated 8-10 dropped to 0-2; ranked No. 1 within six months.

Key numbers: 3 subconscious jobs; 4 removal principles; replay speeds 2x/4x/8x (and to 16x backwards); re-run 5-7 times; pain rated 1-10, target 0-2; countdown breathing 10-7 in, 6-1 out; stay 3-4 minutes in Power APP.

So what: The block is protection, not a flaw; update the threat list rather than fighting the guard. Strip emotion (third person, black-and-white, fast, backwards), add a small change, anchor a peak state. Don't analyze the block, and carry a purpose beyond your profession plus willingness to look foolish. Serious trauma may need more.

Ch 10. The Hero and the Goat

Argument: Poise under pressure is learnable. Pressure arises when stakes are high and the outcome uncertain, pulling the mind into the future; poise comes from resonance, produced by four keys: share your heart not your ego, pursue mastery not the score, love your opponent, and visualize presence not perfection.

Stories & evidence

  • Sinek: giving the audience something beautiful builds mental toughness; playing perfectly can't.
  • Bonnie Blair: valued a 4th-place personal best over a gold.
  • Phil Jackson: the moment the trophy is handed over, "we are no longer a success."
  • Client's four shifts before a world title (gratitude, respect, wanting the best for opponents, rival as necessary); Derin McMains on flow; GSP prays for his opponent.
  • GSP's 80/20 visualization split.
  • Stewart Cink, 2009 Open: "nah, don't got it," no fear of the feeling of failing; won.
  • Sully: absolute focus, "thought of nothing else."
  • Kyla Inaba's adversity ladder: neutral about uncontrollable things is one notch above the field; embracing them as sent for you is two notches.
  • Ski-race story told to Mickelson: two best friends race, photo finish, high-five; you weren't skiing for the race if you'd storm off.
  • Dr. Tribble's resident: in a failing cardiac operation did an unorthodox procedure; "No, but I've thought about it a lot."
  • Ohno's bubble; Great Debaters mantra.

Key numbers: 6 elements of performance; 3 characteristics and 3 obstacles of resonance; 4 keys; ~80% execution / ~20% adversity; Preview 5 minutes before every sleep; stack 3 confidence memories; 5 Newburg questions.

So what: Visualize presence and readiness for anything, exaggerating the pressure beyond what reality can deliver. Use "I expect nothing... I can handle anything." Winning is the goal, not the dream; feelings are yours, outcomes aren't. Wishing your opponent to fail creates negative energy and bad strategy.

Ch 11. Three Hallmarks of Extraordinary Leaders (+ Conclusion)

Argument: Beyond technical expertise, the greatest coaches and leaders do three things: redefine success, connect individuals with a vision beyond themselves, and seek self-mastery while helping others do the same. Leadership is developing people to be their true selves so they can help others do likewise.

Stories & evidence

  • Wooden: peace of mind from knowing you made the effort to become the best you can; he neither scouted opponents nor recruited. Tressel adds "for the group," and flew to learn from the reigning champion he later beat.
  • Frosty Westering: "They're here to beat us, we're here to be us."
  • Collins and Blue Ocean: visionary companies beat themselves, not the competition; contribution first, profits as by-product.
  • Warriors' four values: joy, compassion, mindfulness, competition.
  • SEAL in Hell Week: "I focused on my team; quitting wasn't an option."
  • Brother Lawrence: a dishwasher's presence studied 400 years later.
  • Rapport dialogue: "What's most important about your job?" to "being challenged" to "what does that give you?" to "security," the root value.
  • Pink elephant: "hold on to the ball," not "don't fumble"; Davey Johnson: yelling at one player is yelling at everyone.
  • Jordan loved practice ("pure basketball"); Vermeil: a football player is a person first.
  • Text to a PGA star: stop trying to make birdies, try to be who you are.

Key numbers: 3 hallmarks; rapport weights 55% physiology / 38% tone / 7% words; pace 3 times before leading; one day in seven to recharge; Brother Lawrence studied 400 years later.

So what: Define success as effort, growth and purpose for the group. Give people a purpose (who we are) and a vision (what we'll do for others). Pace before you lead, elicit root values, coach in pictures of what you want, and renew daily. Develop the inner world and relationships first and the rest is added.

Recurring Stories & Figures

  • Lollipop vs. candy store: winning vs. fullness of life (Ch 1, 3, 5).
  • Murphy's own baseball career as the example of identity in performance (Ch 1).
  • The samurai (Bunpachiro in Ch 0; the Code in Ch 5; the samurai "expect nothing" mantra in Ch 6 and 10).
  • Michelangelo's David: removing what isn't you (Ch 1, 4).
  • Georges St-Pierre: fear never disappears (Ch 4); prays for his opponent and 80/20 visualization (Ch 10).
  • Dean Smith / Wooden / Westering / Tressel: success as process and by-product (Ch 1, 2, 4, 11).
  • Wim Hof: focus on the cold (Ch 5) and the retreat hike (Ch 8).
  • "I expect nothing... I can handle anything" (Ch 6, 10).
  • Fearless Four: introduced in Ch 4, used in Ch 8's PGA client, and part of the daily process.
  • Anchoring and the subconscious thermostat: Ch 6, 7, 9.
  • Pugh, Ohno, Cink, Ankiel, Sax, Balko: the athlete case studies that carry Ch 4, 5, 10, 9 and 7.
  • Nelson Mandela: in the Sydney 2000 scenario (Ch 5) and among the mentors in the visualization room (Ch 10).

Loonshots: How to Nurture the Crazy Ideas That Win Wars, Cure Diseases, and Transform Industries

2 markdown files

Quiz

Loonshots Quiz Book

Loonshots: How to Nurture the Crazy Ideas That Win Wars, Cure Diseases, and Transform Industries by Safi Bahcall

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative final exam is at the end. Built from the bahcall-loonshots skill notes, not the book's own wording.

Chapter 1 (Introduction): Structure, Not Culture

Q1 (SA). What is the difference between a loonshot and a moonshot?

A: A moonshot is an ambitious, expensive, widely celebrated goal (a destination). A loonshot is a neglected project, widely dismissed, whose champion is written off as unhinged. Nurturing loonshots is how you reach moonshots.

Q2 (SA). The book's central claim is "structure, not culture." What does it mean?

A: Innovation is an emergent property of group structure. Teams that suddenly stop innovating (Nokia, Merck, Disney after The Lion King) did not change their people or culture; they crossed a phase transition triggered by a control parameter such as group size.

Q3 (MC). In the organizational "tug-of-war" that drives a phase transition, the two competing forces are:

a) creativity vs. discipline b) stake in project outcomes vs. the perks of rank c) artists vs. soldiers d) cost vs. quality

A: b. Small groups: stake dominates. As size grows, rank perks rise and stake falls; when they cross, the system snaps and starts rejecting loonshots.

Q4 (SA). What did Phil Anderson's motto "more is different" mean here?

A: The whole is not just more than, but different from, the sum of its parts. You cannot explain ice by studying one molecule, or a team by studying one person.

Q5 (T/F). The goal is for an innovative organization to be entirely in the loonshot phase. A: False. No group can be fully in both phases at once, except at the edge of a transition. The goal is to hold the edge where both phases coexist, like water at 32°F.

Q6 (SA). Why does the book call "culture advice" like yelling at ice, and what is the alternative image?

A: One molecule yelling at its neighbors cannot unfreeze a block of ice. Structure is like salt on the sidewalk: a small additive that shifts the freezing point.

Q7 (SA). What is "post-hoc culture extraction" and why is it flawed?

A: Picking winners by stock price and reverse-engineering "lessons" from them (the Amgen example, where the real lesson was "pick up the check and hire good lawyers"). Victors rewrite a twisted path into a straight line, like reading the socks of a lottery winner.

Chapter 2: How Loonshots Won a War

Q1 (SA). State Bush-Vail Rule 1 and its two parts (plus the third part added in Ch 4).

A: Separate the phases: (a) separate your artists and soldiers; (b) tailor the tools to the phase (wide spans, loose controls, creative metrics for loonshot groups; narrow spans, tight controls, quantitative metrics for franchise groups); (c) watch your blind side by seeding both P- and S-types (introduced in Ch 4).

Q2 (SA). State Bush-Vail Rule 2 and its parts.

A: Create dynamic equilibrium: love your artists and soldiers equally, and manage the transfer, not the technology. The weak link is never the supply of ideas but the transfer to the field and the feedback back.

Q3 (MC). In the four-quadrant map, "separated but no healthy transfer" is called:

a) stagnation b) chaos c) the Trap d) the Bush-Vail target

A: c. Stagnation = no separation; chaos = everyone told to innovate; the target = separated and exchanging.

Q4 (SA). What happened with early airborne radar, and what did it show about field feedback?

A: Pilots ignored it. The problem was not the technology but a switch-fiddling interface. The fix (the PPI display) came only because Bush forced pilots to explain why to the scientists.

Q5 (T/F). Vannevar Bush's key contribution was a technical breakthrough in radar. A: False. Bush "made no technical contribution whatever"; his job was the touch and balance between the two groups. As a leader, be a gardener, not a Moses.

Q6 (SA). What did Bush's structural fix in 1940 consist of, and what result did microwave radar produce?

A: A civilian agency reporting directly to the President, quarantined in anonymous MIT buildings (separation), with Bush personally pushing the technology to battlefield leaders (transfer). Within ~30 months microwave radar cut Allied shipping losses by 95% and forced the U-boat withdrawal.

Q7 (SA). Why did Jobs 1.0 calling the Apple II team "bozos" matter?

A: It illustrates belittling one side. Artists favor artists and soldiers favor soldiers; a leader must genuinely respect both or one side leaves (Wozniak quit and the Mac launch failed).

Chapter 3: The Surprising Fragility of the Loonshot

Q1 (SA). What are the Three Deaths?

A: Sir James Black: "It's not a good drug unless it's been killed at least three times." Nearly every breakthrough is ridiculed, defunded, or abandoned at least three times before it succeeds.

Q2 (SA). What is a False Fail, and what are the three triage questions?

A: A negative result caused by a flaw in the test, not the idea. Ask: (1) Is the negative outcome due to the idea or the experiment? (2) What would you have to believe for it to be a flaw in the test? (3) How could you evaluate that cheaply?

Q3 (MC). Which is NOT cited as a False Fail example?

a) statins in rats b) the dog "cancer" signal c) Friendster's crashes d) Polavision's failure

A: d. Polavision was a genuine commercial failure (Ch 5). The others were test or execution flaws (rats carry mostly HDL; ultra-high doses; crashes rather than a fad).

Q4 (SA). What does LSC stand for and why "with curiosity"?

A: Listen to the Suck with Curiosity: investigate rejection rather than defend against it. Acknowledgment is not enough; you must probe beneath the surface for the mechanism. Anger is stubbornness; curiosity is persistence.

Q5 (SA). Why separate the inventor and the champion?

A: They are different skill sets. Most inventors cannot or will not promote their own work. Champions are bilingual (artist-speak and soldier-speak), like Deak Parsons, who dragged radar out of neglect "with the persistence of a door-to-door salesman."

Q6 (SA). Walk through the three deaths of Akira Endo's statin.

A: (1) "Diet-heart" had been declared dead and almost nobody attended his talk. (2) No effect in rats; he tested on hens (LDL like humans) and cholesterol fell by nearly half. (3) A dog safety study "showed cancer"; Sankyo killed the program after Endo had left and Merck terminated too, until Brown and Goldstein proved a false positive and pressured a restart. Mevacor was approved in 1987.

Q7 (T/F). Beecham gave up on statins after the rat result and so forfeited a share of enormous value. A: True (a share of $300 billion in the notes): the classic cost of killing on the first animal-model failure.

Chapter 4: The Two Types of Loonshots: Trippe vs. Crandall

Q1 (SA). Define P-type and S-type loonshots with their "tells."

A: P-type: product/technology; "There's no way that could ever work." S-type: strategy/business model/new application of an existing product; "There's no way that could ever make money."

Q2 (MC). Compared with P-types, S-types are:

a) faster to kill you b) easier to copy c) dimmer, slower to kill you, and harder to copy d) rarer in great ideas

A: c.

Q3 (SA). What is the "dangerous virtuous cycle"?

A: P-type loonshots feed a franchise, which funds more P-types; momentum builds tunnel vision (bigger, faster, more) until the wheel turns one too many times.

Q4 (SA). What S-type loonshots did Crandall and the startups use against Pan Am?

A: Two-tier pay (A-scale/B-scale), the Sabre reservation system with yield management, and hub-and-spoke, secondary airports, and 20-minute turnarounds.

Q5 (SA). What is an "S-type moment"?

A: A sudden shock (airline deregulation in 1978, Android given away free) that acts like a solar eclipse, letting the faint light of S-type loonshots show and annihilating the unprepared.

Q6 (SA). How did IBM win the P-type battle and lose the strategy war?

A: It won the PC but missed that customers cared about the software standard and the chip, not the box, handing about $1.5 trillion of value to Microsoft and Intel.

Q7 (T/F). Juan Trippe's skill at P-type deals (the jet-age poker game) was unrelated to Pan Am's fall. A: False. The same P-type instinct that won the jet age bought jumbo jets after deregulation while Crandall's unglamorous strategy won. Pan Am lost money in 18 of its last 22 years and ceased operations in 1991.

Chapter 5: Edwin Land and the Moses Trap

Q1 (SA). Define the Moses Trap and give its three stages.

A: An all-powerful leader anoints the holy loonshot by decree, for love of loonshots rather than strength of strategy. Stages: (1) the dangerous virtuous cycle builds momentum; (2) franchise blinders harden (only loonshots that spin the existing wheel are seen); (3) Moses grows all-powerful and anoints by decree.

Q2 (SA). What was Polavision and why did it fail?

A: Land's 1977 instant-movie system: technically miraculous, commercially dead within a year ($2,500 camera, $30 per 3-minute cassette, not erasable). $200M write-off; Land was forced out.

Q3 (MC). Land's failure with digital was primarily:

a) not understanding the technology b) a failure to see its S-type economics c) lack of lab talent d) lack of funding

A: b. He pushed CCD spy satellites (KH-11) in 1971 yet dismissed digital for Polaroid because "there's no film; there's no way that can make money."

Q4 (T/F). A leader who is both CEO and head of research is a structural strength. A: False. It is a structural warning sign: judge-and-jury leadership.

Q5 (SA). What does "The bottom line's in heaven" represent?

A: Land's answer to an analyst; the Moses creed of launching for scientific and aesthetic appeal over commercial significance.

Q6 (SA). How was Land's first synthetic polarizer connected to the False Fail idea?

A: At 19 he found herapathite crystals in an obsolete-words dictionary entry; the graveyard of unexplained experiments is a good place to find a False Fail.

Q7 (SA). Why does a walled-off brilliant lab not save the company?

A: It sits in the bottom-right quadrant: it postpones decline but does not prevent it. Polaroid's digital camera arrived in 1996; bankruptcy followed in 2001.

Chapter 6: Escaping the Moses Trap

Q1 (SA). Describe the three levels of Rule 3 (system mindset).

A: Level 0: don't analyze failures. Level 1 (outcome mindset): ask why the project failed. Level 2 (system mindset): ask how the decision was made (who, what data, framing, incentives) and change the process.

Q2 (T/F). Rule 3 says to analyze failures only. A: False. Analyze wins too: good decisions can have bad outcomes and vice versa; failing to probe wins reinforces a bad process.

Q3 (SA). What is the PARC Trap and how does it differ from the Moses Trap?

A: PARC: phase separation works brilliantly but loonshots stay parked and never leave (transfer under-forced; "Color is not part of the office of the future"; Kodak burying its 1975 digital camera). Moses over-forces the transfer by decree.

Q4 (MC). What did Jobs learn from Ed Catmull at Pixar?

a) to micromanage creatives b) to mind the system rather than manage the project c) to avoid S-types d) to build more hardware

A: b.

Q5 (SA). Why do creatives need peer feedback, and what are examples?

A: Artists accept feedback from thoughtful peers, not suits. Examples: Pixar's director braintrust and Genentech's scientists responding to scientists. Jobs was kept out of early film feedback.

Q6 (SA). What S-type moves did Apple 2.0 use?

A: The iTunes store and the closed ecosystem. Jobs paid $100M+ to kill Mac clones while near bankruptcy.

Q7 (SA). What did Xerox Texas illustrate about bonus structures?

A: Bonuses forced the franchise to sandbag the loonshot: it couldn't make typewriter numbers and launch the Alto.

Chapter 7: Interlude + Phase Transitions I

Q1 (SA). What are the two things to know about phase transitions?

A: (1) At the heart of each is a tug-of-war between two competing forces. (2) They are triggered when small shifts in a system property (density, temperature) change the balance between those forces.

Q2 (SA). What does "simple, but not simplistic" mean?

A: Keep just enough detail to extract general insight with confidence in its micro origins. Too little explains nothing; too much (137 case studies) also explains nothing.

Q3 (SA). What is the "Yellowstone effect" and its organizational analogue?

A: Suppressing every small fire lets fuel build past the threshold until one catastrophic fire is inevitable (1988 burned 36% of the park). Organizationally, suppressing every small failure invites one catastrophic one.

Q4 (MC). A power-law tail (twice as many 10-acre fires as 20-acre) signals:

a) a stable system b) a system near a transition c) random noise d) an efficient market

A: b.

Q5 (SA). What does percolation theory describe?

A: Whether a connected path exists through random pores, trees, or people. Below a critical density fires die out; above it they engulf everything. It also applies to epidemics, networks, and rock fracture.

Q6 (T/F). Small-world networks are fragile to random failure but robust to attacks on hubs. A: False, reversed. They are robust to random failure but fragile to attacks on the most influential nodes.

Q7 (SA). In the traffic phase diagram, what are the two forces, the two control parameters, and three ways to restore smooth flow?

A: Forces: driver wants cruising speed vs. brakes to avoid the bumper ahead. Parameters: car separation and average speed. Fixes: lower speed limits in heavy traffic, meter on-ramps, ban truck overtaking.

Chapter 8: Phase Transitions II: The Magic Number 150

Q1 (SA). What is the Invisible Axe?

A: The collective behavior above the threshold in which everyone individually favors innovation yet the group rationally rejects loonshots. Politics beats projects.

Q2 (SA). Write the magic number equation and define each variable.

A: M = E · S² · F / G. E = equity fraction; S = management span; F = organizational fitness (project–skill fit ÷ return-on-politics); G = salary step-up per promotion.

Q3 (SA). Compute M for E = 50%, S = 6, F = 1, G = 12%.

A: 0.5 × 36 × 1 / 0.12 = 150.

Q4 (T/F). Dunbar's number is correct in observation and in theory. A: False. Right observation (Brigham Young's companies averaged 150; Gore builds a new plant at 150 parking spaces), wrong theory (extrapolating from monkey brain size).

Q5 (MC). Politics appears first in:

a) the executive suite b) the lowest professional-manager layer c) the research lab d) the board

A: b.

Q6 (SA). Why does the angled transition line matter?

A: A group past 150 can restore loonshot focus by adjusting structure instead of shrinking. The number is not universal, like solids melting at different temperatures.

Q7 (SA). In the Pfizer thought experiment, why is dismissing the loonshot rational at 100,000 people?

A: A 1-in-10 loonshot adds about 1% to revenue after seven years with 99,999 colleagues claiming credit or blame, while belittling it and proposing a modest franchise step could bring a 30% raise next year. In a 50-person firm with equity, the loonshot wins.

Chapter 9: The Fourth Rule: Raise the Magic Number

Q1 (SA). List the six levers of Rule 4.

A: (1) Reduce return-on-politics; (2) use soft equity; (3) increase project–skill fit; (4) fix the middle; (5) bring a gun to a knife fight (chief incentives officer); (6) fine-tune the spans.

Q2 (SA). How do DARPA and McKinsey reduce return-on-politics?

A: DARPA: no career ladder; program managers serve 2–4 year terms with expiring badges. McKinsey: important promotions are evaluated by a senior partner from a distant office or practice who interviews up to two dozen colleagues and clients over about three months.

Q3 (MC). Which span suits a loonshot group?

a) 5 or fewer b) 6 c) 15+ d) always the same as franchise groups

A: c. Wide spans give loose controls and peer problem-solving (Coughran at Google, 180 reports). Narrow spans (≤5) suit franchise groups.

Q4 (SA). Explain the Dead Sea Scrolls test.

A: Before launching a reward, ask what a rational actor would do to maximize the metric. Paying per fragment led shepherds to tear scrolls into scraps. Ford Pinto's "Goals Gone Wild" is another example.

Q5 (SA). Why is the "middle" dangerous and how do you fix it?

A: Far from board oversight, evaluations are complex, and bonuses are one promotion away. Steep grant curves (100% bonuses at top, <10% in the middle) turn it into Survivor. Flatten them, celebrate results not rank, and cut rank perks.

Q6 (T/F). Wage dispersion is associated with higher productivity. A: False. Research finds it lowers productivity and cooperation and raises turnover; a big G is bad.

Q7 (SA). How did MIT win the Red Balloon Challenge?

A: A recursive payout ($2,000 to the spotter, $1,000 to the recruiter, $500 to that person's recruiter, and so on) gave everyone a stake. 4,400 people recruited in 36 hours; all ten balloons found in 8h 52m. Georgia Tech, using charity, recruited 1,400.

Chapter 10: Why the World Speaks English

Q1 (SA). What are the three conditions of a loonshot nursery?

A: Phase separation, dynamic equilibrium, and critical mass.

Q2 (SA). How many 10%-odds loonshots give a good chance of at least one hit?

A: Ten give 65%; two dozen give 92%.

Q3 (SA). State the Needham Question.

A: Why did the Scientific Revolution happen in Europe when China led in paper, printing, compass, gunpowder, canals, literacy, and fleet size?

Q4 (MC). Song China had:

a) all three conditions b) critical mass but neither separation nor exchange c) only separation d) none

A: b. The emperor personally directed astronomy and could end it by decree.

Q5 (SA). Contrast Tycho and Shen Kuo.

A: Equal talent, equal loss of royal patronage. Tycho hopped to Prague (and hired Kepler); Shen had nowhere to go, since private astronomy was illegal, and spent his last decade under house arrest.

Q6 (T/F). Inside a Major, a killed project stays dead; in a nursery it can survive on the next lily pad. A: True (immunotherapy survived in small biotechs after every big pharma passed).

Q7 (SA). What does the Haiti vs. Dominican Republic example show?

A: That adoption questions differ from first-appearance questions. Same island rules out culture, climate, and geography, so institutions explain the difference.

Chapter 11 (Afterword): Loonshots vs. Disruption

Q1 (SA). How do "loonshot" and "disruptive" differ?

A: Loonshot is a real-time label about what leaders believe; disruptive (Christensen) is a hindsight label about effect on a market. They are independent axes, "like height and hair color."

Q2 (T/F). The transistor and PageRank were both disruptive from the start. A: False. Both were sustaining: the transistor was a better switch from the largest company in the country ($20 vs. $1 for a tube, sold first to high-end military buyers); PageRank gave incrementally better results than 17 other search engines.

Q3 (SA). What does "leaf in the tornado" mean?

A: Early-stage projects in fast-moving markets end up somewhere no one predicted, so classifying them by eventual market effect in advance is impossible.

Q4 (MC). In a pharma CEO's survey, how many recent launches landed within 2× of the forecast?

a) 20 of 20 b) 10 of 20 c) 5 of 20 d) 0 of 20

A: d.

Q5 (SA). Give the two market-guess examples.

A: Interferon, the viral "magic bullet," became a $6B multiple-sclerosis franchise; Amgen's EPO, a tiny kidney-disease niche, became a $100B company.

Q6 (SA). Why is IKEA a good test of the two lenses?

A: The disruption lens narrates (true, but useless to Kamprad in 1953). The loonshot lens shows each move challenged a belief (warehouse in the countryside, customers assembling furniture, sourcing in Poland), all S-types forced by a blockade from competitors.

Cumulative Final Exam (10 Questions)

F1 (SA). Why does the book say innovation is a matter of structure and not culture?

A: Teams flip phases when a control parameter (chiefly size) crosses a threshold, driven by the tug-of-war between stake and rank. Small changes in structure can melt steel; one molecule yelling cannot.

F2 (SA). List the four Bush-Vail rules.

A: (1) Separate the phases; (2) create dynamic equilibrium; (3) spread a system mindset; (4) raise the magic number.

F3 (MC). Which pair correctly maps trap to cause?

a) Moses: under-forced transfer; PARC: over-forced b) Moses: over-forced transfer by decree; PARC: under-forced, ideas parked c) both lack separation d) both are chaos

A: b.

F4 (SA). What is the difference between a P-type and S-type loonshot, and how did each relate to Pan Am and Polaroid?

A: P: "won't work"; S: "won't make money." Pan Am died of S-types (Crandall's pay, reservations, hubs); Polaroid's blind side was digital's S-type economics inside a P-type (no film, no money).

F5 (T/F). A negative test result means the idea is flawed. A: False. It may be a False Fail (statins in rats, Friendster crashes, the Comet jets). Run the triage before killing.

F6 (SA). Compute M for S = 10, E = 50%, F = 1, G = 33%, and say what the result implies.

A: 0.5 × 100 / 0.33 ≈ 150. Wider modern spans with aggressive step-ups land at the same number.

F7 (SA). Name three levers for raising the magic number with an example of each.

A: Reduce return-on-politics (DARPA's expiring badges, McKinsey's distant evaluators); soft equity (DARPA visibility and autonomy, open innovation like Red Balloon); fine-tune spans (Coughran with 180 reports vs. franchise groups at ≤5). Others: project–skill fit, fix the middle, chief incentives officer.

F8 (SA). What are the three nursery conditions and how does the framework explain Europe vs. China?

A: Phase separation, dynamic equilibrium, critical mass. China had critical mass but no separation or exchange; Europe's fragmented states allowed rejected ideas and scientists (Copernicus, Tycho) to find another patron.

F9 (SA). How should you steer in real time, and why not by forecasts?

A: By the belief an idea challenges (P: won't work; S: won't pay). Forecasts for loonshots are reliably wrong (0 of 20 within 2×), so fund portfolios and test cheaply.

F10 (SA). What do Level 2 analysis and SRT each ask of you?

A: Level 2 (system mindset): how did we decide and what in the process should change, including after wins. SRT (spirit, relationships, time) are the three "glass balls" a loonshot champion must not drop, per the skill's patterns file.

Arguments & Evidence

Loonshots: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Safi Bahcall

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files in the bahcall-loonshots skill (plus its glossary, patterns, and cheatsheet), so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Ch 1 argues that great teams stop innovating because of structure (phase transitions), not culture. Ch 2 gives the first two rules (separate the phases, create dynamic equilibrium) through Bush's wartime radar work. Ch 3 shows why loonshots are fragile (Three Deaths, False Fails, champions, LSC). Ch 4 splits loonshots into P-types and S-types, and Ch 5-6 show how a leader's love of loonshots becomes the Moses Trap and how a system mindset (Rule 3) escapes it. Ch 7-8 supply the science: control parameters, and the magic number M = E·S²·F/G that explains why politics kills loonshots near 150 people. Ch 9 turns that into Rule 4, six levers to raise M. Ch 10 scales the model up to industries and civilizations (the three nursery conditions, the Needham Question). Ch 11 contrasts loonshots with disruption and says to steer by beliefs, not forecasts.

Ch 1 (Introduction). Structure, Not Culture

Argument: Teams that suddenly stop innovating did not change their people or culture; they crossed a phase transition. Innovation is an emergent property of group structure, so fix structure, not culture.

Stories & evidence

  • *Nokia, Merck, Disney after The Lion King:* examples of good teams that suddenly turned.
  • Miller's piranha (ibrutinib): an idea ridiculed by every large pharma, whose champion was fired by his own board, later bought for $21 billion.
  • Amgen example: reverse-engineering "culture" from a winner; the real lesson was "pick up the check and hire good lawyers."
  • Bahcall's own biotech: a physicist-CEO at a sarcoma patient's bedside and later at his father's leukemia bedside, with dozens of candidate drugs buried because large groups had rejected them.
  • Analogies: water at 32°F; yelling at ice vs. salt on the sidewalk; "more is different" (Phil Anderson).

Key numbers: none beyond the $21 billion ibrutinib sale.

So what: Ask which phase the structure is in and which control parameter put it there. Classify ideas as loonshots or moonshots, and distrust straight-line success stories.

Ch 2. How Loonshots Won a War

Argument: Vannevar Bush (OSRD) and Theodore Vail (Bell Labs) rescued stagnant franchises by building a structure in which loonshots and franchises coexist: phase separation plus dynamic equilibrium.

Stories & evidence

  • Radar's neglect: proposed by two Navy radio engineers in 1922 after a passing ship doubled their signal; the Navy rejected a $5,000 request in 1930 because results "might take two or three years"; still being field-tested on the morning of Pearl Harbor.
  • Bush's 1940 fix: a civilian agency reporting to the President, in anonymous MIT buildings; the Secretary of War rode an experimental radar plane ("I've seen the new radar equipment. Why haven't you?").
  • Pilots ignoring radar: a UI problem; the PPI display came after Bush made pilots explain why.
  • 3M under a Six Sigma CEO: innovation plunged.
  • Jobs 1.0 and the Apple II "bozos": Wozniak quit, and the Mac launch failed.
  • Nursery examples: anti-angiogenesis, a Bond film with a monkey villain, The Adventures of Luke Starkiller.

Key numbers: microwave radar cut Allied shipping losses by 95% within ~30 months; five years to assign one full-time person to radar.

So what: Separate and exchange, tailor tools to the phase, love both groups, get top cover, and manage the transfer, not the technology. Be a gardener, not a Moses.

Ch 3. The Surprising Fragility of the Loonshot

Argument: Every important breakthrough dies at least three times. The decisive skill is investigating failure to separate a True Fail from a False Fail.

Stories & evidence

  • Akira Endo's statin: diet-heart declared dead; no effect in rats, then hens showed cholesterol falling by nearly half; a dog "cancer" study led Sankyo and Merck to terminate until Brown and Goldstein proved a false positive. Mevacor approved in 1987.
  • Beecham quit statins on the rat result.
  • Friendster: Thiel and Howery found users left because of crashes, not because social networks were a fad.
  • Comet jets: metal fatigue from a window design, not jets per se.
  • Deak Parsons: the Navy liaison who dragged radar out of neglect.
  • Folkman: the "counting the arrows" line and Spouse Activation Factor; Gleevec's record trial hides years of rejection.

Key numbers: Endo 16 years, Black's beta-blockers 7, Folkman 32; statins now prevent ~500,000 heart attacks and strokes a year in the US; Beecham forfeited a share of $300 billion; first patient's cholesterol dropped 30%.

So what: Budget for three deaths, run False-Fail triage before killing, appoint and train champions, and practice LSC (anger = stubbornness, curiosity = persistence).

Ch 4. The Two Types of Loonshots: Trippe vs. Crandall

Argument: There are P-type and S-type loonshots. Every innovator has a blind side; Pan Am died of the one Juan Trippe could not see.

Stories & evidence

  • Trippe's jet-age poker game: engines ordered directly from Rolls-Royce to spook Pratt & Whitney; Douglas committed to the DC-8; Boeing conceded the redesign. Boeing's president "felt like an earthquake victim."
  • Crandall's S-types: two-tier pay, Sabre with yield management ("thirty years before Big Data"), hub-and-spoke, secondary airports, 20-minute turnarounds.
  • IBM: won the PC but handed value to Microsoft and Intel.
  • Google: a P-type ranking algorithm plus S-type advertising strategies.
  • S-type moments: airline deregulation (1978), Android given away free.
  • Pie-shop parable and the Harry Lime cuckoo-clock framing.

Key numbers: 120 engines, $40M, four times Pan Am's annual income; IBM's miss worth ~$1.5 trillion; Pan Am lost money in 18 of its last 22 years and ceased operations in 1991.

So what: Name each loonshot's type; if your list is one-sided, seed the other. Expect S-type waves after sudden shocks, and beware the turn too many of a virtuous cycle.

Ch 5. Edwin Land and the Moses Trap

Argument: Land built a Nobel-caliber nursery (Rule 1) but stayed judge and jury of every idea (failing Rule 2). A Moses can will loonshots into existence for a while, until the virtuous cycle spins one turn too many.

Stories & evidence

  • Polaroid's arc: sepia prints (1947), instant color (1963), SX-70 (1972); cameras earned little, film earned a lot.
  • Herapathite: found in a dictionary entry; first synthetic polarizer at 19.
  • Polavision (1977): instant movies; launched with mimes and dancers; "The bottom line's in heaven"; "I wanted you to see what hubris looks like."
  • KH-11: Land argued for CCD spy satellites in April 1971 and won against the military leadership, yet dismissed digital for Polaroid ("there's no film").
  • Walled-off lab: Land banned his own head of engineering from the ninth floor.

Key numbers: sales from $1.5M to $1.4B; Polavision $2,500 camera, $30 per 3-minute cassette, $200M write-off; ten years and half a billion dollars; digital camera in 1996, bankruptcy in 2001.

So what: Phase separation without equilibrium delays but does not prevent decline. A CEO who is also head of research is a warning sign; ask what new income streams a technology enables.

Ch 6. Escaping the Moses Trap

Argument: Jobs 1.0 doubled down on the Moses Trap (NeXT, Pixar Image Computer). Watching Ed Catmull taught him to mind the system rather than manage the project: Rule 3, system mindset. Apple 2.0 was the result.

Stories & evidence

  • Kasparov's levels: Level 0, Level 1 (outcome), Level 2 (system); analyze wins too (a 100:1 lottery; the keeper slipped).
  • NeXT post-mortem: the Cube at $10,000, Businessland sold under 400 units; launch modeled on Polavision's theater.
  • Pixar's braintrust and Genentech scientists as peer feedback; Levinson grilling junior technicians.
  • Toy Story and the IPO showed Jobs the rules working.
  • PARC Trap: "Color is not part of the office of the future"; Kodak's 1975 digital camera buried for a decade; Xerox Texas could not launch the Alto.
  • Apple 2.0: Ive's sealed-off studio, Cook as heir, iTunes store, closed ecosystem; OS/2 failure as a False Fail; $100M+ to kill Mac clones.

Key numbers: Cube $10,000; Businessland under 400 units; $100M+ paid to kill clones.

So what: Analyze decisions, not outcomes; the leader minds the system and champions run projects. Avoid both flanking traps, Moses (over-forced) and PARC (under-forced).

Ch 7. Interlude + Phase Transitions I

Argument: Emergent behaviors can snap. Every phase transition is a tug-of-war between two forces triggered when a control parameter crosses a threshold; find the parameters and you can manage the transition.

Stories & evidence

  • Traffic phase diagram: speed and separation; phantom jams at the Nagoya Dome; fixes are lower limits, ramp metering, truck-overtaking bans.
  • Percolation (Broadbent & Hammersley, 1957) and Watts-Strogatz small-world networks.
  • Yellowstone 1988: suppressing small fires led to a catastrophic one; prescribed burns.
  • Greenspan's "notably rare exceptions" (2008) and Adam Smith's invisible hand as emergent physics.
  • Neil Johnson's virtual terror cells: pro-ISIS pages; clusters grow, merge, split like fire clusters.
  • Hemingway's Theory of Omission applied to models; iron melting at 2,800°F.

Key numbers: 108,086 followers across 196 pages; power-law exponent ≈ 2.5 across nine conflicts; 36% of Yellowstone burned; stopping distance ~6 car lengths at 30 mph vs ~30 at 80 mph; delay doubling 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s.

So what: Name the forces, name two dials, draw the line, and pick the cheaper dial. Power-law tails and clustering signal a system near its edge.

Ch 8. Phase Transitions II: The Magic Number 150

Argument: As a group grows, incentives shift from stake in projects to promotion politics; above a critical size the Invisible Axe appears. That size follows from four structural dials and can be raised.

Stories & evidence

  • Dunbar's number: right observation (Brigham Young's companies; Gore builds a new plant at 150 parking spaces), wrong theory (monkey-brain extrapolation).
  • The 4 p.m. choice: project work vs. lobbying for promotion.
  • Pfizer thought experiment: champion a 1-in-10 drug or belittle it and chase a 30% raise; the answer flips at 50 people with equity.
  • Equation derivation (Appendix B): the no-politics condition, with politics appearing first at the lowest professional-manager layer.

Key numbers: M = E·S²·F/G; E 50%, S 6, F 1, G 12% gives 150; S 10 with G 33% also ≈150; $50B company, 100,000 people, ~$500M (1%) hit with ~10% odds over seven years.

So what: Rejection of loonshots at scale is rational behavior from structure, not bad people. Know your four dials, count soft equity, and remember the line is angled so structure can restore the loonshot phase at any size.

Ch 9. The Fourth Rule: Raise the Magic Number

Argument: DARPA, a ~200-person nursery inside a two-million-person organization, shows how adjusting M's dials keeps very large organizations nurturing loonshots. There are six levers.

Stories & evidence

  • DARPA: no career ladder, 2-4 year terms, expiring badges, publicly known program managers.
  • McKinsey: distant senior partner evaluates promotions over ~3 months.
  • Open innovation: Coors cold-activated can, Kraft melt-resistant chocolate.
  • Project-skill fit: Bahcall's toothpaste project (undermatch); bored Frank Lloyd Wright on a coffee machine (overmatch).
  • Perverse incentives: Dead Sea Scrolls paid per fragment; Ford Pinto's "Goals Gone Wild."
  • Spans: Bill Coughran at Google with 180 reports; Bob Taylor at PARC with 40-50.
  • Red Balloon Challenge: Georgia Tech (charity, 1,400 people) vs. MIT (recursive payout, 4,400 people in 36 hours).

Key numbers: 15+ spans in loonshot groups vs. ≤5 in franchise groups; 100% bonuses at top vs. <10% in the middle; $40,000 prize, ten balloons; $2,000/$1,000/$500 payouts; found in 8h 52m; interviews of up to two dozen colleagues.

So what: Map every HR policy to E, S, F, or G; fix the middle first; audit every reward with the Dead Sea Scrolls test; hire a chief incentives officer; use wide spans only where loonshots live.

Ch 10. Why the World Speaks English

Argument: The scientific method was the mother of all loonshots. It ignited in fragmented Europe, not in richer empires, because Europe was a loonshot nursery among nations meeting three conditions the empires did not.

Stories & evidence

  • The Needham Question: China led in paper, printing, compass, gunpowder, canals, literacy, and fleet size.
  • Kepler's eight minutes: an error of eight arc-minutes (<0.05%) he would not ignore.
  • Tycho vs. Shen Kuo: Tycho hopped to Prague; Shen spent his last decade under house arrest. The emperor declared Shen's system "good enough" after seven years.
  • Royal Society (1660): Boyle's air pump, Papin's piston, Newcomen's steam engine (1712), Nemesis.
  • *Film after US v. Paramount (1948) and biotech vs. pharma* (Roche-Genentech >$30B/yr); immunotherapy surviving in small biotechs.
  • Haiti vs. Dominican Republic, Boston vs. Detroit, and the Qianlong emperor's "nothing to learn" remark.

Key numbers: 10 shots at 10% odds gives 65%; two dozen gives 92%; 200+ Boston biotechs; Copernicus taught for sixty years at Wittenberg.

So what: Score any ecosystem on separation, exchange, and critical mass; all three or it won't ignite. Nurseries keep killed ideas alive on another lily pad; empires bury them.

Ch 11 (Afterword). Loonshots vs. Disruption

Argument: "Disruptive" is a hindsight label about market effect; a loonshot is a real-time label about leaders' beliefs. Steer with P/S-types; use disruptive/sustaining to analyze history.

Stories & evidence

  • Transistor and PageRank were sustaining at the start.
  • Walmart's origin: Walton's wife refused to live anywhere over 10,000 people; Bentonville offered four quail seasons.
  • IKEA: showroom, flat-pack, self-service warehouse, own designers, Polish suppliers, all forced by being banned from trade fairs and cut off from suppliers.
  • Interferon and Amgen's EPO as market guesses wrong in both directions.
  • Low-cost airlines: hundreds of "disruptive" entrants failed while American won with sustaining S-types.

Key numbers: 0 of 20 launches within 2× of forecast; interferon became a $6B MS franchise; EPO's company became $100B; the transistor $20 vs $1 for a tube.

So what: Classify by the belief challenged, treat market forecasts as order-of-magnitude guesses, fund portfolios, and use a nursery to discover your false certainties before a competitor does.

Recurring Stories & Cases

  • Radar / Vannevar Bush: Ch 2 (OSRD), echoed in Ch 3 (Deak Parsons) and Ch 9 (DARPA as OSRD reborn).
  • Statins / Akira Endo: the Three Deaths and False Fail case in Ch 3, and a False Fail template later.
  • Pan Am vs. Crandall and IBM: the blind-side cases of Ch 4.
  • Edwin Land / Polaroid: Ch 5's Moses Trap, with Jobs as his self-declared disciple in Ch 6.
  • Steve Jobs / NeXT / Pixar / Apple 2.0: the arc from Moses to system mindset.
  • Xerox PARC and Kodak's digital camera: the PARC Trap (Ch 6).
  • Forest fires, traffic jams, and terror networks: the phase-transition examples (Ch 7), reused for the organizational model.
  • Dunbar's 150 and the Pfizer thought experiment: Ch 8.
  • DARPA and McKinsey: Ch 9's anti-politics structures.
  • Song China vs. Europe: Ch 10's nursery case; the emperor as Moses.
  • Walmart, IKEA, interferon, EPO: Ch 11's belief-and-forecast cases.

Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World

2 markdown files

Quiz

Range Quiz Book

Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World by David Epstein

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative final exam is at the end. Chapter numbering follows the epstein-range skill (Introduction, Ch 1-12, Conclusion). This quiz is built from that skill's notes, not the book's own text.

Introduction: Roger vs. Tiger

Q1 (SA). What are the Tiger path and the Roger path?

A: The Tiger path is early, narrow, technical, deliberately practiced specialization from the earliest possible age. The Roger path is broad sampling of many activities, unstructured play, and delayed concentration. Federer sampled many sports and specialized late and was still number one in his mid-thirties. Tiger Woods was handed a putter before he could talk.

Q2 (SA). What is the "sampling period" and why is it not a delay?

A: The phase where learners try a variety of activities in unstructured or lightly structured settings, gain a range of proficiencies, and learn their own abilities and proclivities before narrowing. It is integral to development because choosing before sampling means optimizing something you may be poorly matched to.

Q3 (MC). In the study definition, "deliberate practice" requires all of the following EXCEPT:
