A: Space programs, transport networks, flood control, aircraft manufacture, and epidemic and pollution control. His claim is that centralization is misapplied, not always wrong.

Q7 (SA). What does the "parade-ground test" say about pilots?

A: A lavishly equipped demonstration farm shows what is possible under supervision, not what scales.

Chapter 7: Compulsory Villagization in Tanzania: Aesthetics and Miniaturization

Q1 (SA). What is miniaturization?

A: When reality resists, planners retreat into a small controlled zone (model villages, demonstration farms, new capitals) where the plan can be realized, then treat it as evidence about the whole.

Q2 (SA). Give the subsidy-density example from this chapter.

A: One Tanzanian scheme of 300 settlers absorbed four bulldozers, nine tractors, seven lorries, a generator, fifteen administrators, and 150 laborers.

Q3 (MC). Which best describes Nyerere's intent?

a) Extractive and cynical b) Egalitarian, wanting schools, clinics, clean water, and a countryside that would not split into kulaks and laborers c) Purely military d) Purely commercial

A: b. He disavowed compulsion, but allowed it might be necessary to insist farmers grow a certain acreage, and the bureaucracy widened that seam.

Q4 (SA). How did officials handle the villagization campaign after the December 1973 order?

A: Regions competed (Mara reportedly nearly finished); where persuasion failed, famine relief was made conditional on moving, militia supplied transport, and houses were burned to prevent return. Food imports were needed from 1973 to 1975, 1.2 billion shillings, enough to buy a cow for every family.

Q5 (SA). What was the Ruvuma Development Association and what happened to it?

A: It actually practiced Nyerere's stated ideals (spontaneous, local, cooperative). It was banned in 1968 and its assets seized for refusing absorption into party routine.

Q6 (T/F). Scott says Tanzania was as destructive as Stalinist collectivization. A: False. Tanzania's weakness, unwillingness to use Stalinist methods, and peasants' options of flight, smuggling, and foot-dragging made practice far less destructive than theory. Ethiopia under the Dergue ran the same template with military force.

Q7 (SA). What does the Parisian taxi driver example show?

A: Obeying every regulation would halt central Paris, so traffic flows only because drivers master practices outside the code. If following your rules exactly would break the system, the rules are not the system.

Chapter 8: Taming Nature: An Agriculture of Legibility and Simplicity

Q1 (SA). What are Scott's four systemic failures of high-modernist agriculture?

A: (1) Inherited unexamined assumptions from the temperate industrializing West; (2) institutional interest (the more the cultivator knows, the less the specialist matters); (3) cyclopean shortsightedness (productionist focus hides long-term outcomes and externalities); (4) incapacity for complexity (isolating one variable leaves the method unable to assess many-variable practices). Failures 3 and 4 are structural and would occur under the best administration.

Q2 (SA). Why is the experimental plot itself a simplification?

A: Its controls are a construction: weather, soil, landscape, and implicit assumptions about farm size, labor, and what the cultivator wants are held constant. Researchers called pests and bad weather "interference," yet coping with exactly that is the farmer's main concern.

Q3 (MC). The 1970 corn blight illustrates:

a) the benefits of monocropping b) that 71 percent of US corn acreage in six hybrids preceded it; an exotic Mexican landrace supplied the escape c) polyculture failure d) a DDT problem

A: b. The pathogen was old; the vulnerability was new.

Q4 (SA). What did Edgar Anderson find in the Guatemalan garden at Santa Lucia?

A: What looked like an overgrown dump heap was, once mapped, a system of crosswise rows of fruit trees, cacti, coffee, medicinal herbs, maize, banana, cucurbits, and more, at once vegetable garden, orchard, medicinal garden, compost heap, and beeyard. It resisted erosion, held humidity, isolated same-kind plants, maintained fertility, and produced continuously with little effort.

Q5 (SA). Why couldn't the agronomist see that order?

A: Beyond prejudice and institutional interest, complex intercropping is unprovable by the available method because too many variables are in play for unambiguous causal proof. Polyculture resists proof, not necessarily function.

Q6 (T/F). Scott argues that scientific agronomy is worthless. A: False. Modern breeding, pathology, and soil science created knowledge even traditional cultivators use. Local knowledge also has hard limits. The claim is narrower: the method's power is bought by exclusions.

Q7 (SA). What did the DDT case show?

A: The model asked what dose kills mosquitoes and succeeded in its frame (malaria fell). It was blind to residues moving up the food chain; the alarm came from outside the paradigm, leading to eggshell thinning and a ban.

Chapter 9: Thin Simplifications and Practical Knowledge: Mētis

Q1 (SA). Define mētis and name the three conditions under which it is most valuable.

A: Practical, local, experiential intelligence acquired by doing, Odysseus's quality. Most valuable where situations are mutable, indeterminate, and particular.

Q2 (SA). Contrast mētis with technē/epistēmē on scope, test, and stance.

A: Mētis is contextual and local; technē/epistēmē is universal and context-free. Mētis is tested by "did it work?"; technē by "is it explained and verified?" Mētis is partisan (cares about this outcome); technē is impersonal, quantitative, and probabilistic.

Q3 (MC). The best summary of the Squanto maxim ("plant corn when the oak leaves are the size of a squirrel's ear") is:

a) pure folklore b) a compressed reading of a natural succession whose sequence rarely varies, so a near-foolproof frost-avoidance rule that travels c) a scientific formula d) an almanac rule

A: b. Compare the almanac's fixed-date advice (needs correcting for latitude and altitude, fail-safe for the publisher) and Quetelet's lilac formula ("hardly practical").

Q4 (SA). What does work-to-rule prove, and what happened in the Caterpillar action?

A: Actual work processes depend more on informal understandings and improvisations than on formal rules. In the Caterpillar action, workers reverted to the engineers' specified procedures, knowing the officially correct method would cost time and quality.

Q5 (SA). What is "locally superior" knowledge?

A: The harbor pilot outranks the ship's captain inside the harbor; situated knowledge of this port, these sandbars and microcurrents, "must prevail" over the general rules of navigation.

Q6 (SA). How did East German factories rely on mētis?

A: Two employees absent from the org chart kept them running: the jack-of-all-trades who improvised repairs, and the wheeler-dealer who crossed the country in a Trabant to barter for a missing valve. "A key element in the centrally planned economy was underwritten, always unofficially, by mētis."

Q7 (T/F). Scott romanticizes mētis. A: False. Its innovations are recombinations (bricolage), its transmission may favor conservation of skills over daring innovation, and it coexists with domination, monopoly, and exclusion. His objection is to replacing the collaboration between mētis and technē with an imperial scientific view.

Chapter 10: Conclusion

Q1 (SA). State Scott's four rules of thumb for less disaster-prone planning.

A: (1) Take small steps; (2) favor reversibility; (3) plan on surprises; (4) plan on human inventiveness.

Q2 (SA). Explain the two maps test.

A: Map 1 shows the routes the planners provided. Map 2 is a time-lapse of all unplanned movement and activity. Map 2 is far more complex and in older neighborhoods nearly supersedes Map 1. "Planned Brasília is, in a thousand ways, underwritten by unplanned Brasília."

Q3 (MC). The mētis-friendly institution litmus test asks:

a) Is it cheap? b) To what degree does it enhance the skills, knowledge, and responsibility of those who are part of it? c) Is it centralized? d) Is it popular?

A: b. It distinguishes "canned" forms from those open to modification.

Q4 (SA). What contrast do the two war memorials draw?

A: Maya Lin's Vietnam Memorial (low black wall, names in chronological order) virtually requires participation (rubbings, mementos) to complete its meaning. The Iwo Jima statue is symbolically self-sufficient, so visitors receive its message rather than complete it. The first renews mētis ("use it or lose it"); the second is "canned."

Q5 (SA). What is the "abstract citizen"?

A: The standardized, interchangeable planning subject with "no gender, no tastes, no history, no values, no opinions or original ideas, no traditions," the necessary first premise of any large-scale planning exercise.

Q6 (SA). What is the self-fulfilling logic of social engineering?

A: Narrow, controlled environments foster a less skilled, less innovative, less resourceful population (institutional neurosis), which then genuinely does need close supervision. The plan produces the subjects it assumed.

Q7 (T/F). Scott says fixed routines are never efficient. A: False. They are legitimately efficient where the task environment is repetitive, stable, and predictable, and he does not deny the benefits of division of labor or hierarchical coordination for some tasks. But in most human affairs that is seldom the case.

Cumulative Final Exam (10 questions)

F1 (SA). Name the four elements of the recipe for disaster and say which two are the true danger signals.

A: Administrative ordering (legibility), high-modernist ideology, an authoritarian state, a prostrate civil society. Elements 3 and 4, where nobody can say no, are the danger signals.

F2 (T/F). Scott is anti-state, anti-planning, and anti-science. A: False. The state is "the vexed institution that is the ground of both our freedoms and our unfreedoms." Legibility has credited uses (public health, taxation fairness, rule of law, poverty relief, citizenship). His target is "an imperial or hegemonic planning mentality that excludes the necessary role of local knowledge and know-how."

F3 (SA). Walk through how scientific forestry moved from a map to a remade territory and what went wrong.

A: Foresters narrowed vision to commercial wood, derived the Normalbaum and yield tables, then fit the forest to the tables (single-species, same-age, straight rows). The first rotation triumphed; the second collapsed by 20-30% (Waldsterben), and "forest hygiene" tried to simulate lost habitat.

F4 (MC). Which pair of cases best shows miniaturization at work?

a) Haussmann's Paris and the kolkhoz b) Tanzanian model villages and Brasília/the model farm showcase c) Lenin and Luxemburg d) The Squanto maxim and the almanac

A: b. Subsidized showcase zones were read as proof the design would scale (see also the parade-ground test in Ch 6).

F5 (SA). How do Chapters 4 and 5 parallel each other?

A: Lenin : Le Corbusier :: Luxemburg and Kollontai : Jacobs. Each plan entrusts a living process to a cadre with a master science; the critics argue from process, practice, and ground-level experience.

F6 (SA). In what sense did collectivization "succeed" and "fail"?

A: It failed at yields and efficiency (yields stagnated or fell below 1920s levels for half a century) but succeeded at appropriation and control (grain, industrial financing, dissolving the mir). The informal private plots supplied most fruit, vegetables, eggs, and dairy.

F7 (SA). What do work-to-rule, the harbor pilot, and the East German factories have in common?

A: Each shows formal order depends on informal practice (mētis) it neither recognizes nor can create. Formal order is "parasitic on informal processes."

F8 (T/F). Good intentions protect a development scheme from the generic failure. A: False. Tanzania's villagization, under an egalitarian leader and a weak, well-intentioned state, still failed ecologically and economically. The generic developmentalist logic produces generic failure regardless.

F9 (SA). What is thin simplification and why does thinness reduce resilience?

A: A schematic model too impoverished to serve as instructions for a functioning order. "The more schematic, thin, and simplified the formal order, the less resilient and the more vulnerable it is to disturbances outside its narrow parameters." Monocrops and uniform hybrids are examples.

F10 (SA). Apply the four rules of thumb and the two maps test to a hypothetical rollout of a nationwide, simultaneous, irreversible reform. What would Scott advise?

A: Take a small step, observe, then plan the next; favor an intervention that can be undone ("keep all the parts"); design in slack for surprises; assume later participants will improve on the design. Draw Map 2 of the unplanned activity the design silently depends on, and keep a channel open to the people whose knowledge was excluded. (The notes flag nationwide, simultaneous, irreversible rollout as a sign scope has defeated foresight.)

Arguments & Evidence

Seeing Like a State: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

James C. Scott

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files in the scott-seeing-like-a-state skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording. Where the notes give few or no numbers, that is said.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

The Introduction argues that large schemes to improve the human condition fail catastrophically when four elements combine: state simplification (legibility), high-modernist ideology, an authoritarian state, and a prostrate civil society, and that every formal plan is parasitic on informal processes it cannot create. Ch 1-2 (Part 1) show the legibility toolkit applied to forests, land, names, measures, cities, and language. Ch 3-5 (Part 2) show the ideology and the fusion with coercive power: high modernism, the Le Corbusier/Brasilia city and its critic Jane Jacobs, and Lenin's vanguard party and its critics Luxemburg and Kollontai. Ch 6-8 (Part 3) apply this to the countryside: Soviet collectivization, Tanzanian villagization, and the scientific agriculture of legibility and simplicity. Ch 9-10 (Part 4, the missing link) name what the plans left out, mētis, and offer rules of thumb and an institutional litmus test rather than a program.

Introduction

Argument: Schemes fail catastrophically when four elements combine, all necessary and none sufficient: (1) the administrative ordering of nature and society, (2) a high-modernist ideology, (3) an authoritarian state willing to use full coercive power, (4) a prostrate civil society. Elements 1 and 2 alone are ordinary and often benign. The deeper reason for failure is that formal order is "parasitic on informal processes" it neither recognizes nor can create.

Stories & evidence

  • Scott's detour: he began by asking why states are the enemy of "people who move around" (swidden hill peoples, nomads, pastoralists, Gypsies, vagrants, runaway serfs). Sedentarization campaigns recur and rarely succeed. Reframed as legibility projects (taxation, conscription, preventing rebellion), this became a theory of statecraft.
  • The premodern state's near-blindness: it knew "precious little about its subjects," lacked a common metric, and had no synoptic view.
  • Examples of legibility: permanent surnames, standardized weights and measures, cadastral surveys, population registers, freehold tenure, standardized language, city design, transport layout. A cadastral map made to identify taxable holders creates the tenure system it describes.
  • *Work-to-rule (grève du zèle):* observe every rule and production halts, proving that formal rules depend on informal practice.
  • The legible beehive: a modern hive with queen excluder and standardized frames is redesigned around the beekeeper's problem, not the bees'.
  • Scott's guardrails: the state is "the vexed institution that is the ground of both our freedoms and our unfreedoms"; legibility enables public health and relief for the poor; large-scale capitalism is "just as much an agency of homogenization" as the state.

Key numbers: four elements; no other numbers in the notes.

So what: Use the four-element test as a screening test. The lethal ingredient is that nobody can say no. Expect measurement to become prescriptive, and never accept the documented process as the working process.

Ch 1. Nature and Space

Argument: The state narrows vision to a few standardized, aggregable facts so it can see from the center. The decisive move is that state power then reshapes the terrain to match the map. Everything bracketed out of the frame returns later as unpriced cost.

Stories & evidence

  • Scientific forestry (Prussia and Saxony, c. 1765-1800): Beckmann's crews tagged trees in sample plots with color-coded nails by size class; mathematicians derived the Normalbaum and yield tables. Foresters then fit the forest to the tables: underbrush cleared, deadfall removed, single-species (Norway spruce, Scotch pine), same-age, planted in rows.
  • What fell outside the frame: peasants lost fodder, fruit, medicine, resin, grazing, and fuel.
  • Second rotation: nutrient cycling collapsed, soils thinned, storm-felling and species-specific pests hit uniform stands, and site classes dropped. Waldsterben entered the language.
  • "Forest hygiene": nest boxes and schoolchildren tending transplanted ant colonies, simulating a habitat while keeping the monoculture.
  • Door-and-window tax: produced houses with fewer windows.
  • Cadastral mapping and freehold tenure: one legal owner per numbered parcel, replacing plural customary claims. Local measures (a day's plowing, "a farm of two cows") are exact for the task but unreadable from outside.
  • Counterpoint: the Third Estate demanded one weight and one measure; uniform measures underwrote equal citizenship and fair taxation.

Key numbers: about 1765-1800 for the foresters; a 20-30% production loss in the second rotation; an "eighty-year" first rotation; site classes dropping one or two grades.

So what: Write down what falls outside any metric's frame; judge simplified systems on their second rotation, not their first; preserve redundancy you cannot yet price; ask about facts on the ground versus facts on paper.

Ch 2. Cities, People, and Language

Argument: The same simplifying optic is applied to cities, personal names, language, and traffic. Legibility is two-edged: the same capacity that enables vaccination and poverty relief enabled the 1941 Amsterdam map of Jewish residents. State facts are interested, documentary, static, aggregate, and standardized.

Stories & evidence

  • Permanent surnames: until about the fourteenth century most Europeans lacked them. Florence's 1427 catasto showed that state initiative created surnames and that density tracked state reach. In England, clerks invented names when subjects gave none; tying inheritance and copyhold to state-validated claims (Edward I) gave people reasons to adopt them. The 1381 rising followed a decade of poll-tax registrations.
  • Claveria's 1849 Philippine decree: an alphabetized catalogo of names distributed to each town; no document with another name was valid. His registers did not record prior names, destroying the ability to trace history.
  • Grid vs. warren: Bruges versus Chicago; the native-tracker test; the grid's order is visible only from above.
  • Haussmannization (1853-69): demolition, boulevards, sewers, rail for military security, public health, commerce, and display. Zoning regulated facades; the poor were pushed out to Belleville, and eventually the Commune followed.
  • Legrand Star: hub-and-spoke routing makes A-to-hub easy and A-to-B costly.
  • Official language as toll gate: competence in it becomes the currency of advancement.

Key numbers: a third of Florentine households declared a second name, a fifth in secondary towns, a tenth in the countryside; six Christian names covered ninety percent of English males; Claveria's decree in 1849; Haussmann 1853-69; Amsterdam 1941.

So what: Standardize when the alternative is crude intervention, but expect any identity scheme to be reused for purposes you did not choose; keep mappings to old identifiers; regulate outcomes, not surfaces; treat resistance as information about whose interests the old system served.

Ch 3. Authoritarian High Modernism

Argument: High modernism is a faith that scientific and technical progress, applied through the state, can redesign social life from zero. It becomes catastrophic only when it fuses with the other elements. It is not scientific practice and it is not inherently destructive.

Stories & evidence

  • The lineage: Condorcet (1782) on the sciences of man; Saint-Simon's followers; Marx and Engels on nature's forces; WWI and Walther Rathenau's planned war economy at the Office of War Raw Materials.
  • Lenin: studied Rathenau's model as a prototype of a socialized economy and dropped his dismissal of Taylorism as "the scientific extortion of sweat."
  • Concepts introduced: the discovery of society (statistics on fertility, crime, literacy), description becoming prescription, productivism, social taxidermy, Bauman's gardening image.
  • Three liberal-democratic brakes: a believed-in private sphere, a private sector, and working representative institutions. Sen: free press, assembly, and elections prevent famine.
  • Scott's ledger: public health, longevity, and productivity are real gains; the enemies of 19th-century reformers were real-estate interests, entrenched politics, and prejudice.

Key numbers: Condorcet 1782; four elements; three brakes.

So what: Run the four-element test; build the channel for the affected to be heard before you need it; suspect any claim of a single correct technical answer, because its function is to make negotiation illegitimate; discount the future honestly.

Ch 4. The High-Modernist City: An Experiment and a Critique

Argument: Le Corbusier's urbanism is authoritarian high modernism made buildable, justified as science but resting on an aesthetic preference. Brasilia shows formal order and social death at once; Jacobs' street-level critique shows why.

Stories & evidence

  • Le Corbusier's principles: "The Plan: Dictator"; "the death of the street"; functional segregation of work, residence, commerce, and traffic. Cities drawn as seen from miles out to sea.
  • Brasilia: Kubitschek promised "fifty years of progress in five"; Costa won the competition on rough sketches; Niemeyer ran it. An empty, state-owned plateau a thousand kilometers from Rio. Superquadras with a nursery and school each. Real gains: 25 square meters of green space per resident.
  • Subtractions: no corridor street or praça; the Plaza of the Three Powers, vast and empty; "brasilite"; identical facades; nine-year-olds asked to draw "home" did not draw an apartment (Holston).
  • The candangos: about sixty thousand construction workers who squatted, organized, and were heard. By 1980, 75 percent lived in unplanned settlements and the planned city had not reached half its projected population.
  • Chandigarh: rectilinear axes, empty chowks, hawkers banned, another unplanned city at the margins.
  • Jacobs: watching from a second-floor window, she saw the butcher's wife, deli owner, bar patrons, fruit vendor, and laundryman appear to handle a street incident before any police officer; "eyes on the street." A Louisville building's dozen successive uses: "Only an unimaginative man would think he could; only an arrogant man would want to."

Key numbers: superquadra of about 1,500-2,500 residents; about 60,000 candangos; 75% in unplanned settlements by 1980; under half the projected population; 25 m2 green space per resident.

So what: Beauty in the diagram is not evidence of fitness in use; single-use zoning is chosen because it makes planning tractable; what you make legible from the center you may make unnavigable from within; expect the margins to do the work the plan refused.

Ch 5. The Revolutionary Party: A Plan and a Diagnosis

Argument: Lenin's design for making a revolution is the same move as Le Corbusier's design for a city: a living process handed to a professional cadre holding a master science. Luxemburg and Kollontai reply that the process is unknowable in advance and that how the journey is made determines what arrives.

Stories & evidence

  • Lenin: What Is to Be Done? (1903) (party as brain, masses as body; trade-union consciousness; metaphors of general staff, classroom, factory); State and Revolution (egalitarian tone but "absolute and strict unity of will"); The Agrarian Question (the family farm as hand loom, doomed).
  • Luxemburg: a physician, not an engineer; the mass strike is not a pocket-knife; the errors of a real movement are "infinitely more fruitful" than the infallibility of the best central committee. In 1918 she predicted that without elections, free press, and assembly, life dies out in public institutions and an elite is invited to applaud.
  • 1917 itself: in January 1917 Lenin wrote his generation might not see the decisive battles. Workers formed soviets and seized factories; peasants seized land; military collapse and Kerensky's lack of coercive resources broke the regime. Arendt: "The Bolsheviks found power lying in the street, and picked it up."
  • After the seizure: destroying independent soviets, piecework, abrogating the right to strike, grain requisition, collectivization, at the cost of Kronstadt, Tambov, and the Makhnovshchina.
  • Kollontai: the Workers' Opposition saw unions as managers and creators of the communist economy; it was outlawed and she was silenced. "It is impossible to decree communism."

Key numbers: 1903; 1917; 1918 (Luxemburg's prediction); 1921; the notes give few other figures.

So what: Ask what kind of task you are on before choosing the organizational form; watch the metaphors leadership reaches for; broadcast-only channels guarantee the center learns nothing; suppressing criticism disables error correction; distrust the tidy retrospective story.

Ch 6. Soviet Collectivization, Capitalist Dreams

Argument: Collectivization failed at nearly every high-modernist goal it announced yet succeeded at the older goals of appropriation and control. The countryside was redesigned because it then became something the center could see, count, and command.

Stories & evidence

  • American roots: Taylorist agricultural engineers recast the farm as a factory. Thomas Campbell's 95,000-acre Montana wheat operation (Morgan money, federal subsidy, hardy crops, flat virgin land) collapsed in two years under drought and withdrawn price supports.
  • Soviet pilgrims and a hotel-room plan: Russian agronomists toured Campbell's farm; Wilson, Ware, and Riggin planned a half-million-acre Soviet farm in a Chicago hotel room over two weeks. The sovkhoz, Verblud, failed for reasons reducible to context. An 80,000-hectare scheme was divided into thirty-two equal map squares without reference to terrain.
  • Domestic collectivization: communes under-reported land and over-reported population; armed requisition provoked over 150 uprisings and ended in the NEP retreat; Stalin needed grain from middle peasants at one-fifth the market price; total collectivization in 1929-30 culminated the procurement war.
  • The war on the countryside: 25,000 urban plenipotentiaries, "kulak" applied to anyone refusing, over half the livestock slaughtered, the gulag enlarged, the 1933-34 famine (roughly 63 percent of the 1931 harvest confiscated; death estimates from three or four million past twenty). Peasants read the acronym as "second serfdom."
  • Scoreboard: yields stagnated or fell below 1920s levels for half a century; one collective in twenty-five had electricity by 1939; the mir dissolved; private plots supplied most fruit, vegetables, eggs, dairy.
  • Scott's caveats: the record was overdetermined (Lysenko, war, weather, Stalin); centralization is right for space programs, transport, flood control, aircraft manufacture, and epidemic control.

Key numbers: 95,000 acres; half a million acres; 80,000 hectares into 32 squares; over 150 uprisings; one-fifth the market price; 1929-30; 25,000 plenipotentiaries; over half the livestock; about 63% of the 1931 harvest; 3-4 million to over 20 million deaths estimated; 1 in 25 collectives with electricity by 1939.

So what: Ask what a restructuring makes countable and who gains; centralize robust, uniform work and devolve fragile, timing-critical work; never let a lavishly resourced showcase stand as evidence of scale; the informal system carrying your official one is load-bearing.

Ch 7. Compulsory Villagization in Tanzania: Aesthetics and Miniaturization

Argument: Tanzania's ujamaa campaign moved millions into gridded roadside villages under an egalitarian leader and a weak, well-intentioned state, and still failed. The cause was an aesthetic of order mistaken for a scientific proposition, plus miniaturization: subsidized model villages read as proof the design would scale.

Stories & evidence

  • Nyerere's intent: schools, clinics, clean water, tractors, electrification, and no split into kulaks and laborers. He disavowed compulsion yet allowed that insisting on acreage might be needed.
  • Inherited templates: colonial Malawi's lower Shire Valley scheme (a "miniature TVA" with an architect's model; failed almost completely) and Tanganyika's groundnut scheme (three million acres, nine weeks of reconnaissance largely from the air; abandoned by 1950, having grown fewer nuts than it sowed).
  • Operation Planned Villages after December 1973: regions competed; relief made conditional on moving; militia transport; houses burned. About 60 percent of sites were on semiarid land unsuitable for permanent cultivation. Food imports 1973-75.
  • The miniature: a 300-settler scheme absorbed four bulldozers, nine tractors, seven lorries, a generator, fifteen administrators, and 150 laborers.
  • Monocropping overlay: plots surveyed into equal rectangles; communal fields segmented; tea smallholders planted in single blocks to suit extension staff.
  • Dark twin: communal cultivation was far smaller than reported; households let the communal plot lapse while private holdings carried subsistence.
  • Ruvuma Development Association: practiced Nyerere's ideals; banned in 1968.
  • Ethiopia under the Dergue: the same template with military force and cookie-cutter villages of about a thousand people; much of the famine was produced by the resettlement itself.
  • Weak-state mercy: unwillingness to use Stalinist methods and peasant flight, smuggling, and foot-dragging made practice less destructive than theory.

Key numbers: five million people moved; Nyerere's report of 13,065,000 people in 7,684 villages; 300 settlers with 4 bulldozers, 9 tractors, 7 lorries, 15 administrators, 150 laborers; about 60% of sites semiarid; 1.2 billion shillings of food imports (1973-75); three million acres and nine weeks (groundnut scheme); December 1973 order; Ruvuma banned 1968.

So what: Price subsidy and supervision per beneficiary before treating a pilot as evidence of scale; a design justified only by what it negates has no rationale; good intent is not protective; preserve the working exception.

Ch 8. Taming Nature: An Agriculture of Legibility and Simplicity

Argument: Scientific agriculture gains clarity by isolating a few variables, but the experimental plot is itself a radical simplification. Farming as practiced is a locally tuned craft. The failure was not bad science but the imperial pretension that nothing counts as knowledge unless it passes through the aperture of the experimental method.

Stories & evidence

  • West African fields: colonial agronomists read backwardness off four crops at once, unplowed, in no straight rows. Interplanting is the norm on 80 percent of West African farmland.
  • Howard Jones (Nigeria, 1936): the plants sat at proper distances on hillocks, the ground stayed occupied.
  • Sir Albert Howard: fertility includes structure (tilth, aeration, mycorrhizal bridge); approach from the field, not the lab.
  • Edgar Anderson's Santa Lucia garden (Guatemala): a seeming dump heap that was garden, orchard, medicinal garden, compost heap, and beeyard at once, without erosion on a steep slope.
  • Van der Ploeg's Andean potatoes: craft starts with the plot and picks varieties; science starts with an ideal genotype and remakes fields. New genotypes thrive in a narrow band and within three or four years often become incapable of even low production.
  • Davis supermarket tomato: bred thick-walled, uniform, crack-free, picked green for the harvester.
  • 1970 corn blight: 71 percent of US corn acreage in six hybrids; an exotic Mexican landrace supplied the escape.
  • DDT: succeeded within its model (malaria fell) but residues moved up the food chain; the alarm came from outside the paradigm.
  • Four systemic failures: inherited unexamined assumptions, institutional interest, cyclopean shortsightedness, incapacity for complexity.
  • Limits: modern breeding, pathology, and soil science are real achievements; local knowledge has hard limits too.

Key numbers: 80% of West African farmland interplanted; 71% of US corn acreage in six hybrids (1970); 3-4 years until some new genotypes degrade; 1936 (Jones); ten heavenly bodies (the orbit analogy).

So what: Use experimental evidence for few-variable questions but do not read a null result on a many-variable practice as proof it fails; enumerate what a trial held constant; price the fragility of uniformity; ask "useful for what?" over what horizon.

Ch 9. Thin Simplifications and Practical Knowledge: Mētis

Argument: Formal order is "always and to some considerable degree parasitic on informal processes." Mētis, practical, local, experiential knowledge, is the missing ingredient, and high modernism's core error is dismissing it. Mētis and technē are complementary dialects; the objection is to the imperial scientific view that replaces their collaboration.

Stories & evidence

  • Mētis defined: from Detienne and Vernant; Odysseus; hard to teach apart from doing; acquired by practice; rules of thumb whose content is knowing which to apply and when to throw the book away.
  • Technē/epistēmē: settled knowledge; "No rules of technē or epistēmē can explain scientific invention and insight."
  • Work-to-rule: actual work depends on informal understandings; in the long Caterpillar action workers reverted to the engineers' specified procedures, which cost time and quality.
  • Harbor pilot: locally superior to the general rules of navigation.
  • Squanto's maxim: plant corn when oak leaves are the size of a squirrel's ear; a compressed reading of a natural succession (skunk cabbage, willows, red-winged blackbirds, first mayfly hatch) whose sequence rarely varies. Contrasted with the almanac's fixed-date advice and Quetelet's lilac formula.
  • Red Adair test: the oil-well-fire team begins with the unpredictable.
  • East German factories: the jack-of-all-trades and the wheeler-dealer with a Trabant of soap powder and champagne.
  • Other points: bricolage (Lévi-Strauss), partisan knowledge, risk versus uncertainty, Oakeshott's rules as "mere abridgements of the activity itself," neoclassical economics exiling tastes and invention to make its math work.
  • Cautions: mētis can favor conservation of skills and coexists with domination.

Key numbers: Quetelet's lilac rule uses the sum of squared mean daily temperatures since the last frost reaching (4264 C) squared; East Germany before 1989; no other numbers in the notes.

So what: Where work is mutable, indeterminate, and particular, weight practitioner judgment; treat gaps between documented and actual process as load-bearing information; codify rules of thumb after competence, like grammar after speech; ask what a model had to exclude to become calculable.

Ch 10. Conclusion

Argument: The planners "regarded themselves as far smarter and farseeing than they really were and... regarded their subjects as far more stupid and incompetent than they really were." The answer is not less planning but mētis-friendly institutions (multifunctional, plastic, diverse, adaptable) and interventions designed for a contingent future.

Stories & evidence

  • Four rules of thumb: take small steps (Haldane's mouse, rat, man, horse); favor reversibility (Leopold: "keep all the parts"); plan on surprises; plan on human inventiveness. The Yale nutrition circular as a postulate of ignorance.
  • Two maps test: "Planned Brasilia is, in a thousand ways, underwritten by unplanned Brasilia."
  • The two war memorials: Maya Lin's Vietnam Memorial (chronological names, rubbings, mementos including a high-heeled shoe, a glass of champagne, a poker hand, a museum built to hold them) versus the Iwo Jima statue, symbolically self-sufficient.
  • Concepts: the abstract citizen, institutional neurosis, the self-fulfilling logic of social engineering, formal order as subsystem, cultivated natural capital (fish farms, plantations), the resolute singularity of the high-modernist optic.
  • Models: language, common law, democracy. Markets are not an escape hatch: the market is itself a formal system dependent on law, enforcement, trust, and a finite ecosystem.
  • Scott's tempering: supplanted orders were often unjust; high modernism came cloaked in emancipatory ideals; representative institutions force accommodation; ordinary resistance remakes any plan over time. Pruitt-Igoe and Cabrini Green are cited with Brasilia.

Key numbers: four rules of thumb; two maps; two memorials; no statistics in the notes.

So what: In unfamiliar systems step small, stay reversible, and leave slack; draw the second map before shipping; judge institutions by whether they grow the skill and responsibility of their participants; use fixed routines only where the environment is repetitive, stable, and predictable.

Recurring Stories & Motifs

  • *Scientific forestry and Waldsterben:* the canonical thin simplification; first rotation triumph, second collapse (Ch 1; echoed in the monocropping of Ch 7-8 and the tells in the cheatsheet).
  • Brasilia: an empty plateau, the superquadra, and the unplanned periphery that made it livable (Ch 4, again in Ch 7 and as the two-maps example in Ch 10).
  • Facts on paper vs. facts on the ground: cadastral maps, surnames, Tanzania's reported villages, Soviet quotas (Ch 1, 2, 6, 7).
  • The private plot and other dark twins: Soviet private plots, Tanzanian private holdings, landraces, unplanned Brasilia (Ch 6-8, 10).
  • Work-to-rule: the Introduction's proof, the Parisian taxi drivers in Ch 7, and the Caterpillar action in Ch 9.
  • Jacobs, Luxemburg, and Kollontai as mētis-side critics of Le Corbusier and Lenin (Ch 4, 5, 9).
  • Taylorism: from Lenin's embrace (Ch 3) to the farm as a factory (Ch 6) to knowledge as a struggle for hegemony (Ch 9).
  • Miniaturization: model villages, demonstration farms, and Brasilia as a model city (Introduction, Ch 4, 6, 7).
  • Scott's own guardrails: not anti-state, not anti-planning, not romantic about the local, and not pro-market (Introduction, Ch 3, 8, 9, 10).

Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction

2 markdown files

Quiz

Superforecasting Quiz Book

Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction by Philip E. Tetlock & Dan Gardner

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative final exam is at the end.

Chapter 1: An Optimistic Skeptic

Q1 (SA). What does it mean to be an "optimistic skeptic" about forecasting?

A: Hold two truths at once. Skeptic: nonlinear systems (Lorenz's butterfly, the Arab Spring sparked by one street vendor) impose hard limits, and accuracy falls toward chance 3–5 years out. Optimist: much of reality is predictable to some degree under some circumstances, and forecasters can improve if they measure their results.

Q2 (MC). Clocks vs. clouds is best understood as:

a) two kinds of people b) a strict dichotomy of systems c) a spectrum where predictability depends on what you predict, how far out, and under what circumstances d) a way to rank forecasters

A: c. Weather, for example, is reliable at 1–2 days and chimp-level around 8 days.

Q3 (SA). What is the loop that makes weather forecasters improve, and why do most other domains never run it?

A: Forecast, measure, revise. Most domains skip it because consumers don't demand evidence of accuracy, and accuracy is rarely the sole goal (see Q4).

Q4 (SA). Name some goals forecasts serve other than accuracy.

A: To entertain (TV pundits), to galvanize action (activist warnings), to impress (bank outlooks on 2050), and to comfort (partisan reassurance). Because accuracy isn't the only goal, nobody insists on measuring it.

Q5 (SA). What was the Good Judgment Project and what did it find?

A: A research team in the IARPA forecasting tournament (2011–15) with 20,000+ volunteers, ~500 questions mostly 1–12 months out, and over a million judgments. It beat the control group by about 60% in year 1 and 78% in year 2. A small group of "superforecasters" did far better than ordinary forecasters.

Q6 (T/F). The "dart-throwing chimp" finding shows that all experts are useless. A: False. It described the average expert on multi-year questions. On shorter horizons some people show real, testable foresight, and what makes them good is what they do, not who they are.

Chapter 2: Illusions of Knowledge

Q1 (SA). Why did medicine stagnate for so long, and what finally changed it?

A: Doctors trusted the view from the tip of their nose and their own confidence. Progress began when they accepted doubt and ran controlled trials (Archie Cochrane's push for randomized trials). The book argues forecasting today resembles pre-scientific medicine.

Q2 (SA). What are System 1 and System 2, and what is WYSIATI?

A: System 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive judgment. System 2 is slow, deliberate checking. WYSIATI ("What You See Is All There Is") means System 1 builds a coherent story from whatever evidence is at hand and ignores what it doesn't have.

Q3 (SA). Explain "bait and switch" (attribute substitution) with an example.

A: Faced with a hard question, we silently answer an easier one. "Should I fear that shadow?" becomes "Can I recall a lion attack?" Cochrane's doctor swapped "Do I have cancer?" for "Is this the sort of man who would know?"

Q4 (SA). What is the "scientist's test"?

A: Ask, "What would convince me I am wrong?" If you can't answer, you are too attached to your belief.

Q5 (MC). According to the Kahneman–Klein reconciliation, intuition is reliable when:

a) the person is an expert b) the person is confident c) the environment offers valid cues and enough practice to learn them d) the decision is fast

A: c. It works for firefighters and chess players. It fails for stock picking, where valid cues are absent.

Q6 (T/F). Knowing about an illusion switches it off. A: False. Like the Müller-Lyer lines, you can only check it with a ruler. Illusions can be monitored by System 2, not removed.

Chapter 3: Keeping Score

Q1 (SA). What four things make a forecast scorable?

A: (1) A clear time frame, (2) explicitly defined terms, (3) a numeric probability, (4) many forecasts so calibration can be computed.

Q2 (SA). What is the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy?

A: Judging a probabilistic forecast as "wrong" because the less likely outcome occurred, e.g., calling a 70% forecast wrong when the 30% happens. It pushes forecasters toward vague words that can be stretched after the fact.

Q3 (SA). What problem did Sherman Kent's scale address?

A: Words like "serious possibility" meant 80/20 to one analyst and 20/80 to another. Kent mapped words to numeric ranges (e.g., probable ≈ 75% ± 12, almost certain ≈ 93% ± 6). "I'd rather be a bookie than a goddamn poet."

Q4 (SA). Define calibration and resolution. Why do you need both?

A: Calibration: when you say 70%, it happens 70% of the time. Resolution: assigning high probabilities to what happens and low to what doesn't, rather than hovering at 40–60%. Calibration alone can be achieved cowardly; you need to be well calibrated and brave.

Q5 (MC). On the Brier score used in the book, a perfect score is ___ and always saying 50% scores ___.

a) 1.0 / 0.5 b) 0 / 0.5 c) 0 / 2.0 d) 0.5 / 1.0

A: b. 2.0 is maximally wrong (100% confident every time, always on the wrong side). Lower is better.

Q6 (SA). Why is a raw Brier score hard to interpret alone?

A: It depends on question difficulty. A 0.2 may be excellent on hard questions and poor on easy ones, so you need benchmarks and comparison on level playing fields.

Q7 (SA). What did Tetlock's earlier expert-judgment research find about foxes and hedgehogs?

A: Hedgehogs squeeze everything through one Big Idea and are confident and declarative. Foxes use many tools, think in probabilities, and revise. Foxes forecast better and the famous hedgehogs worse. Aggregating many perspectives (the dragonfly eye) is the mechanism.

Chapter 4: Superforecasters

Q1 (SA). What is the difference between a reasonable and a correct judgment? Apply it to the Iraq WMD estimate.

A: Reasonable means justified by what was knowable at the time; correct means the outcome matched. The intelligence community's WMD conclusion was reasonable and wrong. The sin was the "slam dunk" certainty. A 60–70% estimate might have changed the outcome.

Q2 (SA). Why is checklist-style accountability insufficient?

A: It's like checking hand-washing without checking whether patients get better. Only systematic tracking of accuracy is meaningful accountability.

Q3 (SA). How did the GJP build its winning aggregate?

A: It identified the top ~2% by accuracy and update frequency, weighted their forecasts more, then extremized the aggregate (e.g., push 70% toward 85%) to simulate what the crowd would believe if everyone shared all information.

Q4 (SA). How do we know superforecasters aren't just lucky?

A: The regression-to-the-mean test. Fast regression means luck, slow regression means skill. Their year-to-year correlation is ≈ 0.65, with about 70% staying in the top group each year, which indicates skill.

Q5 (T/F). Superforecasters beat intelligence analysts with classified information. A: True, by roughly 30%, and they also beat regular forecasters by roughly 60% and prediction markets.

Q6 (MC). Which is the most accurate description of the superforecasters' edge?

a) superior IQ b) insider information c) habits and methods that can be learned d) luck

A: c.

Chapter 5: Supersmart?

Q1 (SA). Are superforecasters geniuses? What does intelligence contribute?

A: No. They're smart (above ~80% of the population versus ~70% for regular forecasters) but not off the charts. Intelligence and knowledge help only above a modest threshold; method and disposition do the rest.

Q2 (SA). What is Fermi-izing and why does it help?

A: Breaking an unanswerable question into sub-questions, separating the knowable from the unknowable, and making explicit guesses. It exposes assumptions and errors instead of hiding them in a black box ("it dares us to be wrong").

Q3 (SA). Why start with the outside view, and what is anchoring's role?

A: The base rate for the comparison class is the best anchor. We under-adjust from whatever starting point we have, so a meaningful anchor beats a meaningless one. Start outside (how often does this kind of thing happen?), then adjust for the case's specifics.

Q4 (SA). How do you refine a reference class? Give the book's example.

A: Narrow the class to better match the case. US households owning pets: 62%; single-family detached homes: ~73%.

Q5 (SA). What does it mean to treat the inside view as investigation rather than an amble?

A: List the hypotheses (each pathway to "yes"), ask "what would have to be true?" for each, and research the components like a detective.

Q6 (SA). What is "the crowd within"?

A: Assume your first answer is wrong and make a second estimate from a different angle. Averaging the two beats either alone.

Q7 (SA). What is active open-mindedness?

A: Treating beliefs as hypotheses to be tested, not treasures to guard; deliberately seeking views that clash with yours and synthesizing them.

Chapter 6: Superquants?

Q1 (SA). What is the "three-setting dial" and why does it fail forecasters?

A: Gonna happen / not gonna happen / maybe. It's evolutionarily sensible (lion: run, stay alert, relax) but yes and no express certainty, and almost nothing is certain. The honest setting is maybe, subdivided finely.

Q2 (SA). What does a frequent "50%" usually signal?

A: "I don't know." People who use 50% often are measurably less accurate.

Q3 (MC). Epistemic uncertainty is:

a) unknowable even in principle b) knowable in principle but unknown c) pure randomness d) the same as aleatory

A: b. Aleatory uncertainty is unknowable (e.g., rain in Philadelphia a year out). On cloudlike questions supers stay within roughly 35–65% and move out tentatively.

Q4 (SA). What does granularity have to do with accuracy?

A: Forecasters who distinguish more degrees of doubt (ones place) are more accurate than those using fives or tens. Rounding supers' forecasts to coarser values hurt their scores. Finer numbers carry real information.

Q5 (SA). What did the bin Laden compound debate illustrate?

A: Panetta received honest, diverse estimates (about 30% to 90%+) and treated them as the wisdom of the crowd. Obama's "coin flip" may have been triage but also discarded information. Right-but-unreasonable (Maya's "100%") versus wrong-but-reasonable is judged by the reasoning.

Q6 (SA). What's the difference between thinking in probability versus in fate?

A: Probabilistic thinkers ask "how" something happened and accept randomness. Fate-thinkers ask "why" and see events as meant to be; fate-thinking correlates with worse Brier scores.

Chapter 7: Supernewsjunkies?

Q1 (SA). Are superforecasters better only because they update more?

A: No. Their initial forecasts are already much more accurate (about 50% in the book's comparison). Updating then adds to it.

Q2 (SA). What is underreaction and what drives it?

A: Belief perseverance: failing to update enough. Commitment freezes belief, especially when a belief is deep in your "Jenga tower" of identity, expertise, and public statements. General DeWitt (1942) took the absence of sabotage as confirmation that sabotage was coming.

Q3 (SA). What is the dilution effect and what is its cost?

A: Irrelevant details sway judgment (tennis versus skiing, with no bearing on the question). It leads to overreaction to noise: highest-turnover households earned 11.4% versus the market's 17.9%.

Q4 (SA). Describe Tim Minto's updating pattern.

A: On a Syrian-refugee question he updated 34 times with an average move of only 3.5 points, ending with a Brier of 0.07. Frequent and small captures the value of new information without lurching.

Q5 (T/F). Good updating means always moving in small steps. A: False. Move in small steps by default, but jump hard when the basis of the forecast has collapsed. Update in proportion to how diagnostic the evidence is (likelihood ratio).

Q6 (SA). What is the role of Bayes' theorem?

A: A model for updating: the posterior depends on prior belief and how much more likely the evidence is if the hypothesis is true than if false. Supers rarely compute it but follow its logic.

Chapter 8: Perpetual Beta

Q1 (SA). What is the strongest predictor of becoming a superforecaster?

A: Commitment to belief updating and self-improvement, "perpetual beta": growth mindset plus grit, about 3× as predictive as intelligence.

Q2 (SA). Contrast fixed and growth mindsets.

A: Fixed: ability is a trait; the person engages with "right/wrong" but not information that could improve the answer. Growth: ability is built by effort; failure is data. (Mary Simpson joined GJP after missing 2008: "I should be better at this.")

Q3 (SA). What is the cycle behind learning? Give the Keynes example.

A: Try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again. Keynes lost nearly everything in 1920 and 1929, scrutinized his assumptions, and developed something close to value investing.

Q4 (SA). Why do most forecasters fail to get useful feedback?

A: (1) Ambiguous language lets a vague forecast stretch to fit any result (the Forer effect: astrology boilerplate rated 4.2/5 as a personal profile). (2) Time lag plus hindsight bias: experts misremember their past forecasts (about 31 points too high on the Soviet collapse).

Q5 (MC). Why are weather forecasters and bridge players well calibrated?

a) higher IQ b) better training in statistics c) prompt, unambiguous feedback d) bigger datasets

A: c. Calibration is domain-specific and follows feedback quality.

Q6 (SA). What did Polanyi's bicycle illustrate, and what training effect did GJP find?

A: Tacit knowledge needs practice; no manual substitutes. The training booklet gave roughly a 10% improvement and worked best combined with practice.

Chapter 9: Superteams

Q1 (SA). What is groupthink (Janis)?

A: Cohesive groups maintain esprit de corps by developing shared illusions that interfere with critical thinking; agreement is taken as proof of correctness. Bay of Pigs is the example.

Q2 (SA). What did Kennedy change before the Cuban missile crisis?

A: Members were licensed as generalists to question anything; devil's advocates/watchdogs were named; hierarchy and protocol were suspended; outsiders were invited; Kennedy sometimes left the room and withheld his preference so alternatives got a hearing.

Q3 (SA). Why does the wisdom of crowds require independence?

A: Errors must be independent so they cancel. Loud voices, credentials, and premature consensus make errors correlate and pile up.

Q4 (SA). What is precision questioning? Give an example.

A: Respectful, specific probing instead of "you're silly": "What do you mean by 'pastime'?" or "What evidence, over what time frame?" At the Bay of Pigs, it would have stopped at "eighty miles of swamp and jungle?"

Q5 (SA). What is a premortem?

A: Imagine the plan has already failed and explain why. It makes doubts about the leader's plan safe to voice.

Q6 (SA). What were the team results?

A: Teams beat individuals by about 23%; superteams beat prediction markets by 15–30%.

Q7 (SA). What is constructive confrontation (Grove) and what role do "givers" play?

A: Disagree without being disagreeable. Givers share information and help others, lifting the whole team. Team open-mindedness is emergent from communication patterns, not the sum of individual traits.

Chapter 10: The Leader's Dilemma

Q1 (SA). What is the dilemma?

A: Leaders need confidence and decisiveness; good forecasters need humility and openness to changing their minds.

Q2 (SA). How does mission command (Auftragstaktik) resolve it?

A: Deliberate with doubt, decide in time, then execute with resolve. Tell subordinates what to accomplish and why (goal and intent), never how, because decisions "can be shaped only on the spot." Adopted into US doctrine in 1982. Patton: "Tell them what to do, and they will surprise you with their ingenuity."

Q3 (SA). What did Moltke contribute?

A: "No plan survives contact with the enemy's main strength" (the original). Since you can't lay down binding rules, train officers to think, discuss, criticize, and with good reason, disobey.

Q4 (SA). Distinguish deliberation from implementation.

A: Time-box deliberation; an imperfect decision in time beats a perfect one too late. Once decided, commit ("half measures are out of place") until circumstances demand a new decision. The art is recognizing that moment.

Q5 (SA). Distinguish confidence from false certainty. Use Eisenhower.

A: Eisenhower drafted a note taking responsibility for D-Day failure before the landing, then projected calm assurance. Morale comes from composure, not claims of certainty.

Q6 (T/F). Intellectual humility means self-doubt. A: False. It is humility about the problem and compatible with confidence in yourself. Also separate facts from values, and assume competence in adversaries you despise.

Chapter 11: Are They Really So Super?

Q1 (SA). What is Kahneman's critique?

A: System 2 vigilance is exhausting and the illusions can't be switched off, so even supers will eventually fall into them.

Q2 (SA). What is scope insensitivity? Give the forecasting evidence.

A: Answering "how bad does it feel?" instead of the question, ignoring scale (paying about the same to save 2,000 or 200,000 birds). Regular forecasters gave Assad's fall 40% at three months and 41% at six; supers gave 15% and 24% — they partly resisted. Training tip: mentally vary the cutoff date and thresholds.

Q3 (SA). What is Taleb's critique, and where is it right?

A: Only unforecastable black swans matter. He's right that tournaments of months-long questions can't test skill at ~0.1% events, and that fat tails exist in conflict and markets.

Q4 (SA). Distinguish strict from modest black swans.

A: Strictly inconceivable events are rare (9/11 was war-gamed in 1998; WWI was feared for a decade — "gray swans"). Modestly, highly improbable consequential events exist. Consequences of even true surprises unfold through forecastable steps.

Q5 (SA). Can you plan for surprise without forecasting?

A: No. Resilience investment is itself a probability judgment, so make it explicit.

Q6 (SA). How can System 2 corrections become habits?

A: Practice makes outside-view reflexes automatic, like a golf swing; software tools can help.

Chapter 12: What's Next?

Q1 (SA). What is kto-kogo?

A: Lenin's "who, whom": argument and evidence are adornments on a power struggle. Forecasts often serve tribe and career. Examples: Nate Silver after his 2014 Senate forecast; an analyst fired for an accurate but unwelcome call.

Q2 (SA). Why does the book remain optimistic about change?

A: Evidence-based medicine happened despite resistance (Codman's End Result System, which got him expelled, was later adopted). Evidence-based policy, philanthropy, and sports analytics followed, and IARPA funded the tournament despite the wrong-side-of-maybe risk.

Q3 (SA). Why do institutions fear numbers?

A: Numbers expose a failed 70% call while fuzzy language protects you. Blame-game ping-pong (miss 9/11 → over-alarm; WMD false alarm → under-alarm) blocks long-term investment in accuracy.

Q4 (SA). How can big, unscorable questions be addressed?

A: Cluster many small, scorable questions that bear on the big one (Bayesian question clusters), and pair superquestioners (people who ask the right questions) with superforecasters.

Q5 (SA). What is adversarial collaboration?

A: Rivals agree in advance on questions, evidence, and bets that would change their minds, then test them together to depolarize debates.

Q6 (T/F). Brier scoring is a finished, perfect tool. A: False. It's a work in progress (it treats misses and false alarms equally); asymmetric costs can be built in if forecasters are told the rules. Numbers are tools, not totems; imperfect scores still beat none.

Chapter 13 (Appendix): Ten Commandments

Q1 (SA). What was the evidence behind these guidelines?

A: They come from the book and from training experimentally shown to raise accuracy by about 10%.

Q2 (SA). Name the guidelines in order.

A: (1) Triage; (2) break problems into tractable sub-problems (Fermi-ize); (3) balance inside and outside views; (4) balance under- and overreaction to evidence; (5) look for clashing causal forces; (6) distinguish as many degrees of doubt as the problem permits, but no more; (7) balance under- and overconfidence, prudence and decisiveness; (8) look for the errors behind your mistakes without hindsight bias; (9) bring out the best in others and let others bring out the best in you; (10) master the error-balancing bicycle; (11) don't treat commandments as commandments.

Q3 (SA). What is triage in this context?

A: Work questions in the Goldilocks zone; skip clocklike questions (rules of thumb suffice) and cloudlike ones (even models can't beat the chimp).

Q4 (SA). What does "look for clashing causal forces" mean in practice?

A: Doves and hawks each list in advance the signs that would move them, then synthesize a hybrid. Synthesis is an art with no paint-by-numbers rules.

Q5 (SA). What is the theme running through all the guidelines?

A: Each balances opposing errors (inside/outside, under/overreaction, under/overconfidence). Skill comes from practicing the balance, not following a rule. Hence the last guideline.

Cumulative Final Exam

  1. Write a scorable version of "Will the economy get worse?"

A: Add a time frame, a defined measure, and a probability, e.g., "Will US real GDP shrink for two consecutive quarters before 31 Dec 2027, per BEA data? 18%."

  1. A friend says you were wrong because a 75% forecast failed. Respond. A: Wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy; judge calibration over many forecasts.
  2. List the book's eight-step forecasting method. A: Triage; Fermi-ize; outside view; inside view; synthesize (others, markets, crowd within); granular number; update; postmortem.
  3. Why record your reasoning at forecast time? A: Hindsight bias rewrites memory, and feedback is only useful if the original forecast was clear.
  4. Why can't a team just average members' forecasts after a discussion? A: Discussion can destroy independence and create groupthink; protect independent judgment first, then aggregate, and extremize based on private information.
  5. Which uncertainty can a forecaster reduce, and which can't they? A: Epistemic by research; aleatory not, so stay in the 35–65% band.
  6. Explain the leader's dilemma and its resolution. A: See ch10: deliberate with doubt, execute with resolve, mission command.
  7. What are the book's main limits? A: Accuracy fades beyond 3–5 years; fat tails and rare events can't be tested; WYSIATI and scope insensitivity persist; and forecasts often serve power (kto-kogo).
  8. Explain to a colleague, in three sentences, why superforecasters beat experts. A (model): They use a repeatable method (decompose, base rate first, then specifics), give precise probabilities, and update in small steps. They treat beliefs as hypotheses and learn from scored feedback. They also aggregate diverse views, which cancels individual bias.
  9. Applied task: Pick a real question, write your forecast with the method, set a date to score it, and record your reasoning.

Arguments & Evidence

Superforecasting: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Philip E. Tetlock & Dan Gardner

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files in the tetlock-superforecasting skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Ch 1–2 argue that forecasting skill is real but unmeasured, and that our intuition misleads us. Ch 3–4 show how to measure it and who turns out to be good. Ch 5–8 explain how they think (method, probability, updating, mindset). Ch 9–10 apply it to groups and leaders. Ch 11–12 test the limits and ask what could change. Ch 13 packs it into eleven guidelines.

Ch 1. An Optimistic Skeptic

Argument: Forecasting is a measurable, learnable skill, neither a gift nor a fraud. The "dart-throwing chimp" finding applied to average experts on multi-year questions. On shorter horizons some people have real foresight, and what makes them good is what they do, not who they are.

Stories & evidence

  • Lorenz's butterfly and the Arab Spring: one street vendor's act set off a region-wide upheaval. This is the skeptic's case that nonlinear systems limit prediction.
  • Weather forecasting: reliable at 1–2 days, chimp-level at about 8. It improved because meteorologists run the loop of forecast, measure, revise.
  • Expert Political Judgment (EPJ), 1984–2004: the average expert did about as well as random guessing, and worst on long horizons.
  • Good Judgment Project (GJP): 20,000+ volunteers, ~500 IARPA questions, over 1 million judgments. It beat the control group by 60% (year 1) and 78% (year 2).
  • Bill Flack: a retired USDA employee in Nebraska who forecast ~300 questions and was scored on every one. Tom Friedman advises presidents but has never been scored. The difference is the scoring, not intelligence.
  • A one-hour tutorial on basic concepts improved accuracy by about 10%.

Key numbers: ~2% of forecasters were "super"; accuracy falls toward chance at 3–5 years.

So what: Be specific about what you predict, how far out, and under what conditions. Demand scores. Foresight is like eyesight: improving from 20/100 to 20/40 is not hawk-eyed, but it changes your life.

Ch 2. Illusions of Knowledge

Argument: Medicine stagnated for millennia because doctors trusted the view from the tip of their nose. It advanced when they accepted doubt and ran controlled trials. Forecasting today looks like nineteenth-century medicine.

Stories & evidence

  • Archie Cochrane's misdiagnosis (1956): an eminent surgeon told him he was dying. Cochrane, a founder of evidence-based medicine, believed him. The pathology report found no cancer at all. If the skeptic can be fooled, anyone can.
  • Cochrane's reversed-numbers trial: he told cardiologists preliminary results favored the cardiac units, and they demanded he stop the "unethical" trial. He had actually reversed the numbers: home care was ahead. Their reaction exposed their certainty.
  • Galen's logic: the treatment cures everyone except the incurable, who die. This is confirmation bias built into a theory.
  • Bradford Hill's randomized trial template (1921): random assignment balances unknown differences so outcomes can be attributed to treatment.
  • Split-brain patients invent reasons for actions they can't explain. Journalists explain market moves with news that came out after them.
  • Oslo bombing (2011): suspecting an Islamist attack was reasonable. The error was treating the hypothesis as settled.
  • Kahneman–Klein reconciliation: fireground commanders and chess players have valid cues and practice, so intuition works. Stock pickers have neither, so it doesn't.

So what: You can't switch System 1 off. Watch for bait and switch (answering an easier question) and ask "what would convince me I'm wrong?" Confidence signals a coherent story, not a true one.

Ch 3. Keeping Score

Argument: You can't improve what you can't score, and most forecasts can't be scored. Fix that and collect many forecasts, and you find that foxes beat hedgehogs. Aggregating perspectives is the mechanism.

Stories & evidence

  • The Bernanke letter (2010): warning of "risk" from quantitative easing, with no time frame, is unfalsifiable. The book shows how to rewrite it with a date, a defined measure, and probabilities.
  • Sherman Kent and "serious possibility": one analyst read it as 80/20, another as 20/80. Kent proposed a numeric scale ("I'd rather be a bookie than a goddamn poet").
  • Bay of Pigs "fair chance": the author meant 3-to-1 against, but Kennedy heard optimism.
  • Ballmer's iPhone remark: in context it was ambiguous, not laughably wrong.
  • Brier score (1950): 0 is perfect, 0.5 is random, 2.0 is maximally wrong. Scores need benchmarks: 0.2 is excellent in Springfield and poor in Phoenix.
  • EPJ, 284 experts and ~28,000 predictions: hedgehogs (one Big Idea, "furthermore," "just wait") did worse than foxes, even in their own specialty. Fame correlated inversely with accuracy.
  • Galton's ox (1,197 vs. 1,198 lb): the crowd's average was nearly exact. Foxes do inside one skull what crowds do collectively (the dragonfly eye).
  • "Guess two-thirds of the average" (FT/Thaler, 1997): pure logic says 0, but the winning answer was 13 because contestants are human.

So what: A forecast needs a time frame, defined terms, a number, and many instances. Calibration and resolution are both required. Avoid the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy.

Ch 4. Superforecasters

Argument: The Iraq WMD "slam dunk" was a reasonable judgment expressed with unreasonable certainty. The shock led IARPA to run a tournament. It found that ordinary people with the right habits beat professionals, and that their edge was skill, not luck.

Stories & evidence

  • NIE 2002-16HC: "Iraq has... Baghdad has..." There were no red teams, no devil's advocates, and no dissenting paper.
  • Reasonable vs. correct: a 60–70% estimate instead of certainty might have stopped the invasion. Judging a decision by its outcome is the "poker novice" blunder.
  • IARPA tournament: five teams, daily forecasts from Sept 2011 to June 2015, ~500 questions. Teams had to beat the control by 20% in year 1, rising to 50% by year 4.
  • Doug Lorch: a retired IBM programmer. Brier 0.22 in year 1 (5th of 2,800), then 0.14 in year 2 (best). He beat a prediction market by 40% and the control by 60%.
  • First super cohort: 58 people, collective Brier 0.25 vs. 0.37 for everyone else. At 300 days out they beat regulars at 100 days. They beat analysts with classified access by ~30%.
  • The luck test (regression to the mean): year-to-year correlation was ≈ 0.65 (father–son height is ≈ 0.5). About 30% of supers drop out each year and ~70% remain. A coin-flip explanation has under 1 in 100 million odds.
  • Langer's rigged coin flips: Yale students who saw early lucky streaks believed they had skill.

So what: Judge decisions by what was knowable. Meaningful accountability means scored accuracy, not process checklists. Extremizing an aggregate of top performers beat a multi-billion-dollar analytic apparatus.

Ch 5. Supersmart?

Argument: Supers are smart and knowledgeable but not off the charts. What separates them is method: Fermi-ize, take the outside view, then the inside view, then synthesize. Their disposition is that beliefs are hypotheses, not treasures.

Stories & evidence

  • Intelligence threshold: regulars scored above ~70% of the population and supers above ~80%. The big jump is public to forecaster.
  • McNamara's "best and brightest" escalated Vietnam without analyzing their assumptions.
  • Pets example: US households owning pets is 62%, but for single-family detached homes ~73%. This is how you refine a reference class.
  • Arafat exhumation question: with no base rate, bracket it. It must be well above 0 and well below 100, so start near 50%.
  • David Rogg's forecast of an Islamist attack in Western Europe (21 Jan–31 Mar 2015): six attacks in five years gives 1.2 per year. He adjusted to 1.8 per year, then scaled to the 69-day window: ≈ 34%. He posted the whole chain for others to attack.
  • Peggy Noonan on Bush's rebounding approval: all ex-presidents' approval rises, so she skipped the base rate.
  • Summers's rule: double the estimate and move up one time unit.
  • Doug Lorch's reading selector forces ideological and geographic diversity into his news diet.

So what: Base rate first, then the story. Write your reasoning and read it as a stranger. Flip the question's wording to counter confirmation bias. The crowd within is nearly as good as a second person.

Ch 6. Superquants?

Argument: Supers are numerate but rarely use math. What they have is probabilistic thinking: many settings of "maybe" instead of yes/no/maybe. Granularity (single percentage points) predicts accuracy.

Stories & evidence

  • Tversky's three-setting dial: gonna happen, not gonna happen, maybe. It works for lions and fails for forecasting.
  • Bin Laden compound meeting: estimates ran from ~30% to 90%+ (median about 70%). The real Panetta wanted honest disagreement. In Zero Dark Thirty, Maya's "100%" was right and unreasonable. Obama's "coin flip" may have discarded information.
  • Granularity (Mellers): forecasters using tens < fives < ones. Rounding supers' forecasts to 0.05 hurt; rounding regulars to 0.2 barely mattered.
  • Certainty premium: people pay 2–3× more to go from 5% to 0% risk than from 10% to 5%.
  • Rubin's rule: "absolutely" is unacceptable; say 60% and argue whether it's 59.
  • Fate vs. probability: "everything happens for a reason" correlates with well-being but with worse Brier scores. Probabilistic thinkers ask "how," not "why."
  • Munger: without elementary probability you go through life "like a one-legged man in an ass-kicking contest."

So what: Ask how many degrees of maybe you can honestly distinguish. 50% often means "I don't know." Stay in 35–65% on cloudlike (aleatory) questions. Disagreement is data to aggregate.

Ch 7. Supernewsjunkies?

Argument: Supers win partly by updating, but their initial forecasts are already ~50% more accurate. Good updating is as hard as forecasting: steer between underreaction and overreaction with many small steps, but jump when your basis collapses.

Stories & evidence

  • Arafat-polonium: the Swiss lab's unexplained delay was a subtle signal. Flack moved 60% to 65%.
  • General DeWitt (1942): "No sabotage has occurred is a... confirming indication that it will." This is belief perseverance. The Jenga tower is identity, expertise, and public commitments.
  • Dilution effect: irrelevant details (Robert plays tennis, David skis) sway judgment. The highest-turnover households earned 11.4% vs. the market's 17.9%.
  • Tim Minto: 34 updates on a Syrian-refugee question, average move 3.5 points, final Brier 0.07.
  • Ulfelder on Hagel: base rate 23/24 nominees confirmed (96%). With generous likelihood ratios the posterior only dropped to 83%. Hagel was confirmed.
  • Doug Lorch's 95% forecast: it rested on a report that was clearly failing. He went 95% → 55% → 15%, a fresh forecast rather than a gradual retreat.
  • Bait-and-switch update failure: Flack asked "would I visit Yasukuni?" and discounted the tip that Abe would. Abe went.
  • Senate-race example: a Colorado poll moves the GOP candidate 45% → 55%. Bracketing the update (more than 0, less than 10, then 2–9, 3–7) lands at +4, from 60% to 64%.

So what: Update often, in small steps proportional to the evidence's diagnostic weight (likelihood ratio). Know whether you tend to freeze or to swing. When the foundation fails, re-forecast.

Ch 8. Perpetual Beta

Argument: The strongest predictor of becoming a superforecaster is perpetual beta, not IQ: growth mindset plus grit, running try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again. It needs informed practice and clear, timely feedback.

Stories & evidence

  • Mary Simpson: an economics PhD who missed 2008 and lost her savings. She joined GJP because "I should be better at this."
  • Keynes: lost nearly everything in 1920 and 1929, scrutinized his assumptions, and developed something close to value investing.
  • Polanyi's bicycle: tacit knowledge can't be learned from a manual.
  • Forer effect: astrology boilerplate was rated 4.2/5 as a personal profile. Vague forecasts, like horoscopes, can't fail.
  • Hindsight bias: experts recalled their 1988 Soviet-collapse estimates ~31 points too high.
  • Calibration is domain-specific: meteorologists and bridge players are calibrated because feedback is prompt. Police lie-detection confidence grows with experience while accuracy doesn't.
  • Devyn Duffy and Guinea: he postmortemed a win ("we lucked out"). The Arafat postmortem found the team never consulted a radiochemistry expert.
  • Grit (Duckworth): Elizabeth Sloane forecast through brain-cancer treatment. Anne Kilkenny e-mailed a UN agency to learn how refugee data were compiled.
  • Composite superforecaster: cautious, humble, nondeterministic, actively open-minded, numerate, probabilistic, a good updater, and gritty. Perpetual beta predicts ~3× as strongly as intelligence: "75% perspiration, 25% inspiration."

So what: Write your reasoning at forecast time, because memory will rewrite it. Postmortem successes too. Experience (years) isn't feedback (scored outcomes).

Ch 9. Superteams

Argument: Groups can be mad (Bay of Pigs) or wise (Cuban missile crisis) with the same people. Process decides which. Teams beat individuals, and superteams beat markets, by preserving independent judgment while sharing information.

Stories & evidence

  • Bay of Pigs (April 1961): the plan was on the New York Times front page three months earlier. The escape route ran through 80 miles of swamp, and nobody asked "how far?" Cohesion substituted for scrutiny.
  • Cuban missile crisis (Oct 1962): same people, new rules. Kennedy withheld his preference and left the room. He appointed watchdogs, suspended rank, imported outsiders, and forced ten alternatives onto the table. He later put the odds of nuclear war at one-third to one-half.
  • Janis's groupthink: agreement taken as proof of correctness.
  • Wisdom-of-crowds failures: tulips and 2005 housing, where errors piled up instead of canceling.
  • Results: teams +23% over individuals (year 1). A newly minted super placed on a superteam became 50% more accurate. Ordinary teams beat the crowd by ~10%, markets beat ordinary teams by ~20%, and superteams beat markets by 15–30% (caveat: the markets lacked liquidity and real money).
  • Team AOM is emergent: open-minded people who don't engage each other add up to less than their sum.
  • Givers, matchers, takers (Adam Grant): givers like Marty Rosenthal, Doug Lorch, and Tim Minto lifted everyone.
  • Extremizing helped regular teams a lot and information-sharing superteams barely at all.
  • Edmondson's psychological safety: the nurse who tells the surgeon about the sponge.

So what: Form judgments independently first, then share. Keep the leader's view out of the room. Use precision questioning ("what do you mean by...?", "what evidence, over what time frame?") and premortems. Treat unanimity as a symptom.

Ch 10. The Leader's Dilemma

Argument: Leaders must be confident and decisive. Superforecasters must be humble and ready to change their minds. Mission command (Auftragstaktik) dissolves the conflict: deliberate with doubt, then act with resolve, and push decisions down to those who see the ground.

Stories & evidence

  • Moltke: "no plan... extends with certainty beyond the first encounter with the enemy's main strength." So train officers to think, criticize, and with good reason disobey.
  • Prussian war academies debated scenarios collectively. In the US Army of the same era, Eisenhower was threatened with court-martial for publishing tank ideas.
  • Eben Emael (1940): the commander's glider landed 100 km off. A sergeant took charge and knocked out the guns, and another stray sergeant improvised an attack and took 121 prisoners.
  • Hitler at Normandy: reserves could move only on his personal order, and no one would wake him.
  • Eisenhower on D-Day: he wrote the note accepting blame for failure beforehand, then projected calm assurance.
  • Petraeus: unscripted live-fire exercises, and graduate school to meet "seriously bright people with very different basic assumptions."
  • Business echoes: 3M ("we do not tell them how"), Bezos's "disagree and commit," Walmart's leadership academy.
  • Wehrmacht: evil and, man for man, highly effective. Wishful forecasts like Lorch's on Aleppo show values leaking into probabilities.

So what: Give goals and intent, not methods. Project composure, not certainty. Intellectual humility (about the problem) is compatible with self-confidence. Separate facts from values.

Ch 11. Are They Really So Super?
