Argument: Kahneman (illusions can't be switched off) and Taleb (only unforecastable black swans matter) are partly right. But supers showed real resistance to scope insensitivity, black swans are often gray, and even planning for surprise requires probability judgments.

Stories & evidence

  • General Flynn's "unprecedented" conflict claim contradicted datasets on declining battle deaths. The reports on his desk felt like all there was (WYSIATI).
  • Scope insensitivity: ~$10 to clean lakes in one region or all 250,000. Regulars gave Assad's fall 40% at three months and 41% at six, while supers gave 15% and 24%.
  • Black swans: 9/11 was war-gamed in 1998, and WWI was feared for a decade. These are gray swans. Months-long tournaments can't test skill at 0.1% events.
  • Black swans have forecastable anatomy: the consequences of 9/11 (ultimatum, refusal, invasion) were each a scorable short-range question.
  • Lin Wells memo (April 2001): every decade since 1900 had defied the previous one's expectations. Five months later came 9/11.
  • Planning for surprise: Tokyo's earthquake codes make sense and Kansas's would not. Eisenhower: "plans are useless, but planning is indispensable."
  • Fat tails: if war deaths follow a wealth-like distribution rather than a height-like one, a ten-million-death war in 1914 was thousands of times likelier than a bell curve implied.
  • Khosla vs. poker-style investing: black-swan bets (90% fail, 10% change the world) vs. small edges (68% when others say 60%).

So what: Run a scope stress test (vary the deadline and threshold). Google the base rate before calling something unprecedented. Break "unforecastable" shocks into forecastable steps. State the probability behind every resilience investment.

Ch 12. What's Next?

Argument: An evidence-based forecasting revolution is possible, as evidence-based medicine was. But kto-kogo ("who, whom") means forecasts often serve tribe and career more than accuracy. The way forward is scoring, question clusters, superquestioners, and adversarial collaboration.

Stories & evidence

  • Kto-kogo: Lenin's view that argument is an adornment on a power struggle. Nate Silver went from prophet to stumblebum among Democrats after his 2014 Senate forecast. A Santander analyst was fired for an accurate but unwelcome forecast. Dick Morris defended his Romney-landslide call as duty, not belief.
  • Codman's End Result System: record ailment, treatment, outcome, and publish. It got him expelled from Mass General and Harvard, and later the profession adopted it.
  • Other cases of the shift to measurement: evidence-based policy, Gates Foundation evaluations, sports analytics. IARPA funding the tournament is the surprising proof.
  • Blame ping-pong: miss 9/11 and over-alarm, then a WMD false alarm and under-alarm. Both block investment in accuracy.
  • Wieseltier's humanist objection: "where wisdom once was, quantification will now be." Partly right: a hospital can hit 100% survival by refusing sick patients.
  • Korea cluster: rocket launch, nuclear test, rebuffing talks, artillery fire, a naval incident. Each is scorable, and together they approximate "how does this end?"
  • Smack-the-forehead test: a good question makes you say "if only I'd thought of that." Friedman's "Is Iraq the way it is because Saddam is, or vice versa?"
  • Keynesians vs. Austerians: four years passed and no one budged. Signatories of the 2010 letter said in 2014 they'd change nothing.
  • Drezner's pledge: "make a clear prediction and offer a confidence interval... I want to keep score."

So what: Cluster small scorable questions to approach big ones. Pair superquestioners with superforecasters. Settle debates with a joint list of precise bets. Brier scoring is imperfect but beats judging by titles and book sales.

Ch 13 (Appendix). Ten Commandments

Argument: Eleven guidelines from the book and from training shown to raise accuracy ~10%. Each balances two opposing errors, and the last warns against treating any of them as binding.

#GuidelineEvidence / example used
1Triage"Who wins in 2028?" is impossible; narrowing 2016 to plausible contenders is not
2Break problems into sub-problemsPeter Backus's ~26 compatible women in London
3Balance inside and outside viewsSummers's rule; comparison classes even for Kony or Greece
4Balance under- and overreactionUpdating is "dental hygiene"; usually move 0.4 → 0.35, jump on diagnostic signals
5Seek clashing causal forcesDoves and hawks each list what would move them, then synthesize
6As many degrees of doubt as the problem permitsObama on March Madness vs. "fifty-fifty" on bin Laden; "slam dunk" = infinite odds
7Balance under- and overconfidenceScore on calibration and resolution; avoid overcorrecting the last miss
8Look for the errors behind your mistakesPostmortem successes too; don't over-learn from a minor slip
9Bring out the best in othersPerspective taking; Lasorda's dove (too tight kills, too loose loses)
10Master the error-balancing bicycleYou can't learn it from a manual; practice with feedback
11Don't treat commandments as commandmentsMoltke: "two cases will never be exactly the same"

So what: Treat the list as a pre-flight checklist. The book's worked example is a project estimate: use an outside-view rule (past projects ran ~2× over), then adjust, state "70% by 30 June, 90% by 31 August," and schedule the postmortem now.

Recurring Stories to Remember

  • Bill Flack vs. Tom Friedman (ch 1, 12): scored vs. unscored.
  • Iraq WMD "slam dunk" (ch 4, 6): reasonable vs. correct, and the cost of false certainty.
  • Bay of Pigs → Cuban missile crisis (ch 9): same people, different process.
  • Arafat's polonium (ch 5, 7, 8): a case used for the outside view, for updating, and then for the postmortem.
  • Bin Laden compound (ch 6): disagreement as data, and why "50%" throws information away.
  • Moltke and mission command (ch 10): goals and intent, not methods.
  • Codman and Cochrane (ch 2, 12): the medical precedent for forecasting reform.

The Certainty Illusion: What You Don't Know and Why It Matters

2 markdown files

Quiz

The Certainty Illusion Quiz Book

The Certainty Illusion: What You Don't Know and Why It Matters by Timothy Caulfield

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative final exam is at the end. Chapter numbering follows the study notes (Intro = Chapter 0, then Chapters 1-13, then the Conclusion as Chapter 14). Part I (Ch 1-5) is the Science Illusion, Part II (Ch 6-10) is the Goodness Illusion, Part III (Ch 11-13) is the Opinion Illusion.

Chapter 0: Introduction: Adrift in a Storm

Q1 (SA). State the book's thesis, "the certainty illusion."

A: The more we seek certainty, the harder it becomes to find, because the information economy is incentivized to spin exactly the signals we rely on. Distortion follows value: the signals worth faking are the ones people trust most.

Q2 (SA). Name the Three Illusions and the guidepost each corrupts.

A: Science Illusion (the appearance of science replaces science), Goodness Illusion (a messaging strategy that makes a choice feel like the right thing without close examination), and Opinion Illusion (reviews, rankings, and polls are faked, biased, or manufactured).

Q3 (MC). Caulfield calls the problem a "knowledge production crisis" rather than just misinformation because:

a) misinformation is not real b) it is about the degraded methods and institutions that make knowledge, not only downstream lies c) only scientists are affected d) the internet did not exist before 2000

A: b. Upstream incentives (publish-or-perish, hype, predatory journals) keep manufacturing the raw material.

Q4 (T/F). Trust level should be used as a safety indicator: the more trusted a signal, the safer it is.

A: False. Trust level is a risk indicator, not a safety indicator, because the most trusted guideposts are the most worth counterfeiting.

Q5 (SA). How did Caulfield answer the hostile questioner who said "Science is full of shit," and why?

A: He conceded: "Yeah, it is." The man was partly right (predatory journals, hype incentives, salami science, fraud), and more citations would not answer an incentive critique. The productive move is to grant the corruption and argue the repair is better science, not no science.

Q6 (T/F). Because science has problems, the right response is to become a cynical disbeliever of everything.

A: False. That is an anti-pattern: skepticism is a filter, not an off switch, and cynicism destroys your ability to use good evidence. "If not science, what?" The alternative is astrology, tea leaves, and hunches.

Q7 (SA). What does the stat that 81% of Americans rely "a lot" on their own research for big decisions (96% of them online) suggest?

A: Doing your own research does not escape the problem, because it happens inside the same rigged information environment. Related self-check: "I Google, therefore I'm certain."

Chapter 1: The Science-y Veneer

Q1 (SA). What is scienceploitation, and what is its cycle?

A: Using scientific verbiage and hot research topics to sell unproven products and agendas. Cycle: an exciting scientific development makes pop-culture noise, hucksters spot a market, the market floods with products riffing on the science, people get hurt, and public discourse is confused.

Q2 (SA). What is the quantum test?

A: If the word quantum is used to explain a health product or procedure, assume pseudoscience and a fraudster nearby, and stop evaluating. Physicist Mark Freeman has never seen it used accurately with a health product.

Q3 (SA). What is the science-y / scary dyad, and how do you defuse it?

A: Science-sounding jargon plus a fear message, the most durable misinformation engine. Strip the jargon and ask what the claimed harm is; strip the fear and ask what supports the mechanism. Neither usually survives alone.

Q4 (MC). In the stem-cell clinic study (about 250 alternative-medicine clinic websites), what share mentioned any limitation of the evidence?

a) 19% b) 50% c) 75% d) 95%

A: a. Absence of stated risks and limitations is diagnostic of scienceploitation.

Q5 (T/F). The 2004 study on science-y language found that science majors and graduate students were immune to its persuasive effect.

A: False. Science-y language raised persuasiveness regardless of the audience's education level, so build procedural defences, not confidence.

Q6 (SA). What is "science washing"?

A: Michelle Wong's term for using "science" as a generic legitimizing badge (graphs, numbers, technical language) instead of showing relevant research. Check whether there is relevant research applying to this specific claim.

Q7 (SA). Why is "immune boosting" a near-reliable scam marker?

A: You cannot "boost" the immune system as promised, and you would not want to; an overactive immune system is how autoimmune disease behaves.

Chapter 2: Certainty, Dunning-Kruger, and the Humility Fix

Q1 (SA). What is the Galileo gambit and how is it dismantled?

A: Answering evidence by casting yourself as the persecuted truth-teller ("they laughed at Galileo"). Galileo faced a religious orthodoxy, not a scientific consensus; Sagan noted they also laughed at Bozo the Clown; real revolutionaries (Einstein, Darwin, Curie) produced data tested against their era's conventions. Treat it as a last-resort defence and a tell, not an argument.

Q2 (SA). State the Sagan standard and how to apply it.

A: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. Assess plausibility against existing knowledge, assess the claimant (expertise, what they sell, what thousands of researchers supposedly missed), scale the proof to the improbability, and keep the onus on the claimant.

Q3 (MC). The Dunning-Kruger effect, as used here, is:

a) experts underrating themselves b) overestimating knowledge because lacking knowledge impedes recognizing the lack c) fear of public speaking d) trusting only famous people

A: b. A 2019 anti-GMO study found extreme opponents know the least but think they know the most; a large 2022 study replicated this across climate change, nuclear power, vaccination, evolution, and GMOs.

Q4 (SA). Describe the humility fix and Caulfield's exercise.

A: Make intellectual humility ("recognition of one's fallibility as a knower") the default posture. Exercise: list areas where evidence evolved and you changed position, plus grey areas where you are still seeking information. An empty list is itself the finding.

Q5 (SA). What was the finding of "On the Reception and Detection of Pseudo-Profound Bullshit" (Pennycook, 2015 Ig Nobel)?

A: Participants rated syntactically coherent sentences built from random vague buzzwords as at least somewhat profound. A 2019 follow-up found the labelling effect: identical nonsense rated more profound when attributed to a famous author.

Q6 (T/F). Contrarian theories like plate tectonics and H. pylori ulcers justify treating any fringe claim as possibly right.

A: False. Those won because data eventually supported them, raised in scientific venues, not because the proponents proclaimed themselves persecuted.

Q7 (SA). What rule of thumb applies to coaching or wellness offerings full of "transformational," "blind spots," and "optimal levels"?

A: If it sounds like pretentious tripe, it most likely is. Demand a concrete description of what you will do and how it works. Pennycook: "Science that can't be understood is bad science."

Chapter 3: The Hype Machine, Catastrophizing, and Science Investment

Q1 (SA). What is the hype pipeline?

A: The Caulfield & Condit (2012) idea that exaggerated claims of benefit and social impact are generated throughout knowledge production: initial excitement, grant writing, publication, and media representation.

Q2 (MC). Roughly what share of biomedical abstracts contain at least some spin (2017 study)?

a) 5% b) 15% c) nearly 40% d) 90%

A: c. The abstract is often the only thing read, even by academics.

Q3 (SA). What did Sumner et al. (2014) find about health press releases?

A: Of 462 releases, 40% contained exaggerated health advice, 33% exaggerated causation, and 36% exaggerated inferences from animal studies, and the hype was transcribed into the popular press.

Q4 (SA). What did the University of Tsukuba analysis of NIH grant abstracts find?

A: In nearly a million successful NIH abstracts (1985-2020), hype rose roughly 1,400 percent. The team also found a comparably massive increase in hype in NIH's own funding announcements, showing a funder-applicant loop.

Q5 (T/F). Heavy media attention is a sign that a finding is more likely to replicate.

A: False. A 2023 study of 14,000 papers found media attention was negatively associated with replication.

Q6 (SA). What is the "timeline test" for therapy claims?

A: Clinical trials alone take 10-15 years and roughly 90 percent fail, so a "five to ten years or sooner" promise (found in almost 70 percent of the stem-cell newspaper articles Caulfield analyzed) is impossible by construction.

Q7 (SA). What is funding by lottery and why is it proposed?

A: Reviewers decide only basic fundability (meets reasonable standards), then grants are allocated by lottery. The current process is already near-random and biased (a 2018 PNAS study found no agreement among reviewers); a lottery is cheaper, faster, more equitable, and removes the incentive to hype. The Swiss National Science Foundation and the Health Research Council of New Zealand have tried it.

Chapter 4: The Predator Problem

Q1 (SA). Distinguish predatory, hijacked, and vanity/agenda-driven journals.

A: Predatory: charge authors fees with lax or no peer review. Hijacked: criminal clones of a legitimate journal's name and domain to harvest fees ("a fake Gucci handbag"). Vanity/agenda: purpose-built to legitimize a predetermined position (anti-vaccine, climate denial, etc.), typically publishing their own editorial board.

Q2 (SA). List the checks in the red-flag audit for a single supporting study.

A: Publisher (known predatory operator?), author affiliation (vague or mimicking a real institution?), submission-to-acceptance interval, ethics review, methods (control group, blinding, standardization, sample size), and the author's regulatory history. Later chapters add retraction status and citation pattern.

Q3 (MC). Biomedical papers typically take about how long to reach acceptance, and what does two weeks imply?

a) 100 days; no real review b) 2 days; fast review c) 1 year; fraud d) 30 days; normal

A: a. A 2021 study found 91-639 days, averaging around 100.

Q4 (SA). In the O-Shot case, what did the audit of Runels's paper reveal?

A: Publisher OMICS International (later fined $50 million by the FTC in 2019); an ambiguous affiliation ("Medical School Birmingham") that was a modest building far from the real medical school; submitted June 12, accepted June 25; no ethics review by an author previously sanctioned by the FDA; eleven self-reporting women, no control, no blinding.

Q5 (SA). What is the citation-pattern test?

A: Check who cites the work. If the broader academic community does not pick it up, even to contest it, be suspicious. The International Journal of Vaccine Theory, Practice, and Research was cited almost entirely by itself, its own editorial board, and known anti-vaccine advocates.

Q6 (T/F). Appearing in PubMed, Scopus, or a WHO library guarantees a paper is legitimate.

A: False. About 400 publications from hijacked journals were found in the WHO COVID-19 library, and a 2023 study found Scopus carrying work from 67+ hijacked journals.

Q7 (SA). What policy fix does Caulfield propose, and what incentive drives the industry?

A: Prohibit public research funds from paying predatory fees. The incentive is publish-or-perish, with rewards for quantity (in South Africa, quantity-based pay produced up to a 140-fold rise in predatory publications).

Chapter 5: AI and Zombie Science

Q1 (SA). What is the single study syndrome rule?

A: From Ivan Oransky: if a claim is based on one study, be much more suspicious. Always consider the body of evidence. Caulfield calls it the most important takeaway of Part I, because it neutralizes predatory papers, AI fakes, and zombie retractions without detecting each fraud.

Q2 (SA). What is zombie science?

A: Discredited or retracted findings that keep circulating and influencing literature, public perception, and health debates after formal correction.

Q3 (MC). A 2021 analysis of 13,000+ retracted papers found what share of post-retraction references acknowledged the retraction?

a) 5.4% b) 25% c) 50% d) 95%

A: a. Assume retraction status will not reach you passively; check it.

Q4 (T/F). Retracted papers receive less attention than never-retracted papers over time.

A: False. A 2022 University of Michigan analysis of nearly 4,000 retracted papers found they received more attention over ten years, perhaps because they are more exciting and extreme.

Q5 (SA). What is Holden Thorp's two-stage retraction?

A: Stage one decides whether the paper is valid, with no blame, so it can be removed (even provisionally) quickly. Stage two asks who erred, which is slow because careers are at stake. Retractions currently average two to three years (Wakefield took over ten).

Q6 (SA). Why was Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper structurally unable to show causation, and what happened afterward?

A: It described twelve children, with no randomization and no control group. Brian Deer found it was funded by lawyers acting for parents suing vaccine makers. Wakefield lost his licence in 2010, the paper was retracted in 2010 after twelve years, yet in 2015 21 percent of Americans under thirty believed vaccines cause autism.

Q7 (SA). How does motivated reasoning keep zombies alive?

A: For the motivated reasoner the retraction becomes proof of suppression ("Big Pharma can't have those conclusions floating around"), a self-sealing narrative that makes the bogus study seem more valid.

Chapter 6: Health Halos and the Devious Dozen

Q1 (SA). What is a health halo, and what is its real function?

A: A word or phrase that creates an immediate impression of health to influence thinking and behaviour. Its function is to deliver a shortcut to certainty, short-circuiting critical thinking by exploiting our desire to do good.

Q2 (SA). List the Devious Dozen.

A: Natural, holistic, healthy, organic, non-GMO, gluten-free, chemical-free, toxin-free, locally grown, the colour green, immune-boosting, personalized.

Q3 (SA). How do you deconstruct a halo word?

A: Ask what it means (does a regulator define it?), what it implies (usually healthier/safer), and whether the implied claim is supported. The gap between the meaning and the implication is the halo.

Q4 (T/F). Caulfield's point is that every Devious Dozen item is definitively bad.

A: False. His point is narrower: the science is uncertain or mixed for several, and the implied certainty is the deception, not the underlying goal.

Q5 (SA). What did the BMJ Open "immune boosting" study find?

A: Using a "naive computer" across 225+ websites, about 86% portrayed the concept inaccurately (including claims of protection against COVID-19) and fewer than 10% offered any critique. Supplement sales had spiked by as much as 60% in some countries.

Q6 (MC). Pew's 20-country survey on GM foods found what share saying they are safe?

a) 13% b) 40% c) 70% d) 95%

A: a. Nearly half think GM foods are unsafe, despite an unusually complete scientific consensus; this is the largest gap between consensus and public perception of any issue discussed.

Q7 (SA). What did the two JAMA RCTs find on "personalized" diets?

A: The 2018 genetic-diet and 2022 glycemic-response-diet trials found no weight-loss advantage over non-personalized approaches. The best diet is the healthy one you can sustain.

Chapter 7: Pets, Clean Beauty, and "Safe and Sustainable"

Q1 (SA). Explain motte-and-bailey with the clean beauty example.

A: The bailey is the contested claim (clean beauty is definitively safer). When challenged, the defender retreats to the motte, an unarguable truism (we all want safe cosmetics), then treats it as vindicating the original claim. Name the retreat and return to the original claim.

Q2 (SA). Why is "clean" beauty definitionally problematic?

A: There is no definition at Health Canada, the FDA, or the industry, and it is circular (clean means non-toxic, non-toxic means clean). It is, in cosmetic chemist Perry Romanowski's framing, "telling new stories about the same old products."

Q3 (SA). What did Darbre's 2004 paraben study actually show, and what happened to it?

A: It detected parabens in 20 breast tumours with no comparison group, testing whether they could be measured, not whether they cause cancer. Darbre clarified that the paper never claimed causation, but the correction did not reach the public; a 2007 Daily Mail headline helped make paraben-free the founding premise of clean beauty.

Q4 (MC). What do the FDA (2022) and Cancer Research UK (2020) say about parabens in cosmetics?

a) They cause cancer b) The FDA has no information showing an effect on human health as used; CRUK says they do not cause cancer c) They are banned d) They are untested

A: b.

Q5 (T/F). Replacing a demonized ingredient with a "natural" alternative is a safety gain.

A: False. It is substitution risk, an information loss. A 2022 study of ~1,500 "clean" products found most contain a potential allergen, and "clean" toothpaste often drops fluoride (a 2018 review found fluoride-free toothpaste failed to reduce caries).

Q6 (SA). What is the pet-halo transfer?

A: Owners who adopt grain-free, keto, gluten-free, or non-GMO eating are more likely to impose it on pets (2021 study). Grain-free has no evidentiary basis in pets and is linked to canine heart problems under FDA investigation; nearly half of pet food is now labelled grain-free versus 15% a decade ago.

Q7 (SA). Why are successful lawsuit settlements not evidence of safety risk?

A: They are legal outcomes, not scientific findings; courts are notoriously poor with science.

Chapter 8: Ancient Aliens, Wishful Thinking, and the Goodness Bias

Q1 (SA). Define white hat bias.

A: Coined by Allison and Cope (2010): distortion of research-based information in the service of perceived righteous ends. Research on noble topics is more likely to get funded, published, hyped, and believed.

Q2 (SA). How was hydroxychloroquine a white hat bias case?

A: The urgent, righteous goal of a COVID therapy led to publication bias favouring positive results, with positive findings from lower-quality studies carrying more influence than higher-quality RCTs showing no benefit and possible harm.

Q3 (MC). The 2019 University of Southern Mississippi study of 100+ NIH-funded investigators found scientists rated unethical research practices as:

a) equally defensible regardless of cause b) less defensible when the cause was noble c) more defensible when the research was for noble reasons d) irrelevant

A: c.

Q4 (SA). Describe the CBD placebo loop.

A: Placebo responses produce positive trials; positive trials get media coverage; coverage raises expectations and strengthens the placebo response in the next trial (2022 Karolinska study on cannabinoids for pain).

Q5 (T/F). Lower-quality observational studies are more prone to white hat bias than randomized trials.

A: True. Selective analysis and reporting are easier with weaker data.

Q6 (SA). What is the pareidolia check, and what is the problem with ancient-alien claims beyond silliness?

A: Before treating a pattern as evidence, ask whether you wanted to see it. Ancient-alien claims are aimed almost exclusively at non-white civilizations (Giza, Machu Picchu, Rapa Nui, etc.) and never at the Colosseum, reinforcing racist ideas; pseudoarchaeology has been linked to antisemitism, white supremacism, and QAnon.

Q7 (SA). What counterfactual test guards against the goodness bias?

A: Would I accept this method, sample size, or press release if the finding cut against a goal I like? Also: "who would want this to be true?"

Chapter 9: Manly Men and Manly Ideology

Q1 (SA). How is masculinity a "health halo"?

A: "Manly" works like "natural" or "clean": an unargued proxy for good that lets sellers attach unproven interventions. Mallory DeMille: influencers present the pursuit of maximum masculinity as the pursuit of maximum health.

Q2 (SA). What makes masculinity different from safer food or safer cosmetics as a halo?

A: The goal itself is contested, and conformity to traditional masculine norms is consistently associated with worse health outcomes (less help-seeking, more heart disease, risky behaviour, worse mental health, etc.).

Q3 (SA). State Starbird's emotional-signal rule.

A: Whenever content makes you feel politically self-righteous, like about to spike a political football, be extra careful about sharing. Fear, anger, or moral charge is the cue to slow down.

Q4 (MC). Testicle tanning is best summarized as:

a) well supported by animal studies b) no clinical trials and not even animal studies, and possibly harmful c) approved by urologists d) proven to double testosterone

A: b. Urologist Rena Malik says it does not work; Ranjith Ramasamy notes it may decrease testosterone and sperm counts.

Q5 (T/F). Testosterone decline is entirely a myth.

A: False. It is partially real (2021 Miami study, 1999-2016; most experts estimate 20-25% over two decades, not the documentary's claimed 50%), with complex likely causes; none supports a conspiracy to de-masculinize men.

Q6 (SA). What did the Marin County case show about ideology and misinformation?

A: Once anti-vaccine sentiment read as conservative, a wealthy, very Democratic county once known for it became one of the most vaccinated places in America (80% of 5-to-11-year-olds double-vaccinated, over double state and national rates). Ideology amplifies misinformation rather than being its source.

Q7 (SA). What is the 2022 Spanish study's "misinformation fingerprint"?

A: Across ~100,000 pieces of social media misinformation, versus accurate content, it was easier to process, more emotional, scarier, and focused on morality.

Chapter 10: A Good Story and the Certainty Grift

Q1 (SA). Define the certainty grift.

A: Most people want to do good but rarely convert that into behaviour. The goodness illusion bridges the gap with false certainty about both the goal and the path (halos, wishful thinking, scary anecdotes) and sells it for profit, politics, or evidence-free agendas.

Q2 (MC). What share of Americans live a healthy lifestyle (2016 Mayo Clinic Proceedings)?

a) 2.7% b) 27% c) 50% d) 75%

A: a. This intention-behaviour gap is the market map for the grift.

Q3 (SA). List the documentary evidence audit steps.

A: Does it rely on shocking anecdotes? Does it place claims in the broader body of evidence? Separate your emotional response to the production from your assessment of the data. Check whether an uncertain literature has been rendered as a definitive story.

Q4 (SA). What happened in the What the Health study of 160 health science students?

A: After viewing, their nutrition knowledge decreased, agreement with incorrect health claims increased, and many said they would change their diets. Subject-matter training did not protect them.

Q5 (SA). What does Toxic Beauty get wrong about talcum powder?

A: It leaves viewers believing the product-cancer link is clear, supported by billion-dollar settlements. But a large 2020 JAMA study found no statistically significant association between genital powder use and ovarian cancer, and a 2021 review found at most a weak association. Caulfield does not claim there is no connection, only that the literature is uncertain and underwhelming.

Q6 (T/F). Caulfield concludes that stories should be avoided in science communication.

A: False. Stories can be near-essential (Dahlstrom: narrative creates meaning from scattered facts); the problem is anecdote doing the work of data. Narrative is a delivery mechanism, not a truth signal.

Q7 (SA). What is "backlash" (2022 Rutgers study)?

A: People exposed to conflicting health information made more errors, were slower, reported more workload and nutritional confusion, and rejected emerging recommendations outright: "it's all so confusing, so I give up."

Chapter 11: That Earthy Taste! The Opinion Economy

Q1 (SA). What is the opinion economy?

A: The vast, lightly regulated industry that monetizes our belief in strangers' authentic opinions and, in doing so, destroys the authenticity that made them valuable. A trillion-dollar enterprise per the chapter.

Q2 (SA). Why does the wisdom of the crowd fail for online reviews?

A: It requires independent judgments (the ox-weight example); reviewers see each other, so herding (social influence bias: +32% likelihood of a positive rating, +25% in final ratings) and anchoring corrupt the mechanism.

Q3 (MC). The "Goldilocks zone" of ratings that sophisticated fakers target is:

a) 5.0 stars b) 4.2-4.5 stars with small complaints c) 3.0 stars d) 1.0 stars

A: b. All-five-star profiles actually reduce sales, so fakers add minor gripes (the stained blanket).

Q4 (SA). Describe the fake review cycle.

A: A business buys fake reviews to sell more, spends the extra revenue on ads with the platform hosting the fakes, so the platform, business, and fake reviewer profit; only the customer loses.

Q5 (SA). How did Oobah Butler make The Shed at Dulwich the top-ranked London restaurant?

A: A $13 burner phone for TripAdvisor verification, an appointment-only site with a menu of moods, styled fake food photos, and fake reviews (praising the "earthy taste" with a stained-blanket complaint). It rose from 18,149th of 18,149 to number one, with no food ever served; he refused all bookings, adding exclusivity.

Q6 (T/F). Having thousands of reviews averages out bias.

A: False. Garbage in, garbage out scales with the garbage: roughly 25-30% may be unreliable, and only 1.5% of one apparel company's customers wrote reviews (an extreme-value sample).

Q7 (SA). What are incentivized reviews and how much do they inflate ratings?

A: Reviews paid or discounted into existence; not technically fake, but they inflate ratings 40-70% and require FTC disclosure.

Chapter 12: Reviews Are Often Wrong

Q1 (SA). What did the 2016 Amazon vs. Consumer Reports study find?

A: Across 1,200+ products, higher Amazon ratings scored higher with Consumer Reports only 57% of the time. Consumer Reports scores predicted used-product resale prices; star ratings had essentially no relationship to them.

Q2 (SA). Give the two mechanisms Donald Lichtenstein offered for consumer review inaccuracy.

A: Non-comparativeness (consumers evaluate one product in isolation) and timing (they review right after purchase, before living with the product).

Q3 (SA). State the knowledge asymmetry rule.

A: The more expertise separates you from the provider, the less your review tracks quality. Use reviews only for experience (wait times, courtesy), not clinical quality, which patients cannot judge.

Q4 (MC). What do studies find about online physician ratings?

a) They closely predict clinical outcomes b) No clear relationship with clinical outcomes or peer-assessed performance c) They predict mortality d) They are all fake

A: b. Yet 84% of surveyed Americans would not see a physician rated under four stars.

Q5 (T/F). Tech-savvy users can reliably spot machine-generated fake reviews.

A: False. They detected them at rates indistinguishable from random guessing. Assume-you-can't-detect rule: treat your ability as near zero.

Q6 (SA). What did Marco Zenone's alternative cancer clinic analysis find?

A: 1,000+ reviews across 39 clinics averaged 4.4 stars (the believably good Goldilocks range), dominated by stage-four and terminal patients, for treatments with no supporting evidence; patients using alternative therapies for cancer have worse outcomes.

Q7 (T/F). Knowing that fakes exist protects you from them.

A: False. 52% of Australians suspect they have fallen for fakes and 86% of Germans still call reviews credible. Three in four Americans overestimate their ability to sort credible from bunk, and the most overconfident spread more falsehoods.

Chapter 13: An Escape Plan: Polls, Taste Makers, and Liking What You Like

Q1 (SA). List the main steps of the escape plan for reviews.

A: Be very skeptical of online reviews; seek side-by-side comparisons in standardized environments; use independent expert outlets (Consumer Reports, Wirecutter, video reviews); use multiple comparative sources; ignore star ratings and aggregates; check your own motivated reading.

Q2 (SA). What are the four poll questions (Frank Graves)?

A: How big is the sample (~1,000 reasonable nationally)? Is it representative (random, not self-selecting)? Who did the research (survey experts or an influencer)? Any obvious biases, such as a sponsor with a vested interest? Also check question wording.

Q3 (SA). What is the spiral of silence?

A: People withhold opinions they believe are in the minority, so visible consensus silences dissent. A 2019 study found likes directly changed personal opinion as consensus cues.

Q4 (MC). FiveThirtyEight recomputed IMDb rankings using only women's ratings. Only what share of 4,000+ films had more ratings from women than men?

a) 2.4% b) 25% c) 50% d) 80%

A: a (97 films). The Godfather fell from second to tenth. Lesson: an aggregate is a population; change the population and the "objective" answer changes.

Q5 (SA). What is the deliberate taste-widening experiment?

A: For a set period, engage attentively with things you claim to loathe, with iconography bracketed off. Caulfield's year of yacht rock, Fleetwood Mac, AC/DC, and disco expanded his "this is great" list by 30-40%, though some dislikes never budged.

Q6 (T/F). Caulfield recommends sharpening your skill at filtering real reviews from fake ones.

A: False. Experts say individual consumers cannot do it; substitute sources rather than sharpen your filter.

Q7 (SA). What are incidental similarities?

A: Non-political common ground that increases felt closeness and thereby openness to opposing political views; a route into contested conversations.

Chapter 14: Conclusion: A Path Forward?

Q1 (SA). List the Certainty Six.

A: (1) Pause and recognize the ecosystem isn't rigged for accuracy, asking "is this accurate?" before sharing. (2) Watch for scienceploitation. (3) Resist the allure of science hype. (4) Take a closer look when goodness is used as marketing. (5) Always consider the existing body of evidence. (6) Like what you like.

Q2 (SA). What are the three sub-tests of Certainty Six #2?

A: Is the claim riding a hot topic (electricity, radiation, now stem cells, genomics, nanotech, microbiome, quantum)? Does actual research support it or just buzzwords (word salad)? Do scientific trappings appear in a field already associated with pseudoscience?

Q3 (SA). What are the steps of the body-of-evidence test?

A: Refuse single study syndrome; check your personal biases on the topic first; check retraction status and venue (search the title and see whether a breadth of academics cite it); ask what the scientific consensus is and find it via responsible aggregators (science communicators, journalists, university and government resources, credible professional bodies).

Q4 (T/F). The public tends to overestimate how strong scientific consensus is.

A: False. It underestimates it, because consensus "often isn't sexy" and contrarian views are overrepresented.

Q5 (SA). What is the Fundamental Fix?

A: Fix how science is funded, done, and communicated: reward quality over quantity; shut down fake journals; retract bad science faster and make retractions unmistakable; fund replication and negative results; open data; enforce integrity; and have publicly funded researchers correct the record when their field is spun.

Q6 (MC). What discriminates valid contrarianism (plate tectonics, bacterial ulcers) from grift?

a) the charisma of the speaker b) venue: raised and tested in scientific venues versus ranting on podcasts and cable news c) popularity d) age of the claim

A: b.

Q7 (SA). How did Caulfield apply the test to his own book?

A: He found studies he planned to cite skewed toward predatory venues and cut them ("Punt."). He admitted his own work sits inside the same distorting incentives, and answered by running the body-of-evidence test on his sources rather than abandoning citation.

Cumulative Final Exam

  1. State the thesis of the book in two sentences and explain why trust level is a risk indicator.

A: The more we seek certainty, the harder it is to find, because the guideposts we rely on (science, goodness, opinion) attract distortion in proportion to their value. The signals worth faking are the ones people trust most.

  1. Name the Three Illusions and, for each, one countermeasure from the book.

A: Science Illusion (body-of-evidence test / single study rule / red-flag audit); Goodness Illusion (health halo deconstruction / separate the goal from the intervention); Opinion Illusion (review escape plan / four poll questions).

  1. A clinic's website cites one study as proof its therapy works. Describe what you would check.

A: Single study syndrome rule; red-flag audit (publisher, affiliation, acceptance interval, ethics review, methods, author history), retraction status, citation pattern, then the scientific consensus via aggregators. Also check whether risks and limitations are stated and whether a legitimate governing body (e.g., ISSCR) says it is clinic-ready.

  1. What do the Galileo gambit, the pseudo-profound bullshit finding, and the science-y language studies have in common?

A: All manufacture the illusion of certainty: persecution framing converts missing evidence into evidence of suppression; vagueness is mistaken for profundity; opacity is rated as credibility regardless of education.

  1. Explain how hype and predatory publishing both trace back to the same incentive, and what fix addresses it.

A: Publish-or-perish and quantity-over-quality rewards (and funding that rewards exaggerated promises). Fixes: reward quality, block public funds paying predatory fees, funding by lottery, understatement as default.

  1. Why does a retracted paper like Wakefield's keep circulating?

A: Post-retraction citations rarely note the retraction (5.4%), retracted papers attract more attention, slow retraction lets misinformation entrench, and motivated reasoners fold the retraction into a persecution story.

  1. A product says it is "toxin-free" and "natural." Walk through the deconstruction.

A: Ask what the words mean (regulator definition?), what they imply, whether supported. Dose makes the poison; appeal to nature fallacy (arsenic, venom, lightning); try "evil-spirits-free"; read the ingredient list; ask what replaced removed ingredients (substitution risk).

  1. Someone responds to your evidence with "surely you want safe cosmetics?" Name the move and your reply.

A: Motte-and-bailey. Restate the original contested claim (that this product is definitively safer than alternatives) and return the discussion to it.

  1. How can a noble cause bias research and a documentary? Give two examples.

A: White hat bias (hydroxychloroquine and COVID; CBD placebo loop) and the certainty grift via a good story (Toxic Beauty talc; What the Health). Noble goals lower the evidence bar; production quality and anecdote make weak data feel definitive.

  1. You are choosing a washing machine, a physician, and a poll to believe. Apply the book's guidance to each.

A: Washing machine: independent comparative expert testing (Consumer Reports, Wirecutter), multiple sources, ignore star ratings (57% agreement, no link to resale prices). Physician: knowledge asymmetry means reviews track experience not clinical quality; use with extreme caution. Poll: four questions (size ~1,000, representative, who did it, sponsor bias). Throughout, assume you cannot detect fakes, pause, and "like what you like."

Arguments & Evidence

The Certainty Illusion: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Timothy Caulfield

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files, glossary, patterns, and cheatsheet in the certainty-illusion skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording. Chapter numbering follows the skill (Intro = Ch 0; Conclusion = Ch 14).

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

The Introduction diagnoses a "certainty illusion": the guideposts we use to cut through noise (science, goodness, and opinion) are so valuable that they have become the prime targets of distortion, producing a knowledge production crisis and not merely a misinformation problem. Part I (Ch 1-5) shows the Science Illusion: the science-y veneer, the hype machine inside research itself, predatory and hijacked journals, and zombie science, with "never rest on one study" as the load-bearing defence. Part II (Ch 6-10) shows the Goodness Illusion: health halos and the Devious Dozen, clean beauty and pet food, white hat bias, masculinity as a halo, and the power of a good story to sell false certainty into the gap between wanting to do good and doing it. Part III (Ch 11-13) shows the Opinion Illusion: a manufactured review economy, ratings that barely predict quality, fakes you cannot spot, and an escape plan built on expert comparatives, poll-quality questions, and liking what you like. Ch 14 converts the diagnosis into a systemic fix and a personal toolkit, the Certainty Six.

Ch 0. Introduction: Adrift in a Storm

Argument: We have more access to knowledge than ever and less certainty, because science, goodness, and opinion are now so valued that they are being counterfeited. The trust level of a signal is a risk indicator, not a safety indicator. The deeper problem is a knowledge production crisis (degraded methods and institutions), not just downstream misinformation.

Stories & evidence

  • The hostile questioner: after a lecture on health misinformation, a man asks "why should we trust you?" and says "Science is full of shit." Caulfield concedes "Yeah, it is," because the critique is partly right (predatory journals, hype incentives, salami science, fraud) and is about incentives, not facts.
  • University of Pittsburgh (2023): beliefs about COVID treatments, among physicians as well as the public, were predicted by partisan cable news preference and not by exposure to scientific research.
  • Trust in science as branding: about 90% say they trust science while also embracing astrology and conspiracies.
  • Own-research paradox: 81% of Americans rely "a lot" on their own research for big decisions, and 96% of those do it online.
  • Framings: the WHO's "infodemic," the "great flattening of knowledge," and Sagan's "candle in the darkness" for science as process, not institution.

Key numbers: ~10% of clinical trials reach clinical application; 81% / 96% own-research figures; ~90% say they trust science.

So what: Diagnose which guidepost a claim leans on before judging it. Concede real institutional failures, defend science as a process done well and with humility, and avoid cynical disbelief of everything ("if not science, what?"). Awareness alone is partly protective.

Ch 1. The Science-y Veneer: Quantum Leaps, Scienceploitation, and Science-y Fear

Argument: Scientific-sounding language works as a credibility technology whether or not any relevant science exists, and its power comes from opacity, not comprehension. Add fear and you get the most durable engine of misinformation.

Stories & evidence

  • Stem cells for sale: with Zarzeczny and Murdoch, Caulfield examined about 250 alternative-medicine clinic websites advertising stem-cell therapies (sourced from bone marrow, umbilical cord blood, even apples). The ISSCR says proven treatments are very few (certain blood and immune disorders via bone-marrow transplant, plus tissue-specific transplants like skin and cornea).
  • Skincare analysis (2015, with Rachul and Percec): most stem-cell products were presented as ready for use, few substantiated claims, fewer mentioned risk.
  • The Manhattan beautician microneedling "apple stem cells" into a thrilled client who cited tighter skin and Hungarian apples.
  • Science-y language studies: a 2013 study on "trappings of science"; a 2004 study showing persuasiveness regardless of education (science majors and grad students included); a 2023 study showing vague claims later misremembered as definitive; a 2020 Ohio State study on jargon disengagement.
  • Historical prototypes: Mesmer's animal magnetism (1779); Eben Byers and Radithor (radium water).
  • Quantum: physicist Mark Freeman has never seen the word used accurately with a health product.
  • Negativity bias: a 2019 17-country experiment found negative news physiologically activates people everywhere.

Key numbers: only 19% of stem-cell clinic sites mentioned any limitation; science-y language raised persuasiveness regardless of education.

So what: Run the quantum test; demand a plain-language mechanism; check the field's own governing body; treat missing risks as diagnostic; split any scare into its science-y half and scary half; ask whether "science" is used honorifically or descriptively. Expect it to work on you and build procedures, not confidence.

Ch 2. Certainty, Dunning-Kruger, and the Humility Fix

Argument: People most confident about contested science tend to know the least, and the moves they reach for (the Galileo gambit, pseudo-profound bullshit) exist to destabilize evidence. The counter is intellectual humility plus a proportional standard of proof.

Stories & evidence

  • The New Age Bullshit Generator: a shimmering passage attributed to Hemingway turned out to come from a generator built after its creator sat through a debate involving Deepak Chopra.
  • Pennycook's Ig Nobel study (2015): random vague buzzword sentences were rated at least somewhat profound; a 2019 follow-up showed the labelling effect (famous attribution raises perceived profundity). "Consciousness consists of four-dimensional superstructures of quantum energy" fuses science-y and pseudo-profound.
  • Knowledge overconfidence: a 2019 anti-GMO study ("extreme opponents know the least, but think they know the most") and a large 2022 replication across climate change, nuclear power, vaccination, evolution, and GMOs.
  • Narcissism and conspiracy: a 2022 review (need for dominance, control, uniqueness); a 2017 German study (conspiracy belief for uniqueness); a 2022 study of overconfident, wrong conspiracy believers who overestimate agreement from others.
  • Soft Galileo gambit: Gwyneth Paltrow's "we were just early" response to the jade egg fine and gluten-free critique.
  • Real contrarians: plate tectonics and H. pylori won through data, not self-proclaimed persecution.

Key numbers: 2015 Ig Nobel study; 2019 labelling effect; multiple 2019-2022 overconfidence studies (no single headline percentage).

So what: Treat Galileo talk as a last-resort tell; scale proof to improbability and keep the onus on the claimant; interrogate the claimant (expertise, what they sell); run a humility inventory (an empty list is the finding); demand "what you do and how it works."

Ch 3. The Hype Machine, Catastrophizing, and Science Investment

Argument: The vocabulary hucksters exploit was manufactured by the legitimate research community, because funding incentives reward exaggerated promises at every stage. The same machinery inflates harms (catastrophizing), and the fix is de-hyped science, not less science.

Stories & evidence

  • University of Tsukuba analysis: nearly a million successful NIH abstracts (1985-2020) showed hype rising about 1,400 percent, with a comparable rise in NIH's own funding announcements.
  • Economic-impact promises: Texas (2009) projected 230,000 jobs and $88 billion from stem-cell investment; New Jersey 20,000 jobs and $71.9 billion; California's 2004 analysis projected $6.4-12.6 billion in health-care savings and persuaded voters to commit $3 billion. None of the therapies exist two decades later.
  • Press releases (Sumner et al., 2014): 462 releases; 40% exaggerated advice, 33% causation, 36% animal-to-human inference.
  • Replication: a 2023 study of 14,000 papers found media attention negatively associated with replication.
  • Grant lottery: Page & Barnett's proposal; trials by the Swiss National Science Foundation and New Zealand's Health Research Council.
  • Caulfield's anecdote: a 2013 genomics workshop where a senior researcher told him to stop criticizing genomics or the money would go to stem cells.
  • Stem-cell news analysis: almost 70% of articles promised therapies in "five to ten years or sooner."

Key numbers: ~1,400% hype rise; ~40% of abstracts with spin (2017); ~90% clinical trial failure; 10-15 years for trials; ~15% Canadian grant success rates; over 600 years of researcher time wasted in one Australian competition.

So what: Be wary of "breakthrough" and "revolution" language; discount near-term clinical timelines; read past the abstract and check the press release against the paper; invest in science generally but discount every specific promise; apply equal skepticism to catastrophizing.

Ch 4. The Predator Problem: Predatory Journals, Hijacked Titles, and Fake Peer Review

Argument: Pay-to-publish journals, cloned journals, and purpose-built advocacy "journals" have flooded the literature with real-looking papers that reach guidelines, policy, media, and marketing. Publication is no longer a credibility signal; the specific venue and citation pattern are.

Stories & evidence

  • The O-Shot: Dr. Jen Gunter called Dr. Charles Runels's PRP genital injection "potentially very dangerous"; Runels posted "just some of the research," a small study of eleven self-reporting women with no control or blinding. Audit: publisher OMICS International (fined $50 million by the FTC in 2019); affiliation "Medical School Birmingham" (a modest building, 250 miles from the real school); submitted June 12, accepted June 25; no ethics review; author previously sanctioned by the FDA. Clinics worldwide sell the procedure, and outlets such as Cosmopolitan and the Daily Mail ran uncritical coverage.
  • P-Shot follow-up: a 2022 JAMA paper on PRP for erectile dysfunction ("paucity of evidence"); a 2021 Sexual Medicine Society of North America statement says not for routine practice.
  • Vaccine journal: citation analysis of the International Journal of Vaccine Theory, Practice, and Research found nearly all citations from itself, its editorial board, or known anti-vaccine advocates.
  • Contaminated databases: ~400 hijacked-journal publications in the WHO COVID-19 library; Scopus carrying 67+ hijacked journals.
  • Institutional blind spots: a 2020 study of 20 Canadian universities found no policy language discouraging predatory publication; a small Canadian study linked it to greater reward.
  • Policy reach: Moher and Lalu found 800+ policies citing papers from a single predatory publisher.

Key numbers: 11,000-16,000 predatory journals; 750,000+ articles a year; ~$400 million spent annually; 91-639 days (avg ~100) to acceptance versus under two weeks; South Africa up to a 140-fold rise.

So what: Run the red-flag audit on any single study; treat quick acceptance as near-proof of no review; check who cites it; do not treat PubMed, Scopus, or WHO libraries as validation; fix incentives by blocking public funds from paying predatory fees; verify the venue first when a claim is both counter-consensus and convenient.

Ch 5. AI and Zombie Science

Argument: Generative AI will multiply plausible fake science faster than experts can filter it, while discredited research already refuses to die. The durable defence is refusing to rest any conclusion on one paper.

Stories & evidence

  • The Wakefield zombie: the 1998 Lancet paper described twelve children with no randomization or control; a press conference asserted a link; the Daily Mail, New York Times, CNN, 60 Minutes, and Jenny McCarthy (Larry King Live, Oprah) amplified it. Brian Deer found it was funded by lawyers acting for parents suing vaccine manufacturers. Wakefield lost his licence in 2010 (the GMC found him "dishonest" with "callous disregard"); The Lancet retracted in 2010 after twelve years. In 2015, 21 percent of Americans under thirty believed vaccines cause autism (the same figure in an Alberta survey of nearly 3,000).
  • Post-retraction citation: a 2021 study of 13,000+ retracted papers (5.4% acknowledged); an Economist analysis of 20,000 retracted articles (84% received post-retraction citations, 95,000 in total, cited onward in 1.65 million papers); a 2021 study of the Wakefield literature (337 references, ~62% not noting the retraction).
  • Retraction attention paradox: a 2022 University of Michigan analysis of nearly 4,000 retracted papers.
  • AI: a Northwestern/University of Chicago study found academics could not identify ChatGPT-written abstracts; Eurasia Group's 2023 "weapon of mass disruption"; Sandra Wachter's "loss of the middleman."
  • Other zombies: ivermectin for COVID and the retracted 2019 police-shootings study (condemned by 850+ academics, echoed by Donald Trump after George Floyd's murder).
  • Proposals: Holden Thorp's two-stage retraction; the U.K. parliament's April 2023 proposal of a retraction process of no more than two months; Oransky's swamp metaphor.

Key numbers: 5.4%; 84% / 95,000 / 1.65 million; 89% of authors unaware a cited article was retracted (2022); retractions average two to three years; ~$2.5 trillion a year in global R&D.

So what: Never accept a claim resting on one paper; check retraction status; treat unusually exciting findings as higher risk; do not argue the persecution framing on its terms; push for fast, visible, two-stage retraction; with AI, shift from detecting individual fakes to structural habits (body of evidence, source legitimacy, citation patterns).

Ch 6. Health Halos and the Devious Dozen

Argument: A health halo is a word that makes a product feel healthier or safer than the evidence supports. Its real function is to deliver a shortcut to certainty by exploiting our wish to do good, and it measurably changes what we buy, eat, and taste.

Stories & evidence

  • The Devious Dozen: natural, holistic, healthy, organic, non-GMO, gluten-free, chemical-free, toxin-free, locally grown, the colour green, immune-boosting, personalized.
  • Immune-boosting end to end: the immune system is a balanced network, not a muscle; overactivity causes autoimmune disease and anaphylaxis. Supplement sales spiked up to 60% in some countries during COVID-19. The BMJ Open "naive computer" study of 225+ websites found ~86% portrayed the concept inaccurately, fewer than 10% critiqued it.
  • Trusted outlets: the NYT, Harvard Health, and Mayo Clinic ran "boost your immune system" headlines; a Columbia study found 60% of links shared on social media are never opened.
  • Non-GMO: 2016 NAS, Purdue, Health Canada, FDA, FAO, WHO agree no link between GE foods and disease; Pew (20 countries) found nearly half think GM foods unsafe and only 13% say safe.
  • Personalized: two JAMA RCTs (2018 genetic diet; 2022 glycemic-response diet) showed no weight-loss advantage.
  • Halo effects on behaviour: perceived healthiness increases portions and calories; taste research (two slices of the same apple) shows belief changes reported taste. A 2018 University of Chicago study found people judge good and bad faster than they expect.
  • Organic and local: organic farms generally have lower yields; transport is ~5-10% of food's footprint versus >80% from production.
  • Absurd halos: gluten-free sparkling water, non-GMO Triscuits.

Key numbers: ~86% inaccurate and <10% critical; 13% say GM foods safe; up to 60% supplement spike; 60% of shared links unopened.

So what: For each halo word ask what it means, what it implies, and whether that is supported; expect behavioural effects; treat "holistic" as a red flag; try "evil-spirits-free"; ask for the RCT behind "personalized"; judge practices, not labels, and eat the overall pattern of real food.

Ch 7. Pets, Clean Beauty, and "Safe and Sustainable"

Argument: Halos migrate into any market where love, guilt, and insecurity live (pet food, cosmetics), and when challenged defenders retreat from a contested claim to an unarguable platitude. Naming that retreat (motte-and-bailey) is the practical defence.

Stories & evidence

  • Parabens end to end: Darbre's 2004 study found parabens in 20 breast tumours with no comparison group and tested whether they could be measured, not whether they cause cancer; she later clarified this, but a 2007 Daily Mail headline said women absorb up to 5 lbs of chemicals a year. FDA (2022): no information showing an effect on human health as used; Cancer Research UK (2020): "Parabens do not cause cancer"; Schwarcz: very weak estrogenic properties and less allergenic than alternatives. Rubin and Brod (JAMA Dermatology, 2019) warned of contact dermatitis and unnecessary avoidance. A 2020 crowdsourced urine study showed avoidance lowers measured parabens, with no evidence of health benefit.
  • Substitution risk: a 2022 study of ~1,500 "clean" products at Target and Walgreens found most contain a potential allergen; fluoride-free toothpaste failed to reduce caries (2018 review); several "clean" companies recalled products for mold, yeast, and bacteria.
  • The founder's admission: Drunk Elephant's Tiffany Masterson said "I don't think they are bad for you" but removed parabens because "consumers don't want them."
  • Pet food: nearly half of pet foods are labelled grain-free (up from 15%); 88% of veterinary professionals with dogs and 73% with cats say grain-free is not healthy; a 2021 study found owners impose their diets on pets; a 2013 UC Davis study of 67 home-prepared diets found major imbalances; the FDA warns raw pet food is more likely to carry Salmonella.
  • Motte-and-bailey in politics: urban tanks behind "safer streets," fluoride removal behind "toxin-free water," abortion bans behind "avoiding unnecessary deaths."

Key numbers: 20 tumours; ~1,500 products; 15% to nearly half grain-free; 88% / 73% of vets; 45% of pet products contain ingredients not on the label.

So what: Name the retreat and restate the original claim; ask what a "free-from" ingredient did and what replaced it; demand a definition; separate "we should study this" from "this is unsafe"; check the messenger's conflict of interest; do not impose your food ideology on animals.

Ch 8. Ancient Aliens, Wishful Thinking, and the Goodness Bias

Argument: Wishful thinking distorts the production, publication, and reporting of science itself. When a research goal seems noble, weak data are called conclusive, low-quality studies get amplified, and questionable practices look defensible. Bias need not be self-serving to wreck an evidence base.

Stories & evidence

  • Ancient aliens: Caulfield's own rocket-on-a-Mayan-sarcophagus moment (actually a king's descent into the underworld) and the face on Mars. Pseudoarchaeology (Stephanie Halmhofer) targets non-white civilizations (Giza, Machu Picchu, Sacsayhuamán, Pumapunku, Teotihuacán, Rapa Nui) and links to antisemitism, white supremacism, occult fascism, and QAnon. A 2013 Finnish study tied pareidolia to religious and paranormal belief.
  • White hat bias (Allison and Cope, 2010): research on noble topics gets funded, published, hyped, believed.
  • Hydroxychloroquine: a 2021 study found a publication bias favouring positive results; low-quality positives outweighed RCTs showing no benefit and possible harm.
  • Scientists' own ethics: a 2019 University of Southern Mississippi study of 100+ NIH-funded PIs found unethical practices rated more defensible for noble research.
  • Press bias: a 2015 analysis found rigour had no effect on press coverage; media are more likely to cover low-quality observational studies.
  • CBD: crowdfunding claims riddled with misinformation (Caulfield, Snyder, Zenone, 2020); a 2022 Karolinska study found placebo responses drive pain reduction in cannabinoid RCTs and are boosted by media coverage of earlier placebo-driven positives.

Key numbers: 100+ NIH PIs surveyed; no effect of rigour on coverage; no single headline figure.

So what: Ask the counterfactual; check study type before conclusion; do not use press attention as a quality proxy; treat strong desire for an outcome as a warning; look for feedback loops; be open to wonder but not closed to facts.

Ch 9. Manly Men and Manly Ideology

Argument: Masculinity has become a health halo, so bro-wellness products inherit unearned certainty. Unlike safer food or cosmetics, the goal itself is contested, and conformity to traditional masculine norms is consistently associated with worse health.

Stories & evidence

  • Testicle tanning: from Tucker Carlson's The End of Men and guest "Raw Egg Nationalist"; no clinical trials, not even animal studies; urologist Rena Malik says it does not work; Ranjith Ramasamy warns of lower testosterone, lower sperm counts, and infertility. Providers fuse the manliness halo with the natural halo.
  • Testosterone trend: a 2021 University of Miami study (1999-2016); most experts estimate 20-25% over two decades, not the documentary's claimed 50%; causes include obesity, diabetes, diet, sleep, chemicals, and COVID.
  • The Liver King: raw organ meat and "ancestral living" business while spending $11,000 a month on steroids and growth hormone.
  • Manhood threat: a 2021 Duke study (social pressure to be masculine elicits aggressive cognition); a 2022 Lethbridge study (masculinity stress and willingness to pay for red meat); Sarah DiMuccio's "So, they order the steak"; a 2022 NYU-team study found masculinity-driven political effects especially strong among liberal men.
  • Marin County: a Democratic, anti-vaccine-prone county became one of the most vaccinated once anti-vaccine sentiment read as conservative.
  • Misinformation fingerprint: ~100,000 social media pieces (2022 Spanish study).
  • Health costs of norms: a 2017 systematic review, a 2021 depressive-symptoms study, and 2020 suicidal-ideation work.

Key numbers: 20-25% versus 50% testosterone decline; $11,000 a month; 80% vaccinated in Marin (5-to-11); ~100,000 posts.

So what: Separate goal from intervention; question goals presented as axiomatic; treat "no trials, not even animal studies" as a full stop; use Starbird's rule before sharing; remember ideology amplifies misinformation from any side; the evidence-based alternative is exercise, sleep, real food, no smoking, little or no alcohol, and see a physician if worried.

Ch 10. A Good Story and the Certainty Grift

Argument: A good story usually wins: production quality and narrative structure manufacture certainty, even for trained audiences. Layered on halos and wishful thinking, this closes the gap between our wish to do good and our failure to act, and the certainty grift monetizes that gap.

Stories & evidence

  • Toxic Beauty (2019) and talc: moving stories of women with ovarian cancer plus billions in settlements; a large 2020 JAMA study found no statistically significant association with genital powder use, and a 2021 Gynecologic Oncology review found at most a weak association. Caulfield does not claim no connection.
  • What the Health (2017): shown to 160 health science students (2020 Sam Houston State study); knowledge decreased, agreement with incorrect claims increased, many said they would change diets.
  • Why stories work: Jonathan Haidt ("story processor, not logic processor"); fMRI work; a 2020 University of Florida analysis of Vaccines Revealed (transportation, para-social relationships); Dahlstrom on particulars versus patterns; Jonathan Jarry on post hoc reasoning.
  • Documentaries' legitimate power: a 2016 study of an environmental documentary; University of Antwerp (2021) on Blue Planet shifting journalists' and politicians' attention.
  • Backlash: 2022 Rutgers study on conflicting health information.
  • Kindness: a 2020 Ohio State study of motives for being kind.

Key numbers: 2.7% of Americans live a healthy lifestyle (2016 Mayo Clinic Proceedings); 160 students; billions in talc settlements.

So what: After any documentary ask whether it is anecdote-driven and contextualized in the body of evidence; treat emotional conviction as data about the production; never read settlements as scientific validation; keep using stories for real data, honestly representing uncertainty; most people (including opponents) are well meaning.

Ch 11. That Earthy Taste! The Opinion Economy and Biases in the Machine

Argument: Online ratings feel like authentic crowd certainty, which is exactly why a trillion-dollar opinion economy manufactures and distorts them. Even genuine reviews are skewed by who writes them and by biases unrelated to quality.

Stories & evidence

  • The Shed at Dulwich: Oobah Butler (a $13 burner phone for TripAdvisor verification, a mood-based menu, shaving-cream and bleach-cake photos, fake reviews with a stained-blanket gripe) moved from rank 18,149 of 18,149 in London to number one, with 89,000 page views in a day, serving no food and refusing every booking.
  • Fake review cycle: Curtis Boyd of the Transparency Company.
  • Biases: anchoring; social influence bias (+32% likelihood of positive rating, +25% final ratings); choice supportive bias; marketing placebo effects (pricier wine, a discounted energy drink working less); precarious manhood ("Real Men Don't Buy 'Mrs. Clean'"); weather (rainy-day reviews lower); NYC hotel ratings (couples 8.19 highest, business travellers 7.61 lowest).
  • Sampling: MIT Sloan found only 1.5% of an apparel company's customers wrote reviews; super contributors dominate.
  • Trust: 88% trust reviews as much as or more than experts or friends; ~70% of shoppers filter by rating, commonly at four stars.

Key numbers: 25-30% unreliable; 4.2-4.5 star Goldilocks zone; incentivized reviews inflate 40-70%; one Yelp star = 5-9% revenue; fake reviews influence ~$791 billion in US online spending and directly affect ~$152 billion (World Economic Forum estimate).

So what: Assume a quarter to a third of reviews are unreliable; ask who profits from half a star; treat a believable 4.2-4.5 as neutral, not credible; assume herding; prefer independent comparative testing for objective quality.

Ch 12. Reviews Are Often Wrong, and You Can't Spot the Fakes

Argument: Checked against expert assessment or market reality, consumer ratings barely beat a coin flip, and they are worst where stakes are highest. Nobody, including experts and algorithms, can reliably identify a modern fake review.

Stories & evidence

  • The 2016 accuracy study: 1,200+ products, Amazon stars versus Consumer Reports; higher-rated products beat the Consumer Reports pick only 57% of the time; resale prices tracked Consumer Reports, not stars. Donald Lichtenstein: non-comparativeness and timing.
  • Alternative cancer clinics (Marco Zenone): 1,000+ reviews across 39 clinics averaging 4.4 stars, dominated by stage-four and terminal patients, for treatments with no supporting evidence; patients using alternative cancer therapies have worse outcomes.
  • Physician ratings: physicians are 64% more likely than other businesses to get five stars and 194% as likely to get one star; 84% of Americans would not see a physician under four stars; no clear relationship with clinical outcomes. Ratings reward likability.
  • Detection: machine-generated reviews defeated tech-savvy users at rates indistinguishable from guessing; three in four Americans overestimate their detection ability; 52% of Australians suspect falling for fakes; 86% of Germans call reviews credible.
  • Negative campaigns: about 50 fake negatives can overtake a competitor hotel in visibility.

Key numbers: 57%; 64% / 194%; 84%; 4.4 stars; 3 in 4; ~50 fake negatives.

So what: Use comparative expert testing for objective products; do not choose professionals by rating; assume you cannot detect fakes; treat a believably good average as neutral and a wall of cure narratives as a warning; the higher the stakes and desperation, the stronger the incentive to manipulate.

Ch 13. An Escape Plan: Polls, Taste Makers, and Liking What You Like

Argument: You cannot extract reliable signal from consumer reviews, so substitute independent comparative expert sources, apply explicit quality criteria to polls, and recognize that aggregated opinion shapes what you believe you like. Deliberately widening taste is freeing and a small bridge across polarization.

Stories & evidence

  • FiveThirtyEight's IMDb recount: of 4,000+ films, 97 (2.4%) had more ratings from women than men; for 90%, male ratings outnumbered female by at least two to one; for 51%, more than five to one. Women-only rankings dropped The Godfather from second to tenth, The Godfather II from third to twenty-second, and The Empire Strikes Back from thirteenth to forty-first.
  • Critic demographics: 64% of reviews of the 100 highest-grossing films were by white men; 89% of "top critic" reviews by white critics.
  • Caulfield's year of music: a punk-rock snob listening to yacht rock, Fleetwood Mac, AC/DC, and '70s disco; his "this is great" list grew 30-40%; some dislikes never budged. His rough split of taste: ~70% iconography, 25% quality, 5% random exposure.
  • Stated versus measured taste: 60% of liberals in one study said they liked R&B but tested as liking it less than conservatives; education and childhood music exposure correlated with liking fewer artists; critic reviews influenced song liking more than listening did.
  • Social effects: a 2019 study on likes as consensus cues; the spiral of silence; Kelefa Sanneh on social-not-musicological algorithms; Frank Graves on "faux research."
  • Bridging: incidental similarities; the Berkeley/Yale Fox-to-CNN study of forced exposure moving even hardcore partisans.

Key numbers: 2.4% (97 films); 90% / 51%; 64% / 89% critic demographics; ~1,000 respondents for a national poll; 30-40% taste expansion.

So what: Use two or more independent comparative sources and ignore aggregate scores; ask the four poll questions (size, representativeness, who, bias); see visible consensus as a force; ask who is in any aggregate; audit your own motivated reading; try what you have written off; "if you are a fan, you are a fan."

Ch 14. Conclusion: A Path Forward?

Argument: The systemic repair is to change how science is funded, done, and communicated, shifting incentives from quantity and hype to quality and impact. The personal repair is the Certainty Six.

Stories & evidence

  • Caulfield applies the rule to himself: while writing, he found cited studies skewed toward predatory venues and cut them ("Punt."), acknowledging his own work sits inside the same incentives. The literature on polluted literature is itself polluted, and the answer is to run the test on his own sources.
  • Spain's most prolific academic: meat researcher José Manuel Lorenzo Rodriguez reportedly published 176 papers in 2022 (one every two days), a system that "has created monsters."
  • Accuracy nudge: Pennycook and Rand show a prompt about accuracy improves the quality of news shared.
  • Salami science: Russell Funk; a 2023 survey found 20% of researchers admit sacrificing quality for quantity.
  • Innovation slowdown: a 2023 Nature analysis of 45M papers and 3.9M patents found disruptive research has declined sharply since 1945 (>90% by one measure).
  • Contrarians with venues: plate tectonics and bacterial ulcers were raised at scientific venues, supported by data.
  • Rapid translation: COVID vaccines, built on decades of prior work, are the rare real example.
  • Caulfield's own bias: he is a sucker for studies showing exercise, sleep, and social connection are good.

Key numbers: 176 papers in 2022; 45M papers / 3.9M patents, >90% decline; 20% of researchers sacrifice quality.

So what: Run the Certainty Six: pause ("is this accurate?"), watch for scienceploitation, resist hype, scrutinize goodness marketing, consider the body of evidence, like what you like. For extraordinary claims check retraction status, venue, citations, and consensus via aggregators; assume you underestimate consensus; judge contrarians by venue, not storyteller; push for the Fundamental Fix (quality over quantity, faster visible retractions, funded replication and negative results, open data, researchers correcting the record).

Recurring Stories to Know

  • Wakefield and the vaccine-autism paper (Ch 5; echoes in Ch 4, 9, 14): the model zombie, with citations, celebrity amplifiers, and a 21% belief figure.
  • The O-Shot / OMICS International (Ch 4): the red-flag audit in action, one predatory paper propping up an industry.
  • Stem cells (Ch 1, 3, 14): clinic websites (19% mentioned limits), apple stem-cell skincare, and failed economic-impact promises.
  • Immune-boosting (Ch 1, 6): a near-reliable scam marker, ~86% of sites inaccurate, supplement spike.
  • Parabens and clean beauty (Ch 7; echoed in 8, 10): from Darbre's 20 tumours to a lasting premise.
  • *Talc and Toxic Beauty*** (Ch 7, 10): settlements are not science.
  • Hydroxychloroquine, CBD, and COVID treatments (Ch 0, 8): white hat bias and the cable-news-predicts-beliefs finding.
  • The Shed at Dulwich (Ch 11): fake reviews can make a nonexistent restaurant number one.
  • Amazon versus Consumer Reports, 57% (Ch 12): consumer ratings barely beat a coin flip.
  • Testicle tanning and the Liver King (Ch 9): bro-science with no trials and a steroid habit.
  • The hostile questioner (Ch 0, 13 echo): the "science is full of shit" concession, and the Pittsburgh finding that physicians' cable news preference predicted COVID treatment beliefs.
  • The 2.7% healthy-lifestyle figure (Ch 10): the intention-behaviour gap the grift monetizes.

The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics: The Science of Success

2 markdown files

Quiz

Psycho-Cybernetics Quiz Book

The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics: The Science of Success by Maxwell Maltz

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. The book is an omnibus of five volumes, and the skill numbers its 24 chapters sequentially, so related chapters are grouped two to a section here (each question names the chapter it comes from). Questions are short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), or multiple-choice (MC). A cumulative final exam is at the end.

Section 1: Chapters 1-2 (Frustration, the Tomorrow Illusion, Conscience)

Q1 (SA). What does "Psycho-Cybernetics" mean, and where does the word come from? (Ch 1)

A: Psycho = mind; cybernetics comes from the Greek kybernetes, "helmsman." Together: steering your mind toward a productive, useful, worthwhile, predetermined goal. The point of the image is that the engine always runs; the question is who has the wheel and where the port is.

Q2 (T/F). In Chapter 1, frustration is mainly an event caused by circumstances, so the first fix is to change your circumstances. (Ch 1)

A: False. Frustration is a habit of self-relation, broken by changing your opinion of yourself. Maltz says no one can make you feel frustrated "without your consent," and he warns against waiting for conditions to change first (there are "no ifs" to happiness).

Q3 (MC). Which of these is NOT one of the Twelve Faces of Frustration? (Ch 1)

a) You wear a mask b) You repeat your mistakes instead of growing through them c) You retire from life d) You work too few hours

A: d. The twelve include not being true to yourself, destructive imagination (no goal), not knowing how to relax, aiming at unhappiness, frustration as habit, not accepting weaknesses, no compassion, the mask, repeating mistakes, retiring from life, considering yourself a loser, and not accepting yourself for what you are.

Q4 (SA). What happened with the seventeen-year-old boy Maltz operated on in Latin America, and what does Maltz ask the reader? (Ch 1)

A: Maltz repaired the boy's cleft lip; the boy had shouted "I'm going to die!" on the table. Two weeks later, handed a mirror, he stared at a face he had never seen and cried "I'm going to live!" Maltz asks the reader: are you going to live? No surgeon can operate on emotional disfigurement, so "be your own plastic surgeon."

Q5 (SA). What is the "Tomorrow Illusion" (Mañana, Incorporated) and what is the remedy? (Ch 2)

A: The habit of deferring your life to a better tomorrow that never arrives; members "never get dividends." Remedy: do the constructive thing today and postpone only the destructive one ("wait till tomorrow, I'll give vent to my anger tomorrow").

Q6 (SA). How does Maltz reinterpret "conscience"? (Ch 2)

A: He rejects "conscience doth make cowards of us all" and says we make cowards of our conscience. Conscience is simply your opinion of yourself, audible after a blunder. "I can't live with my conscience" means "I can't live with myself," which is a fixable self-image problem.

Section 2: Chapters 3-4 (Happiness, Crises, and Success)

Q1 (SA). What are the steps of the Happiness Habit in Ch 3, and what escape clause does Maltz build in? (Ch 3)
