A: Decide happiness is now, not conditional; dig out buried assets; own your free eight hours and spend them on what you like; live in a climate of happiness; help someone; and start each morning with a small smile in the mirror and a resolution to do your best. Escape clause: "if you fail, you fail: there's no disgrace in it, and the next day, you try all over again."

Q2 (SA). Name the seven characteristics of the failure mechanism as listed in Ch 3, and say how they map onto F-A-I-L-U-R-E. (Ch 3)

A: Fear, Aggressiveness, Insecurity, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness. Ch 24's acronym uses Anger and Inferiority for the second and third letters; the rest match.

Q3 (SA). What are the "wonderful computer" and the "decompression chamber"? (Ch 3)

A: The wonderful computer is Maltz's name for the goal-striving mechanism in the mid-brain (smaller than a hazelnut), which diagnoses your health, not your disease. The decompression chamber is a designated room in your mind where, under frustration, you regroup and give yourself another chance.

Q4 (MC). In Maltz's definition, success is best described as: (Ch 4)

a) accumulating achievements b) a growing self-image ("a success to yourself") c) beating competitors d) avoiding all failure

A: b. "You will not be a success if you make a million dollars but leave your self-image impoverished."

Q5 (SA). Spell out S-U-C-C-E-S-S. (Ch 4)

A: Sense of direction, Understanding, Courage, Compassion, Esteem, Self-acceptance, Self-confidence.

Q6 (SA). What are the Four Principles of Relaxation and the four operating conditions for the servo-mechanism? (Ch 4)

A: Relaxation: forgive others; forgive yourself; see yourself at your best; keep up with yourself. Operating conditions: one thing, one thought, one goal at a time; live in the present; use anxiety creatively to reach the goal; if a situation defies solution, sleep on it, not with it.

Q7 (T/F). If you set a goal and fail one day, you have failed. (Ch 4)

A: False. "If you set a goal and fail one day, this is no failure at all." Reset the goal tomorrow. Maltz compares it to an athlete who cannot win every day; reaching most of your goals makes you a champion in the art of living.

Section 3: Chapters 5-6 (Self-Respect, Understanding, Sincerity; Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness)

Q1 (SA). Why can't self-respect be obtained from other people's opinions, and how is it kept alive? (Ch 5)

A: "If you don't have self-respect, no one will give it to you." It is generated internally and spent outward; giving it to others keeps it replenishing. It is a lifelong job (a plant you keep watering), not a state you complete.

Q2 (SA). What specific "understanding" does Maltz say is key to dignity, and how does Goal Builder 2 practice it? (Ch 5)

A: That you have the right to live happily, pleasurably, and with self-respect. You walk a familiar street asking of each passerby "Does he believe he has the right to be happy?", then go to the mirror, write UNDERSTANDING, say "Do I have rights? Yes. Yes, I do," and erase the word but keep the feeling.

Q3 (T/F). Sincerity is just niceness and needs no particular precondition. (Ch 5)

A: False. Sincerity is the capacity to face reality without evasion, and it requires enough confidence in yourself to do so.

Q4 (SA). What is the "tell" that your self-respect is low, even when you admire others? (Ch 5)

A: Envy. If you downgrade yourself, you can still admire others, "but your respect will be tainted with envy," and others sense it.

Q5 (SA). What is the anxiety audit (Goal Builder 5), and what does Maltz predict it will show? (Ch 6)

A: Write down today's worries, then last week's, last month's, and a year ago's; check whether each was realistic. Maltz predicts many, "perhaps most," were unrealistic, giving you evidence of your own overreaction rate to apply to today's fears.

Q6 (MC). Which is NOT one of the Five Ways to Vanquish Emptiness? (Ch 6)

a) Stop sleepwalking b) Resign from Mañana Incorporated c) Renew your sense of direction d) Wait for a sanction from others that you are somebody

A: d. The list also includes enriching your self-image and orienting outward by giving your self-respect away. Maltz says "No one else has to sanction that you are somebody."

Q7 (SA). When is anxiety useful and when is it dead weight? What does a goal do to uncertainty? (Ch 6)

A: Anxiety is creative while choosing and dead weight after the decision (a fifty-pound weight carried all day). "When you reach for a goal, you bend uncertainty to your will," turning an open-ended threat into a bounded problem.

Section 4: Chapters 7-8 (Active Forgiveness and Opportunity; Mirror Watchers and Prison Walls)

Q1 (SA). What makes forgiveness "active" in Ch 7, and what must be included? (Ch 7)

A: It is a daily, all-out operation ("each day is D-day"), not a mumbled word followed by a catnap. Forgive others' faults, imperfections, wrongs done to you, and wrongs you only imagine they did; then forgive yourself for all your mistakes and flaws.

Q2 (SA). What is the torture-scene exercise in Goal Builder 8 meant to show? (Ch 7)

A: After picturing an enemy torturing a prisoner and noticing your recoil, Maltz turns it: "what about your own cruel self-torture? Is this not equally horrifying?" It makes you apply to yourself the standard you instantly apply to a stranger. Self-condemnation is torture you wouldn't tolerate from someone else.

Q3 (T/F). After a big loss, you should revise your self-image downward to stay realistic. (Ch 7)

A: False. "No matter what you lose... you must keep faith in yourself." Keep past successes ready on the "screen of your mind" and don't decide in advance that opportunity is for the other guy.

Q4 (SA). Describe Creative Mirror Watching and the diagnostic question it uses. (Ch 8)

A: Look at yourself honestly, turn away, and notice whether your face triggered a torrent of criticism; ask whether you feel that hostile when a friend walks into your home. Then close your eyes, picture a good friend's face, feel it, write FRIEND on the glass, and say "I will be a friend to myself." It looks behind the face at who you intend to become, not at flaws (prosecution) or surface (narcissism).

Q5 (SA). What does "stop cooking up failure" mean? (Ch 8)

A: Don't mentally prepare the botched interview or rejected pitch in vivid detail in advance. That is mental rehearsal in reverse and it programs the servo-mechanism with the dreaded outcome.

Q6 (SA). What is the point of the convicted-criminal caricature in Goal Builder 10? (Ch 8)

A: Overdrawing a snarling, riot-starting prisoner lets you feel how ludicrous it is to obsess over guilt and deny yourself self-respect; your real self-condemnation then looks like a role nobody cast you in. Maltz adds a fairness footnote: many inmates have constructive attitudes and deserve compassion.

Section 5: Chapters 9-10 (Tranquility and the Active Life; Integrity, Survival, Goal Builders)

Q1 (SA). What does the "Daily Dozen for Tranquility" spell, and what is its stance on peace? (Ch 9)

A: TRANQUILITY: Tension, Resistance, Arrogant aggressiveness, Negation as a way of life, Quandary, Unbelief, Inferiority, Life of loneliness, Laissez-faire, Irritation, Trepidation, Yesterday Incorporated. Tranquility is active: you wage war on these forces; passivity leaves you helpless and tense.

Q2 (SA). In what order do effort and relaxation come in the tension drill? (Ch 9)

A: Effort first: brighten your day with something constructive, get up, fight off worries, live fully, then "after a good go at your goals, you are ready for your trip to the good land - tranquility." Chronic tension arises from trying to relax instead of pursuing goals.

Q3 (MC). In the Retirement Mechanism, "Retreat" is paired with: (Ch 9)

a) Return b) Courage to Act c) Responsibility d) Friend

A: a. Other pairs include Eviction to Conviction, Mañana to Today, Ennui to Emancipation, No direction to Goal Orientation, and Traitor to Friend.

Q4 (SA). What are Goal Builders 11 and 12, and what does each have you say or write? (Ch 9)

A: 11, Tranquility: listen (in imagination or reality) to sounds that soothe you, then write TRANQUILITY and say "I will be tranquil today." 12, No Retirement Clock: listen to a ticking clock, write CLOCK, and say you must not use your time to retire from life or "kill" time.

Q5 (SA). Describe the Goal Builder program's structure and its progression. (Ch 10)

A: Fourteen Goal Builders, one per week, six days of application and one day of rest. Each typically has a seeing component, a mirror component (write the word in erasable pencil or lipstick), a spoken first-person statement, and an erasure. Progression: constructive thinking, constructive imaging, constructive action.

Q6 (SA). What is "survival with self-respect," and what is the five-part protocol (Goal Builder 14)? (Ch 10)

A: Surviving a crisis without downgrading your opinion of yourself. Accept the fear, nervousness and panic; accept yourself regardless of what the audience thinks; stop expecting yourself to fail; bring images of past successes to mind (they replace nervousness and cushion a real failure); then do your best.

Q7 (T/F). The exaggerated stadium scenario (125,000 people, 250,000 eyes) is meant to be realistic. (Ch 10)

A: False. It is a deliberate caricature; by rehearsing a crisis far worse than yours you return to your real problem correctly scaled. Maltz admits "this picture scares me, too."

Section 6: Chapters 11-12 (Chief Purpose and 21 Days; The Self-Image)

Q1 (SA). What is the 21-day rule and why does Maltz frame it as he does? (Ch 11)

A: "For a person to experience a noticeable change in a mental picture, a minimum of twenty-one consecutive days must elapse." He refuses to debate the theory and hands the judgment to the reader: practice for 21 days, then judge for yourself.

Q2 (SA). What is "Divine Discontent"? (Ch 11)

A: Negative feedback you receive when you are not moving toward your ultimate goal (man is teleological). Chronic discontent is data about direction, not a character flaw.

Q3 (SA). Explain the two-ocean-liners image. (Ch 11)

A: Same engine, same sea: a crewed ship with a goal reaches port 9,999 times out of 10,000; one with no crew and no goal runs aground before clearing the harbor. The difference is the goal and the helmsman.

Q4 (MC). According to Ch 12, the self-image is best described as: (Ch 12)

a) a floor under your abilities b) a ceiling on the effectiveness with which you can use your true potential c) a fixed personality trait d) the sum of your skills

A: b. Behavior, feelings and abilities are always consistent with it; performance outside the effectiveness range produces tension and a pull back.

Q5 (T/F). To change your self-image you must first actually improve yourself. (Ch 12)

A: False. It can be revised by repainting the mind-picture; a person "only puts to use the talents he already possesses."

Q6 (SA). When does positive thinking fail? (Ch 12)

A: "When it is compatible with a person's self-image, positive thinking does undoubtedly function, but when it is incompatible with the self-image, it absolutely will not work." Fix the picture first.

Q7 (SA). What do the circus elephant and the pike teach? (Ch 12)

A: Old limits can outlive their cause. The grown elephant stays at a stake it could uproot; the pike, after battering a glass partition separating it from minnows, starves surrounded by food once the glass is removed. Check whether the constraint still exists.

Section 7: Chapters 13-14 (The Quiet Place; Goals and The Method)

Q1 (SA). How do you build and use the Quiet Place? (Ch 13)

A: Construct it once in imagination, furnished to your taste (a beach house, a cloud, a distant planet - the constraint is comfort, not realism). Two rules: completely isolated and nobody else knows where it is. Enter it at least once a day; it takes an instant, like picturing the Golden Gate Bridge.

Q2 (SA). What did Truman's "foxhole" show? (Ch 13)

A: Truman described a foxhole in his mind where he allowed nothing to bother him and retreated into it whenever anything bothered him. Maltz cites it as proof the technique scales to high-stakes work and is used mid-crisis, not only on weekends.

Q3 (T/F). Relaxation is a temperament some people have and others don't. (Ch 13)

A: False. It is learned, a skill with a training curve; and your response to events, not the events, determines whether you are calm or agitated.

Q4 (SA). State the Method (mental rehearsal) as Maltz specifies it. (Ch 14)

A: Ten minutes a day, alone, eyes closed, body still. Build one situation in vivid five-sense detail; be a participant, not an onlooker; see yourself succeed (past actions are irrelevant); "begin by knowing you have arrived"; hold the feeling. Twenty-one consecutive days.

Q5 (MC). Synthetic experience works because: (Ch 14)

a) the subconscious is gullible b) the nervous system cannot distinguish a vividly imagined experience from a real one c) affirmations are magic d) it distracts you from failure

A: b. Successful affirming needs Desire, Information, and Repetition.

Q6 (SA). Give at least six of the nine rules for wording an affirmation. (Ch 14)

A: Strictly personal (I, me, my); positive; present tense; not progressive ("I am going to"); not comparative; avoid "able to" and "can"; balanced (no opposites or extremes); realistic (no absolutes or perfection); no time limits ("time limits are deadly; they create tension").

Q7 (SA). What does it mean that "you supply the goal; the mechanism supplies the how"? (Ch 14)

A: You define the objective and never specify the route; conscious micromanagement of the how is interference with the automatic guidance system.

Section 8: Chapters 15-16 (Negative Feedback and Plan of Action; Happiness and Exercises)

Q1 (SA). Complete the line and give the three steps: "Negative feedback is never a ___." (Ch 15)

A: STOP sign. Steps: (1) be aware of it, (2) evaluate it as unwanted/unacceptable (the outcome, not yourself), (3) take measures to correct at once. Repeated, this becomes an automatic reflex.

Q2 (SA). What do the instrument-panel, tennis-net and golf-hazard images teach? (Ch 15)

A: A warning light is information, not judgment ("no one becomes upset"), and only an occasional glance at negatives is needed; attention stays on the objective. The tennis player doesn't watch the net, the golfer the water.

Q3 (SA). What are Maltz's three prohibitions for being effective with others, and what is the underlying diagnosis of inhibition? (Ch 15)

A: Avoid trying too hard to impress them; avoid doing or saying things for the effect you believe they'll have; avoid thinking about what they think of you. Inhibition is excessive negative feedback (over-monitoring), including hurt by what you think they think.

Q4 (SA). List the five parts of "Your Own Plan of Action." (Ch 15)

A: Crystallize your thinking; develop a written plan and a deadline; develop a real desire ("Is it really worth it to me?"); develop self-confidence from past successes; develop determination. Deadlines belong on plans, never on affirmations.

Q5 (SA). How does Maltz define happiness, and what is its relation to goals? (Ch 16)

A: Quoting Dr. John A. Schindler: "a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant a good share of the time." It is a cultivable habit and a by-product of striving for goals, experienced in the present. Perpetual happiness is nonsense; gray days are normal.

Q6 (SA). What is the manipulation test? (Ch 16)

A: If you react automatically to outside circumstances that tell you to be angry or upset, you are being manipulated and letting outer conditions dictate how you feel. "If you learn the habit of happiness, you are the master instead of the slave."

Q7 (MC). Which is NOT one of the Mirror Magic six-day drills? (Ch 16)

a) Morning breathing and the question "Am I a friend to myself?" b) Garbage disposal c) Closing the front door on the past d) Counting to twelve

A: d. (Counting to twelve is the anger protocol in Ch 22.) The traffic-light drill is also in the set: a red light stands for fear of failure holding you back, and green means move forward with the confidence of past successes. The drills attach to events that already happen daily.

Section 9: Chapters 17-18 (Theater of the Mind and Origin Story; Relaxation and Habits)

Q1 (SA). What was the woman's reaction to her scar surgery, and what did Maltz discover? (Ch 17)

A: A woman in her mid-twenties had a deep indented scar from a car accident. After a successful removal, she said "I really don't see any improvement," and then, looking at the "before" photos, "It looks better, but I don't feel better." Her real wound was an unhappy romance that ended two years earlier, months before the accident; her self-image was poor.

Q2 (SA). Who are you in the theater of the mind? (Ch 17)

A: Producer, director, writer, actor or actress, hero or villain, the film technician in the booth, and the audience. There is no external critic in the room.

Q3 (T/F). Maltz says the subconscious is a second mind that judges your goals. (Ch 17)

A: False. It is "not a 'mind' but a goal-striving servomechanism" that is impersonal: fed success goals it works as a success mechanism, fed negative aims as a failure mechanism.

Q4 (SA). Why is worry "mental rehearsal running backwards"? (Ch 17)

A: Worry is imagination seeing what can happen to you before the event; it is the same technique with the opposite content. If you can worry, you can already visualize, so point it toward the goal.

Q5 (SA). What are the two roadblocks to relaxation in Ch 18? (Ch 18)

A: (1) Refusing to accept your limitations ("you can do only so much"; ask "what am I accomplishing at this pace?"). (2) Holding grudges against others and yourself. "Compassion and love are parents of relaxation"; you cannot have peace of mind while you hate.

Q6 (SA). What does the tense millionaire illustrate? (Ch 18)

A: A wealthy man with a mahogany dining room, two cars and staff who bolts his food, paces, lights and drops a cigar, and cannot relax; "he has even forgotten who he is." Asked who he is, he says only "Mr. X." Strain jams the mechanism, and material success does not buy relaxation. You must see him in your mind, not just think about him.

Q7 (SA). What are the three winning habits? (Ch 18)

A: Do the practice exercises regularly, like washing your hands; understand the importance of your mind (sustaining a single mental picture); realize the power of your self-image.

Section 10: Chapters 19-20 (Happy Living and Emotional Scars; Masks and Accepting Weakness)

Q1 (SA). Name the Four Miracle Drugs for emotional scars. (Ch 19)

A: Accept your limitations; forget your mistakes; forgive others; see yourself at your best.

Q2 (SA). List the Seven Rules for Happy Living. (Ch 19)

A: Get the happiness habit; declare war on negative feelings; strengthen your self-image; learn how to laugh; dig out your buried treasures; help others; seek activities that make you happy.

Q3 (T/F). Maltz thinks any bitterness after an unfair blow is a sign of failure. (Ch 19)

A: False. A few days of resentment is understandable, "maybe even desirable," cleansing your system. What is forbidden is letting the scar permanently dominate your thoughts.

Q4 (SA). In the unfair-firing case, how does Maltz tell you to forgive the director? (Ch 19)

A: Not by deciding he was right, but by considering what fear or insecurity may have driven him (it took courage to hire someone inexperienced, and he may have feared responsibility for your mistakes), and because you are human and not always fair yourself. Then remove the scar and return to positive goals.

Q5 (SA). Why does accepting your weakness make you strong? (Ch 20)

A: It gives you a floor under you in a crisis: "You turn a crisis into an opportunity, not an opportunity into a crisis." Masks and the "tough guy" or "perfect woman" scripts are attempts to stand on nothing.

Q6 (SA). What question does Maltz ask about self-punishment, and what is the answer? (Ch 20)

A: "If you punish yourself for your mistakes, what do you gain?" Nothing; so be kind to yourself.

Q7 (SA). In the "Be Yourself" exercise, what are the three lists and what does the gap between them mean? (Ch 20)

A: Words you'd use to describe yourself; words you think others would use; words you'd like to describe you. The gap between 1 and 2 is the mask; the gap between 1 and 3 is working material for the self-image. You also write a biography of the person you'd like others to see, and a list of reasons it would be impossible (many are expired conditions still being obeyed).

Section 11: Chapters 21-22 (Pressure, Individuality and Friends; Peace of Mind and Living Fully)

Q1 (SA). Why do some people stay calm under pressure, and what are the Bing Crosby and Whistler stories used for? (Ch 21)

A: "Their self-image holds up." Bing Crosby calmly picked up the dropped script and came in on cue. Whistler, discharged from West Point after "Silicon is a gas," later said "If silicon had been a gas, I would have been a general" - the point is adaptability: sometimes to succeed you must change your plans.

Q2 (SA). State the crisis protocol. (Ch 21)

A: Set your goals; believe in them; bring back your triumphs; don't be afraid to be nervous; recognize your power in a crisis. Intervene on the expectation of failure, not on the symptom.

Q3 (SA). List the Five Rules for Winning Friends. (Ch 21)

A: Be a friend to yourself; reach out to people; imagine you're the other person; accept the other fellow's individuality; try to meet others' needs (talk to people, not at them, and listen).

Q4 (SA). What is the daily vacation and why daily? (Ch 22)

A: A flight into the quiet room of your mind every day. Even with a 35-40 hour week (versus 60-80 hours in Maltz's youth) people are still tense; tension accrues daily and can't be settled in arrears by an annual vacation.

Q5 (SA). Describe "Delay Your Response" and its success criterion. (Ch 22)

A: Identify your over-reaction domains in advance (e.g., money on a tight budget). At the point where you know you can no longer check the anger, count slowly to twelve. At twelve you may still be irritated, but rage is subdued and your actions are controlled. The aim is control of action, not absence of feeling.

Q6 (T/F). Retiring from a job and retiring from your self-image are the same thing. (Ch 22)

A: False. Retiring from a job is optional; retiring from the self-image is always self-inflicted ("No police come in the middle of the night and enforce this indignity upon you; you do it to yourself"). Keep a goal every day.

Q7 (SA). What goes on inside the "pleasant room in your mind"? (Ch 22)

A: Rest, but also work: make peace with yourself, accept insecurities, re-picture cherished memories, set present goals, and imagine a future free of resentment and worry.

Section 12: Chapters 23-24 (The Daily Dozen; Thoughts To Live By)

Q1 (SA). Name the first five of the Daily Dozen (12 Ways to a New Self-Image) and the twelve in order if you can. (Ch 23)

A: First five: Truth, Imagination, Relaxation, That Winning Feeling, Good Habits. Full list: Truth, Imagination, Relaxation, That Winning Feeling, Good Habits, The Aim of Happiness, Unmasking, Compassion, Accepting Your Weakness, Living with Your Mistakes, Being Yourself, Never Retiring.

Q2 (SA). How do success pictures relate to failure pictures? (Ch 23)

A: You don't delete failure pictures; you crowd them out by repeatedly visualizing the roles and situations you've relished, until success pictures "blot out" the failure pictures.

Q3 (SA). What is the practical forgiveness test in Daily Dozen item 3? (Ch 23)

A: Before renewing a years-old grudge, ask whether the act you condemn is one you, "in your own imperfection, might have committed."

Q4 (SA). What is the F-A-I-L-U-R-E acronym? (Ch 24)

A: Fear, Anger, Inferiority, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness - a failure mechanism "made up of past defeats."

Q5 (SA). What does Maltz say is the only difficulty in therapeutic forgiveness, and why do we resist? (Ch 24)

A: Securing your willingness to cancel the debt with no reservations. We resist because we take comfort in condemnation: "As long as we condemn another, we can feel superior to him." True forgiveness sees that the debt itself was never valid.

Q6 (SA). What are the Five Roadblocks of Frustration, in short? (Ch 24)

A: (1) Worrying after the decision as well as before; (2) worrying about yesterday and tomorrow; (3) doing too many things at once; (4) wrestling problems around the clock (cure: sleep on it, not with it); (5) refusing to relax.

Q7 (SA). What lesson does the hurdler-turned-salesman carry, and what is the Yesterday Tomorrow Complex? (Ch 24)

A: A hurdle champion who became a mediocre salesman broke his leg trying to jump hurdles at a reunion; in the cast he recalled he became a champion through practice and overcoming failures, so he applied the same tenacity to selling and became top-flight within a year ("Failure teaches success"). The Complex: 60 percent of what we see deals with yesterday, 20 percent with tomorrow, leaving little for today (1,440 minutes a day).

Cumulative Final Exam

  1. A friend has lost her job and says, "Positive thinking never works for me." Using the book, diagnose why and what to do.

A: Positive thinking incompatible with the self-image "absolutely will not work" (Ch 12). Fix the picture first through the Method (Ch 14): ten minutes a day, participant view, 21 consecutive days; affirmations that feel like lying come after.

  1. What is the single master framework of the book, and how does it explain both Maltz's surgical successes and his failures?

A: The self-image: behavior, feelings and abilities are consistent with it, a ceiling on effectiveness. Changing a face often changed the picture; the woman who said "It looks better, but I don't feel better" still held a poor self-image from an earlier broken romance (Ch 12, 17).

  1. Explain the servo-mechanism and what "you supply the goal, it supplies the how" means for how you set goals.

A: The subconscious is an impersonal, goal-striving machine: success mechanism when fed success goals, failure mechanism when fed negative aims. State the objective (present tense, positive, no time limits) and never specify the route (Ch 14, 17).

  1. Why is worry evidence that you can already use the Method?

A: Worry is mental rehearsal in reverse (Ch 17); "stop cooking up failure" (Ch 8) and point the same imagination at the goal.

  1. A colleague makes a serious error and says, "I'm just a failure." Apply negative feedback.

A: Negative feedback is never a STOP sign: be aware, evaluate the outcome (not the person) as unwanted, correct at once, then return attention to the objective (Ch 15); one day's failure is no failure (Ch 4); self-punishment buys nothing (Ch 20).

  1. Compare the Four Principles of Relaxation (Ch 4), the Two Roadblocks (Ch 18), and the Four Miracle Drugs (Ch 19). What do they share?

A: Forgiveness of others and self, accepting limitations, and seeing yourself at your best recur in all three; "compassion and love are parents of relaxation."

  1. Describe therapeutic forgiveness and why it is hard.

A: Cancel the debt with no reservations, seeing the debt was never valid; hard because condemnation lets us feel superior (Ch 24). Honesty check: could I have committed this act (Ch 23); a few days of bitterness are fine, permanent residence is not (Ch 19).

  1. You have stage fright before a big presentation. What does Maltz tell you to do, and what does he tell you not to do?

A: Set the goal, believe in it, bring back past triumphs, permit the nervousness, then act (Ch 10, 21). Do not fight the symptom; intervene on the expectation of failure.

  1. Compare the Quiet Place (Ch 13), the pleasant room and daily vacation (Ch 22), and the decompression chamber (Ch 3).

A: All are private mental retreats built in advance and entered often. The Quiet Place is furnished once and entered at least daily; Ch 22 stresses a daily vacation and that it is a working room too; Ch 3's is a room for regrouping under frustration.

  1. Applied task: Pick one situation you handle badly and run the Method for 21 consecutive days (10 minutes, eyes closed, participant view, full sensory detail), mark each day off, and judge at day 21. Alongside it, pick one six-day Mirror Magic drill attached to a daily event.

Arguments & Evidence

The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Maxwell Maltz

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (the anecdotes, cases and images the book uses), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the chapter files, glossary, patterns and cheatsheet in the maltz-psycho-cybernetics skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not Maltz's own wording. Chapter numbers follow the skill (24 files covering an omnibus of five separately published volumes). Note: this is not a book of studies. Maltz's evidence is mainly clinical anecdote, vivid analogy and exercises the reader is told to test personally; he cites no experiments in these notes.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Maltz, a plastic surgeon, noticed that fixing a face sometimes transformed a personality and sometimes changed nothing, and concluded that the operative image is inside the face, not on it. Book One (Ch 1-4) diagnoses frustration as a habit of self-relation and defines success as a growing self-image (S-U-C-C-E-S-S). Book Two (Ch 5-10) builds self-respect through forgiveness, mirror work and fourteen weekly Goal Builders. Book Three (Ch 11-16) is the systematic course: define Psycho-Cybernetics, state the self-image as a ceiling, then teach the Quiet Place, the Method (ten minutes of mental rehearsal for 21 days), negative feedback as course correction, and the happiness habit. Book Four (Ch 17-23) retells the origin story and adds the theater of the mind, relaxation, emotional scars, acceptance of weakness, pressure, friends and the Daily Dozen. Book Five (Ch 24) distills everything into two acronyms (F-A-I-L-U-R-E and S-U-C-C-E-S-S), therapeutic forgiveness and the Five Roadblocks. Material repeats across volumes by design.

Ch 1. The Art of Overcoming Frustration

Argument: Frustration is a habit of self-relation, not an event, and it is broken by changing your opinion of yourself, not your circumstances. Psycho-Cybernetics means steering your mind to a productive, predetermined goal; it is a practice, not a reading ("positive doing").

Stories & evidence

  • The cleft-lip origin: as an intern Maltz delivered a baby with a cleft lip; the father fainted and Maltz felt responsible, pushing him toward plastic surgery.
  • The seventeen-year-old in Latin America: shouted "I'm going to die!" on the table; two weeks later, handed a mirror, he stared at a face he had never seen and cried "I'm going to live!" Maltz asks the reader whether they carry an emotional disfigurement and says to be your own plastic surgeon.
  • The concentration-camp survivor who had a tattooed number removed from her arm: do you have tattooed numbers on your mental arm?
  • The woman who said the book "didn't do anything for me" had only read it.
  • "Sally and the $30,000": happiness is not conditional on external windfalls.
  • Twelve Faces of Frustration (diagnostic checklist).

Key numbers: twelve faces; one goal a day within your capabilities.

So what: Run the Twelve Faces scan, name the one face you wear today, set one achievable goal, and remember frustration needs your consent.

Ch 2. Winging Away / The Road to Self-Respect

Argument: Frustration is kept alive by the Tomorrow Illusion and by misreading conscience (really the self-image punishing you). Forgiveness, treated as a procedure, dissolves both.

Stories & evidence

  • Conscience reinterpreted: against Shakespeare, "we make cowards of our conscience"; "I can't live with my conscience" means "I can't live with myself."
  • The mirror operation: a surgeon's routine (cap, gown, mask, gloves, incision) applied to the face of the mind: identify the scar, scrub in at the mirror, excise ("You're my friend. I like you."), close, post-op check.
  • The treasure story against himself: a rumor of a million dollars on the eighteenth floor of his building; Maltz found his butler on the terrace in a white coat with pick and shovel hacking at the rock garden. Everyone digs outside for treasure buried in the self-image.
  • The tennis doubles-partner image of self-criticism ("Let's play ball together").
  • Compliment people while they are alive, not at the funeral.

Key numbers: none stated; the "Mañana Incorporated" members get no dividends.

So what: Postpone only your resentment, never your goal. Stop criticizing yourself first (criticism of others stops as a side effect), and treat forgiveness as an operation, not a word.

Ch 3. Happiness and Unhappiness / Winning Out Over Crises

Argument: Happiness is a habit you install deliberately, and a crisis is survivable because you carry a built-in servo-mechanism ("your wonderful computer") that works if you stop jamming it with worry.

Stories & evidence

  • The ringing telephone: at a lecture a phone kept ringing; Maltz took the receiver off the hook. Remove the small aggravation before it recruits you into a big one.
  • The morning protocol: think kindly of yourself on waking, smile at the mirror, resolve to do your best, accept in advance that if you fail you try again tomorrow.
  • The wonderful computer: the goal-striving mechanism in the mid-brain, smaller than a hazelnut, which no committee of scientists could build.
  • Seven key characteristics of frustration (Fear, Aggressiveness, Insecurity, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness); resentment is "the gout of the mind."
  • The decompression chamber in the mind.

Key numbers: the free eight hours outside work and sleep; seven characteristics.

So what: Attach happiness to a fixed daily trigger (the mirror on waking), protect the free eight hours for activities you like, and build the decompression chamber before you need it.

Ch 4. On To Success!

Argument: Success is a growing self-image ("you cannot be a success unless you are a success to yourself"), and S-U-C-C-E-S-S is the repair checklist. Its mechanics: relax, one thing at a time, and let a Success Cycle run.

Stories & evidence

  • S-U-C-C-E-S-S: Sense of direction, Understanding, Courage, Compassion, Esteem, Self-acceptance, Self-confidence.
  • Twelve Faces of Success as the inverse of Ch 1's list.
  • The house-and-lawn analogy: you mow the lawn and paint the house but let weeds grow over the self-image.
  • The eighty-two-year-old in Maltz's Monterey workshop: "I'm eighty-two, and I'm practicing to be ninety."
  • The athlete who cannot win every day: reaching most of your goals makes you a champion in the art of living.
  • The "emotional sunglasses" worn even at the pillow.

Key numbers: seven ingredients, twelve faces, four principles of relaxation, four operating conditions.

So what: Define success internally, run the Four Principles of Relaxation (forgive others, forgive yourself, see yourself at your best, keep up with yourself), and treat one day's failure as no failure at all.

Ch 5. Self-Respect / Understanding / Sincerity

Argument: Self-respect is a need, assembled from understanding (that you have rights), sincerity (facing reality without evasion), and daily reaching for the best in yourself. It cannot be imported from others' opinions.

Stories & evidence

  • Goal Builder 2 (Understanding): walk a familiar street asking whether each person believes he has the right to be happy; some slouch and avert their eyes, others walk erect without swaggering; then write UNDERSTANDING on the mirror and say "Do I have rights? Yes. Yes, I do."
  • Funhouse mirrors: harmless as amusement, crippling as self-distortion.
  • Self-respect as savings: "even more basic than money."
  • Envy as the tell: admiration tainted by envy.

Key numbers: fourteen goal builders, one per week, six days on, one off.

So what: Generate self-respect internally and spend it outward; run one Goal Builder at a time; read envy as a low-self-respect signal.

Ch 6. Uncertainty / Resentment / Emptiness

Argument: Each enemy of self-respect is mechanically fixable: uncertainty yields to a goal, resentment to a rationally audited anxiety, emptiness to direction.

Stories & evidence

  • The circling airplane: a plane leaves New York, goes over Philadelphia, circles back, heads to Chicago, drifts toward Canada, circles back and never lands. That is a life with no sense of direction.
  • The anxiety audit (Goal Builder 5): list today's, last week's, last month's and last year's worries; Maltz predicts most were unrealistic.
  • Goal Builder 6 (Getting Rid of Emptiness): write a goal and test it: is it yours, does it mean something to you, can you achieve it, do you have a fighting chance?
  • Emptiness as a locked airport locker holding your integrity.
  • Five Ways to Vanquish Emptiness (stop sleepwalking, resign from Mañana Inc., renew direction, enrich self-image, orient outward).

Key numbers: five ways; Yesterday Tomorrow Complex of 60% yesterday and 20% tomorrow.

So what: Do not personalize uncertainty, spend anxiety before the decision and not after, and give yourself at least one goal that means something to you.

Ch 7. Opportunity / Real Forgiveness

Argument: Forgiveness is active, a daily all-out operation ("each day is D-day"), not a word you mumble; and opportunity is visible only to someone whose self-image hasn't already ruled them out.

Stories & evidence

  • The Philadelphia cab driver: his ex-wife phoned at 3 a.m. after twenty years of silence just to say hello; Maltz put away his lecture notes and spoke off the cuff. What you refuse to cancel does not decay, it waits.
  • Half-living: the middle-aged man who answers "I'm still alive; I get by."
  • Goal Builder 8 (Forgiveness): an arrow on the mirror, "From forgiveness to self-respect"; the torture-scene exercise ("Is this not equally horrifying?" about your own self-condemnation).
  • Grudges as history: Suspicion, Resentment and Greed joined forces to pin Forgiveness to the mat.

Key numbers: none stated.

So what: Forgive daily, include wrongs you only imagined, forgive yourself for specific items, and never renounce your self-image after a loss.

Ch 8. Mirror Watchers / Tear Down Those Prison Walls

Argument: The mirror works only in its creative form (looking behind the face at who you intend to become); misused it becomes narcissism or prosecution. Most confining walls are self-installed.

Stories & evidence

  • The friend test: compare your commentary on your reflection with your reaction when a friend enters your home; then picture a good friend's face and write FRIEND on the glass.
  • Goal Builder 10 (convicted-criminal caricature): a snarling prisoner who shakes the bars, beats his plate with a fork and attacks the kindly warden, so overdrawn that guilt obsession looks ludicrous. Footnote: inmates Maltz lectured include many with constructive attitudes who deserve compassion.
  • The maladjusted pigeon performing a response after its conditions have gone.
  • The woman who couldn't talk: inhibition presents as incapacity and dissolves when the self-image changes.
  • Cooking up failure as reverse rehearsal.

Key numbers: none stated.

So what: Look at yourself as at a friend, write then erase the word, and test each "wall" before accepting it.

Ch 9. Tranquility / The Active Life

Argument: Tranquility is won actively, by combat against twelve named forces; relaxation is the reward after goal-directed effort. Retirement from life is a ten-part mechanism with constructive alternatives.

Stories & evidence

  • TRANQUILITY acronym: Tension, Resistance, Arrogant aggressiveness, Negation, Quandary, Unbelief, Inferiority, Life of loneliness, Laissez-faire, Irritation, Trepidation, Yesterday Incorporated.
  • French Resistance analogy: dynamiting a munitions train is good; sabotaging your own worthwhile goals is the same skill on the wrong target.
  • Retirement Mechanism pairs: Retreat/Return, Eviction/Conviction, Withdraw/Courage to Act, Mañana/Today, Ennui/Emancipation, No direction/Goal Orientation, Traitor/Friend, and others.
  • Goal Builders 11 (Tranquility, soothing sounds) and 12 (No Retirement Clock, listening to a ticking clock).

Key numbers: twelve forces; ten retirement components.

So what: Schedule relaxation after a real go at your goals, attack manufactured tension (not unavoidable tension), and keep a goal every day however small.

Ch 10. Integrity / Survival / Goal Builders

Argument: Book Two closes with its payload: fourteen Goal Builders turn ideas into physical practice, and survival with self-respect means getting through a crisis without downgrading your opinion of yourself.

Stories & evidence

  • The program structure: one per week, six days on, one off; sequence from Self-Respect through Survival; each has seeing, mirror, spoken and erasure parts.
  • Goal Builder 14 (Survival): a speech to a stadium enlarged for 125,000 people, you forget your name, brush your teeth with soap, think of 250,000 eyes. Maltz: "Obviously, it's a caricature... this picture scares me, too."
  • The survival statement: "I will accept my fear. And my nervousness. And my panic."
  • Past successes as failure insurance: they displace nervousness now and ease acceptance of an actual failure.
  • Self-respect as a plant you keep watering as long as it lives.

Key numbers: 14 goal builders; 125,000 people; 250,000 eyes.

So what: Serialize the practice, speak the sentence to the mirror, simulate a crisis worse than yours to right-size it, and accept the fear explicitly.

Ch 11. Chief Purpose / Two Images / As a Man Thinks

Argument: Book Three is a 21-day program built on one definition (steering your mind to a predetermined goal) and one rule: you can only prove it by doing it. Chronic discontent is directional feedback.

Stories & evidence

  • The man at the airline counter who says "I don't know," or "a ticket to anywhere you choose."
  • The giant earth-moving machine: hands on the wheel or run into a ditch.
  • The two ocean liners: a crewed ship with a goal reaches port 9,999 times out of 10,000; one with no crew and no goal runs aground before clearing the harbor.
  • Divine Discontent: man is teleological and gets negative feedback when off heading.
  • The opening promise: "Now! You can teach yourself how to use Psycho-Cybernetics in 21 days!" with judgment handed to the reader.
  • "Avoid debating" and "Confusion is helpful."

Key numbers: 21 consecutive days; 9,999 of 10,000.

So what: Name the port before touching the wheel, commit to 21 days before judging, and run the method rather than debating it.

Ch 12. Self-Image / Perception / The Process of Thinking

Argument: The self-image is the ceiling on effectiveness; behavior, feelings and abilities are always consistent with it. You can change it by repainting the picture, without first improving yourself, and positive thinking incompatible with it will not work.

Stories & evidence

  • The circus elephant: chained as a calf to a stake, the grown elephant stays put though it could uproot a tree.
  • The pike and the minnows: after battering a glass partition the pike stops trying and starves once the glass is removed.
  • "PARIS IN THE / THE SPRING": most readers miss the doubled word, showing we see what we expect.
  • Effectiveness range: performance outside it produces tension and a pull back.
  • Observation, Retention, Selection as the creative-thinking sequence.

Key numbers: none stated.

So what: Work on the picture before the skill, read tension at the edge of performance as a boundary marker, and check whether the glass is still there.

Ch 13. The Quiet Place / Relaxation

Argument: Relaxation is learned and is the enabling condition for everything else; the core tool is a mental retreat built once and entered daily.

Stories & evidence

  • Marcus Aurelius on retreats: you can retire into yourself whenever you choose.
  • Truman's foxhole: "a foxhole in my mind where I allow nothing to bother me."
  • The construction protocol: a beach house on an uncharted Pacific island, a cloud, deep in the earth or a distant planet; total isolation and privacy; entry as quick as picturing the Golden Gate Bridge.
  • The daily statement read each day for 21 days.

Key numbers: at least once a day; 21 days for the recitation.

So what: Build the place before the crisis, keep it private, and enter it daily; your response, not events, sets your state.

Ch 14. Goals / Synthetic Experience / The Method

Argument: The nervous system cannot tell a vividly imagined experience from a real one, so you can manufacture success experience and reprogram the self-image. You supply the goal; the mechanism supplies the how.

Stories & evidence

  • The Method: ten minutes daily, eyes closed, one situation in sensory detail, as participant, "begin by knowing you have arrived," 21 consecutive days.
  • Synthetic experience requires Desire, Information, Repetition.
  • Nine affirmation rules and a Descriptive Statement checklist ("Is my goal high enough? Reach out!").
  • Controlled-attention drill: review the day in reverse as you fall asleep.
  • "Act the way you want to be (in your imagination), and you'll be the way you act."
  • The law works impersonally, like gravity.

Key numbers: 10 minutes; 21 consecutive days; nine rules.

So what: Think from the goal, not about it, avoid time limits on affirmations, and never micromanage the how.

Ch 15. Negative Feedback / Plan of Action / Tired People

Argument: Mistakes are steering corrections, never a STOP sign. Excess attention to the negative indicator, or to what others think, is the malfunction.

Stories & evidence

  • Three steps: be aware, evaluate the outcome as unwanted, correct at once.
  • The instrument panel: "When one of the panels lights up, no one becomes upset."
  • The tennis player and the net; the golfer and the water.
  • Three prohibitions with others: don't try to impress, don't act for effect, don't think about what they think.
  • Plan of Action (five parts) and Personal Balance Sheet (eleven headings plus six life areas).
  • Tired people: fatigue from unresolved negative feeling and goalless effort.

Key numbers: three steps; five-part plan.

So what: Glance at negatives, concentrate on positives, correct at once, and put deadlines on written plans, not on self-image work.

Ch 16. Happiness / Exercises and Techniques

Argument: Happiness is a cultivable habit of thinking, a by-product of striving for goals, and it is the way to stop being manipulated by circumstances. Book Three ends with concrete drills.

Stories & evidence

  • Dr. John A. Schindler's definition: "a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant a good share of the time."
  • Mirror Magic: morning breathing plus "Am I a friend to myself?", emptying the wastebaskets, closing the front door on yesterday, the red traffic light as fear of failure.
  • The daily 21-day recitation ("This is the beginning of a new day...") and "Just For Today" (twelve hours; "I am going to spend my time making things happen").
  • Emerson: "Do the thing, and you will have the power."

Key numbers: 21 days; six-day drills; twelve hours; "mark off 21 consecutive days."

So what: Attach drills to events that already happen, expect gray days, and don't wait for perfect conditions.

Ch 17. Theater of the Mind / Truth / The Power of Imagination

Argument: The origin story in full: correcting faces transformed some patients, but the exceptions taught Maltz that the operative image is inside. The subconscious is an impersonal servo-mechanism that becomes a success or failure mechanism depending on goals fed.

Stories & evidence

  • The successes: fearful people became bold, a mean adolescent won acceptance, a listless middle-aged man felt hope rise.
  • The woman with the cheek scar: mid-twenties, scar from a car accident; "I really don't see any improvement"; "It looks better, but I don't feel better." The real scar was an unhappy romance two years earlier.
  • The theater of the mind: you are producer, director, writer, actor, technician and audience.
  • The method actor playing a king and worry as imagination running backwards.
  • The movie queen standard that makes young girls certain they are ugly.

Key numbers: none beyond the two-year romance.

So what: Feed the mechanism goals rather than inferiority data, and use the imagination you already use for worry.

Ch 18. Relaxation / Why Not Be a Winner? / Habits

Argument: "Easy does it." Strain is the modern failure; relaxation is a precondition for success, blocked by refusing limitations and holding grudges.

Stories & evidence

  • The tense millionaire: mahogany dining room, drumming the table, gobbling food "as if his hands were two shovels," lighting and dropping a cigar, ending as "Mr. X."
  • You can't push yourself into sleep.
  • Franklin: "He that can take rest is greater than he that can take cities."
  • Kennedy at the podium as visible relaxation under high stakes.
  • Habits applied to drinking, weight, smoking, overwork and dress.
  • Three winning habits and dead aim on the target.

Key numbers: two roadblocks; three winning habits.

So what: Ask "what am I accomplishing at this pace?", forgive, and treat relaxation as a readout of the self-image.

Ch 19. Seven Rules for Happy Living / Cast Off Your Emotional Scars

Argument: Emotional scars are deeper than physical ones and keep generating new injury until you resolve to heal them; seven rules and four miracle drugs are the remedy.

Stories & evidence

  • The unfair firing: hired by a publishing company after clerical bank work, criticized by an impatient director, fired; Maltz's ruling is a few days of bitterness is fine, then forgive by considering the director's fear.
  • The wounded man who vows to refuse anyone any favor and takes it out on his sister, the postman, the cat.
  • The ointment of kindness applied gently.
  • Seven Rules (including learning to laugh and helping others) and Four Miracle Drugs.

Key numbers: seven rules; four drugs; "a few days" of resentment.

So what: Do not hold a grudge against yourself, and heal the scar rather than waiting for others to acknowledge it.

Ch 20. Masks / Sex and the Self-Image / Accept Your Weakness

Argument: Accepting weakness gives you a floor to stand on; masks and imported standards are attempts to stand on nothing, and self-punishment buys nothing.

Stories & evidence

  • "You turn a crisis into an opportunity, not an opportunity into a crisis."
  • The tough guy and the perfect woman as masks.
  • The homely boy who got the dance with the pretty girl: a self-image that permitted him to ask.
  • "You're as beautiful as you feel."
  • Be Yourself exercise: three description lists, a biography, and a written list of reasons change is impossible.

Key numbers: three lists.

So what: Be kind to yourself, treat the gap between self-description and perceived image as the size of your mask, and check which "impossibilities" are expired. (The skill notes the social framing of the sex chapter is dated.)

Ch 21. Individuality / Functioning Under Pressure / Winning Friends

Argument: People stay calm under pressure because their self-image holds up; friendship starts from being a friend to yourself.

Stories & evidence

  • Bing Crosby drops his script ten seconds before air and comes in on cue.
  • Whistler at West Point (1854): "Silicon is a gas"; later, "If silicon had been a gas, I would have been a general."
  • Overcoming stage fright: the actress is helped by the crisis protocol (goal, belief, triumphs, permit nerves, go) rather than reassurance.
  • Five Rules for Winning Friends.
  • Maltz's first patient as a turning point.

Key numbers: five rules.

So what: Intervene on the expectation of failure, not the fear symptom; talk to people, not at them.

Ch 22. Peace of Mind / You Can Live Fully At Any Age

Argument: Take a daily vacation in a pleasant mental room, delay your response to anger, and never retire from your self-image.

Stories & evidence

  • The pleasant room rebuilt from a childhood retreat, a working room for accepting insecurities and setting goals.
  • Daily vs annual vacation: workweeks fell from 60-80 hours in Maltz's youth to 35-40 and people are still tense.
  • The $180 dentist bill: the linoleum and TV are absorbed, then the bill triggers the count to twelve.
  • Maltz's own routine past sixty: alternating days of surgery and writing.
  • "Revitalizing cream" for the self-image.

Key numbers: count to 12; $180; 60-80 versus 35-40 hours.

So what: Know your over-reaction domains in advance and aim for control of action, not absence of feeling.

Ch 23. Daily Dozen / Rave Notices

Argument: Twelve concepts (the same as Book One's Faces of Success) are daily instruments; repetition crowds out failure pictures with success pictures.

Stories & evidence

  • Twelve items: Truth, Imagination, Relaxation, That Winning Feeling, Good Habits, The Aim of Happiness, Unmasking, Compassion, Accepting Your Weakness, Living with Your Mistakes, Being Yourself, Never Retiring.
  • Quotes: Shelley, Emerson ("Self-trust is the first secret of success"), Aristotle and Ovid on habits.
  • The grudge test: the act may be one you would have committed.
  • Kennedy, months dead, still vivid in the theater of the mind.
  • Rave notices: "You've re-written the script."

Key numbers: twelve items.

So what: Run the twelve as a daily pass, stoke the winning feeling, and remember habits can be changed with work.

Ch 24. Thoughts To Live By

Argument: Book Five distills the system into two acronyms, defines forgiveness as cancelling an invalid debt, and diagnoses frustration through five roadblocks.

Stories & evidence

  • F-A-I-L-U-R-E and S-U-C-C-E-S-S, with Schopenhauer on compassion and a Shaw adaptation on keeping the self-image "clean and bright."
  • Therapeutic forgiveness: "As long as we condemn another, we can feel superior to him"; the surgical standard of no halfway measures.
  • The hurdler who became a salesman: broke his leg at a reunion, thought in the cast, returned with the tenacity that made him a champion, and became top-flight in a year.
  • Maltz's own failure: failed organic chemistry as a Columbia premed, retook it over the summer and earned an A.
  • Casals at ninety-three: "Every day I am reborn."
  • The Daily Requirements of Man (a second twelve).

Key numbers: 60% yesterday and 20% tomorrow; 1,440 minutes in a day; five roadblocks; an A.

So what: Cancel the debt with no reservations, sleep on a problem rather than with it, and remember that fearing mistakes is the greatest failure.

Recurring Stories to Remember

  • The woman with the cheek scar (Ch 17, with echoes in 1 and 19): "It looks better, but I don't feel better."
  • Maltz's cleft-lip origin and the seventeen-year-old (Ch 1, 17): the mirror, "I'm going to live!"
  • The mirror word (Ch 2, 5-10, 16): write it, say it, erase it; keep the feeling.
  • The pike and the elephant (Ch 12, 20): expired constraints still obeyed.
  • The tense millionaire (Ch 18): wealth without relaxation.
  • Goal Builder 14's stadium and the actress's stage fright (Ch 10, 21): accept the nervousness, recall triumphs.
  • Facial surgery as the standard for forgiveness (Ch 2, 24): no partial measures.
  • Truman's foxhole and the daily vacation (Ch 13, 22): private retreats.

The Genius Myth: A Curious History of a Dangerous Idea

2 markdown files

Quiz

The Genius Myth Quiz Book

The Genius Myth: A Curious History of a Dangerous Idea by Helen Lewis

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. The book has an introduction and 19 chapters, so chapters are grouped two or three to a section, each with short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative final exam is at the end. Built from the notes in the lewis-genius-myth skill, not the book's own wording.

Section 1: Introduction, Ch 1 (Avonian Willy) and Ch 2 (Secular Saints)

Q1 (SA). What is Lewis's core distinction about genius?

A: Grant acts of genius, but reject a class of geniuses. Individuals do extraordinary things, but that doesn't make them a superior sort of human ("Special People" is the book's alternative title).

Q2 (SA). What is the "had to was" shift in the word "genius"?

A: Greek and Roman genius was a visiting spirit or guardian, something you had. The Renaissance "great men" and then the Romantics made it something you were. That switch enables the "special people" idea and sets up disappointment when the person turns out to be deplorable.

Q3 (MC). In the Berners-Lee vs. Musk test, fame tracks:

a) the size of the contribution b) performing the cultural role of genius (provocative statements, extreme work habits, unusual personal life, self-mythologizing) c) IQ d) number of patents

A: b. The more original inventor is less famous because he doesn't perform the role.

Q4 (SA). Name the four stages of the Shakespeare pipeline in Ch 1, with one detail for each.

A: Preservation (the First Folio, assembled by two actor-friends seven years after his death; without it eighteen plays, including Macbeth and The Tempest, vanish). Popularization (Restoration impresarios like Davenant rewrote freely: flying witches, a happy-ending Lear). Canonization (Garrick's 1769 Stratford Jubilee: odes, mulberry-tree relics, zero performances of the plays; bardolatry is born). Monetization/nationalization (Shakespeare as the argument for English pre-eminence, an imperial export, a tourist asset).

Q5 (T/F). Lewis argues that reverent treatment is what keeps a great work alive. A: False. Irreverent reuse, not reverence, kept Shakespeare alive. Kid-glove treatment can kill a living tradition.

Q6 (SA). What is Vasari's method, and what are two of the archetypes it fixed?

A: Biography as fable: a whole life honed to a few details that illustrate a moral. Archetypes include the art monk (Michelangelo), the scatter-brained polymath (Leonardo), the prodigy who corrects the master, and the arrogant visionary vindicated (Brunelleschi and the egg).

Q7 (SA). What does the Gauss test (Brian Hayes) teach, and what is the invariant in the story?

A: Source the anecdote. The schoolboy 1-to-100 story doesn't appear until 1856, gains the arithmetic series in 1938, and evolves toward narrative fitness (whips dropped as readers got squeamish). The invariant is the prodigy, marked from childhood, whose gift is indistinguishable from magic.

Section 2: Ch 3 (Galton's Good Breeding) and Ch 4 (Terman's Termites)

Q1 (SA). Describe Galton's method in Hereditary Genius (1869) and its fatal flaw.

A: He listed eminent men, counted eminent relatives, and concluded ability is inherited. The flaw is the nepotism confound: he could not separate inherited talent from inherited resources, connections, and opportunity.

Q2 (SA). What is the Austen Problem?

A: Eminence-based selection (for example, sourcing from a biographical dictionary and cutting short entries, as Havelock Ellis described) loses Jane Austen. A genius needs a story as well as achievements; uneventful excellence fails the filter.

Q3 (T/F). Gauss supports Galton's thesis, since Galton's statistics depend on him. A: False. Gauss's family tree gave no hint of genius and his brother was a laborer, so he is a counter-example to Galton's thesis.

Q4 (MC). IQ testing was originally invented by Binet to:

a) rank humanity b) find children who needed help c) select future leaders d) support immigration limits

A: b. Binet feared "brutal pessimism" about fixed intelligence. Goddard brought the tests to America and used them for classification.

Q5 (SA). What was the result of Terman's Study of the Gifted?

A: About 1,500 high-IQ Californian children tracked for life. They were physically healthier than average, 90% college-bound, with 1,500 papers and 100+ patents, but produced no genius by Galton's standard: eminent, not illustrious. Terman himself admitted in 1947 that America hadn't produced a Shakespeare or Newton.

Q6 (SA). Which two future Nobel laureates did Terman's team reject, and why does it matter?

A: William Shockley and Luis Alvarez (both physics Nobels) were excluded for scoring too low. It shows childhood IQ tests can't identify genius.

Q7 (SA). What is the Flynn Effect, and what is its lesson?

A: IQ scores rose about 3.3 points per decade across the 20th century (a 1900s child answers "dogs hunt rabbits," a modern one "both are mammals": schooling in abstraction, not smarter brains). Be very cautious comparing groups or eras.

Section 3: Ch 5 (Cyril and Hans) and Ch 6 (Shockley and the Genius Sperm Bank)

Q1 (SA). What was the "too-perfect correlation" tell in Burt's data?

A: His twin IQ correlations (0.944 reared together, 0.771 apart) stayed identical to three decimals while his sample grew from 21 to 53 pairs. Invariant statistics across changing samples signal fabrication.

Q2 (SA). What is the "genius exemption," and why is it circular?

A: Eysenck's defense of Burt: geniuses may fudge figures to confound "vulgar mediocrities." If the result is wrong, then he wasn't a genius, so the defense is circular and disqualifying.

Q3 (T/F). Lewis concludes that heritability of intelligence is a myth. A: False. Following Harden's middle ground, intelligence is partly heritable and IQ predicts educational and career outcomes. The myth is treating the number as an inerrant ranking of human worth.

Q4 (SA). What does "scenius" mean, and what is Paul Graham's Leonardo example?

A: Collective genius of a place and time. "To make Leonardo you need more than innate ability; you also need Florence in 1450." Milan, same size and 300 km away, produced no Leonardo. Shockley's Florences were California, Caltech during the quantum revolution, and Bell Labs.

Q5 (MC). How did Shockley become "the father of the transistor"?

a) he built the point-contact device b) Brattain and Bardeen built it; Shockley, excluded from the patent, threatened revolt, was put at the center of publicity, answered the press, and wrote the textbook c) he won a patent lawsuit d) Bell Labs named him

A: b.

Q6 (SA). What is the "omni-expertise cascade," and what is Lewis's advice for rebutting a figure like Shockley?

A: A Nobelist in one field is treated as authority in another (a physicist at a genetics conference), escalating extremity under backlash, "just asking questions," spurious precision. Refute him as wrong, not evil: moral condemnation alone hands him a martyr's costume.

Q7 (SA). What did the Repository for Germinal Choice show, and what did Doron Blake conclude?

A: Robert Graham's "Nobel" sperm bank was branded falsely: Shockley was the only laureate to admit donating, and no laureate donations produced a child. Doron Blake (IQ 180, magazine covers, bullied) concluded, "I don't think you can breed for good people."

Section 4: Ch 7 (Marilyn and Me) and Ch 8 (So You Want to Be a Genius?)

Q1 (SA). How does Marilyn vos Savant illustrate "genius as self-fulfilling prophecy"?

A: Her childhood score sat unnoticed for thirty years; once Guinness printed it, attention produced more attention ("Ask Marilyn," books, public opinions on everything). Nothing about her changed; her life did.

Q2 (SA). What are galaxy-brainedness and the high-IQ society pathology?

A: Galaxy-brainedness is the willingness to hold opinions on everything (Jarvik calling relativity, the Big Bang, and black holes wrong). High-IQ societies (Mensa, Mega, Triple Nine) suffer constant schisms and lawsuits, showing a big number doesn't confer judgment or humility.

Q3 (MC). What do IQ tests mainly select for, per Lewis after sitting the Mensa test?

a) persistence b) speed c) creativity d) self-marketing

A: b. Not measured: showing up daily, the ego to insist you're right, and the ability to market yourself as the spirit of the age.

Q4 (SA). Explain the Potus problem.

A: Great discoveries create the conditions for their own under-appreciation. The West Wing made "POTUS" ordinary; Shakespeare's psychological complexity is now every drama's baseline; zero once took centuries and now a child grasps it.

Q5 (SA). What is the multiple problem, and what is its number?

A: Ogburn and Thomas (1922) documented 148 cases of simultaneous independent invention. Inventions become inevitable once preconditions exist, but we remember one name: the one who claimed credit harder, filed first, or self-mythologized.

Q6 (SA). What is the Matthew Effect, and what is the "forty-first seat"?

A: Merton: to those who have, more is given; recognition converts into labs, grants, first-author credit, and press. The forty-first seat is the Académie française seat the illustrious never got (Descartes, Pascal, Molière, Rousseau, Diderot, Flaubert, Zola, Proust all missed it).

Q7 (T/F). In Lewis's account, Fleming's discovery of penicillin involved no luck in his career choices. A: False. He chose medicine because of his brother, St Mary's because of water polo, and bacteriology to stay in the rifle club; the mould story also omits the assistant who connected it to an earlier experiment.

Section 5: Ch 9 (The Rebel) and Ch 10 (Monsters and Tortured Artists)

Q1 (SA). What is the Galileo syndrome (Galileo gambit)?

A: Taking opposition as evidence of insight: "if everyone says I'm wrong, I must be right." Lewis's line: "You're probably not Galileo."

Q2 (MC). The "hoofbeats to horses" heuristic says:

a) heretics are usually right b) assume the mainstream/obvious explanation while staying open c) never trust experts d) zebras are common

A: b.

Q3 (T/F). Galileo was martyred and died in disgrace for his telescope. A: False. He sought papal permission, died in his bed, and was above all a superb lens-maker (3x to 8x to 15x to 20x magnification), also an empiricist, self-publicist, and politician. "Eppur si muove" first appears in 1757, a century after the trial.

Q4 (SA). What is the Semmelweis reflex, and why is it a problem for the myth?

A: Authorities' knee-jerk rejection of challenges (handwashing rejected; he died in an asylum). It is real but rare, and it is the exception that makes the myth. Most "they laughed at him" stories (Edison's phonograph was an instant hit; Columbus didn't prove the earth round) are false.

Q5 (SA). What does "benefit of clergy" mean in Orwell's use, and what is the propaganda test?

A: The medieval exemption of clerics from civil courts, transferred to artists: being an artist is no excuse for abuse. Propaganda test: separation of art and artist is impossible when the art is propaganda for the crime (Polanski's "celebrations of sexual sadism"; Goode's plays).

Q6 (SA). What does Simon Stephens's "contradiction, not causality" mean?

A: The gift did not cause the crime; they coexist. Alcoholics who make great art don't make it because of alcoholism. Goode was a criminal and a kind mentor, an abuser and a maker of good art. "The cult of the individual is a lie... we are dividuals."

Q7 (SA). How did the "special person" aura work in the Chris Goode case?

A: It stifled doubt: critics who feared being philistines praised work they found "boring... or theatrically unfruitful," objections were read as pathology, queerness and left politics served as a shield, and an all-male, largely unpaid ensemble was recruited with nudity and sexual contact written into the advert. Afterward he was erased from the internet rather than reckoned with.

Section 6: Ch 11 (Great Wives) and Ch 12 (Keepers of the Flame)

Q1 (SA). What did Sofia Tolstaya do for Tolstoy?

A: Married at 18 to a 34-year-old, she had sixteen pregnancies, copied War and Peace seven times, edited, kept diaries he mined, supplied material, and kept working in bed after childbirth.

Q2 (SA). What is the "reader thesis" (A. N. Wilson)?

A: What bound the Tolstoys was that she was his reader; the marriage broke when a rival reader, the disciple Chertkov, replaced her. Swap Sofia for Chertkov and you swap Anna Karenina for unreadable tracts.

Q3 (SA). What is the Wife Glitch, and what is "Yoko-ing"?

A: Schaffer's Wife Glitch: someone who anticipates needs, orders the home, tends raw emotion, and fills weaknesses with her strength, "and means it." Yoko-ing is blaming the wife for the decline she was holding back.

Q4 (T/F). Einstein's first wife Mileva Marić was a fellow physics student and early sparring partner. A: True. The notes describe his contract for her (laundry kept, meals in his room, stop talking when told), after which she was replaced and the "Einstein priests" wrote her out.

Q5 (SA). How did Life magazine and Lee Krasner shape Pollock's legacy?

A: Life's 1949 "Is he the greatest living painter?" and the 1951 "Irascibles" photo created abstract expressionism as a movement (excluding Krasner). As widow she sold one or two Pollocks a year, preferably to museums, and almost single-handedly forced up prices ($2M for Blue Poles in 1973; $140M for No. 5 decades later).

Q6 (SA). What was Jo van Gogh-Bonger's playbook?

A: Widowed at about 29 with a baby, she (1) hung the work where people live, (2) paired paintings with letters so the life sold the art, (3) converted a hostile critic, (4) organized a 484-work show in 1905, (5) bought back Starry Night because "uncomfortable is good," and (6) kept family on the board (three descendants sit on the museum board). Her diary was withheld until 2009.

Q7 (MC). Which of these is NOT given as a keeper's tool in Ch 12?

a) sanitizing (Burns) b) copyright control (Beckett's estate forbidding women in male roles) c) rationing access to papers d) public auditing of estates

A: d.

Section 7: Ch 13 (A Cover Version) and Ch 14 (Alchemy)

Q1 (SA). What is the shared premise of Yesterday and Cover Version, and how do they differ?

A: A man is the only person who remembers the Beatles. Yesterday (Curtis): great talent cannot be repressed. Cover Version (Barth): the songs alone don't land without the personalities, era, manager, producer, and luck.

Q2 (SA). Which two figures does Lewis say Yesterday omits, and why does it matter?

A: George Martin (producer) and Brian Epstein (committed manager). The film's manager is a cynical shark who could have made the star anyway, an insult to Epstein's integrity.

Q3 (SA). What is the counterfactual test, in one question?

A: "Would I buy this from a stranger?" Value the work, not the name. Think of a hit as work x persona x moment x sponsor x luck.

Q4 (T/F). The Decca rejection proves the Beatles were an unrecognized revolution. A: False in Lewis's account. The audition setlist was mostly covers plus three forgettable originals, and George Martin heard potential, not a revolution.

Q5 (SA). Give two near-misses from Craig Brown's account of the Beatles.

A: (any two) Paul's parents met because bombers flew on one night and not the next; Ringo nearly died of peritonitis; Paul failed Spanish and stayed down a year, meeting George; they dodged conscription; they found Epstein as they considered quitting; Ringo nearly emigrated but the forms were too many.

Q6 (SA). Distinguish conceptual and experimental innovators (Galenson). Who is an example of each?

A: Conceptual: big-idea makers who peak early and are most often called geniuses (Picasso). Experimental: slow refiners over decades (Cezanne). Culture glorifies the conceptual because it explains why we aren't geniuses.

Q7 (SA). According to Simonton, when should a genius die for the myth, and how did the Beatles fit?

A: Young (Mozart) or very old (Goethe), never at sixty. The Beatles ended at their peak (George was 27) and refused to reform; Lennon was murdered in 1980 and sainted; McCartney lived long enough to become patriarch and manager of the catalogue.

Section 8: Ch 15 (The Deficit Model) and Ch 16 (Disruptors)

Q1 (SA). What is the deficit model?

A: The idea that genius extorts a price: for every credit a debit, with oddness as the currency (Beethoven deaf, Milton blind, Mozart a child who couldn't handle adulthood). The flaw makes the gift feel earned.

Q2 (SA). Name the three biopic tropes Lewis identifies.

A: Inspiration as a blinding flash, genius as an unworldly being, and suffering as payment. Also: the lone rebel against an uncaring regime, and the great man as the sun with everyone orbiting.

Q3 (SA). What is the Hawking timeline test?

A: Ask whether the suffering precedes or follows the work. Hawking did his best work before his deterioration, so the link between illness and insight is narrative, not causal.

Q4 (SA). What is the "shadow film" The Laws of Madness and what does it teach?

A: Michael Laudor (schizophrenia, Yale Law Review editor) got a 1995 NYT profile hitting every deficit beat, a $600K+ memoir deal and $1.5M film rights. Off his medication, he killed his girlfriend, believing her an impostor. Intelligence did not save him, though the myth said it could. It is the corrective to A Beautiful Mind.

Q5 (T/F). Silicon Valley's success was built largely without public institutions. A: False. Its scenius rested on no non-competes in California, Stanford, and Department of Defense funding (GPS via Naval Research; the internet via DARPA). It was publicly nurtured and privately mythologized.

Q6 (MC). Disruption theory (Christensen), as Lewis critiques it, ignores:

a) cheap rivals b) lobbying, shaping of laws, weak antitrust, and giants buying rivals (Facebook bought about thirty companies in two years) c) venture capital d) customers

A: b.

Q7 (SA). What is the "genius asshole" archetype?

A: Jobs as the "Genius Entrepreneur," who convinced everyone that the assholery was indivisible from the genius (Wozniak: a nicer Apple "may never have made the Macintosh"). Lewis treats it as a story the geniuses tell about themselves, an empirical claim nobody has tested.

Section 9: Ch 17 (Thomas Edison) and Ch 18 (Elon Musk)

Q1 (SA). What did Lewis identify as Edison's real conceptual breakthrough, and how did it arise?

A: The phonograph (1877), an accidental byproduct while the lab was hunting telephone diaphragms; a finger on a vibrating membrane suggested a stylus and a record.

Q2 (SA). How was the lightbulb "de-mythed"?

A: Incandescence (Davy, 1802-09), a carbon rod in vacuum (Jobard, 1838), and a working prototype (Swan, 1860) preceded him. Edison's problem was not conceptual: a better vacuum (Sprengel pump), a longer filament (Batchelor's carbonised thread: 40 hours), and reliable supply. The grid was his most underrated innovation.

Q3 (SA). What was the "access-for-hype machine"?

A: Favoured reporters got exclusives; Edison mentioned imminent breakthroughs; reporters got a story, Edison got publicity. One Herald writer received eight shares in Edison Electric. A genius created by an admiring group with a commercial interest in his veneration.

Q4 (SA). What are Mac and Conger's "three problems," and what is the lesson?

A: SpaceX was a physics problem, Tesla a manufacturing problem, Twitter a social and psychological one. Genius is not a transferable skill.

Q5 (SA). What numbers and facts illustrate the Twitter outcome and the taxpayer scaffolding under Musk's firms?

A: Fidelity marked the $44B purchase down 71% to about $10B. SpaceX was rescued by a $1.6B NASA contract (Dec 2008) and Tesla buyers got $7,500 credits.

Q6 (SA). Who was Mary Beth Brown, and what does "MB" stand for in Lewis's argument?

A: Musk's assistant for twelve years, the "only bridge" between him and his interests, let go in 2014 reportedly after asking for executive-level pay (Musk disputes). "MB" stands for all the support structure ("the rest of us") that moderates a genius; shedding her and the grown-ups preceded the Twitter chaos.

Q7 (T/F). Lewis says Musk has shown no acts of genius at all. A: False. Reusable rockets (and making EVs desirable) are acts of genius; the problem is his becoming a special person, an omni-expert radicalized by his own platform. It is both/and, not either/or.

Section 10: Ch 19 (Conclusion: An Idea That Won't Stay Dead)

Q1 (SA). What is the secularization arc (Fara)?

A: Greek/Roman possession, then the Romantic secular saint, then the Victorian number, then today's granular data; each an attempt to pin down genius's random, unpredictable nature.

Q2 (SA). List the four functions of the myth in Lewis's functional account.

A: (1) A mechanism for letting the weird prosper; (2) a mechanism for managing envy (we're just Gauss's classmates); (3) a way to reconcile ourselves to monstrosity paired with achievement; (4) sneaking admiration for the one who gets away with it.

Q3 (SA). What are the "two wastes" (Gould, Spencer)?

A: Some talents are scorched by indulgence; far more are extinguished for lack of support (cotton fields, sweatshops, marriage bars, segregation). "Before he can remake his society, his society must make him."

Q4 (SA). Why does Lewis think AI doesn't remove the need for genius myths?

A: LLMs are prediction machines lacking originality; great works are unpredictable, wrong by the previous rules. Substitute ChatGPT for Dostoevsky "and the magic is gone." We need myths, and myths need people.

Q5 (SA). State Lewis's prescription.

A: Attach "genius" to acts and works, not persons (the painting, the transistor, War and Peace, not Shockley or Tolstoy). Celebrate talent, be humble about where it's found and whether it's recognized, and nurture as many seeds as we can.

Q6 (T/F). Lewis advises debunking the myth entirely and denying talent and achievement. A: False. She warns against "debunking into nihilism" and notes the myth is load-bearing: remove it only if you replace its functions.

Cumulative Final Exam

  1. State Lewis's thesis in one sentence and explain "had to was."

A: Grant acts of genius, deny the class. Genius shifted from something you had (a visiting spirit) to something you are, which creates "Special People" who get latitude nobody else gets.

  1. Run the six-step "distortion audit" on any famous figure. Name the steps.

A: Potus (what did the world lack before them?); multiples (who else got there?); adjacent possible (which components had just arrived?); Matthew Effect (how did recognition compound, who got the forty-first seat?); weirdness (which eccentricities were folded into the legend?); luck (which trivial decisions routed them here?).

  1. What did Terman's study, Burt's data, and the Mensa-type societies each show about IQ and genius?

A: Terman: high childhood IQ predicts a good life, not genius (missed Shockley and Alvarez). Burt: identical correlations across changed samples signal fraud, and the "genius exemption" defended it. High-IQ societies: schisms show a number confers no judgment or works of genius.

  1. How did Galton, Shockley, and Musk each end up in "Galton's territory"?

A: Galton founded eugenics from the idea of inherited, countable genius; Shockley became an omni-expert eugenicist and donated to the genius sperm bank; Musk's myth led him to population collapse, "woke mind virus," and IQ/breeding talk. The notes say the myth "ends where it began: Galton."

  1. Explain scenius with two examples from the book and what the myth leaves out.

A: Florence in 1450 (Leonardo); Shockley's Caltech and Bell Labs; Silicon Valley (Stanford, DARPA, no non-competes). The myth credits only the individual and omits place, time, identity, and public funding.
