  1. Why is "they all laughed at him" suspect, and what test should you apply when you feel like Galileo?

A: Most such stories are false (Edison's phonograph was an instant hit; Columbus didn't prove the earth round) and Semmelweis is the rare exception that fuels the myth. Hoofbeats to horses: assume the obvious, stay open, and set an update trigger before the evidence arrives; you're probably not Galileo.

  1. What do the great-wife, widow, and Beatles-support chapters share?

A: Genius runs on invisible others: Sofia Tolstaya (reader, copyist, editor), Krasner and Jo van Gogh-Bonger (legacy managers), George Martin and Brian Epstein (producer and manager). Ask "who cooked the dinner?" and who holds the papers.

  1. What are the propaganda test and the Hawking test for?

A: Propaganda test: whether art and artist can be separated (not if the art argues for the perpetrator's perversion). Hawking test: whether suffering preceded or followed the work, to check whether a suffering-insight link is narrative.

  1. Compare Edison and Musk using three shared features.

A: (any three) a media-built myth (reporters with equity; fans and platform); conceptual early peak followed by calcification or omni-opinion ("the Edison horizon"); "hardcore" long-hours culture; reliance on hidden support (teams, the grid, NASA contracts, an MB); playing the genius in public ("they want it").

  1. Applied task: Pick a living "genius" in the news. Run the distortion audit and the three-problems test, list who cooked the dinner, and write one sentence that attaches "genius" to an act rather than the person.

Arguments & Evidence

The Genius Myth: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Helen Lewis

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the chapter files in the lewis-genius-myth skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Lewis's thesis is to grant acts of genius but deny a class of geniuses. The Introduction and Ch 1-2 show that "genius" is a manufactured status: Shakespeare, Vasari's fables, and the Romantics built the templates. Ch 3-7 follow the attempt to turn genius into a measurable, inherited quantity (Galton, Terman, Burt, Eysenck, Shockley, vos Savant), which led to eugenics, fraud, and sperm banks. Ch 8 lists the distortions that really decide who gets the label. Ch 9-12 take apart the seductive myths: the lone rebel, the licence for monsters, the invisible great wife, and the estates that manage reputations after death. Ch 13-15 use the Beatles and biopics to show luck, co-authors, and the deficit model. Ch 16-18 bring it to Silicon Valley, Edison, and Musk, and Ch 19 explains why the myth persists and prescribes attaching "genius" to works, not persons.

Introduction: The Genius Myth

Argument: "Genius" is not an objective category but a myth-making process: societies anoint exceptional people to display what they value, then grant those "special people" latitude denied to everyone else. Acts of genius are real; a class of geniuses is not.

Stories & evidence

  • Had to was: Greek/Roman genius was a visiting spirit or guardian (daimonion, furor divinus); the Renaissance and the Romantics made it an identity.
  • The Musk referendum: arguing whether Musk is a genius is really arguing about what society values and tolerates; the right exaggerates, the left denigrates.
  • Berners-Lee vs. Musk test: the more original inventor is less famous because he doesn't perform the role of genius.
  • Eysenck's tell: posterity is likelier to call you a genius if you behave oddly, die young or very old, or disregard normal restrictions.
  • Story requirement: a person becomes a "genius" only when a story is woven around them.

Key numbers: none stated.

So what: Ask who tells the story and why. The label converts taste into pseudo-fact and eccentricity into entitlement.

Ch 1. Avonian Willy

Argument: Even the most deserving genius needed people who worked to make him one. Reputation is manufactured and monetized.

Stories & evidence

  • First Folio: two actor-friends assembled it seven years after Shakespeare's death; without it eighteen plays (including Macbeth and The Tempest) vanish.
  • Restoration rewrites (Davenant): flying witches, a happy-ending Lear, ballet in The Tempest. Irreverence kept the work alive.
  • Garrick's 1769 Stratford Jubilee: odes to "Avonian Willy," mulberry-tree relics, no performances of the plays; bardolatry is born. Macklin called Garrick's cult a "golden calf."
  • Biographical vacuum: a 40-page life written a century later; the vacuum fills with conspiracy (Oxford, Bacon, "a woman") or relic-worship.
  • Estates as brands: Einstein's "priests" hid his first child until 1986; the university licensing his image has earned about $250M; Picasso's name on a Citroen; "Genius Bar," Genius.com, "Genius" pills.

Key numbers: 7 years (Folio after death); 18 plays at risk; 1769; about $250M (Einstein image licensing); 1986.

So what: Find the preservers (Heminges and Condell) and marketer (Garrick) in any canon. When the toothpicks outnumber the performances, canonization has become commerce.

Ch 2. Secular Saints

Argument: Vasari's Lives turned artist biography into fable and planted templates we still use; the Romantics then added nature, madness, illness, and moral exemption.

Stories & evidence

  • Vasari's archetypes: the art monk (Michelangelo, boots fused to his skin), the scatter-brained polymath (Leonardo), the prodigy who corrects the master, and the arrogant visionary vindicated (Brunelleschi and the egg).
  • Story-fitness selection: Artemisia Gentileschi's rape-and-revenge legend is remembered; Sofonisba Anguissola, court painter to Philip II who died at 93, is not.
  • Gauss test (Hayes): the schoolboy story first appears in 1856, gets the arithmetic series in 1938, goes viral with E. T. Bell's gothic version, and drops the whips as readers get squeamish.
  • Romantic additions: Rousseau's Emile; Kant's "nature's elect"; Byron ("we of the craft are all crazy"; the incest scandal absorbed into legend); tuberculosis as the genius's disease; Weininger's suicide in Beethoven's death-room.
  • Walden debate: Thoreau's laundry; the premise that the genius must return to nature is itself the myth.

Key numbers: 1856 and 1938 (Gauss versions).

So what: Treat every anecdote as a fable: find the earliest source, what was added, what vanished, and the invariant. Prodigy stories discourage the rest of us as "the less distinguished classmates."

Ch 3. Galton's Good Breeding

Argument: Galton replaced the Romantic lightning strike with genius as rare, innate, inherited, and measurable, founding both modern statistics and eugenics. His method confused reputation with ability and couldn't separate genetics from nepotism.

Stories & evidence

  • **Hereditary Genius (1869):** list eminent men, count eminent relatives, conclude ability is inherited. Eminent: 1 in 4,000; illustrious: 1 in a million.
  • Nepotism confound: Merivale on the Atkyns judges ("a snug little party of jobbers"). Galton's nephews-vs-sons control was admitted to be beyond him.
  • Environment omitted: de Candolle's 18 factors (rickets, lead, sex bars, religious exclusion, serial pregnancy, colour bars, independent wealth...).
  • Gauss counter-example: Galton's statistics depend on Gauss, whose family gave no hint of genius; Gauss praised Sophie Germain's "superior genius" for overcoming obstacles.
  • Carlyle's Great Man theory: history as the biography of great men, written defensively against an age that "accounts for" heroes.
  • Havelock Ellis and the Austen Problem: cut short entries from a biographical dictionary and you lose Jane Austen.
  • **Kantsaywhere:** Galton's utopia of breeding licences and labour colonies; Pearson and Fisher held the Galton chair, with buildings renamed in 2020.

Key numbers: 1 in 4,000 eminent; 1 in a million illustrious; 95% "mediocre"; 18 factors.

So what: Before accepting "talent runs in families," control for nepotism and access. Check whether your selection method rewards drama over quality.

Ch 4. Terman's Termites

Argument: IQ testing was invented to help struggling children and hijacked to rank humanity. Terman's study of high-IQ children produced eminent but not illustrious adults, rejected two future Nobelists, and showed childhood tests can't find genius, though the label bent the children's lives.

Stories & evidence

  • Binet vs. the single number: Binet feared "brutal pessimism"; Simon called Stern's single mental age a betrayal.
  • Flynn Effect: a 1900s child says "dogs hunt rabbits," a modern one "both are mammals."
  • Goddard: moron/imbecile/idiot bands; the debunked Kallikak study; legacy in the 1924 Immigration Act, Buck v. Bell (1927), and Nazi sterilization laws.
  • Terman's study (1921-): healthier than average, 90% college-bound, 1,500 papers, 100+ patents, no genius. Terman's 1947 admission: no Shakespeare or Newton since Jamestown.
  • Shockley and Alvarez both rejected as boys, both later won physics Nobels.
  • Thumb on the scale: teacher nominations skewed to confident, eloquent boys; poor and minority schools under-sampled; "royal jelly" label.
  • Cox Miles' ruler method: IQs for the dead from encyclopedia entry length (Goethe 210, Newton 190, Cervantes and Copernicus 105, Shakespeare absent).
  • Worked cases: Jess Oppenheimer (I Love Lucy) logged as conceited with no sense of humour; "Sara Ann," a physics graduate who never worked as one.

Key numbers: about 1,500 children; IQ 140 then 135; about 3.3 points per decade (Flynn); 1921; 90% college-bound; 100+ patents.

So what: Precocity is not adult originality. "Gifted" predicts comfortable eminence, not breakthrough, and labelling a child is an intervention.

Ch 5. Cyril and Hans: Twin Flames

Argument: Burt and his pupil Eysenck produced falsified or "unsafe" data in service of hereditarian views and were protected for decades by the mythology that a genius may bend the rules.

Stories & evidence

  • Too-perfect correlation: Burt's twin correlations (0.944 together, 0.771 apart) unchanged to three decimals while his sample grew from 21 to 53 pairs.
  • Phantom collaborators: "Miss Howard" and "Miss Conway" published only in Burt's own journal while he edited it; over half its forty contributors appear to be Burt pseudonyms.
  • Genius exemption: Eysenck's defense that geniuses may fudge figures; if wrong, he wasn't a genius. Hearnshaw's "justifiable prerogative of a great man" reappears as Corr's "Sometimes you need a pariah."
  • Eysenck's ecosystem: tobacco funding (GBP 800,000), cancer-prone personality, astrology, gout as a genius correlate (rich middle-aged men both eat richly and have careers).
  • Pelosi's 30-year pursuit: 1992 BMJ article softened; a 2019 open letter listing 61 papers; King's College judged 26 co-authored papers "unsafe."
  • Eleven-plus: Burt's political legacy of selection that stratifies by class.
  • Harden's middle ground: intelligence is partly heritable; ranking worth by it is the error.

Key numbers: 0.944 and 0.771; 21 to 53 pairs; twenty coincidences; GBP 800,000; 61 papers; 26 papers; 30 years.

So what: Unchanging decimals are fingerprints of fraud. Spot the defender's script, not just the man. Institutions protect stars; correction lags stature by decades and comes from outsiders.

Ch 6. William Shockley and the Genius Sperm Bank

Argument: Rejected from Terman's study, Shockley won a Nobel through scenius, then believed his own genius label, strayed into eugenics as an omni-expert, alienated everyone, and ended as a footnote.

Stories & evidence

  • Scenius: Paul Graham's Leonardo and Florence line; Milan, 300 km away, made no Leonardo. Shockley's Florences were California, Caltech, and Bell Labs (nine Nobels, monopoly-funded freedom).
  • Insulation by identity: pulled over unshaven with a loaded gun, he got the gun back.
  • Credit grab: Brattain and Bardeen built the point-contact transistor; Shockley, excluded from the patent, threatened revolt and became "the father of the transistor." Bardeen left and won a second Nobel.
  • Management: "climbing by moonlight and unroped," lie-detector tests, then the Traitorous Eight left, leading to Fairchild and Intel.
  • Omni-expertise cascade: a physicist at a genetics conference; "1 IQ point per 1% Caucasian ancestry"; moral condemnation lets him pose as a persecuted empiricist.
  • Persecuted becomes persecutor: his own scores were 129 and 125 (mother 161), yet he proposed $1,000 per IQ point below 100 as a sterilization bonus.
  • Sperm bank (Repository for Germinal Choice): Shockley the only laureate to admit donating, at about 70; no laureate donations produced a child; Doron Blake (IQ 180) concluded you can't breed for good people.
  • *Syl Jones interview and Playboy 1980:* a self-image that blocks self-correction.

Key numbers: nine Nobels at Bell Labs; IQ 129 and 125; $1,000 per IQ point; 69th percentile (sciences) and 45th (quadratics) at college entry; Blake's IQ 180.

So what: Achievement is talent x place x time x identity; the myth reports only the first. Refute cranks as wrong, not evil.

Ch 7. Marilyn and Me

Argument: A childhood test score sat unnoticed for thirty years; once printed, an obscure woman became "the smartest person in the world." IQ can't identify genius, but the label can manufacture one, and high-IQ societies show a number doesn't make you right or able to run a meeting.

Stories & evidence

  • Marilyn vos Savant: 178th of 613 in her high-school class, married at 16, divorced twice; after the 1985 Guinness entry came "Ask Marilyn" and public omni-opinions. Her score itself is contested (228 vs. the school board's ceiling of 167).
  • Galaxy-brainedness: Jarvik calling relativity, the Big Bang, and black holes wrong; high-IQ polls on foreign policy were useless.
  • Mensa and others: a new "aristocracy of brains" (fireplace tiles, yellow map pins); randomly assigned volunteer roles collapsed; Mega, Triple Nine, Cincinnatus, and Prometheus fought schisms and lawsuits; members' own preferred label was "Outsider."
  • Towers' three groups: well-adjusted, marginal, and dropouts ("the psychological walking wounded").
  • Lewis sits the Mensa test: it rewards speed, dated assumptions, and arguable synonyms.
  • Langan's Koko post: IQ used to compare Somalis to gorillas.
  • Mega Society log: credentialism by number resolved by fiat.
  • Guinness retires the category (1990); GWAS shows even eye colour is polygenic.
  • Hawking: "People who boast about their IQ are losers."

Key numbers: 178th of 613; scores of 228 vs. 167; 1985; 1990; 30 years.

So what: The label is a lens that creates its own object. Count the schisms as the empirical refutation of "high IQ means works of genius."

Ch 8. So You Want to Be a Genius?

Argument: The label is distorted by the Potus problem, multiples, the adjacent possible, the Matthew Effect, a taste for weirdness, hedgehogs, and white-elephant art, and plain luck.

Stories & evidence

  • Eysenck's list flipped: male, lose a parent before 10, born in February, die at 30 or 90 but never 60: features picked from biographies afterward.
  • Potus problem: The West Wing; Shakespeare's complexity now baseline; zero once took centuries.
  • Multiples (Ogburn & Thomas, 1922): telephone, natural selection, calculus, aeroplane, logarithms, Neptune; credit goes to the one who claimed harder (Newton smearing Leibniz; Wallace naming his book Darwinism).
  • Adjacent possible: printing press (moveable type + paper + ink + wine press); YouTube (cameras + broadband); Babbage ahead of time; Edison as manufacturer.
  • Timing: even Einstein and Picasso lost contact with the implications of their own revolution.
  • Matthew Effect and forty-first seat: Descartes, Pascal, Molière, Rousseau, Diderot, Flaubert, Zola, Proust; science advances one funeral at a time.
  • Be weird: Franklin's belief in transmigration; ninety-nine insane ideas and one gravity.
  • Hedgehog vs. fox (Berlin): Tetlock's foxes forecast better.
  • White elephant vs. termite art (Farber): Ulysses, awards campaigns.
  • Luck (Fleming): brother, water polo, rifle club; Dubos: "every decision is like a murder."

Key numbers: 148 simultaneous inventions; 1922; eight missed Académie names.

So what: Run the six-step distortion audit: Potus, multiples, adjacent possible, Matthew, weirdness, luck. What survives is the act; what falls away was the myth.

Ch 9. The Rebel

Argument: The lone heretic vindicated against the establishment flatters contrarians from scepticism into conspiracism: "if everyone says I'm wrong, I must be right." For every Newton of mathematics there's a Newton of alchemy.

Stories & evidence

  • Galileo gambit: ivermectin "truthers" (Heying, Weinstein), Mark Rylance on garlic and chemo, Freeman Dyson on climate.
  • They didn't all laugh: Edison's phonograph was an instant hit; Columbus didn't prove the earth round; Semmelweis (handwashing, died in an asylum) is the exception that makes the myth.
  • Impressionists: Leroy's "wallpaper in its early stages"; Impression, Sunrise sold for 800 francs.
  • Galileo unmythed: "Eppur si muove" first appears in 1757; he sought papal permission, died in his bed, and was a superb lens-maker (3x to 8x to 15x to 20x); Kepler borrowed his telescope.
  • *Dyson's Scientist as Rebel:* exemplar Thomas Gold (right about the ear, wrong about moon dust and abiogenic oil); phlogiston, mesmerism, phrenology, polywater.
  • Ivermectin timeline: early scepticism reasonable, then Merck says no evidence and Nature reports the evidence evaporating; contrarians whose identity is heterodoxy can't update, and speculation spirals to vaccine-Nuremberg rhetoric.
  • Theft as fame-maker: Impression, Sunrise (1985), Mona Lisa (1911).

Key numbers: 1757; 800 francs; magnification 3x, 8x, 15x, 20x.

So what: Opposition is not evidence. Source "they laughed at him," set an update trigger before the evidence arrives, and remember rebels have power and consequences.

Ch 10. Monsters and Tortured Artists

Argument: The tortured-genius aura works as a licence that stifles doubt, at any scale. Orwell's rule stands: being an artist is no excuse for abuse.

Stories & evidence

  • Orwell on Dalí: benefit of clergy; neither denounce the cad nor defend the untouchable genius. If Shakespeare's hobby were raping children, we would not tell him to carry on for another King Lear.
  • Chris Goode mechanism: a cultivated sensitive-outsider persona; work that eroticized adult-child relationships; an all-male, largely unpaid ensemble recruited at 18 to early thirties with nudity and sexual contact written into the advert; "check-ins" as consent theatre; critics fearing the Mary Whitehouse trap; queerness and left politics as shield. Arrested for child-abuse images, died by suicide on bail, then erased from the internet.
  • Smuggled argument: calling him a genius told viewers they were cool enough to see the deeper message.
  • Weinstein and Dederer's question: "What do we do with the art of monstrous men?" Polanski: Oscars, "not rape rape," "philistine collusion," until MeToo.
  • Stephens: contradiction, not causality; "all his plays were suicide notes" sentimentalizes addiction and abuse; "dividuals."

Key numbers: ensemble aged 18 to early 30s (no other figures).

So what: Apply the propaganda test. Prefer friends to fans, who can hold contradiction. Reckon; don't erase.

Ch 11. Great Wives

Argument: Behind most acknowledged geniuses stands a wife who feeds, copies, edits, manages, shields, and mirrors him, and whose sacrifice is written out or recast as hindrance.

Stories & evidence

  • Tolstoy and Sofia: married at 18 to a 34-year-old, sixteen pregnancies, copied War and Peace seven times, supplied material (her grief for a dead son became Anna's "eternal fear"); he wrote a play condemning wet nurses when she couldn't breastfeed; "a genius, and a parasite."
  • Reader thesis (Wilson): the marriage broke when the disciple Chertkov (2,000 letters, secretary-copyists, a secret will) replaced her as reader. She was admitted only after he lost consciousness; her memoir was suppressed for eight decades.
  • Wife Glitch (Schaffer): anticipates needs, fills weaknesses, "and means it." Institutions can substitute (nunneries for Hildegard, a Cambridge college for Newton, a Tokyo hospital for Kusama).
  • Wife as mirror: Gertrude Stein's The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas.
  • Vera Nabokov: agent, translator, secretary, driver, substitute lecturer, pistol in handbag after Lolita.
  • #thanksfortyping (Holsinger): thanks for typing whole manuscripts five times while nursing and teaching; an economist thanking his professor-wife for "managing the entire infrastructure of our lives."
  • Einstein's contract for Mileva Marić: laundry, three meals in his room, no personal relations; later replaced and written out by the "Einstein priests."
  • Adam Smith's dinner: cooked by his mother, then a cousin. New Yorker cartoon: "significantly less impressive once you realise these guys had free child care."

Key numbers: 16 pregnancies; 7 copies of War and Peace; 2,000 letters; 8 decades of suppression; age 18 vs. 34.

So what: Ask "who typed it?" and "who cooked the dinner?" The male dominance of "genius" partly reflects who gets a wife. Ask what you owe those harmed in the production of the work you admire.

Ch 12. Keepers of the Flame

Argument: Legacies are made and unmade by keepers (widows, heirs, executors, friends, magazines) who select, suppress, sanitize, price, and package.

Stories & evidence

  • **Life and the Irascibles:** the 1949 headline and 1951 group portrait created abstract expressionism as a movement, excluding Krasner; Hedda Sterne regretted being the one woman included.
  • Lee Krasner: painted small in a bedroom while Pollock had the barn; after his 1956 crash took the barn and painted seventeen-foot canvases; as widow sold one or two Pollocks a year and forced up prices.
  • Sonia Orwell: fourteen weeks a wife, thirty years a widow running the estate.
  • Jo van Gogh-Bonger: widowed at about 29 with a baby, 200+ paintings in a boarding house in Bussum; paired art and letters, won over a critic who first called it "nearly vulgar," staged a 484-work show in 1905, bought back Starry Night ("uncomfortable is good"); diary withheld until 2009; descendants on the museum board.
  • Hamilton's guardians: Donne's son, Marvell's "widow," Pope's feud with a pirate publisher, Boswell for Johnson, Burns sanitized (a revisionist biographer got a bullet in the post).
  • Copyright as control: the Beckett estate forbids women in male roles; le Carré's womanizing was published eight years later.
  • Reversals: Pollock "Stanley Kowalski with a paintbrush"; Krasner now the critical darling (Whitechapel, Whitney, MoMA, Barbican), but the market lags.
  • Grocer story: Life said the grocer "bought" a Pollock; he took it against unpaid debts.

Key numbers: $2M (Blue Poles, 1973); $140M (No. 5); Pollock $200M (2015) vs. Krasner record $11M (2019); 484-work show (1905); 14 weeks and 30 years (Sonia Orwell); 2009.

So what: Use the Jo checklist for any estate. Ask who holds the papers, who sits on the board, and who was cropped from the group photo.

Ch 13. A Cover Version

Argument: Two films from the same premise (a man is the only one who remembers the Beatles) give opposite answers: Yesterday says talent will out; Cover Version says talent isn't enough without persona, era, manager, producer, and luck. Each author wrote the theory of success his own life taught.

Stories & evidence

  • Counterfactual test: In Cover Version, "In My Life" from an unknown twentysomething doesn't land; the protagonist becomes Townes Van Zandt (died at 52).
  • "Star Wars wouldn't sell today" (Barth).
  • Auteur fetish: "One Man Only" campaign; Ed Sheeran's real co-writers; 60,000 songs a day.
  • Omitted Fifth and Sixth Beatles: Martin and Epstein.
  • The authors' lives: Curtis (Harrow, Oxford, Blackadder, Four Weddings, "never been knocked out") vs. Barth (twenty-five unproduced scripts, one Simpsons episode).
  • Credit: Curtis says he never read the script; Barth got a shared "Story by" credit and a share of net profit that "lost money" by Hollywood accounting; Alan Smithee.
  • Age: at thirty-two "you are no longer a person who could be."

Key numbers: 25 unproduced scripts; 60,000 songs a day; 12 notes; age 52 (Van Zandt); age 32.

So what: Value a hit as work x persona x moment x sponsor x luck. The more comforting story outsells the truer one.

Ch 14. Alchemy

Argument: The Beatles became the band through near-misses, collaborators, a demographic and media moment, and the right lifecycle: one member to die young and one to live long. Genius is a story with a beginning, middle, and end.

Stories & evidence

  • Near-miss biography (Craig Brown): bombers on one night and not the next; Ringo's peritonitis; Paul failing Spanish; conscription dodged; Epstein arriving as they considered quitting; Sutcliffe staying in Hamburg; Ringo's emigration forms.
  • Origin smoothing: John "barely noticed" Paul (1967) vs. "immediately impressed" (1983).
  • Losing it (Brown): John and Paul "lost it" too; Barth: old bands "don't look right."
  • Decca reconsidered: mostly covers plus three forgettable originals; Martin heard potential. Please Please Me was raw and sub-three-minutes; Little Richard was "way ahead."
  • Adjacent possible: television, Little Richard, post-war stability, George Martin (classically trained, Goons producer), Boomer bulge, charts, Ed Sullivan.
  • Age curves: Beard (peak by 40); Simonton (steep rise, gentle decline); Darwin at 50, Copernicus at 70, Disraeli PM at 64. Galenson's conceptual (Picasso) vs. experimental (Cezanne).
  • Perspiration: Gladwell's Hamburg hours (the "10,000" spuriously precise); Get Back shows songs emerging from aimless jamming.
  • When to die (Simonton): Mozart young, Goethe very old, never sixty; the Beatles ended at their peak (George was 27); Lennon murdered 1980; McCartney as patriarch and catalogue manager (Glastonbury at 80).

Key numbers: George was 27; peak by 40; "never sixty"; 1980; Glastonbury at 80.

So what: Count the coin flips. Early rejection isn't proof of hidden genius. Don't rank the dead partner above the living one, because death mythologizes.

Ch 15. The Deficit Model

Argument: Genius is said to extort a price, with oddness as currency. Biopics are today's Vasari: inspiration as flash, genius as unworldly, suffering as payment, which feels just, sells tickets, and warps real lives.

Stories & evidence

  • Examples of deficit: Beethoven deaf, Milton blind, Mozart a child who couldn't handle adulthood, Picasso needing women's "blood."
  • *Nash (A Beautiful Mind):* the bar-scene "vision"; the spy plot as delusion; Nash said supernatural ideas came "the same way" as mathematical ones.
  • *Hawking (The Theory of Everything):* skates over marriages and abuse allegations; best work came before deterioration; Penrose, equally impressive and later a Nobel laureate, stays obscure; Wilczek: idolization "corrosive."
  • Turing: already a Cambridge Fellow at Bletchley, but the film makes him friendless.
  • Oppenheimer: a rare attempt at genius as organizational.
  • **The Laws of Madness (Laudor):* schizophrenia, Yale Law Review editor, a 1995 NYT profile, a $600K+ memoir deal and $1.5M film rights (Ron Howard; Brad Pitt); off medication he killed his girlfriend; A Beautiful Mind* was released three years later.
  • Nobel's rule of three vs. CERN's hundreds.

Key numbers: $600K+ memoir; $1.5M film rights; 1995; three years later; Nobel cap of 3.

So what: Use the Hawking test: suffering that follows the work is narrative, not cause. Intelligence does not save you; the unmade shadow film is the corrective.

Ch 16. Disruptors

Argument: Silicon Valley is a site of scenius built by public institutions yet mythologized as rugged individualism and "disruption." The 2020s turned from wonder to cynicism.

Stories & evidence

  • Scenius conditions: no non-competes in California, Stanford, DoD funding (GPS via Naval Research; the internet via DARPA), post-war wealth attracting scientists.
  • Disruption (Christensen): cheap rivals dislodge bloated incumbents; reality includes lobbying, weak antitrust, and Facebook buying thirty companies in two years (Instagram, WhatsApp).
  • Genius asshole: Jobs the "Genius Entrepreneur," Wozniak the "Genius Engineer"; Wozniak: a nicer Apple "may never have made the Macintosh." Boy-kings: daughters named after Roman emperors, laser eye surgery, guns, gold, and potassium iodide.
  • Cynical turn: Swisher's Burn Book; Gladwell mocked in 2010; crypto as con (SBF), NFTs, social networks, generative AI.
  • Geopolitics: Musk, Altman, and Thiel as arguments that America still leads, as Shakespeare argued for England. Menlo Park, New Jersey gave its name to Menlo Park, California.

Key numbers: thirty companies in two years (Facebook).

So what: Every "self-made" founder stands on DARPA, Stanford, and a tax code. Ask "who bought whom?" Both wonder and cynicism are myth responses.

Ch 17. Thomas Edison: The Lightbulb Moment

Argument: At Menlo Park the Romantic genius gave way to the modern workaholic. Edison's real conceptual breakthrough was the phonograph; the lightbulb was incremental and team-built; the grid was underrated; and the myth was co-produced by reporters with shares in his company.

Stories & evidence

  • Phonograph (1877): an accidental byproduct of hunting telephone diaphragms; the lab ignored it for six months; the "flash" was a midnight-dinner collaboration. Scientific American demo ("How do you do?").
  • Myth revisions: deafness as superpower; schooling argument; "Tom" Edison (he was "Al").
  • Access-for-hype machine: a Herald writer received eight shares in Edison Electric; filament explorers (one claimed 98 days in the same clothes).
  • Lightbulb de-mythed: Davy (1802-09), Jobard (1838), Swan (1860); Sprengel pump; Batchelor's carbonised thread (40 hours); platinum "for ever" filaments burned out in minutes; lost the current war to Westinghouse; company becomes GE.
  • Had it, then didn't: ore-milling, litigation, a movie camera actually an employee's, the lab fire, the electric-car battery killed by the Model T; couldn't grasp radio.
  • Sage phase: opinions on women, Turks, the soul; the "Edison Test" (Einstein reportedly flunked it); his name invoked against the New Deal.
  • Selfish genius: Tesla left after a reneged bet; neglected first wife; a failson lending the name to the "Magno-Electric Vitalizer."
  • Latimer footnote: one of the few Black engineers hired, for patent-fight opposition research.

Key numbers: 1877; six months ignored; 40 hours (Batchelor's filament); 8 shares; 98 days.

So what: Credit the manufacturing and the grid; use the reporter-with-shares test (who profits from calling this person a genius?). Early-peaking conceptual innovators calcify as the myth grows.

Ch 18. Elon Musk: Extremely Hardcore

Argument: Musk shows acts of genius (reusable rockets, making EVs desirable) and has succumbed to being a special person. Genius is not transferable: SpaceX was physics, Tesla manufacturing, Twitter social and psychological.

Stories & evidence

  • Extremely Hardcore email (Nov 2022): long hours, three months' severance for refusers.
  • Genius as prism: silly decisions read through the Tony Stark lens.
  • High on his own supply: sycophants, Fidelity marking the $44B purchase down 71% to about $10B.
  • Leg-ups: Zip2 launched with a $28,000 gift from his father, sold for $307M; pushed out of X.com but made $180M.
  • "They want it" (Goldman): playing the genius in public (Diablo 4, feuds, the sink).
  • Valley ascetic: seven meals a week, sixty-day silent retreats, blood transfusions from a teenage son.
  • Autism as badge: "geek syndrome" (Silberman, 2001); the post about "high T alpha males and autists" (history: big butch lads backed Nazi Germany; Bonhoeffer and Sophie Scholl resisted).
  • Cult of the brilliant engineer: Google hired Schmidt and Facebook hired Sandberg as "grown-ups"; Zunger's rebuttal to Damore.
  • Taxpayer scaffolding: SpaceX rescued by a $1.6B NASA contract (Dec 2008); Tesla buyers' $7,500 credits.
  • Stockholm syndrome of the hardcore; the Glass Onion Miles Bron template; Delaware texts ("1.),, Solve Free Speech").
  • The missing MB: Mary Beth Brown, twelve years as the "only bridge," let go in 2014 (Musk disputes the reason); a successor said Musk is "special in this world... our job to protect him."
  • Full circle to Galton: population collapse, "woke mind virus," IQ and breeding.

Key numbers: $44B to about $10B (-71%); $28,000; $307M; $180M; $1.6B; $7,500; 12 years; 2014.

So what: Acts of genius, yes; special person, no. Run the three-problems test and the support-structure inventory before any "genius" takes on a new domain.

Ch 19. Conclusion: An Idea That Won't Stay Dead

Argument: We used to have God, now we have geniuses: an ineffable quality like sanctity that every era tries and fails to pin down. The myth survives because it makes better stories and does social work. The prescription is to return "genius" to acts and works and nurture the many seeds exclusion has wasted.

Stories & evidence

  • Secularization arc (Fara): possession, then secular saint, then Victorian number, then granular data.
  • Four functions: space for the weird, envy management, reconciliation with monstrosity, admiration for the one who gets away with it (Picasso as pure id, Trump as analogue, Larkin's shit in the shuttered chateau).
  • Picasso reversed: revered because of his selfishness; he made himself the sun.
  • Two wastes (Gould, Spencer): scorched by indulgence; far more extinguished by lack of support. "Before he can remake his society, his society must make him."
  • Why Great Man theory won't die: better stories; Vasari's readers wanted gossip; Nobel's cap of three vs. CERN's hundreds.
  • AI and the artist: LLMs are prediction machines; Baldwin's connection across time; "substitute ChatGPT for Dostoevsky and the magic is gone."
  • Impossible standards: private lives are fully accessible, yet the archetypes stagger on.

Key numbers: none stated beyond Nobel's three.

So what: Attach "genius" to the painting, the transistor, War and Peace. Don't debunk into nihilism; replace the myth's functions. "There are many seeds of genius in the world. We must nurture as many as we can."

Recurring Stories & Figures

  • Gauss: the evolving schoolboy anecdote (Ch 2), Galton's counter-example (Ch 3), and Lewis's "classmates" envy logic (Ch 19).
  • Shockley: rejected by Terman (Ch 4), the Nobel and credit grab, the sperm bank (Ch 6), and the omni-expert arc in Ch 9 and 16.
  • Burt and Eysenck: Burt's data in Ch 5 and in Shockley's thesis (Ch 6); Eysenck's "portrait" (Ch 0, 8).
  • The Beatles: the counterfactual films (Ch 13) and the alchemy of near-misses and endings (Ch 14).
  • Edison: the Gauss-style myth revisions and the phonograph (Ch 9, 17), the multiples (Ch 8), and the echo in Musk (Ch 18).
  • Musk: the referendum (Introduction), the Valley genius (Ch 16), and Galton again (Ch 18).
  • Tolstoy and Sofia: the type-case great wife (Ch 11), and the extinguished talents (Ch 19).
  • Galileo and Semmelweis: the lone-rebel archetype (Ch 9), carried into Dyson, Burt, Eysenck, and Shockley.
  • Einstein: his priests hiding his first child (Ch 1), Mileva Marić (Ch 11), a last-of-a-kind figure (Ch 14), and the "Edison Test" (Ch 17).
  • Shakespeare: the bardolatry pipeline (Ch 1), a baseline of complexity (Ch 8), and the Folio and Garrick as early keepers (Ch 12).
  • Hawking: the Hawking test (Ch 15) and his IQ quote (Ch 7).
  • Pollock, Krasner, and van Gogh: the Art Widow and Jo's playbook (Ch 12).
  • Picasso: the conceptual innovator (Ch 8, 14) and the revered selfishness (Ch 19).

The Unaccountability Machine: Why Big Systems Make Terrible Decisions — and How The World Lost Its Mind

2 markdown files

Quiz

The Unaccountability Machine Quiz Book

The Unaccountability Machine: Why Big Systems Make Terrible Decisions — and How The World Lost Its Mind by Dan Davies

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. Each chapter has short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative final exam is at the end. Chapters follow the skill's numbering: Introduction, Chapters 1-10, and the three Intermissions (3i, 5i, 7i) in book order.

Introduction

Q1 (SA). What is the "decisions, not events" stance, and what two explanations does it set aside?

A: Treat outcomes as the output of decision-making systems. It sets aside conspiracy (hidden motive) and cock-up (individual blunder). Systems have no hidden motivations (a consistent output is their purpose) and they don't make "mistakes" (they live with consequences or die of them). Individuals are named only as needed to describe the system ("if it hadn't been them, it would have been someone else").

Q2 (SA). What is a "decision-making system," and who are "the decided-upon"?

A: A decision-making system is any arrangement (algorithm, handbook, rule book, committee procedure) that produces decisions from standardised information rather than an individual reacting to circumstances. The decided-upon are the many people affected by decisions they had no part in and cannot address a person about.

Q3 (MC). Which is NOT one of the three revolutions in the Introduction's lens?

a) managerial b) cybernetic c) neoliberal d) digital

A: d. Managerial happened and was forgotten; cybernetic looked promising but never arrived; neoliberal (early 1970s) succeeded.

Q4 (SA). What contrast does the Dugdale/Truman example draw?

A: In 1954 Sir Thomas Dugdale resigned over the Crichel Down affair even though it was unclear he was personally involved; as minister in charge he bore responsibility. Truman kept "The Buck Stops Here" on his desk in 1953. Sixty-six years later Trump said "the buck stops with everybody" about a shutdown. The intervening industrialisation of decision-making removed the link that made the earlier answer available.

Q5 (T/F). The Introduction argues that declining accountability is mainly a moral decline in rulers' character. A: False. It treats this as largely a consequence of fewer decisions being made by identifiable humans at all.

Q6 (T/F). Regulating the algorithms behind AI loan and insurance decisions is, on this view, a complete answer to unaccountable decisions. A: False. Automated decisions are a visible special case; the committees writing the rules are themselves bound by opaque rule books designed to prevent attribution to any individual.

Chapter 1: 'Something's Up'

Q1 (SA). Define an accountability sink and give the diagnostic test.

A: An arrangement in which there is nobody to blame: a powerless person who conveys the decision plus a policy with no route of appeal. Test: is there any information from the affected person that could change the outcome? If not, it is a sink.

Q2 (SA). State the fundamental law of accountability.

A: The extent to which you can change a decision is precisely the extent to which you can be accountable for it, and vice versa. Ask "who can override this?"

Q3 (SA). What happened in the Schiphol ground squirrel story, and what does it show?

A: In April 1999, 440 ground squirrels from Beijing arrived at Schiphol on a KLM flight without import papers and were put through an industrial shredder built for worthless male chicks (the same machine had taken 200 more squirrels, dozens of turtles and a flock of parakeets). A sensible-looking ministry policy covered most cases; the pet-squirrel craze was the unanticipated input; no channel fed results back to those who could change the policy; staff had acted "formally correctly." It shows how a sink produces gruesome outcomes with nobody to blame.

Q4 (MC). Why is the common law described as a good accountability sink?

a) You can argue with the judge b) It is a sink, but it evolves through slow reputational feedback (precedent weighted by judges' seniority and promotion) c) It removes all rules d) It is unwritten

A: b. A sink is bad when there is no such feedback channel at all.

Q5 (T/F). Relying on frontline disobedience as the only safeguard against a bad policy is realistic. A: False. It is neither psychologically plausible nor managerially realistic to expect someone to follow orders 99 per cent of the time and then act independently on the hundredth.

Q6 (SA). What are "control fraud" and "self-organising control fraud"?

A: Control fraud (Bill Black): a criminal takes over a bank and installs incentives that produce fraudulent loans and declared profits, with legitimate-looking cash transfers. Self-organising control fraud (Davies' coinage): the system is so criminogenic that banks organise themselves into fraud with no link between bosses and low-level crooks; executives need only set unrealistic targets and underinvest in compliance.

Q7 (T/F). Davies argues that restoring middle-manager discretion is a simple fix for sinks. A: False. "Naive de-sinking" reintroduces caprice, unfairness and racism; many policies exist precisely to prevent those. Legitimate reasons for sinks include legal liability shields, insurance underwriting and avoiding corrosive interpersonal conflict.

Chapter 2: Stafford Beer

Q1 (SA). What is Beer's black box axiom?

A: "It is not necessary to enter the black box to understand the nature of the function it performs." Draw a boundary, assume nothing about internals, observe how it reacts to its environment, and iterate: do more of what works and less of what doesn't.

Q2 (SA). Distinguish clear box, muddy box and black box.

A: Clear box: something you control directly, like a factory machine. Muddy box: more analysis would help but at disproportionate effort. Black box: you decide you lack the understanding to treat it otherwise; being a black box is a decision by the observer, not an objective property.

Q3 (SA). What does POSIWID mean, and what does it not mean?

A: "The purpose of a system is what it does." It is not cynicism and says nothing about the intentions of the people working there. Example: the purpose of the Schiphol pet hotel was to shred squirrels, because the system was set up to ensure compliance with import regulation at lowest cost.

Q4 (SA). Explain the resource bargain.

A: A unit operates autonomously only to the extent that this doesn't jeopardise the broader system (budget, space, management time, goodwill). Bargains are kept until the situation changes, then renegotiated. Model: a platoon told to take a bridge, with only two expected messages, "bridge captured" or "external factor intervened, renegotiate."

Q5 (MC). Homeostasis differs from economists' equilibrium because it:

a) is always optimal b) carries no implication of optimality, only that forces return the system there c) ignores feedback d) applies only to machines

A: b.

Q6 (T/F). Beer's 1947 army unit of soldiers labelled "psychopathological" showed that an outside theory of their minds was needed first. A: False. He chose variables, plotted trends, refused to assume, and followed feedback. The result was a "crash course" method that raised the educational age of troops, which his superiors told him was called operational research.

Q7 (SA). Why is central planning criticised here "on two counts"?

A: It's planning (a national economy is too complicated to write down) and it's central (getting the information and centralising it is the more wicked problem). The Soviet example: adding up different grades of wire, switches and fastenings.

Chapter 3: Aliens Among Us

Q1 (SA). Why does Davies prefer "decision-making system" to "artificial intelligence"?

A: It drops the question of whether an organisation is "really" intelligent and asks only whether it makes decisions and whether they can be traced to identifiable humans. If not, attribute the output to the system ("Boeing did this").

Q2 (SA). How does cybernetics ground the principle of diminishing accountability?

A: The amount of individual accountability a system can support is inversely related to how far it must be treated as a black box. As organisations grow more complicated, accountability falls structurally. Ashby's example: four mutually connected parts have twenty circuits, and knowing all twenty still doesn't describe the whole.

Q3 (SA). How does the Fox News voting-machine case illustrate "not conspiracy, not cock-up"?

A: Internal emails show no scheme: individuals each reacted to immediate pain points (audience figures, share price, angry viewers) and assumed someone else would stop anything catastrophic. Yet it wasn't an accident: a long series of local decisions to stir up rage accumulated into a system-wide commitment to serve the angriest, least-informed viewers. That was a real decision that nobody made.

Q4 (MC). Boeing's technical pilot Mark Forkner is cited as an example of:

a) good management b) scapegoating the one person whose paperwork is legible while corporate intent goes unproven c) a whistleblower d) the paperclip maximiser

A: b. It is "proof the accountability sink worked."

Q5 (T/F). Explainability research is mostly applied to favourable decisions. A: False. It is almost never applied to favourable decisions; it is funded to explain refusals. Ask who benefits from the box staying closed.

Q6 (SA). What is the "responsibility gap," and why does Davies say AI ethics is already business ethics?

A: The gap is the problem of assigning liability when an automated system causes harm. Corporations have operated above the black-box threshold for centuries, so AI's accountability problems already exist in non-computational form, under far weaker rights of explanation.

Q7 (T/F). Deep but partial expertise raises confidence in proportion to reliability. A: False. It raises confidence disproportionately to reliability (financiers' "it's different this time"; the State Department underperforming a parrot trained to say "don't start a war").

Intermission: Computing Ponds and Rabbit Holes

Q1 (SA). What did Beer mean by "fabric"?

A: A substrate with the properties of a computer that doesn't depend on anyone specifying the algorithm ahead of time.

Q2 (SA). Why did Beer's computing pond fail?

A: The iron filings fed to the Daphnia (to make them respond to a magnetic field) left the water with a growing suspension of tiny permanent magnets, which collapsed any organisation that began to form. The medium's own dynamics destroyed the signal.

Q3 (SA). State the explainability paradox.

A: Explanation is demystifying (it shows how the conjurer put the rabbit in the hat), so "explainable" and "genuinely intelligent" pull in opposite directions.

Q4 (SA). What is the "pencil-and-paper test"?

A: Ask whether the result could in principle have been produced with pencil and paper given unlimited time. If yes, there is no magic, just iterated simple operations.

Q5 (T/F). Fabric-style methods are valuable mainly because they are fast and efficient. A: False. They are usually neither fastest nor most efficient; they earn their keep only if they can do things conventional methods cannot do at all.

Chapter 4: How to Psychoanalyse a Non-human Intelligence

Q1 (SA). State Ashby's law of requisite variety.

A: Anything that aims to regulate a system needs at least as much variety as that system. A system can be stable only if every source of variability from the environment is matched by equal or greater variety in the regulator. Beer called it the cybernetic equivalent of Newton's laws of motion.

Q2 (SA). What is variety, and why isn't it intrinsic?

A: The number of states a system can be in. It is a property of how you choose to describe the system, so you must choose your black boxes and say which states you count.

Q3 (MC). The practical way to apply the law, per Davies, is to:

a) count bits exactly b) compare whether regulator variety is greater or less than input variety c) hire more staff d) ignore it

A: b. "We all know what someone looks like when they're overloaded."

Q4 (SA). Name the moves of variety engineering and give an example of each.

A: Attenuation (continuous temperature becomes "too hot/too cold" for a thermostat); amplification (build regulatory subsystems using another source of variety, e.g. a thermostat per cage across a hundred cages); regulation by veto (Ashby's homeostat: sensors veto unacceptable states until all are satisfied); splitting the problem (regulate temperature apart from food and water, but only if variables are truly separable; smashing a Rubik's Cube into 26 sub-cubes solves nothing).

Q5 (SA). Why is an accountability sink recast here as a "solution as much as a problem"?

A: Building cause-and-effect subsystems so managers don't decide case by case is variety amplification; unappealability is its side effect.

Q6 (T/F). You can literally amplify variety. A: False. That would breach the second law; you do the stereo-amplifier trick by building regulatory subsystems inside the wider regulator.

Q7 (SA). What are ataxia and purpose tremor?

A: Wiener's two failure modes in the automated gunsight: feedback too weak (the gun trails its target) and too strong (it oscillates and overcorrects). Named after cerebellar injury symptoms; the moment control engineering became cybernetics.

Chapter 5: Cybernetics Without Diagrams

Q1 (SA). Name the five systems of the Viable System Model and the function of each.

A: 1 Operations (makes change in the world); 2 Regulation (prevents clashes: timetables, quartermaster); 3 Integration/optimisation (coordinates the System 1s, strikes and polices resource bargains, handles residual variety); 4 Intelligence (the "there and then", watching the environment not yet in contact with operations); 5 Philosophy/identity (balances 3 against 4 by fixing what kind of organisation this is).

Q2 (SA). How can you tell System 2 from System 3?

A: System 2 is the management everyone agrees is necessary; System 3 is the management people complain about. System 3 managers often pretend to be System 2.

Q3 (SA). What are the two failure modes of management by exception?

A: Micromanagement (System 3 fights System 1's variety single-handed, gets bloated, neglects coordination) and excessive delegation (no bargains or planning; conflicts settled by politics and hoarding). System 3 should be sized to the residual variety.

Q4 (T/F). Forecasting is a form of System 4. A: False. Forecasts are the here-and-now in another form; a real System 4 looks at what isn't yet relevant.

Q5 (MC). An algedonic signal is best described as:

a) a quarterly report b) a channel letting any level signal directly to the top that something threatens catastrophic consequences c) a type of resource bargain d) a System 2 timetable

A: b. Modelled on a train's emergency brake; resource the channel and the translation capacity at the receiving end. Frequent red-handle signals indicate missing or dysfunctional systems further down.

Q6 (SA). Distinguish information from data.

A: Variety counts as information only if it has a causal role in decision-making, arriving in time and in a form the receiver can act on. Otherwise it is data sitting on disk.

Q7 (SA). How does the chapter read the 2008 crisis through the VSM?

A: Central banks (a System 1 of government with independence as its resource bargain) named the calm ("Great Moderation," "NICE times," "Goldilocks economy") while a debt bubble built. Their "forecasting" was here-and-now extended, so System 4 was weak; 2006-07 warnings stayed data; only Lehman's bankruptcy acted as an algedonic squeal. The root was System 5: an identity that defined certain information as none of their business.

Intermission: Decerebrate Cats

Q1 (SA). What does a decerebrate cat illustrate?

A: An animal with its higher brain severed can still walk, right itself, eat and groom, but cannot generate its own responses to change. An organisation that has hollowed out Systems 4 and 5 likewise still runs operations but cannot act purposively.

Q2 (SA). What warning sign marks a decerebrate organisation?

A: Attention runs only to the immediate surroundings (this quarter's revenue, current staffing level) and planning capacity has disappeared.

Q3 (T/F). Smooth day-to-day operations are good evidence of adaptive health. A: False. The decerebrate cat grooms itself; operational competence says nothing about adaptive capacity.

Q4 (SA). What are the only two outcomes when a shock hits a decerebrate organisation?

A: It finds resources from somewhere to re-establish intelligence and identity, or it collapses. The crisis is deferred, never avoided.

Q5 (SA). What was Beer's stock example, and what is Davies' practical corollary?

A: A university whose operations run smoothly while the capacity to decide what it's for has gone. Corollary: if you can see a company actively decerebrating itself, update your resume and call recruiters.

Chapter 6: Economics and How It Got That Way

Q1 (SA). What are the steps of the Ricardian Vice?

A: (a) Model a feature of the economy, stripping away nearly all complexity; (b) make strong, often questionable simplifying assumptions; (c) derive the conclusion; (d) act as if it has been proved about the real world.

Q2 (SA). Walk through Ricardo's England/Portugal example.

A: Cloth costs 100 labour-hours in England and 90 in Portugal; wine costs 120 in England and 80 in Portugal. Portugal is absolutely better at both, but relative prices differ (a bolt of cloth is worth nine-eighths of a barrel of wine in Portugal, five-sixths in England), so Portugal gains by making only wine and trading. The arithmetic is airtight; the vice is the leap from it to claims about real international trade.

Q3 (MC). Which is NOT one of the four conditions to check before trusting an optimisation model?

a) commodity good b) observable marginal cost curve c) independent spot markets d) high consumer brand loyalty

A: d. The fourth is negligible strategic interaction.

Q4 (SA). In what sense is economics a "variety-engineering technology" and "identity-creating function"?

A: It attenuates society to price and quantity so it can always give a definite answer, and it does System 5's job for policymakers by telling rulers what they don't have to think about (e.g. cost-benefit analysis lets whole approaches be rejected without consideration).

Q5 (T/F). Observing a market outcome licenses the inference that it is optimal. A: False. None of the four sources (Smith, Hayek, equilibrium proofs, market efficiency) licenses that, and the inference is "a huge accountability sink."

Q6 (SA). Why can't safety information go through cost-benefit analysis?

A: "This aircraft has a faulty stall sensor which might cause it to crash" is fundamentally not a statement about expected costs, however comfortable you are pricing a life; it needs a separate channel.

Q7 (SA). What do "homo economicus" and the "representative individual" do?

A: Homo economicus cares only about price and quantity and is perfectly informed and able to read other agents' minds. The representative individual/firm assumes identical preferences or aggregates all producers into one, dodging strategic interaction.

Chapter 7: If You're So Rich, Why Aren't You Smart?

Q1 (SA). Distinguish management accounting from financial reporting.

A: Management accounting measures process efficiency and allocates costs to specific decisions. Financial reporting summarises the whole enterprise for financiers on standard periods and conventions, and so attenuates variety.

Q2 (SA). State the attributability test.

A: The extent to which a cost can be attributed to an output is exactly the extent to which it could be avoided if you weren't producing it. Also, allocating costs a manager cannot influence is pure harm.

Q3 (SA). What is business hallucination?

A: A firm acting on a picture of itself generated by reporting conventions rather than by its actual production process.

Q4 (SA). Summarise the skincare factory example.

A: Two lines from essentially the same cream: bulk barrels for construction workers, and small beauty tubs at ten times the price. Marketing is treated as a period cost, so the luxury line looks more profitable while the bulk line absorbs a disproportionate share of fixed packaging cost allocated by direct labour. Consultants compare in-house manufacturing (carrying beauty overheads) with a cheap external supplier; manufacturing is sold; the marketing and research costs don't vanish; and two years later consultants are hired to explain the slump.

Q5 (MC). The fast-food "chicken efficiency" story shows:

a) the danger of measuring the wrong efficiency b) the value of cost allocation c) the benefits of consultants d) a successful bargain

A: a. Managers stopped frying an hour before closing, lost sales, and hit 100 per cent.

Q6 (T/F). Consultants can supply the managerial class with its identity function. A: False. Telling clients what they want to hear is better for repeat business, so consultancy can never supply it; their real product should be a repaired feedback loop. They also work as accountability sinks (professional scapegoats).

Q7 (SA). How do "Ricardians win arguments"?

A: By collecting the numbers: whoever designs data collection decides what is measured and ignored. The only reliable counters are data collected for a different purpose or an internal inconsistency in their model. (A single death can be encoded as liver failure, mercury poisoning or murder.)

Intermission: Meanwhile, in Chile

Q1 (SA). Name Cybersyn's components and their role.

A: Cybernet (several hundred repurposed telex machines carrying production data); Cyberstride (statistical software judging whether data fell in the normal range and classifying departures as blip, trend change or new normal); the Operations Room (about a dozen managers with wall displays negotiating resource bargains); Checo (an economic simulator, planned but never delivered).

Q2 (SA). Map Cybersyn onto the VSM.

A: Operations Room = System 3; Cybernet = partial System 2; Cyberstride = variety engineering matching the room to data inflow; Checo = intended System 4.

Q3 (T/F). Cybersyn was an attempt at computerised central planning of the economy. A: False. It was a management-by-exceptions system built on the VSM, and management cybernetics already shows a centrally planned economy cannot meet requisite variety.

Q4 (SA). Which part proved most practically useful?

A: Cybernet: during a trucking strike it let the government track deliveries and secure essential supplies.

Q5 (SA). What does "out of scale" mean here?

A: The control system's channel capacity plainly cannot match the variety it regulates; a few hundred telex machines against an industrial economy fails the laugh test.

Q6 (SA). Name two further problems with Cybersyn.

A: Installing it provoked reaction from operations (building a regulator changes the regulated system), and interventors in nationalised factories passing on central orders undercut the devolved-autonomy logic. Chile also nationalised faster than it could manage, without an overall industrial plan.

Chapter 8: Enter Friedman

Q1 (SA). What are the three moves of the Friedman doctrine?

A: (1) Look through the corporation to individuals; (2) replace actual shareholders with an abstract "representative shareholder" black box that cares only about profits; (3) invite the executive to split his moral self into judgements "as a person in his own right" and decisions "in his capacity as a businessman."

Q2 (SA). Why does Davies call the doctrine a "personal accountability sink"?

A: It lets managers attribute bad consequences and lost independence to a separate work-self bound by one simple principle.

Q3 (SA). Why is debt a "variety attenuator" for lenders?

A: The lender need only answer two questions (is the rate attractive compensation for time and risk; will I be paid back?), and so can make far more investments than they could supervise. With heavy debt, the payment signal swamps all other information.

Q4 (SA). Describe the leveraged buyout mechanism.

A: Put up roughly 10 per cent of your own money, borrow 90 per cent, then make the acquired company borrow to repay your creditors. Debt forces focus on cash; limited liability caps the buyer's loss at the initial 10 per cent; risk shifts to workers, suppliers, customers and managers.

Q5 (T/F). Courts have found a legal "fiduciary duty to maximise shareholder value." A: False. Courts have never found a duty to run a company one way rather than another; the phrase is legal jargon used outside its legal context, moral exhortation in sonorous tones.

Q6 (MC). "Financialisation," per Davies, is best understood as:

a) a parasite on the real economy b) the growing importance of financial aspects of the whole system, since finance is how resource bargains are struck c) a conspiracy d) a tax policy

A: b.

Q7 (SA). What did Jensen (with Meckling) contribute?

A: A rigorous mathematical footing for the doctrine: "managerial behaviour" (slacking, pursuing social goals with shareholders' money), "agency costs" (shareholders' difficulty checking managers), and "ownership structure" as the fix (debt and stock options to make managers act as if a personal owner were watching).

Q8 (SA). What is "pre-emptive self-buyout"?

A: Companies behaved as if already under a leveraged buyout to avoid becoming targets, spreading the pathology without the transaction.

Chapter 9: The Morbid Symptoms

Q1 (SA). What is "reversing the polarity"?

A: Following Jerome Levy, the investing class exists to serve the working class by insuring them against loss. The neoliberal era ran this backwards, with unemployment itself as the variety attenuator, so the working class insured the corporate sector against the business cycle. It produced the Great Moderation.

Q2 (SA). Why does cutting middle management and outsourcing destroy information?

A: Middle managers were the processing (translation/transduction) capacity at communication boundaries. Outsourcing replaces internal boundaries with contracts that carry essentially two states ("going as anticipated" or "it's stopped working"). Because the channel mostly says OK, spare bandwidth for "conditions are changing" always looks cuttable.

Q3 (SA). What does "the one-bit channel and the scream" mean for populism?

A: Where the population's channels carry very few bits, the only message possible is "Help! the Current State of Affairs is Intolerable to me." Respond to the fact of the scream, not its content; the movement's existence is the signal.

Q4 (MC). In the GE example, what was done to avoid spoiling future smooth growth after a one-off $2bn gain?

a) paid special dividends b) closed factories and made over 1,000 people redundant c) raised prices d) acquired a rival

A: b.

Q5 (T/F). Marmot's Whitehall studies found that civil service grade predicted mortality independent of income, smoking and family history. A: True. This is the "status syndrome"; being out of control is physiologically harmful.

Q6 (SA). Why do short-term targets privilege costs over revenues?

A: Management controls costs within a quarter; revenue requires finding a customer, winning the order, making the product and getting paid, which is impossible in a quarter.

Q7 (SA). What was the "blind spot in the control parameters" before the financial crisis?

A: Only government deficits were monitored; private-sector debt sat outside the control system and was seen as positive by the post-Friedman corporate control system.

Q8 (SA). What is "el pueblo"?

A: Allende's name for the System 5 box: the last-resort absorber of information, which hardly ever does anything and has no postal address; even in a dictatorship there is a collective veto if things become intolerable.

Chapter 10: What Is to Be Done?

Q1 (SA). What is Davies' single private-equity reform, and why?

A: Any entity taking control of an operating company should guarantee its debts. It closes the accountability sink (limited liability) that lets buyers take on debt and extract cash while bad news cannot travel upstream. Don't try to regulate "excessive" borrowing; requisite variety says that is doomed.

Q2 (SA). What is the three-step argument against economists in charge?

A: (1) Any system set up to maximise a single objective can go bonkers. (2) Every maximiser needs a higher-level system watching over it. (3) So the economists can't be in charge, not as they currently are.

Q3 (MC). Which describes "viability over maximisation"?

a) Firms should maximise long-run profit b) Corporations have no motives; what looks like a profit motive is an imbalance between here-and-now and there-and-then, and viable systems seek stability c) Firms should maximise employment d) Firms should be nationalised

A: b.

Q4 (SA). What do Galbraith and Simon contribute?

A: Galbraith's technostructure (a managerial class across business, government, military and media working to maintain stability, whose executives mainly handle uncertainty) and Simon's behavioural theory of the firm (profits are a constraint, not a goal to be maximised). They described what was in front of them, and suggest the fix is changing the terms of the battle between capital and the managerial class.

Q5 (T/F). Davies says we should insist that an identifiable human is always available to blame for automated decisions. A: False. Important decisions will be made by actual robots; repair the feedback link instead ("I blame the system" becomes literal).

Q6 (SA). What is the proposed role of AI in communication?

A: A variety amplifier for two-way communication: summarising large text up to a smaller decision-making system and expanding short instructions down, rather than just making existing structures run faster.

Q7 (SA). What does "Only cybernetic problems are soluble" mean?

A: If a problem is organisational, its complexity comes from the people in the organisation, so they have enough variety to match it; the problem can't be bigger than the people whose misdirected efforts created it.

Final Exam (10 questions)

Q1 (SA). What is an accountability sink, and what single question tests for one?

A: A combination of a powerless human interface and an unappealable policy, so there is nobody to blame. Test: is there any information the affected person could supply that would change the outcome?

Q2 (SA). State Ashby's law and the quick way to apply it.

A: Only variety can absorb variety; a regulator needs at least as much variety as what it regulates. Quick check: compare whether regulator variety is greater or less than input variety, rather than counting bits.

Q3 (MC). Which pairing is correct?

a) System 4 - regulation b) System 3 - intelligence c) System 5 - philosophy/identity, balancing 3 against 4 d) System 2 - identity

A: c.

Q4 (T/F). POSIWID is a claim about individuals' bad intentions. A: False. It says nothing about the intentions of people in the system; it's about reading purpose from output and a description of how System 5 preserves viability.

Q5 (SA). Give the Ricardian Vice and the four-condition check in one answer.

A: Prove something in a stripped-down model and act as if proved about the world. Before trusting an optimisation model, check: commodity good, observable marginal cost curve, independent spot markets, negligible strategic interaction.

Q6 (SA). How do decerebration and outsourcing connect across Chapters 5i and 9?

A: Systems 4 and 5 produce no directly measurable output, so they are easy to cut; thinning middle management removes translation capacity at boundaries, and outsourced contracts carry only "OK" or "stopped." The result is an organisation that functions until the environment changes structurally.

Q7 (MC). The attributability test says a cost is attributable:

a) in proportion to direct labour b) exactly to the extent it would be avoided by not producing the output c) if the accountant says so d) if it is a period cost

A: b.

Q8 (SA). Trace how Friedman's doctrine, debt and the LBO combine, and what the effect is on the working class (Ch 8-9).

A: The doctrine supplies a single maximising goal and a personal accountability sink; debt (and the LBO's 10/90 structure) swamps all signals but cash and shifts risk onto workers, suppliers, customers and managers; with corporate shock-absorbing capacity cut, the polarity reverses and the working class absorbs volatility, with the population's only channel a one-bit scream.

Q9 (SA). What does Davies prescribe for maximising systems and for the "decided-upon"?

A: Pair every maximiser with a higher-level supervisor, keep the top level of any autonomous system a non-maximiser, and give the decided-upon a red handle to signal intolerability. Set survival conditions rather than maximisation targets.

Q10 (SA). Why is the Cybersyn story relevant to the VSM and to requisite variety?

A: Cybersyn was a management-by-exceptions design (Operations Room = System 3, Cybernet = partial System 2, Cyberstride = variety engineering, Checo = intended System 4) that was badly out of scale to the Chilean economy; it also provoked reaction, and it was ended by the 1973 coup before it could fail informatively.

Arguments & Evidence

The Unaccountability Machine: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Dan Davies

Each chapter has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files (plus glossary, patterns and cheatsheet) in the unaccountability-machine skill, so it reflects that summary of the book, not the book's own wording. The skill's notes carry few statistics, so "Key numbers" sections are short by nature.

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

Davies argues that over the last century the developed world industrialised decision-making, so that important institutions run on processes and standardised information rather than on individuals reacting to circumstances, and accountability (the link between deciders and the decided-upon) atrophied. Ch 1 names the mechanism, the accountability sink; Ch 2-4 supply the toolkit from Stafford Beer and Ross Ashby (black boxes, POSIWID, requisite variety, variety engineering) and treat organisations as non-human decision-making systems. Ch 5 builds the Viable System Model (five functions) as a diagnostic, with the Decerebrate Cats intermission showing what happens when the higher functions are cut. Ch 6-7 turn the lens on economics (the Ricardian Vice, markets as computing fabric) and accounting (business hallucination), with the Chile intermission showing the road not taken. Ch 8 explains how the Friedman doctrine, debt and the leveraged buyout gave corporations a single maximising goal; Ch 9 traces the consequences (reversed polarity, lost translation capacity, the one-bit scream of populism); Ch 10 prescribes viability over maximisation, guaranteeing the debts of controlled companies, red handles for the decided-upon, and acceptance that robots will make decisions while feedback is repaired.

Introduction

Argument: Over the last century the developed world industrialised decision-making: important institutions are run by processes and systems operating on standardised information, not by individuals reacting to circumstances. The result is the atrophy of accountability. To understand it, treat outcomes as the output of decision-making systems rather than conspiracy or cock-up, and read history through three revolutions (managerial, cybernetic, neoliberal).

Stories & evidence

  • Dugdale vs Truman vs Trump: Sir Thomas Dugdale resigned in 1954 over the Crichel Down affair (a fairly trivial malpractice concerning requisitioned Dorset farmland), though it was never clear he was personally involved. Truman kept "The Buck Stops Here" on his desk in 1953. Sixty-six years later, asked who was responsible for a government shutdown, Trump said "the buck stops with everybody."
  • The three revolutions: the managerial revolution happened and was forgotten; the cybernetic revolution looked promising but never arrived; the neoliberal revolution of the early 1970s succeeded.
  • Cybernetics' brain drain: the founders discovered information representation, which proved commercially decisive for electronic circuits, so the talent went to the computer industry.
  • Chile 1973: the neoliberal/cybernetic debate did happen, "with helicopters and guns at La Moneda."

Key numbers: Dugdale 1954; Truman 1953; 66 years between Truman's desk sign and Trump's answer; the neoliberal revolution in the early 1970s; 11 September 1973.

So what: Ask where a decision went, not who erred. Read a system's consistent output as its purpose. Look for the rule book behind the algorithm. Cover the three revolutions before reaching for character flaws.

Ch 1. 'Something's Up'

Argument: The twenty-first-century polycrisis is at root a crisis of accountability. Organisations have built accountability sinks (a powerless human interface plus an unappealable policy) that absorb negative feedback; the resulting inability to learn from unanticipated situations guarantees periodic catastrophic failure.

Stories & evidence

  • Schiphol squirrels (April 1999): 440 ground squirrels from Beijing landed on a KLM flight without import papers; they could not go on to Athens or be sent back, and were put through a shredder built for worthless male chicks. The machine had earlier taken 200 more squirrels, dozens of turtles and a flock of parakeets. A sensible-looking ministry policy, a delegating airline, a low baseline of destruction accepted, no feedback channel, and the pet-squirrel craze as the unanticipated input. Staff were "formally correct"; the alleged fault was an "assessment mistake," i.e. failing to disobey.
  • The common law as a good sink: you can't argue with a judge, but precedent is weighted by judges' seniority and reputation and promotion reflects decisions made over time. Fundamentalism and strict constructionism try to remove that channel.
  • Bill Black's control fraud, extended by Davies to self-organising control fraud in banks (unrealistic targets plus underinvestment in compliance).
  • Peter Dale Scott's parapolitics / the deep state (Turkish shorthand originally) as the part of government where accountability is intentionally diminished.
  • Placeholder numbers: the 3 per cent deficit rule and 2 per cent inflation target as examples of numbers with no analysis behind them becoming fundamental constraints; junior officials' round numbers becoming continental policy.
  • Kings vs priests: a king's orders can be argued with; a priest interprets the Word. Discontent grows when king-shaped structures are run by priest-like managers.
  • The IMF as scapegoat: clever in a journal, indefensible to a hungry crowd.

Key numbers: 440 squirrels (plus 200 earlier); 99 per cent obedience vs the hundredth case; 3 per cent deficit rule; 2 per cent inflation target.

So what: Ask what the frontline person can change. Write down the assumptions a policy encodes. Build an exceptions route and check it is used. Keep a slow reputational feedback channel in any sink you must retain. Expect crises on a schedule (a Minsky-shaped dynamic). Recognise legitimate reasons for sinks (liability shields, underwriting, avoiding corrosive interpersonal conflict) before removing them; naive de-sinking brings back caprice and unfairness.

Ch 2. Stafford Beer

Argument: Beer built management cybernetics on one move: define a complex system by its behaviour, draw a box around it, and refuse to open it. From that follow the black box axiom, homeostasis, POSIWID, and a management theory based on neither control nor delegation but on accountability via the resource bargain.

Stories & evidence

  • Beer's 1947 army unit: an army psychologist with no medical qualification was handed illiterate soldiers diagnosed with "psychopathological personalities." They couldn't write home or handle 4 + 3, yet scored darts aloud and computed accumulator bets instantly. He chose variables, plotted trends, refused to assume, and followed feedback, producing a "crash course" method that raised the educational age of troops. His superiors told him it was called operational research.
  • Pre-Partition India: he had earlier tracked shifting allegiances the same way.
  • The platoon told to take a bridge: the model of a resource bargain, with two expected messages.
  • Homeostat and feedback examples: ship's gyroscopic stabiliser (stabilising feedback) vs Hendrix amplifier (destabilising feedback).
  • Soviet planning: adding up different grades of wire, switches and fastenings got the system into serious trouble.
  • Hayek on prices: prices derive from transactions through which knowledge percolates; the central planner's dilemma.
  • Beer's Sigmoots: informal cross-level meetings where anyone could bang a shoe on the table.
  • Applied backwards to Ch 1: the purpose of academic publishing is to generate citations for academics and profits for publishers; the purpose of the Schiphol pet hotel was to shred squirrels.

Key numbers: 1947; the soldiers could not handle 4 + 3 yet scored darts aloud ("21 — that's 15 and a double 3 to go").

So what: Treat complex systems as black boxes and study behaviour. Judge organisations by what they consistently produce, separately from intentions. When change stalls, look for homeostatic forces. Structure autonomy as a resource bargain. Expect the consultant's paradox: a good diagnosis says people's own organisation prevents them achieving their goals, which triggers self-defence.

Ch 3. Aliens Among Us

Argument: Treat corporations and large organisations as non-human decision-making systems whose outputs must be attributed to the system, not to any individual. Individual accountability shrinks not because managers are sneaky but because complexity forces everyone, insiders included, to treat the organisation as a black box. "Systems don't make mistakes and don't have intentions," so conspiracy-versus-cock-up is the wrong question.

Stories & evidence

  • Fox News and the voting-machine defamation case: internal emails show individuals reacting to audience figures, share price and angry viewers, each assuming someone else would stop anything catastrophic. Yet the audience didn't arrive believing in stolen elections by chance: local decisions to stir up rage accumulated into a system-wide commitment. A real decision that nobody made.
  • Boeing and Mark Forkner: charging the one pilot with legible paperwork while corporate intent goes unproven.
  • Ashby's four-part example: four mutually connected parts have twenty circuits; knowing all twenty still doesn't describe the whole.
  • Searle's Chinese room, read as an argument about accountability; Bostrom's paperclip maximiser as the model for firms that prioritise financial results over extinction-level harm.
  • Overconfident partial expertise: financiers' "it's different this time"; the State Department underperforming a parrot trained to say "don't start a war."
  • Explainability: research is funded to explain refusals, almost never favourable decisions.

Key numbers: four parts and twenty circuits (Ashby).

So what: Attribute systemic outputs to the system by name. Expect accountability to fall as organisations grow.
