Distrust confidence in proportion to how much you know about a subset of a complex system. Treat "we need explainability" as a claim about who is allowed to see inside. Apply the AI-ethics agenda to corporations, which crossed the black-box threshold centuries ago.

Intermission: Computing Ponds and Rabbit Holes

Argument: The cyberneticians kept trying to build computation from living or physical "fabric" (ponds, petri dishes, compass needles) rather than algorithms written in advance. The appeal is a system with no comprehensible logic that nonetheless gives good answers, which is in direct tension with explainability.

Stories & evidence

  • Beer's computing pond: a tank of algae, larvae and Daphnia, with iron filings ingested by the Daphnia so they would respond to a magnetic field. Initial conditions were meant to correspond to a computing problem and the pond's evolution to represent the solution; neither correspondence was specified. It failed because the water filled with tiny permanent magnets, collapsing any developing organisation.
  • Beer and Gordon Pask's ferrous sulphate petri dish, "tuned" with feedback to discriminate frequencies.
  • Electronic turtles/tortoises that drive toward or flee light, showing complex behaviour from simple connections.
  • The conjurer and the rabbit: explanation demystifies.

Key numbers: None in the notes.

So what: Apply the pencil-and-paper test to impressive AI. Expect explainability and surprise to trade off. A substrate's own dynamics are a failure mode. Opaque methods are justified only when they do what conventional methods cannot.

Ch 4. How to Psychoanalyse a Non-human Intelligence

Argument: Diagnose an organisation by checking whether its regulators have as much variety as what they regulate. Ashby's law of requisite variety is load-bearing: a system achieves stability only if every source of environmental variability is matched by equal or greater variety in the regulator.

Stories & evidence

  • The squirrel survival facility: squirrel-plus-cage as a black box (weight, body temperature, heart rate, ambient temperature, light/dark), a survival set, a regulator. Lighting is a one-bit switch; temperature is matched by a continuous heater or attenuated into "too hot/too cold" (a thermostat); a hundred cages need thermostats (amplification); staff and husbandry policies attenuate. "That is a squirrel farm, and it is also an organisation."
  • Ashby's homeostat: four compass needles acting as voltmeters; a dragged needle cycles through settings (a veto), a mid-range needle stops. Four inputs of thirty states each give 810,000 combinations, yet it reached stability quickly and recovered when disturbed.
  • Wiener's automated gunsight: ataxia (too weak, gun trails) and purpose tremor (too strong, oscillation).
  • Vehicle controls test: train (one handle), car (steering wheel), plane (joystick).
  • Rubik's Cube smashed into 26 sub-cubes as a failed split of a non-separable problem.
  • Beer's gibe about hiring the greatest geniuses to memorise the phone book.
  • Wiener vs Shannon on information: entropy with a negative sign vs unpredictability; British cyberneticians followed Wiener, hence "variety."

Key numbers: 810,000 combinations (4 inputs x 30 states) in the homeostat; one-bit lighting switch; twenty-six sub-cubes.

So what: Check requisite variety at every regulatory link before blaming people. Fix mismatches by attenuating input, amplifying the regulator through subsystems, or splitting separable problems. Prefer comparison to measurement. Every black-box boundary is an act of attenuation, so say what you decided not to look at. Match observation frequency to the rate variety is generated. The accountability sink is a variety amplifier, "a solution as much as a problem."

Ch 5. Cybernetics Without Diagrams

Argument: Any organisation capable of surviving indefinitely must contain five functions (operations, regulation, integration, intelligence, philosophy), each matched in information-handling capacity to the variety it faces, plus channels fast and legible enough to turn data into action. When a big system fails, find which function is missing, under-resourced or mismatched.

Stories & evidence

  • Analogies for the five systems: musicians, conductor, tour manager, artistic director and Elton John; or soldiers, quartermaster, battlefield commander, reconnaissance and field marshal. Identity as information management: a consistent identity lets you refuse Wagner's Ring cycle for an Elton John tour.
  • The 2008 crisis read cybernetically: a central bank as a System 1 of government with independence as its resource bargain. The 2000s named the calm ("Great Moderation," "NICE times," "Goldilocks economy") while a debt bubble and house-price spiral built. Forecasting (inflation forecast targeting) was here-and-now extended. Warnings in 2006-07 stayed data; Lehman's bankruptcy was the algedonic squeal. The root failure was System 5, an identity that defined certain information as none of their business.
  • Train driver's emergency brake as the model for the algedonic channel.
  • System 2/3 test: System 2 is the management everyone agrees is necessary; System 3 is the one people complain about.

Key numbers: Five systems; warnings in 2006-07.

So what: Diagnose by function, not org chart. Size System 3 to residual variety. Treat "problem child" units as unrecognised viable systems. Build System 4 around what is not yet relevant. Check channels for bandwidth, speed and translation capacity. Protect red handles. When 3 and 4 are chronically mismatched, look at System 5.

Intermission: Decerebrate Cats

Argument: An organisation that has stopped attending to some kinds of information looks alive but has lost the ability to act purposively; it survives only while its environment stays unchanged, and collapses at the first real shock.

Stories & evidence

  • The decerebrate cat: with its higher brain severed it still walks, rights itself, eats and grooms, but cannot generate its own responses to change and needs sheltering.
  • Beer's university example: teaching happens, terms start and end, accounts balance, but the capacity to decide what the institution is for has gone. A shock (funding regime change, demand collapse) leaves it with no function to respond.
  • Davies' corollary: if you see a company actively decerebrating itself, update your resume.

Key numbers: None in the notes.

So what: Judge health by what an organisation attends to, not whether operations run. Treat disappearing planning and horizon-scanning as an early warning. The crisis is deferred, never avoided.

Ch 6. Economics and How It Got That Way

Argument: Economics is best understood as a variety-engineering technology: a rhetoric and modelling style that attenuates society to price and quantity so it can always give a definite answer. That made it the identity-creating function (System 5) of modern governance and generates predictable blind spots.

Stories & evidence

  • Ricardo's England and Portugal: cloth costs 100 hours in England and 90 in Portugal; wine 120 and 80. Portugal is better at both, but relative prices (cloth worth nine-eighths of a barrel of wine in Portugal, five-sixths in England) make specialising in wine pay. Airtight and non-trivial (Samuelson could name no other proposition in the social sciences that was both). The vice is the leap to claims about real trade, where adding commodities, inputs, brands, firms, investment, strategy or noting that countries import goods similar to those they export lets you generate any conclusion.
  • Competitive-markets model of discrimination: "shows" it can't survive competition, so competition is treated as a substitute for anti-discrimination law.
  • Electricity example: the four conditions (commodity good, observable marginal cost curve, independent spot markets, negligible strategic interaction); marginal cost curve as the one concept engineers independently invented (a load balancing table).
  • Four sources of "market as computing fabric": Smith's invisible hand, Hayek's socialist calculation debate, post-war equilibrium proofs, financial-economics market efficiency.
  • Safety statement: "This aircraft has a faulty stall sensor which might cause it to crash" is not a statement about expected costs.
  • Economics' vocabulary: "ad hoc" as an insult; microfoundations, homo economicus, representative individual.

Key numbers: 100 and 90 labour-hours (cloth), 120 and 80 (wine); nine-eighths vs five-sixths; four conditions.

So what: Read any economic argument as an attenuation device and ask what it licensed you to stop thinking about. Separate tractability assumptions from assumptions that smuggle in the conclusion. Never infer optimality from a market outcome. Route information not expressible as expected cost (safety, red handles) through separate channels. Judge economics on the practical deficiencies of the systems it builds, not on moral failings of economists.

Ch 7. If You're So Rich, Why Aren't You Smart?

Argument: Managers are the System 1 of a structure whose higher functions are supplied by economists, but the channel is broken because economists don't speak accounting, the language of management. Inside firms, financial-reporting numbers built for one purpose get used for decisions they were not designed for, so companies hallucinate.

Stories & evidence

  • The skincare factory: bulk barrels for construction workers and small tubs for the beauty market at ten times the price, from essentially the same cream. Marketing as a period cost flatters the luxury line; fixed packaging cost allocated by direct labour penalises the bulk line. Consultants compare in-house manufacturing (carrying beauty overheads) with a cheap external supplier; manufacturing is sold; marketing and R&D costs don't vanish; two years later consultants explain the profit slump.
  • Chicken efficiency: a fast-food chain judged managers on the proportion of each bird sold; managers stopped frying an hour before closing, lost sales, and hit 100 per cent.
  • One death, three encodings: liver failure, mercury poisoning, murder.
  • Einstein reads the phone book: 1960s firms computerised existing paper bookkeeping instead of rethinking it; "the decision nobody made."
  • Consultants as accountability sinks and "brains for hire": renting middle-manager expertise costs the same hours at higher rates.
  • The Chandler pattern; Machiavelli's constraint (a prince not wise cannot be well advised).

Key numbers: Ten times the price (beauty tubs); 100 per cent chicken efficiency; one hour before closing.

So what: Ask what decision each number was collected for. Allocate a cost to a manager only if stopping the output would avoid it and the manager controls that part of the bargain. Disagreements over allocation are disagreements about the production process. Beat Ricardians with data collected for another purpose or an internal inconsistency. Budget for excess management capacity. "Learn the numbers by looking at the business, never the business by looking at the numbers."

Intermission: Meanwhile, in Chile

Argument: Cybersyn was not computerised central planning but a large-scale management-by-exceptions system built on the viable system model, and it was so badly out of scale to the Chilean economy that it could never have been a fair test.

Stories & evidence

  • Cybernet: several hundred repurposed telex machines (found idle in a government building) carrying production data, more reliable than phoned numbers and leaving a record. During a trucking strike it let the government monitor deliveries and secure essential supplies.
  • Cyberstride: statistical filter classifying departures as blip, trend change or new normal; the automated descendant of Beer's hand-drawn steelworks charts.
  • Operations Room: about a dozen managers with wall displays (hand-drawn slides projected; Beer said CRT flicker was distracting).
  • Checo: economic simulator, planned but never delivered.
  • Interventors placed in nationalised factories undercut devolved autonomy; Chile nationalised faster than it could manage.
  • The coup: ended the experiment; it didn't get to fail informatively.
  • Violence as a variety amplifier: one guard with a gun controls a prison.

Key numbers: Several hundred telex machines; about a dozen managers.

So what: Build the exception filter before the command centre. Compare channel capacity to environmental variety first. Expect reaction from the regulated. Cheap instrumentation can beat the war room. Design experiments that can fail legibly.

Ch 8. Enter Friedman

Argument: The Friedman doctrine solved a real crisis (corporations at the end of the 1960s had lost any sense of purpose amid an explosion of environmental variety) by supplying a single maximising goal and a personal accountability sink, at the price of denying that the organisation exists as a decision-making system. Debt and the leveraged buyout gave it teeth.

Stories & evidence

  • The doctrine's three moves: look through the corporation to individuals; substitute a "representative shareholder" black box; invite the executive to split into a person and a businessman. Social responsibility is "the moral equivalent of taxation."
  • Jensen and Meckling: managerial behaviour, agency costs, ownership structure (debt and stock options as the fix).
  • The buyout example: corporate jets, country club memberships, lavish expenses, obsolete product lines, cosy relationships with sclerotic customers. The firm puts up 10 per cent, borrows 90, buys the company, makes it borrow to repay the acquisition debt. Interest is tax-deductible where dividends are not. Perks stop; risk sits with workers, suppliers, customers and managers; limited liability caps the buyer's downside at 10 per cent.
  • "Fiduciary duty to maximise shareholder value": cited to Friedman, but courts have never found such a duty; semantic drift from increase to maximise and profits to shareholder value.
  • Efficient market hypothesis as ideology; Economic Value Added (Joel Stern); private equity's strong System 5.
  • Pre-emptive self-buyout and definition creep once wasteful targets ran out.
  • Capitalism vs managerialism: the unremarked class struggle of the 1970s-80s that managers lost.

Key numbers: 10 per cent equity / 90 per cent borrowed; downside capped at the initial 10 per cent.

So what: Ask what information a single-maximising-end doctrine licenses you to throw away. Read heavy debt as an information problem first. "Fiduciary duty" outside law is exhortation in costume. Look for the personal accountability sink. Structures beat individuals: neither Friedman nor Welch is the villain. Expect definition creep when legitimate targets run out.

Ch 9. The Morbid Symptoms

Argument: Having cut away the middle management and civil-service capacity that absorbed volatility, the corporate and political systems reversed the old bargain and made the working class the shock absorber. When that broke, the only channel left to the population was a one-bit scream, which is what populism is.

Stories & evidence

  • The Welch/GE model: always make the quarterly number; costs are controllable in a quarter, revenues not; layers of middle management go; annual rank-and-yank of the bottom 10 per cent kept for its threat; GE offset a one-off $2bn gain by closing factories and making over 1,000 people redundant; financial services grew until subjective estimates dominated earnings; the mortgage arm "jacked up the volume without controls" and misrepresented loan quality, ending in a $1.5bn Justice Department settlement.
  • Levy, Marx, Kalecki, Keynes, Friedman's natural rate / NAIRU: unemployment as variety attenuator, giving the Great Moderation.
  • Time inconsistency (Prescott and Kydland): independent central banks as Odysseus tied to the mast; read cybernetically as accountability channels working "too well."
  • Outsourcing as a one-bit channel: "going as anticipated" vs "it's stopped working."
  • Case and Deaton's deaths of despair; Marmot's Whitehall studies: grade predicts mortality independent of income, smoking and family history.
  • Allende's "el pueblo" as the System 5 box.
  • Pre-crisis blind spot: only government deficits monitored; private-sector debt unwatched.
  • Elections and polls: proportional systems carry more information than first-past-the-post; a monthly poll has a shorter lag than an annual one.

Key numbers: Bottom 10 per cent (rank and yank); $2bn one-off gain; over 1,000 redundancies; $1.5bn settlement; one bit.

So what: Before cutting "redundant" management, ask which boundary it sits at. Ask who absorbs volatility. Build bandwidth for "conditions are changing." Watch what the control system doesn't monitor. "If you consistently demand the impossible, you will inevitably get the unethical." Respond to the fact of the scream, not its content. Make recommendations.

Ch 10. What Is to Be Done?

Argument: Quieten the signal that drowns out all others by making anyone taking control of an operating company guarantee its debts, so corporate decision-making can return to viability rather than maximisation. Stop letting a maximising discipline sit at the top of governance, and build real channels for the decided-upon to signal intolerability.

Stories & evidence

  • Elizabeth Warren's eight-part private equity plan: only one point (guarantee the debts) is needed cybernetically. Limited liability is a resource bargain introduced for US joint-stock corporations in the 1820s, not a principle of natural justice; keep its original purpose for small non-controlling investors.
  • Galbraith's technostructure and Herbert Simon's behavioural theory of the firm: profits as a constraint, not a goal to be maximised.
  • Brian Eno's 77 Million Paintings: a purposive non-maximiser; businesses as artists, not paperclip maximisers.
  • Keynes' dentists: economists as competent technicians.
  • Transformer networks as variety amplifiers for two-way communication.
  • Beer's household dial (the original red-handle alert, never built beyond his son's shed prototype) and the Cwarel Isaf meeting with Brian Eno.
  • Oil company example for POSIWID.
  • Only cybernetic problems are soluble.

Key numbers: 8-part Warren plan, of which 1 point is needed; 1820s.

So what: Fix systems by closing the sink, not by writing rules that must out-vary the situations they govern. Set survival conditions, not maximisation targets. Pair every maximiser with a supervisor and a red handle. Demote economics to a competent technical trade. Use AI as a variety amplifier. Accept that robots will make decisions; repair feedback because people are less angry when listened to. "I blame the system" will have to be said literally.

Recurring Stories & Examples

  • Schiphol squirrels (Ch 1, 2, 4): the accountability sink and POSIWID in one case; the squirrel survival facility returns as the variety-engineering model in Ch 4 and as the permutation-maths reference in Ch 9.
  • Stafford Beer (Ch 2, 3i, 7i, 10): army unit, computing pond, Cybersyn, the household dial and Brian Eno.
  • Ashby's homeostat (Ch 2, 4): four needles, 810,000 states, regulation by veto.
  • Boeing and Fox News (Ch 3): systems whose output was harm with nobody deciding.
  • The 2008 crisis (Ch 5, 9): System 4 and 5 failure, algedonic squeal of Lehman, private-sector debt as blind spot.
  • Ricardo's England/Portugal (Ch 6, 7): the template of the Ricardian Vice, returning inside firms as accounting.
  • Jack Welch / GE (Ch 8, 9): rank and yank, making the numbers, outsourcing.
  • The leveraged buyout (Ch 8, 10): 10/90 financing, the debt klaxon, and the "guarantee the debts" fix.
  • Chile, 1973 (Intro, 7i, 8, 9): Cybersyn, the Chicago Boys, the coup and "el pueblo."
  • Decerebration (Ch 5, 5i, 7, 9): cutting System 4/5, middle management and planning.
  • Paperclip maximiser / maximisers going "bonkers" (Ch 3, 10).

This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends

2 markdown files

Quiz

This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends Quiz Book

This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends by Nicole Perlroth

How to use: Cover the answers, answer from memory (out loud or in writing), then check. Anything you miss is a section to reread. The book has 25 short chapters (Prologue plus Ch 1-24), so they are grouped 2-3 per section, each with short-answer (SA), true/false (T/F), and multiple-choice (MC) questions. A cumulative 10-question final exam is at the end. Questions are built from the study notes on the book, so they reflect that summary, not the book's own wording.

Section 1: Prologue, Ch 1, Ch 2 (Kyiv, Closet of Secrets, The Fucking Salmon)

Q1 (SA). Why does Perlroth call Ukraine a "test kitchen," and what does it mean when attacks on Ukraine slow down?

A: Russia used Ukraine to rehearse every tool (election malware, disinformation, media trapdoors, then grid attacks), a "cruel version of the scientific method": test a capability, demonstrate it, move on. When attacks slow, "that means they've moved on."

Q2 (MC). NotPetya is best described as:

a) a criminal ransomware gang's payday b) a state weapon of mass destruction wearing ransomware's mask c) a North Korean attack on Sony d) a bug in Microsoft's update system

A: b. No payment could recover the data. It hit Merck, Pfizer, Maersk, FedEx and even Russia's own Rosneft and Evraz, with $10 billion+ in damage.

Q3 (SA). What is the "vulnerability paradox" from the Prologue?

A: Ukraine survived partly because it was not fully automated (no Internet of Things, paper ballots counted by hand), while the US plugs in 127 devices a second and has the world's largest attack surface. At the NSA, offense outnumbers defense roughly 100 to 1. Connectivity is the exposure.

Q4 (T/F). In Ch 1, Perlroth found that the NSA's main method was cracking encryption algorithms. A: False. The algorithms "held up quite nicely." The NSA routed around encryption: a flawed random-number standard, paying RSA to make it the default, chip-factory backdoors planted by the CIA, and hacking Google and Yahoo servers before data was encrypted.

Q5 (SA). Define a zero-day and say why exploiting one is "God mode."

A: A software or hardware flaw with no existing patch; the vendor has had "zero days" to defend. Exploiting one is like having a spare key to a locked building that works no matter how vigilant the administrator is.

Q6 (MC). In Ch 2, the Italian exploit sellers' deflection ("talk about my salmon") became shorthand for:

a) the trade's refusal to say whom it sells to and whom it won't b) a food-safety scandal c) Stuxnet's code name d) a vendor ethics board

A: a. In the notes, a non-answer about buyers is the answer, since a seller with limits would state them.

Q7 (SA). What is "Langner's mirror argument"?

A: Stuxnet used seven zero-days to reach air-gapped centrifuge controllers and wreck roughly a fifth of Iran's centrifuges. The same techniques apply to power, water and chemical plants, and the largest concentration of vulnerable industrial systems is in the United States. A weapon built for one target becomes a template for everyone.

Section 2: Ch 3, Ch 4, Ch 5 (The Cowboy, The First Broker, Zero-Day Charlie)

Q1 (SA). How did John Watters start the public zero-day market, and how much did he pay for the company?

A: In 2002 he bought bankrupt iDefense for $10 and let two young researchers pay hackers for bugs, the first open bounty program. He sold it to Verisign for $40M in 2005.

Q2 (SA). Why did Microsoft's Trustworthy Computing memo make zero-days more valuable?

A: Gates's 2002 memo froze products, retrained ~10,000 developers, created a hacker hotline and Patch Tuesday. Microsoft bugs became rarer, so a remote Windows exploit went from pennies to six or seven figures. Scarcity made them expensive.

Q3 (MC). Why did iDefense lose out within about three years?

a) hackers stopped finding bugs b) secret government contractors paid far more for silence (e.g., $150,000 vs. $400) c) Microsoft sued it d) Verisign shut it down

A: b. Once secret buyers paid more for silence than defenders paid for disclosure, rational hackers hoarded.

Q4 (SA). In Ch 4, why does "Jimmy Sabien" say "access is king," and what did agencies actually want to buy?

A: Cyberweapons are useless without a way in. Agencies wanted the full stealthy kill chain (entry, beaconing, exfiltration, obfuscation, persistence). A reliable, invisible, persistent exploit, when all three appear together, is "ka-ching."

Q5 (T/F). Government agencies in the early market pooled purchases so they never paid twice for the same exploit. A: False. Agencies bought the same exploits two, three, four times because nothing is shared and each wants "the win" and the budget that follows.

Q6 (SA). What were a hacker's five options for a serious bug (Ch 5), and which one paid?

A: (1) Tell the vendor and risk threats or lawsuits; (2) keep and use it; (3) publish for credit and shame; (4) sell to a disclosure broker like iDefense for a few thousand; (5) sell to a government directly or via a broker for far more, with silence and no credit. Only option five paid.

Q7 (MC). "No More Free Bugs" (March 2009) is notable because:

a) vendors welcomed it b) it pushed hackers away from vendors and toward buyers the government men at the back of the room were happy to see c) it created HackerOne d) it ended the underground market

A: b. Charlie Miller, Dino Dai Zovi and Alexander Sotirov launched it after Google tried to get Miller fired for reporting an Android bug for free. The government men didn't clap: fewer patches, more sellers for them.

Section 3: Ch 6, Ch 7 (Project Gunman, The Godfather)

Q1 (SA). What did Project Gunman find, and what lesson did it teach?

A: In 1984 the NSA found Soviet magnetometer implants inside the US embassy's IBM Selectric typewriters, capturing keystrokes before encryption touched them. Lesson: encryption alone is never enough; ask where data exists in the clear.

Q2 (SA). Give the key numbers of the Selectric implants.

A: First implant traced to a 1976 shipment, found in 1984 (eight years undetected); 16 typewriters bugged (13 in Moscow, 3 in Leningrad); Deeley's internal bounty for finding it was $5,000.

Q3 (T/F). The Gunman team found the bug quickly because they started with the typewriters. A: False. They spent ten weeks on crypto gear because it was the "obvious" leak point; the typewriters were last. This is "searching where you expect the bug, not where it is."

Q4 (MC). The Soviets forbade their own staff from typing classified material on electric typewriters. The notes call this:

a) an unrelated policy b) a tell the Americans ignored: if an adversary protects itself against a vector, assume they weaponized it c) a Cold War myth d) proof the typewriters were clean

A: b.

Q5 (SA). What is Robert Morris Sr.'s complexity confidence threshold, and how does Gosler's Chaperon implant illustrate it?

A: Total confidence in 10,000 lines of code or fewer, zero confidence above 100,000. Gosler's Chaperon implant hid undetected in under 3,000 lines. "Even if you found something, you could never be confident you found everything."

Q6 (SA). What is "Before Gunman / After Gunman" and the "Willie Sutton principle"?

A: BG/AG is Gosler's periodization: before Gunman the US was "in la-la land"; after, it broke into "anything with a pulse." Willie Sutton: go where the data is; passive collection dies when data moves to endpoints.

Q7 (SA). What was the SIGINT Enabling Project, and what was Crypto AG?

A: SIGINT Enabling: a Snowden-leaked 2013 budget line for covertly influencing commercial product designs so they are exploitable while appearing secure. Crypto AG: a Swiss encryption vendor whose machines were spiked so US decoders could read clients' traffic, the NSA's own "Gunman."

Section 4: Ch 8, Ch 9 (The Omnivore, The Rubicon)

Q1 (SA). State the "intravenous principle."

A: Once the needle (implant) is in, the same access can replenish fluids or deliver a lethal dose. Reconnaissance implants are latent attack tools; ask what a payload swap would cost.

Q2 (MC). By 2013 the NSA's Genie program managed about:

a) 850 implants b) 8,500 implants c) 85,000 implants d) 8.5 million implants

A: c. Up four times in five years, targeting routers, switches, firewalls and encryption devices.

Q3 (SA). What is the "moral hazard of shared technology"?

A: In the Cold War the US and USSR ran different tech. Now everyone runs the same Windows, Oracle, Gmail and iPhones, so weakening a target's stack weakens your own. "There are no patents on vulnerabilities."

Q4 (SA). What was Keith Alexander's "third option," and why was Stuxnet designed to look like accidents?

A: Between failed diplomacy and airstrikes (World War III), a deniable, gradual cyberattack. The worm accelerated the failure rate centrifuges already had (~10%/yr), so Iranian engineers blamed themselves.

Q5 (SA). List what Stuxnet's chain used and what made its targeting precise.

A: Seven zero-days (four Microsoft, three Siemens), including a .LNK USB jump, printer-spooler spread, stolen Taiwanese code-signing certs and a Siemens Step 7 default password. It fired only on PLCs controlling clusters of exactly 164 centrifuges at 800-1100 Hz, designed with NSA legal review.

Q6 (T/F). Because Stuxnet's payload was tightly targeted, it could not spread beyond Natanz. A: False. Precision does not equal containment: the constraint on what it damaged did not constrain where it spread. It escaped in June 2010, and Biden's reaction was "Sonofabitch... they went too far."

Q7 (SA). What was Stuxnet's outcome, and what broader precedent did it set?

A: About 2,000 of 8,700 centrifuges destroyed by early 2010. Using a novel weapon legitimized it for everyone and lowered the bar for attacking critical infrastructure; Hayden called it "a whiff of August 1945."

Section 5: Ch 10, Ch 11 (The Factory, The Kurd)

Q1 (SA). What is NOBUS and when did it collapse?

A: "Nobody But Us": patch low-hanging fruit anyone could find, but keep exploits that supposedly only the US can weaponize. It collapsed from ~2012 as Russia and China honed the same router-hacking skills.

Q2 (SA). What is the "weaponization gap," and what did VRL sell?

A: Finding a bug is a pain, weaponizing it is a bigger pain, and making it 100% reliable is the biggest. VRL (five ex-TAO hackers, "Maryland Five," Reston) sold push-button exploits, using "fuzz farms" so exploits never crashed or tipped off targets.

Q3 (MC). Which describes the "contractor laundering layer"?

a) contractors cleaned up leaked code b) contractors bought in shadier foreign markets agencies couldn't legally touch and delivered finished tools via special contract vehicles with no provenance questions c) contractors audited the NSA d) contractors sold only to allies

A: b.

Q4 (SA). Give three numbers showing the US tilt toward offense in Ch 10.

A: NSA breaking-and-entering budget of $652M in 2013, twice its network-defense budget; a new $25.1M zero-day procurement line (~625 zero-days/year); Cyber Command budget from $2.7B to $7B by 2012. RAND: average zero-day secret ~7 years but ~25% found within 18 months.

Q5 (SA). What was the Wassenaar Arrangement and what did the US do about it?

A: A 1996 nonbinding export-control regime; surveillance tech was added to its control list in 2012-13. The US, uniquely, never adopted the changes into law after objections from EFF, Google and the pen-testing industry.

Q6 (SA). What is the "purple briefing / black briefing" (two folders) red flag?

A: Contractor tradecraft: a memorized defensive cover story (purple) for outsiders and the real offensive job (black). Evenden's red flags: you aren't told the job before arriving, two folders on day one, and a lot of money overseas.

Q7 (SA). Trace the mission creep in Evenden's Project Raven work.

A: Track ISIS, then show Qatar funds the Muslim Brotherhood, then hack Qatar, then FIFA officials, then a template spearphish for a UAE dissident journalist (the "template" got sent), then in late 2015 the US First Lady's staff. CyberPoint's fingerprints were on hacks of ~400 people; contracts then moved to the Emirati LLC Dark Matter.

Section 6: Ch 12, Ch 13 (Dirty Business, Guns for Hire)

Q1 (SA). What was Desautels' ethical model and why did it fail?

A: A reputation-driven broker who sold only to US entities and turned down ~85% of offers on gut instinct ("Bushido"). It failed because ethics don't survive an opaque market: sellers wriggled out of exclusivity, and one middleman defeated "US-only."

Q2 (SA). What did the Hacking Team breach (July 5, 2015) reveal?

A: Phineas Fisher dumped 420 GB of contracts, source code and email. Hacking Team sold Remote Control System to the FBI, DEA, CIA (via a front) and to Sudan ($1M), Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Russia, Morocco, Bahrain, Ethiopia and others, despite denials and a supposed human-rights veto board. Desautels' Flash zero-day was baked into it; he shut down his zero-day business.

Q3 (T/F). Perlroth's exposes of Hacking Team shrank the market by shaming buyers. A: False. They showed have-not governments what they were missing: "no intelligence agency on the planet was going to miss out." Sunlight doesn't always disinfect this market.

Q4 (MC). An "ideal state" broker-grade exploit needs:

a) a phishing email and a user click b) zero target interaction, about 98.9% reliability, and a "clean fail" c) a public CVE number d) a vendor patch

A: b.

Q5 (SA). What is "zero-click," and why does it matter for NSO's Pegasus?

A: Infection with no target interaction ("over the air stealth installation"). It removes the one defense users had (don't click). Pegasus also detects battery drain, shuts down and waits for WiFi to exfiltrate.

Q6 (SA). How was Pegasus first caught in the wild?

A: In August 2016 Ahmed Mansoor got suspicious texts and forwarded them to Citizen Lab's Bill Marczak instead of clicking. Marczak found a chain of three Apple zero-days with files naming "Pegasus" and "NSO." Lookout helped; Apple patched for ~1 billion users. Pegasus was traced to 67 servers, 400+ targets, operators in 45+ countries.

Q7 (SA). What does the "AK-47 defense" and the Mexico case tell you about vendor ethics committees?

A: "When you're selling AK-47s, you can't control how they'll be used once they leave the loading docks." NSO had never been denied an export license; in Mexico Pegasus hit soda-tax advocates, anticorruption activists, lawyers for the 43 disappeared students and journalist Carmen Aristegui and her 16-year-old son. Ethics committees were marketing, not safeguards.

Section 7: Ch 14, Ch 15, Ch 16 (Aurora, Bounty Hunters, Going Dark)

Q1 (SA). What is the "Fog of Peace" and how did it matter in Operation Aurora?

A: Grosse's inversion of the fog of war: so many benign alarms that a real nation-state attack hides in them, and the bias is toward the innocent explanation ("probably another intern"). At Google, the intern's first instinct nearly buried the fastest attack the company had seen.

Q2 (SA). What did China want in Aurora, and what was Google's response?

A: Google's source code (permanent access) and dissidents' Gmail accounts (the Five Poisons). Google confiscated machines, reset every password, redirected Google.cn to Hong Kong, and on Jan 12, 2010 became the first US company to publicly name China. Motto: "Never again."

Q3 (T/F). Google's stand against China proved lasting: the company never reconsidered the Chinese market. A: False. Within a year executives pushed re-entry; later came Dragonfly (secret censored search) and a Beijing AI lab. Principle eroded against market size.

Q4 (SA). What are Moussouris' three hacker motivations, and how did Microsoft apply them?

A: Compensation, recognition, and "intellectual happiness." If you can't win on money, win on the other two. Microsoft scoped its bounty to beta IE/Windows (June 2013 pilot, permanent that November) so defense didn't bid against government offense.

Q5 (MC). Zerodium's published price list included:

a) $80K Chrome, $100K Android, $500K iPhone, up to $1M-$2.5M for zero-click/remote jailbreaks b) $5 per bug c) a flat $10,000 rate d) no published prices

A: a. Google's own leet-themed bounties started at $1,337 and reached $1.5M for a full Android remote jailbreak by 2020.

Q6 (SA). What was Muscular, and why did the smiley face matter?

A: An NSA-GCHQ man-in-the-middle on Google and Yahoo internal data-center links (444,743 Yahoo address books grabbed in one day). A hand-drawn smiley face on the slide turned an ambiguous diagram into a declaration of war; intent, not just capability, escalates.

Q7 (SA). Describe the San Bernardino outcome and Project Zero's doctrine.

A: The FBI sought an order forcing Apple to write backdoored software; Cook refused ("the equivalent of cancer"). A week before trial the DOJ dropped the case after buying a zero-day for $1.3M. Project Zero (Aug 2014) attacks the whole ecosystem and publishes bugs after a 90-day vendor deadline, trading patch-lag risk for long-term hardening.

Section 8: Ch 17, Ch 18 (Cyber Gauchos, Perfect Storm)

Q1 (SA). What does "atado con alambre" explain about Argentine hackers?

A: "Held together with wire": MacGyver resourcefulness born of scarcity. The "embargo on cool shit" forces reverse-engineering to the metal, producing deep exploitation skill, while US engineers "skim the surface."

Q2 (MC). Ivan Arce's summary of selling to buyers outside the West: "A guy from the NSA and a guy from Iran show up with big bags of cash..."

a) "...you call the police." b) "...do you perform an ethical analysis? Or do you weigh the bags?" c) "...you sell to neither." d) "...you auction publicly."

A: b.

Q3 (SA). Why do brokers approach a hacker after he burns an exploit onstage?

A: They are buying the researcher's relationship and future work "for a rainy day," not the burned exploit.

Q4 (SA). Why did Alfredo Ortega, the Cyber Gaucho, refuse to sell?

A: Not from morals ("I don't think spying is bad") but survival: "It's like being a physicist in the 1930s with the atomic bomb. You'd get killed."

Q5 (SA). What is the plagiarized-weapon boomerang?

A: Shamoon (Aug 2012) wiped 30,000 Saudi Aramco computers and was essentially copied from the US/Israeli code used months earlier on Iran's oil networks. Using a cyberweapon teaches the target to rebuild it cheaply.

Q6 (SA). What did the Bowman Dam scare teach?

A: "The first assessment is almost always wrong." Officials nearly retaliated believing Iran was in a 245-ft Oregon dam; it was a 20-ft New York flood-control dam with its sluice gates disconnected for maintenance.

Q7 (T/F). The "glass houses" problem meant the US could demand a ban on all government hacking. A: False. The NSA does exactly that, so the US could only draw the line at commercial IP theft (the 2015 Xi-Obama deal, followed by a ~90% drop in Chinese industrial attacks for ~18 months).

Section 9: Ch 19, Ch 20 (The Grid, The Russians Are Coming)

Q1 (SA). What is the tell that an intrusion is pre-positioning for attack rather than espionage?

A: It targets control systems with "die"/"turnoff" commands. Hultquist: the Russians were "not there to collect intelligence on the price of gas."

Q2 (SA). Describe the December 23, 2015 Ukraine blackout.

A: Sandworm (GRU Unit 74455) hijacked SCADA, an invisible cursor opened breakers at 30 substations, changed the operator's password, killed emergency phone lines and backup power. 230,000 people were in the dark for about 6 hours: a message, "We can torch you."

Q3 (MC). Sandworm's BlackEnergy evolved from:

a) a $40 DDoS tool (Cr4sh) b) Stuxnet source code c) a Chinese Aurora payload d) Hacking Team's toolkit

A: a. It was delivered in harmless-looking modules over months, only becoming a weapon once assembled.

Q4 (SA). State the VEP and why it tilts toward hoarding.

A: The Vulnerabilities Equities Process weighs keeping vs. disclosing a zero-day (widespread technology favors disclosure). With vast offense budgets it "always weighs more heavily on hoarding." EternalBlue was withheld about 7 years, a decision Daniel came to regret.

Q5 (SA). What did Heartbleed show?

A: That open-source ubiquity is not open-source security: OpenSSL secured millions of systems but was maintained by one engineer on $2,000/year.

Q6 (SA). What was the Russian aim in 2016, and how did the IRA operate?

A: Not necessarily a Trump win but bruising Clinton and casting doubt on legitimacy. The Internet Research Agency amplified real divisions (Heart of Texas vs. United Muslims of America, "Woke Blacks"), reaching 126M Facebook users and 288M Twitter impressions.

Q7 (T/F). Podesta's email theft required a sophisticated zero-day. A: False. Fancy Bear phished him with a fake Google password alert; an aide's "legitimate/illegitimate" typo ("This is a legitimate email") helped hand over 60,000 emails.

Section 10: Ch 21, Ch 22 (The Shadow Brokers, The Attacks)

Q1 (SA). Why is "capabilities vs. descriptions" the key distinction between Snowden and the Shadow Brokers?

A: Snowden leaked descriptions of programs; the Shadow Brokers leaked working exploit code ("the keys to the kingdom"). Losing the weapon is far worse than losing the manual.

Q2 (SA). Why did the leak expose NOBUS as false?

A: Many exploits hit bugs anyone could find in Cisco, Fortinet and other firewalls securing American networks, yet the NSA held them for years instead of disclosing.

Q3 (MC). The NSA tipped Microsoft to patch EternalBlue (MS17-010):

a) years earlier b) a month before the April 2017 dump, with attribution left blank c) after WannaCry d) never

A: b. Infections hit 400,000 machines within two weeks of the dump.

Q4 (SA). Compare WannaCry and NotPetya.

A: WannaCry (May 12, 2017): North Korea's Lazarus group, 200,000+ orgs in 150 countries in 24 hours, ~50 UK hospitals hit, botched (under $200K collected), stopped by an ~$11 kill switch (Marcus Hutchins). NotPetya (June 2017): Russia's GRU wiper, via M.E.Doc supply chain, EternalBlue + EternalRomance + MimiKatz, $10B+ damage.

Q5 (T/F). NotPetya was confined to Ukraine because it was delivered through a Ukrainian tax program. A: False. "The internet has no borders": any company with even one Ukraine-connected machine was hit (Maersk, Merck, FedEx, Mondelez, Chernobyl's monitors, Russia's Rosneft). Insurers invoked the war exemption.

Q6 (SA). What does "patch exists does not equal patched" mean?

A: A patch (MS17-010, March 2017) doesn't protect legacy systems: critical infrastructure runs Windows XP, patches need approval and rare maintenance windows, and automated patching is a "no-no."

Q7 (SA). What was the U.S. official line after WannaCry, and what did Brad Smith propose?

A: Bossert: the tools were ours but we're not responsible for how others use them, while quickly naming North Korea (and a NotPetya op-ed blaming Russia was killed). Smith proposed a "Digital Geneva Convention": no peacetime attacks on civilians, hospitals, the grid or elections, no IP theft, mutual response. Ironically, as he spoke, Pentagon hackers were planting logic bombs in the Russian grid.

Section 11: Ch 23, Ch 24 (The Backyard, Epilogue)

Q1 (SA). What does "Eternal is the perfect name" mean?

A: A leaked exploit persists wherever patching lags, which is most civic infrastructure. EternalBlue hit Allentown, a San Antonio jail and Baltimore ($18M cleanup) even though it was long patched.

Q2 (SA). Explain "NOBUS is dead twice over."

A: Adversaries independently steal your tools (Legion Amber, a Chinese group that took the NSA's exploits ~a year before the Shadow Brokers) and buy equivalent capability (the Gulf, e.g., Crowdfense at $3M for iPhone exploits).

Q3 (MC). The "perception hack" is:

a) altering vote totals b) small, amplifiable attacks that erode confidence in election legitimacy c) a phishing technique d) a type of ransomware

A: b. Cheaper and more corrosive than altering votes; the gravest 2020 interference came from within.

Q4 (SA). What did the nuclear-plant intrusions show?

A: Russia inside Wolf Creek (Kansas) and Cooper (Nebraska), mapping for a future attack; at Saudi Arabia's Petro Rabigh an attack switched off safety locks, the last step before an explosion.

Q5 (SA). What is Perlroth's bottom-line verdict on the "Cyber Pearl Harbor"?

A: Not a single unseen event but a decade-long, normalized plague: "death by a thousand hacks."

Q6 (SA). Give four elements of the epilogue's remediation plan.

A: Examples: "move slowly and fix your shit" and security from inception; "build it like it's broken" (compartmentalize crown jewels, Apple sandboxing); CHERI chip redesign; MFA and fast patching (98% of attacks start with phishing); keep elections offline with paper trails and protect voter rolls; reinstate the cybersecurity coordinator and mandate critical-infrastructure standards.

Q7 (SA). How should the VEP be reformed?

A: Add civilian agencies (HHS, Transportation); move oversight from NSA to DHS with IG/PCLOB audits; set expiration dates; take credit for disclosures (GCHQ's BlueKeep); close the NDA loophole for purchased zero-days; pass the stalled PATCH Act. Also use US buying power to demand exclusivity plus patching, and set red lines (hospitals, elections, planes, nuclear plants).

Cumulative Final Exam (10 Questions)

Q1 (SA). State the book's central thesis in two sentences.

A: The US spawned and bankrolls the global zero-day market and built the most powerful cyber arsenal, but because the world runs the same technology it could neither keep those weapons secret nor defend its home front. Hoarding boomeranged (EternalBlue into WannaCry, NotPetya and attacks on US towns, hospitals, the grid and nuclear plants): "It wasn't Ukraine. It was us."

Q2 (SA). Why does defense lose the bidding war for bugs, and what is the counter-strategy?

A: Governments pay far more to keep holes open than vendors pay to close them (a Chrome bug earns ~3x more on the government market; iPhone jailbreaks reach $2-2.5M). Compete on recognition, openness and intellectual challenge, and scope bounties to beta software (Google, Microsoft, HackerOne, Project Zero).

Q3 (MC). Which pair best illustrates "pre-encryption capture / hack the endpoint"?

a) Gunman typewriters and NSO's Pegasus b) Stuxnet and Shamoon c) iDefense and Zerodium d) Aurora and OPM

A: a (also Muscular). Encryption is beaten where the data sits in the clear.

Q4 (SA). Name three boomerang examples where using or building a weapon came back on the US or its allies.

A: Stuxnet escaped and inspired Shamoon (copied code); the Shadow Brokers dump of EternalBlue powered WannaCry and NotPetya; Legion Amber stole NSA exploits; Snowden and Stuxnet were blueprints that globalized capability.

Q5 (SA). What is the intravenous principle and which two chapters' stories show it?

A: Every espionage implant is a latent weapon since the payload can be swapped from surveillance to destruction. Ch 8 (Genie's ~85,000 implants) and Ch 9 (Stuxnet crossing from espionage to attack); also Ch 19's Sandworm pre-positioning.

Q6 (T/F). Vendor ethics boards, export approvals and "no-trace" branding are reliable safeguards in the spyware trade. A: False. They are marketing, not safeguards (Hacking Team's veto board, NSO never denied a license). The only question that matters is who the end user is and whom you won't sell to; a non-answer ("the fucking salmon") is the answer.

Q7 (SA). Why is attribution risky, and what examples does the book give?

A: It is spoofable and the first assessment is usually wrong: Bowman Dam near-retaliation, the Shadow Brokers' mock-Russian English, Guccifer 2.0's Cyrillic metadata and Google-Translate Romanian, NotPetya disguised as ransomware.

Q8 (MC). According to the book, what share of attacks start with phishing or stolen credentials rather than zero-days, and what is the top defense?

a) 10%, firewalls b) 50%, antivirus c) 98%, multifactor authentication plus long unique passwords and fast patching d) 98%, air gaps only

A: c.

Q9 (SA). What do Ukraine (Russia's test kitchen) and Xinjiang (China) have in common, and why does it matter?

A: Adversaries rehearse their best tools on a soft proxy (their own people or a neighbor) before turning them on the West: "the Chinese use their best tools against their own people first... Then they turn those tools on us." Watch the testing ground.

Q10 (SA). If you were advising the NSA on a newly found wormable bug in a widely used Microsoft protocol, what would the book tell you to do and why?

A: Disclose it now. Score prevalence x reliance x severity; wormable plus widely deployed is a disclose-now case. NOBUS is dead (others will find or steal it), holding EternalBlue about 7 years was indefensible by the VEP's own criteria, and a stockpile is a single point of catastrophic failure.

Arguments & Evidence

This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: Key Arguments, Stories & Evidence by Chapter

Nicole Perlroth

Each section covers a chapter or a group of closely related chapters and has: Argument (the claim), Stories & evidence (what the book uses to support it), Key numbers, and So what (the lesson). Built from the full text of the chapter files in the perlroth-how-the-world-ends skill, so it reflects that summary of the book (journalism reported through about 2020), not the book's own wording. Chapter numbering follows the skill (Prologue = Ch 0).

The Big Arc in One Paragraph

The Prologue and Ch 1-2 open with Ukraine as Russia's test kitchen, the Snowden documents, and the secretive trade that supplies the NSA's tools. Ch 3-5 trace how a public bounty market for zero-days was outbid by secret government buyers. Ch 6-10 show why the NSA turned to offense (Gunman, Gosler, TAO, Stuxnet) and how contractors industrialized weaponization. Ch 11-13 follow the trade as it escaped US control into mercenary and spyware firms. Ch 14-16 describe the tech industry's defensive turn (Aurora, bounties, Project Zero, the crypto wars). Ch 17-20 show the market globalizing and the boomerang beginning: Iran, China, North Korea and Russia learn and strike, from the Ukraine blackout to the 2016 election. Ch 21-23 deliver the payoff: the Shadow Brokers leak EternalBlue, which powers WannaCry and NotPetya and then hits American towns, hospitals and nuclear plants. Ch 24 offers a remediation plan: build as if already broken, fix the human layer, and rebalance policy from hoarding to defense.

Prologue, Ch 1, Ch 2: Kyiv; Closet of Secrets; The Fucking Salmon

Argument: The country with the greatest offensive cyber advantage is also the most vulnerable, and its advantage rests on a trade in zero-days that nobody will explain. Ukraine shows what is coming; the Snowden trove shows the NSA wins by going around encryption; the sellers' silence shows the market's structure.

Stories & evidence

  • Ukraine as test kitchen: five years of Russian attacks (2014 election malware, disinformation, grid blackouts in 2015 and 2016) culminating in NotPetya on Constitution Day, June 27, 2017. Ukrainian experts called it a cruel version of the scientific method.
  • Attribution by resources: the grid attack was routed through Singapore, the Netherlands and Romania and delivered in benign pieces, yet sophistication and no profit motive pointed to a state.
  • NotPetya as disguise: it mimicked Petya ransomware, but no payment could recover data. It hit Merck, Pfizer, Maersk, FedEx, a Cadbury factory in Tasmania and Russia's own Rosneft and Evraz; Chernobyl's 2,500 computers went dark in seven minutes.
  • Ukraine's armor was backwardness: no Internet of Things, paper ballots counted by hand; the US built the "world's largest attack surface."
  • The closet (Ch 1): Perlroth worked the Snowden documents in a windowless Times storage closet in 2013. The NSA lobbied standards bodies for a flawed random-number formula, paid RSA to make it the default, had the CIA plant chip-factory backdoors, and hacked Google and Yahoo servers before encryption.
  • Hints of a market: references to "commercial partners" implied a gray market of brokers and contractors; Mariner 1 (a missing hyphen destroyed a $150M spacecraft) and a $50 hotel-lock hack illustrate flaws everywhere.
  • The salmon dinner (Ch 2): at a 2013 industrial-security dinner in Miami, Italian exploit sellers Luigi Auriemma and Donato Ferrante deflected the question of whom they sell to. Ralph Langner, who first attributed Stuxnet to the US and Israel, called them mercenaries.
  • Langner's mirror argument: Stuxnet used seven zero-days to wreck roughly a fifth of Iran's centrifuges; the same techniques apply to US power, water and chemical plants.

Key numbers: NotPetya $10B+ (Merck and FedEx ~$1B each), 80% of Ukraine's computers wiped; 127 devices plugged in per second in the US; NSA offense roughly 100 to 1 over defense; seven zero-days in Stuxnet; seven years to answer the book's questions.

So what: Treat a neighbor's blackouts as rehearsal footage for your own. Use profit motive as the first attribution filter. Ask "who else has this, and where did it come from?" rather than "is the NSA spying?" And treat a seller's refusal to name buyers as the answer.

Ch 3-5: The Cowboy; The First Broker; Zero-Day Charlie

Argument: The public bounty market (iDefense) and the vendors' hostility to researchers pushed hackers toward secret government buyers, who paid far more for silence. Secrecy is a precondition of a zero-day's value, so the trade resists exposure, and "No More Free Bugs" accelerated the shift.

Stories & evidence

  • John Watters and iDefense (Ch 3): a Texas investor with no computer background bought bankrupt iDefense for $10 in 2002 and let two researchers pay hackers for bugs, the first open bounty program. Early hunters included Tamer Sahin ($75 = a month's rent) and Greg McManus, a New Zealand sheep farmer.
  • Vendor hostility: Microsoft called disclosure "information anarchy"; Oracle's security chief called bounties immoral.
  • Trustworthy Computing: Gates's 2002 memo (after Code Red, Melissa, ILOVEYOU, Nimda) froze products, retrained ~10,000 developers, and created Patch Tuesday. Microsoft bugs became scarce, hence valuable.
  • Priced out: mystery contractors offered $150,000 for bugs iDefense paid $400 for; iDefense's per-bug price rose $400 to $4,000 to $50,000 and still lost. Watters sold to Verisign for $40M (2005) after putting in $7M.
  • Jimmy Sabien (Ch 4): a pseudonymous Beltway broker explains access is king, agencies want the full kill chain, firmware persistence survives wipes, and agencies bought the same exploit two to four times (he once told four agencies to go to lunch together). The Grugq's Forbes interview posing with a bag of cash halved his business.
  • Cash-and-trust market: hotel-room demos, Israeli middlemen with $500K in cash, Western Union; Watters's verdict was dark markets are inefficient and prices only climb.
  • Charlie Miller (Ch 5): ex-NSA analyst sold a Linux zero-day for $50,000 after an $80,000 ask was accepted "too quickly" elsewhere and the exploit failed on the target variant. He defied four NSA officials who flew to St. Louis, and published the first public account of the government's prices ("The Legitimate Vulnerability Market," Carnegie Mellon talk with a redacted $50,000 check).
  • No More Free Bugs (March 2009): after Google BCC'd Miller's boss over a free Android exploit, Miller, Dino Dai Zovi and Alexander Sotirov told hackers to stop reporting for free. The government men at the back did not clap: fewer patches, more sellers for them.

Key numbers: $10 purchase; $40M sale; $75 early bounty; $400 / $150,000 gap; ~$1M for ten exploits and ~$50K for a Windows bug in the mid-1990s; post-9/11 cyber spending up 50%+ in five years; over a hundred contractors, "probably only a dozen that know what they're doing"; $50,000 Linux exploit; prices cited 2006-07 ranged $60-250K.

So what: Whoever pays most for a bug decides whether it gets fixed. Punishing researchers is a subsidy to the underground. Government markets are cash-based, trust-based and inefficient, which drives prices up and leaves buyers unable to guarantee exclusivity.

Ch 6-7: Project Gunman; The Godfather

Argument: The NSA's zero-day appetite is a reaction to a 1984 shock: an adversary can capture data before encryption touches it, and beyond a few thousand lines of code no one can guarantee a system is clean. That drove the pivot from passive interception to "hacking the endpoints."

Stories & evidence

  • Gunman (Ch 6): Reagan-approved 1984 operation (Walter Deeley) to replace every piece of electrical equipment at the Moscow embassy and examine the old gear at Fort Meade. The NSA tagged 250 replacement typewriters, shipped under armed escort; the Soviets "coincidentally" disabled the elevator so ten tons went up by hand.
  • The search: ten weeks on crypto gear and fax/teletypes found nothing. On July 23, 1984 one analyst noticed an extra coil in a Selectric power switch; X-ray revealed a magnetometer implant that converted keystroke mechanics into magnetic disturbances and radio-burst data.
  • Warning signs ignored: an antenna in the embassy chimney; Soviets forbade their own staff from using electric typewriters for classified work.
  • Gosler (Ch 7): Sandia scientist, founding director of the CIA's Clandestine Information Technology Office (1996). Chaperon studies (1985): subverters vs. evaluators; his implants (one used Zork text to leak secret variables) were never found by evaluators; in Chaperon 2 only Gosler found the new implant among ~100 engineers.
  • Complexity threshold: Morris Sr. (1987) said total confidence at 10,000 lines or fewer, none above 100,000. Linux grew from 176K to 15M lines, F-35 8M, Vista 50M.
  • Historical warnings: Thompson's "Reflections on Trusting Trust" (1984), Ware (1967) and Anderson (1972) reports.
  • Crypto AG and SIGINT Enabling: vendors spiked or influenced so the US could read traffic; "complete enabling" of two VPN chip makers.
  • Adversary tiers I-VI: V-VI spend years and billions inserting zero-days into the global supply chain.

Key numbers: 1976 first implant, found 1984 (eight years); 16 bugged typewriters (13 Moscow, 3 Leningrad); $5,000 bounty; 250 typewriters; Gosler implant under 3,000 lines; Sandia funding $500K (1990) to $50M (1995).

So what: Ask where data exists in the clear. Read an adversary's defensive habits as intelligence about their offense. Verification does not scale with code size, so design assuming implants exist, and red-team your own detection by planting implants and measuring whether evaluators find them. Every capability the US built to exploit endpoints can be built to exploit ours.

Ch 8-9: The Omnivore; The Rubicon

Argument: After 9/11 the NSA industrialized hacking into near-indiscriminate global collection, creating a moral hazard (backdoors in shared technology are backdoors into America), and then Stuxnet crossed from espionage to physical destruction, proving a weapon built from zero-days cannot be kept in the box.

Stories & evidence

  • TAO and the ROC: jeans-and-T-shirt hackers on 24/7 shifts at Fort Meade; recruits arrived by unmarked bus with red "uncleared" badges; ~$40K starting salary.
  • Genie and the assembly line: ~85,000 implants by 2013; units for finding bugs, honing implants, reaching hard targets, and "fourth-party collection" piggybacking on others' hacks.
  • Operation Shotgiant: NSA penetration of Huawei's HQ from 2007, used to reach Huawei's customers.
  • Weak controls: a dozen LOVEINT cases were demoted, none prosecuted; FISA court approved 1,748 of 1,789 applications unchanged (2012); the 2008 Russian-seeded USB incident led the Pentagon to superglue USB ports.
  • Stuxnet (Ch 9): Keith Alexander's "third option" for Bush. Joint operation Olympic Games (NSA, Unit 8200, CIA, Mossad, energy labs). The worm crossed the air gap via a human with a thumb drive, spread through a chain of seven zero-days with stolen Taiwanese certs, used Step 7's default password, and fired only on 164-centrifuge clusters.
  • The replay trick: like looping security footage, it fed monitors normal readings for 13 days, then spun rotors to 1400 Hz and down to 2 Hz on a 27-day cycle.
  • Escape and exposure: left Natanz in June 2010 (leading theory: an Israeli-added spreading mechanism; Biden: "Sonofabitch... they went too far"). Kaspersky, Symantec, Microsoft and Langner reverse-engineered it; Langner's TED talk named the US.
  • Hayden's frame: "a whiff of August 1945."

Key numbers: ~85,000 implants (4x in five years, 3/4 in Iran, Russia, China, North Korea); 1,748 of 1,789 FISA approvals; 500 KB worm, 50x larger than anything seen, 100x the Apollo 11 code; ~2,000 of 8,700 centrifuges destroyed; ~10%/yr baseline failure; 164 centrifuges, 800-1100 Hz; declassification set for 2039.

So what: Every surveillance implant is an attack capability with a deferred payload. Depth (kernel, firmware) beats breadth. When you and your adversary run the same technology, every secret exploit is a liability you carry for them. Precision does not equal containment; using a novel weapon legitimizes it for everyone.

Ch 10-11: The Factory; The Kurd

Argument: Offense-over-defense spending and contractor laundering created a private weaponization industry; then the trade escaped American control, as US-trained talent flowed to repressive governments and the US declined to regulate exports.

Stories & evidence

  • NOBUS: keep exploits supposedly only the US can weaponize (Hayden's "four acres of supercomputers" test); collapsed from ~2012 as Russia and China caught up.
  • VRL (Ch 10): five ex-TAO "Maryland Five" left in 2008 for autonomy, built Vulnerability Research Labs in Reston, kept secret 12 years; acquired by Computer Sciences Corp. in 2010. They commissioned foreign hackers (Argentina, Malaysia, Italy, Australia, France, Singapore), weaponized in fuzz farms, and delivered via "special contract vehicles." Perlroth's reporting hit walls (contracts booked as "$2.9M for computer peripheral equipment").
  • Turbine and the Spiegel catalog: Turbine to manage millions of implants autonomously; catalog items such as Surlyspawn (keystrokes off air-gapped machines, the digital Gunman).
  • Burn economics: multimillion-dollar zero-days are "virtually never deployed in anger."
  • Sinan Eren (Ch 11): Kurdish hacktivist, Immunity Inc.'s second employee (founder Dave Aitel, whose refusal to name customers is another "fucking salmon"). He quit in 2009 after a Turkish general demanded personal training; his homemade ethic (cross-reference Amnesty reports, sell only to high-scoring governments) was individual and unenforceable.
  • Wassenaar: surveillance tech added in 2012-13; US never adopted it.
  • Project Raven (Ch 11): David Evenden went to Abu Dhabi in 2014 for 2-4x salary; the two folders (purple vs. black briefing); mission creep from ISIS to Qatar, FIFA, a London journalist (the Rori Donaghy email), and the US First Lady's staff in late 2015. He refused to move to Dark Matter and tipped the FBI.

Key numbers: $652M offense (2x defense) in 2013; $25.1M zero-day line (~625 zero-days/yr); Cyber Command $2.7B to $7B, staff 900 to 14,000; RAND: ~7-year average secrecy, ~25% found in 18 months; $1.7B pen-testing industry; ~400 victims of CyberPoint hacks; Wassenaar 1996.

So what: NOBUS is a wasting asset. The valuable work is reliable weaponization. Contractors let agencies buy where they legally can't, removing accountability. Self-regulation doesn't hold; offensive contracts drift from terrorists to whoever the client dictates. Two folders and a hidden job description are red flags.

Ch 12-13: Dirty Business; Guns for Hire

Argument: In an opaque market, personal ethics and vendor ethics committees cannot survive money and middlemen. Spyware makers hand nation-state phone surveillance to any government with a seven-figure budget, and abuse follows.

Stories & evidence

  • Adriel Desautels (Ch 12): Boston broker (Netragard; motto "We Protect You From People Like Us"). Origin sale: a $16,000 joke price for an MP3 zero-day. He accepted ~15% of offers, enforced exclusivity with 3x pay and NDAs, and cited "Bushido." Exclusivity eroded to "2-3 months, then non-exclusive."
  • The collapse: his Adobe Flash zero-day went to Hacking Team via a trusted US buyer's "friendly" Italian client. On July 5, 2015 Phineas Fisher dumped 420 GB; Desautels found his exploit in spyware sold to Sudan, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopia and others and shut down his zero-day business.
  • Hacking Team: customers included the FBI, DEA, CIA (via a front), Sudan ($1M), Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Russia, Morocco, Bahrain; it dropped Sudan and Russia only in 2014. Coverage of its abuses served as an advertisement to have-not governments.
  • NSO and Pegasus (Ch 13): founded 2008 by Unit 8200 alumni Shalev Hulio and Omri Lavie; pivoted to surveillance after the FBI's 2011 "going dark" testimony; Francisco Partners bought control for ~$120M (2014). Zero-click, "room tap," and battery-conscious design.
  • Ahmed Mansoor: the "million-dollar dissident," hit by Hacking Team, Gamma, then a three-zero-day Safari Pegasus chain; he forwarded the texts to Citizen Lab instead of clicking. Sentenced in 2018 to 10 years.
  • Mexico: soda-tax advocates, anticorruption activists, lawyers for the 43 disappeared students, journalist Carmen Aristegui and her 16-year-old son; lures escalated to "your daughter was in an accident."

Key numbers: ~98.9% reliability and "clean fail"; Windows/Exchange remote $100K-$250K, urgent $500K-$1M; broker cut 3%-60%; 420 GB leak; Pegasus $500K install + $650K for 10 phones; ~1 billion users patched; 67 servers, 400+ targets, 45+ countries.

So what: Weaponized exploits are defined by silence (zero interaction, near-perfect reliability, clean failure). Exclusivity over copyable code is trust, not control. Do due diligence on the buyer; "we only sell to friendlies" dies at the first middleman. Once spyware ships, abuse is a matter of when. Independent watchdogs and a target who doesn't click are the real detection.

Ch 14-16: Aurora; Bounty Hunters; Going Dark

Argument: Aurora and Snowden pushed the tech industry, not the government, to the front line of defense. Google named China, bounties and Project Zero tried to drain the exploit supply, and Silicon Valley turned on the NSA over Muscular and the FBI's backdoor demand.

Stories & evidence

  • Aurora (Ch 14): China's 2009 breach (Legion Yankee) of Google via an IE zero-day on a Taiwan server delivered by a "Go Kill Yourself" chat link to Beijing staff. The goals were source code and dissidents' Gmail (the Five Poisons). The intern's "probably another intern" reflex nearly buried it; the Fog of Peace.
  • Response: Adkins, Grosse, Marquis-Boire, Brin, and Mandiant; "Upchuck Hour"; 250 engineers sleeping on campus; machines confiscated, passwords reset, Google.cn redirected to Hong Kong, public naming on Jan 12, 2010. "Never again," then Dragonfly within a year.
  • Bounties (Ch 15): Google's leet bounties ($1,337, $31,337), Facebook's no-cap approach, Microsoft's beta bounty through Moussouris' two-year data campaign (June 2013 pilot, first payout to a Google engineer, permanent in November). HackerOne (2014, Rice, Moussouris, the Three Dutchmen, $9M from Benchmark). Zerodium's price list from Chaouki Bekrar after Vupen lost its export license.
  • Pentagon and OPM: Hack the Pentagon (2016, 1,400+ hackers; a Synack hacker breached classified networks in under 4 hours); the OPM breach (~1M+ federal employees' data, fingerprints) spurred action.
  • Muscular (Ch 16): NSA-GCHQ interception of Google and Yahoo data-center links, with a smiley face on the slide; Google encrypted internal links.
  • Project Zero (Aug 2014): Chris Evans's team found 1,600+ critical bugs; 90-day disclosure; Ian Beer neutered iOS exploits used against Uighurs.
  • Crypto wars: PGP, Clipper Chip (1996), iPhone 6 encryption (2014), San Bernardino. Cook's refusal; the FBI paid $1.3M to an American hacker for a zero-day and dropped the case.

Key numbers: 2 billion lines of Google code (estimated); $100K no-questions signing bonuses; Google bounties $500 minimum, $1.5M for Android jailbreak by 2020; Zerodium $80K Chrome / $100K Android / $500K iPhone / $1M-$2.5M zero-click; Microsoft ~$250K bounty year one, 200K reports/year; 444,743 Yahoo address books in a day; $1.3M for the iPhone zero-day.

So what: You can't outbid governments; win on recognition, openness and intellectual challenge, and scope bounties to beta software. Name-and-shame deters silence and recruits talent. Covert interception damages trust more than compelled access. A backdoor for the good guys is a target for everyone. Principle erodes against market size.

Ch 17-18: Cyber Gauchos; Perfect Storm

Argument: The market is now global and self-sustaining, and US offense taught every adversary: Iran, China and North Korea each learned and struck back where America was undefended.

Stories & evidence

  • Argentina (Ch 17): "atado con alambre"; Cesar Cerrudo turning traffic lights on and off; Ekoparty with Zerodium as Platinum Sponsor; Core Security's Gera Richarte and Ivan Arce; Alfredo Ortega (the Cyber Gaucho) broke voting machines in under 20 minutes and refused to sell out of survival instinct.
  • Brokers and relationships: Juliano Rizzo demoed a six-figure exploit onstage and foreign brokers swarmed afterward for his next one; a Gulf-state buyer closed a deal in a Palermo club.
  • Failed fix: Dan Geer's buy-the-market idea (outbid everyone 10x, patch) was too late. Arce: "Do you perform an ethical analysis? Or do you weigh the bags?"
  • Flipped moral map: older hackers lived through the Dirty War (30,000 desaparecidos); to Argentines the US looks different than "good Western governments."
  • Shamoon (Ch 18): Aug 15, 2012, Iran wiped 30,000 Saudi Aramco computers, copied from US/Israeli code, then bank DDoS (BofA, JPMorgan, Citi, NYSE) with 70+ Gbps vs. banks' 40.
  • Failed infrastructure bill (2012): McConnell: "if we were attacked, we would lose."
  • Bowman Dam (Aug 2013): officials nearly retaliated against the wrong dam.
  • PLA Unit 61398: traced by Mandiant and the NYT to a Shanghai tower; DOJ indicted five soldiers.
  • Sands (Feb 2014) and Sony (Dec 2014): Iran and North Korea wiper-plus-doxxing playbooks, a model for 2016.
  • 2015 deals: Iran nuclear deal and Xi-Obama IP-theft agreement paused attacks.

Key numbers: Iran's cyber budget $76M to $1B+; the cost of ~3 F-35s; ~90% drop in Chinese industrial attacks for ~18 months; Sony: 70% of computers wiped; Aramco 30,000 computers; Bowman: 245-ft Oregon dam vs. 20-ft New York dam; Ali Abbasi hacked a grid controller onstage in 5 seconds.

So what: Sell-only-to-good-governments is a Western assumption. Stuxnet and Snowden were blueprints; deterrence fails because barriers are low and capability is buyable. Deploying a cyberweapon is free R&D for the target. Glass houses limit which norms the US can demand. Verify attribution before retaliating. Offense without hardened defense leaves the private sector holding the bag.

Ch 19-20: The Grid; The Russians Are Coming

Argument: Russia pre-positioned in critical infrastructure and demonstrated it could turn off the lights; at home the US defense posture was thin and the VEP tilted toward hoarding while Russia ran an election-interference campaign built on America's own divisions.

Stories & evidence

  • Sandworm (Ch 19): GRU Unit 74455, named by iSight's John Hultquist for Dune references. BlackEnergy began as a $40 DDoS tool; delivered in staged modules; KillDisk cleaned up. Targeted GE Cimplicity, Siemens and Advantech software.
  • Rehearsal in media companies: Starlight and TRK; Starlight's lawyer clicked an Excel file in April and 200 machines were infected by October.
  • The December 23, 2015 blackout: invisible cursor opened breakers at 30 substations; 230,000 without power for ~6 hours. Hultquist had told the Pentagon a month earlier, "they're going to turn off the lights."
  • Defensive collapse: DHS's top four cyber officials resigned in four months of early 2013; a 2010 bipartisan letter warned of outages "for at least months to two years"; the grid bill was killed. Two decades of FUD trained people to tune out.
  • Printout defense and VEP (Ch 20): the White House emergency plan was literally a printout; EternalBlue ("not dirty," WMD-class) was withheld about 7 years; Heartbleed's OpenSSL ran on one engineer on $2,000/year.
  • 2016 interference: IRA (Prigozhin; Heart of Texas vs. United Muslims of America staged standoffs; "Woke Blacks"); Fancy Bear phished Podesta (60,000 emails); Guccifer 2.0, DCLeaks and WikiLeaks laundered the loot; voter rolls probed in all 50 states, Arizona and Illinois breached, VR Systems hacked.
  • Response failure: McConnell refused a bipartisan attribution statement; Obama's sanctions and 35 expelled diplomats were "barely a spanking"; NYT editors buried the DNC story.

Key numbers: 230,000 people, 30 substations, 6 hours; 198 critical-infrastructure incidents in 2012 (+52%); 1,000+ firms in 84 countries (Energetic Bear); EternalBlue 7 years; 126M Facebook users and 288M Twitter impressions; 60,000 Podesta emails.

So what: Control-system implants with "die/turnoff" targeting are land mines, not cameras. Adversaries rehearse on soft proxies. The VEP is structurally biased toward hoarding. Information warfare amplifies real divisions and aims at legitimacy and turnout. Partisan paralysis and symbolic sanctions don't deter.

Ch 21-22: The Shadow Brokers; The Attacks

Argument: The nightmare of hoarding came true: someone stole the NSA's arsenal and dumped it, and within weeks EternalBlue powered two of history's most destructive attacks. Washington deflected responsibility.

Stories & evidence

  • The Shadow Brokers (Ch 21): Aug 2016 auction of "Equation Group" tools (Kaspersky's name for TAO); 300 MB samples; Halloween "Trick or Treat?" dump; April 2017 password reveal and ~20 exploits including EternalBlue and DoublePulsar.
  • Jake Williams: ex-TAO, recognized the tools as authentic and was outed with real NSA code words; felt his government didn't have his back.
  • Wrong suspects: Hal Martin (a hoarder with 50 TB, not the leaker); Vault7 (CIA, Joshua Schulte) was separate; Israel showed the US that Kaspersky was pulling Top Secret files, "spies hacking spies hacking spies."
  • NOBUS exposed: exploits hit Cisco and Fortinet firewalls anyone could have found. The NSA quietly tipped Microsoft a month before the dump (MS17-010, attribution blank).
  • False flags: the mock-Russian broken English read like a native English speaker faking it.
  • WannaCry (Ch 22): May 12, 2017, North Korea's Lazarus group; ~50 UK hospitals, Renault, Telefonica, FedEx; no working decryption; Marcus Hutchins triggered an ~$11 kill switch and was later arrested.
  • NotPetya: GRU via Linkos Group's M.E.Doc ("Ukraine's TurboTax"), six weeks after breaching Linkos; EternalBlue + EternalRomance + MimiKatz; Maersk, Merck, FedEx/TNT, Mondelez, DLA Piper, Reckitt Benckiser, Cadbury Tasmania, Chernobyl, and Russia's Rosneft. Insurers invoked the war exemption.
  • Accountability dodge: Bossert deflected on lost tools; a Bossert NotPetya op-ed blaming Russia was killed to avoid angering Putin. Brad Smith's "Digital Geneva Convention" speech (Nov 9, 2017), while Pentagon hackers planted logic bombs in the Russian grid.

Key numbers: up to 1M Bitcoin demanded; ~20 exploits in the final dump; 400,000 infections in two weeks; WannaCry 200,000+ orgs, 150 countries, 24 hours, under $200K collected, ~$11 kill switch; NotPetya $10B+; Hal Martin 50 TB.

So what: Losing working code is far worse than losing descriptions. A stockpile is a single point of catastrophic failure. A wormable leak arms every future attacker. Irreversible "ransomware" is a wiper in disguise. A patch existing is not protection. Accountability dodges and selective attribution undermine deterrence.

Ch 23-24: The Backyard; Epilogue

Argument: The boomerang reached American towns, hospitals and nuclear plants, producing not a Cyber Pearl Harbor but "death by a thousand hacks." The remedy is to build assuming compromise, fix the human layer and foundations, and rebalance policy from offense to defense.

Stories & evidence

  • Eternal EternalBlue (Ch 23): Allentown, a San Antonio jail and Baltimore ($18M). The NSA deflected with Rogers's Toyota-truck analogy (Microsoft's Burt: "It's already a bomb") and the "91% disclosed" statistic, meaningless without denominators.
  • NOBUS dead twice: Legion Amber stole the NSA's tools about a year before the Shadow Brokers and used them against Five Eyes and for nuclear-propulsion tech; the Gulf (Crowdfense, $3M iPhone exploits; the Bezos WhatsApp hack; Khashoggi).
  • China: a two-year Uighur watering-hole attack using 14 iOS zero-days (Project Zero's find); "best tools against their own people first."
  • Iran and Nitro Zeus: US logic bombs in Iran's grid; 2,700 hits on Trump's 2020 campaign; escalation after the Suleimani strike.
  • Russia: pax mafiosa (TrickBot, Evil Corp); inside Wolf Creek and Cooper nuclear plants; Petro Rabigh safety-lock attack ("All that's missing is some political motivation").
  • 2020 election: CISA's Krebs, Cyber Command's TrickBot/IRA takedowns, Microsoft's legal action, and Nakasone's "defend forward"; Election Day was "just another Tuesday on the internet," but the perception hack came from within.
  • Epilogue: the internet built at a biker bar in 1976 (Dave Retz: "Everything is vulnerable"). Remedies: "move slowly and fix your shit," security from inception, "build it like it's broken" (Casey Ellis), CHERI, MFA, open-source census/bill of materials, offline elections, reinstating the cyber coordinator, VEP reform, red lines.

Key numbers: $18M Baltimore; 14 iOS zero-days over two years; $3M Crowdfense; 2,700 attacks on the 2020 campaign; 98% of attacks begin with phishing; 80-90% of modern software is open source; Windows zero-day ~$1M; 2018 elimination of the cyber coordinator.

So what: A leaked exploit persists wherever patching lags. Attacks on confidence are cheaper than attacks on votes. Paying ransoms funds the threat. Coordinated action (CISA, Cyber Command, companies) can blunt interference. Expiration dates, civilian VEP seats, DHS oversight, and using US buying power for patching terms are the policy fixes.

Recurring Stories Across the Book

  • Stuxnet: the espionage-to-attack line (Ch 2, 9), the blueprint (Ch 17), the plagiarized Shamoon (Ch 18), the lesson ignored at NotPetya (Ch 22).
  • EternalBlue: hoarded ~7 years (Ch 20), dumped by the Shadow Brokers (Ch 21), WannaCry and NotPetya (Ch 22), Allentown and Baltimore (Ch 23).
  • Ukraine as test kitchen: Prologue, the 2015 blackout (Ch 19), NotPetya (Ch 22); echoed by Xinjiang (Ch 23).
  • "The fucking salmon": the Italians (Ch 2), Aitel (Ch 11), vendors' vagueness at NSO (Ch 13).
  • Gunman as origin story: the NSA's pivot to offense (Ch 6-7), pre-encryption capture reappears in Muscular (Ch 16) and Pegasus (Ch 13); Aurora as Silicon Valley's Gunman (Ch 15).
  • Gosler's complexity problem: reappears at Google scale (Ch 14) and in the open-source argument (Ch 20, 24).
  • Hacking Team and CyberPoint/Mansoor: the same slide from "friendly" to abusive (Ch 11-13).
  • The 2016 playbook: Sony as model (Ch 18), the IRA and Fancy Bear (Ch 20), the perception hack (Ch 23).
  • Moussouris and bounties: the incentive model to scale (Ch 15, 24).
  • Heartbleed: open-source security theater (Ch 20, 24).
  • Ralph Langner: Cassandra of PLC sabotage and the first to name the US (Ch 2, 9).
